*Sūkṣmāgama* T1013, p. 1)
Śrī.
May there be auspiciousness.
May there be no obstacle!
Homage to the Guru! Homage to Gaṇapati! Homage to the chosen deity!
The Ritual for Worship according to the *Sūkṣmāgama*:
[I worship] the Leader of all, who flows swiftly,
the Cause, residing within the mouth of the Kalabha.
Every morning, I constantly bow down to the son of Pārvatī, who is like the Pārijāta tree.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the worship of Śiva;
sacrifice is considered to be of two kinds: for one's own sake and for the sake of others.
For the twice-born who observe the Śiva-vow, the practice is undertaken for one's own sake;
two types of rules are prescribed: ending with the lamp and ending with the sacrificial oblation (haviṣya). || 2 ||
It is stated by the noble ones born in the land of Āryadeśa that, among all initiations for the supreme goal of the twice-born Śivas, the initiation of Śiva is preeminent. (3)
Therefore, O Śiva, one should worship all the gods in this [rite] performed by the twice-born;
it is declared to be of four kinds, ending with the lamp and ending with the oblation (havis).
Then [he described] the conclusion of the dance, including the offering of oblations, according to the full extent of his resources,
as well as purification, sipping water, bathing, bathing with ashes, and the libation to the ancestors.
Next, the opening of the door, followed by the three breath-controls (recaka) and so forth,
as well as the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement on the hands (karanyāsa), characterized by the Great Principles (mahātattva) and other elements.
Now, for them, one should contemplate the mandala, the color, the syllables of the deity’s utterance,
the knotting and the subsequent cutting, and their origin within the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
(2) Purification of the self, the ritual placement of the digits (kalānyāsa), the distinction of flowers as auspicious or inauspicious,
the worship of the gateway, and thereafter the purification of the site.

The purification of the vessels for the substances, the characteristics of the consecration (abhiṣeka), the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the water of honor (arghya), and the characteristics of the fragrant substances (gandhadravya). || 9 ||
He caused the recitation of the Viśītāri mantra at the time of offering the arghya, along with the three fragrances and eight flowers,
while the great bell was struck seven times.
The time for the secret covering-cloth comes after the purification of the *liṅga*;
the face, feet, and back [are purified] after the purification of the pedestal.
His seat, his time, and the mudrā; thereafter, the worship of the five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇa-pūjā) and their colors and forms. || 12 ||
Then, at the conclusion of that, one should perform the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā) according to the distinction of their respective classes,
followed by the procedure for the door, the udumbara post, and the rites for incense and lamps.
Then follows the ritual of the lustration (nīrājana), the food offering (naivedya), the fire sacrifice (agnikārya),
the worship of the retinue, and thereafter the worship of all the deities.
Their characteristics, as well as the colors, the offering of food, and the characteristics of the daily festival, followed by the worship of the sandals (pādukā), are likewise described. || 15 ||
The characteristics of the ghaṭikā and the fruit of worship beyond that—one who understands all such matters as these is a true worshiper. (16)
At dawn, remembering Śiva, Daṇḍapāṇi, the elder brother of Śiva, went outside the village and thereafter discharged his excrement, urine, and other waste. (17)
The wise man should place the sacred thread at the root of his ear or upon his hand;
having placed the sun to his right, he should face south during the night. (18)
Taking a blade of grass from the ground, with the body held straight and without reciting [mantras], one should not look toward the sun, water, fire, the moon, a cow, or a brahmin. (19)
Near a temple, at a well, in a storehouse, or in ashes;
in fields, in the shade of trees, by a river, or within lakes. (20)
A man should not perform both [actions] at a shrine, near a tree, on the shore of the great ocean, or under a lunar asterism. || 21 ||
Having taken a lump of clay in his right hand from the middle of the water,
he should go to the bank of the water and thereafter perform the purification.
One should cleanse the penis with mud the size of an axle, then cleanse the anus five times;
likewise, one should thoroughly cleanse the feet and hands five times each, and [the face] three times.
Having discarded [the water] on another part of the bank, the wise man should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
holding the purifier (pavitra) in his hand, he should do so with three or five blades of darbha grass.
The purifier (pavitra) should be knotted with a clockwise turn and four finger-breadths in length;
on dry land, one should place the right foot while keeping the left foot in the water.
With his hand shaped like a cow’s ear, he should drink water in which a *māṣa* bean has been submerged;
having drunk it three times with the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. (26)
One should touch the mouth with the thumb; one should touch the face with the hand;
one should touch the ears with the thumbs and little fingers, and touch the outer parts with the thumbs.
Having touched the navel with the little finger, one should touch the heart with the thumb;
then, touching the head with all the fingers, one performs the five salutations and the six-limbed ritual.
Purity and sipping water (ācamana) have been prescribed; thereafter, one should perform the ritual bath (snāna).
Having taken earth for the bath, one should apply it, with a greater amount on the right side. (29)
Thereafter, one should sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra and, having divided it three times,
consecrate it with the Brahma-tīrtha using the Kavaca-mantra according to the prescribed sequence.
First with earth from the north, then in sequence in the eight directions,
and finally with earth from the south, one should prepare the Śivatīrtha.

The wise one should touch [the body] with the middle finger and the heart-mantra, starting from the crown of the head down to the feet; thereafter, he should perform his bath and carry out the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having formed the *kalaśa-mudrā*, one should perform the ritual bathing with [water] consecrated by the mantras;
the wise person should then drink that water which has been submerged in black gram (*māṣa*) while reciting those same mantras.
Having recollected the Dadhikrā mantra, one should sprinkle [the water] on the head in due order;
for the twice-born, the five sacred sites (pañcatīrtha) are prescribed to be applied to the right hand.
One should offer water to the Sun and perform breath control (prāṇāyāma);
having recited the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred and eight times, one should perform the ritual worship (upasthāna). || 35 ||
One should perform the libation for the gods, sages, and ancestors;
one should offer it with the little and middle fingers for the sake of perfect satisfaction. 36.
Recalling each respective mantra, one should perform the libation for the ancestors between the thumb and the forefinger at the tips of the fingers of the sages.
The *brāhma* [tīrtha] is at the base of the big toe, while the *agnitīrtha* is likewise on the sole;
having washed one's feet, one should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). (38)
Having entered a cowshed with either a leaf of the *pālāśa* tree or a lotus leaf,
one should take fresh cow dung and form it into a ball with the left hand.
One should burn everything with the Aghora mantra and collect [the ashes] with the Vaktra mantra;
then one should apply the ashes with the Brahmavidyā-mantras and their limbs, using the leaf-mantras and vessel-mantras.
Then, after the ashes— collected from the embers of a fire and consecrated with mantras by one learned in the Vedas—
have entered the temple, the preceptor, composed in mind, shall enter last.
Having worshipped the clay on the door-panel and [the name] in its center by means of one's own name,
and having recited the Aghora-weapon mantra, one should perform the opening of the door-panel.
At the conclusion of the worship, having honored Rudra, one should bind [the protection] with the armor-mantra (kavaca),
while facing north and seated upon a beautiful seat.
Having placed the ashes in one's own left hand, one should purify them with the Astra-mantra;
then, having recited the Śiva-mantra a hundred times, one should perform the bath with the ashes.
It is proclaimed that for men, [the state of] ash is always [attained] through sinful conversation;
therefore, the preceptor, having performed the binding of the ten directions with the Astra-mantra alone, [should proceed].
First, worship with the hands should be performed using perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
one should first practice inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka). 46.
One should exhale the abdominal air by pressing the nose with a finger;
then, like a liquid, one should properly fill the belly with external air. (47)
Pūraka has been fully described; thereafter, one should practice kumbhaka.
One neither takes in nor releases the breath situated within or without. (48)
Because it consists of a full jar (pūrṇakumbha), it is therefore called "kumbhaka" (the jar-like breath-retention).
One should likewise practice the exhalation and other [breathing techniques] with a duration of twelve mātrās. (49)
The placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement on the hands (karanyāsa) are declared to be threefold;
they constitute the creation and the maintenance for both celibate students and householders.
The dissolution of the forest-dwellers and ascetics is thus praised:
[it proceeds] from the little finger on the right hand up to the thumb, and likewise from the thumb down to the little finger on the left.
One should place the ten seed-syllables and perform the placement for emanation and maintenance;
the right thumb should be the beginning, and likewise the left little finger.
Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the five Brahmans (pañcabrahmannyāsa) and then carry out the placement of withdrawal (saṃhāranyāsa);
it begins with the left thumb and ends with the right thumb.
Thereafter, one should place the limbs of Śiva and then place the weapon (astra) on the palms of the hands;
this is declared to be the karanyāsa, and after that follows the aṅganyāsa.
The placement according to the order of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) is declared to extend from the crown of the head down to the feet,
[placing the mantras] respectively on the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and the feet.
From Īśāna to Sadyojāta, [the mantras] should be placed from the feet up to the heart;
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the feet, the private parts, the heart, the mouth, and the head.
From Sadyojāta up to Īśāna, the placement of the limbs beginning with the heart occurs;
one should perform the placement of the Heart-mantra on the heart and the Head-mantra on the head. (57)
Having placed the *śikhā* [mantra] on the crest-lock and the *kavaca* between the breasts,
one should place the *astra* in the region of the hands and the *netra* upon the eyes. (58)
This is declared to be the *sthitinyāsa*; the wise one should perform the placement of the elements beginning with earth.
In brief, the principle (*tattva*) is established within the great principles (*mahātattva*) beginning with earth. (59)
I shall describe the mandala for the Earth, the syllables for the recitation of the deities, and the individual nyāsa for each [limb], beginning with the thumbs, in their proper order. (60)
One should place the golden square mandala, whose presiding deity is Brahmā, by pronouncing the five [syllables] from the thumb to the knees. (61)
The white-colored Vaṇya is presided over by Viṣṇu;
then, from the knees up to the navel, there are four [syllables] beginning with *hviṃ*. 62.
One should recite "Hauṃ" three times for the triangle, which is said to have seven flames, red in color, and presided over by Rudra; this extends from the navel to the throat.
The six-cornered [mandala] has Vāyu as its presiding deity; it is black and has Īśvara as its cause.
This is indeed declared to be the Vāyu-maṇḍala; one should utter "Aiṃ" twice.
One should specifically perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) from the throat up to the forehead;
[one should meditate on] the smoke-colored, circular mandala of space as Sadāśiva.
From the forehead up to the tip of the crest-lock, one should recite the mantra Śivottara once;
this is declared to be the characteristic of Earth, and one should cut through the five knots.
First is the knot of the penis; second is the knot of the navel;
third is the knot of the abdomen; and fourth is the knot of the throat. (67)
One should cut the fifth head-knot with the very weapon of Śiva. This is declared to be the cutting of the knots; one should then effect the purification of the self. (68)
One should first unite oneself with the *haṃsa* and the heart;
[one should place it] at the tip of the crest-lock, twelve finger-breadths [above], resembling pure crystal. (69)
Afterwards, having meditated upon it as being like dry wood by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*,
one should burn it with the seed-syllable of fire (*agnibīja*), conjoined with the circle of fire (*agnimaṇḍala*).
Having meditated upon this form of ash, beginning from the big toe and ending at the crown, surrounded by a halo of flames, one should then immerse it in nectar.
One should contemplate the nectar below the moon-crested [Soma] and the downward-facing lotus of the Praṇava, once the auspicious Suṣumṇā has been pierced at the crown of the head.
One should lead the self there [into the heart], but one should not even mentally conceptualize it as a swan;
rather, [one should contemplate] the auspicious Lord who consists of all knowledge and comprises all the gods. (73)
Having thus joined [the mantras] according to the rule, which destroys all death,
one should then perform the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), beginning from the head and ending with the northeast (Īśāna).
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās beginning from the head;
Īśāna should be placed on the five heads, and Puruṣa on the faces.
One should place the Praṇava on the upward-facing mouth, starting from the east and proceeding in order;
likewise, one should place it on the heart, the neck, the chest, the abdomen, the navel, and the back.
One should [place the seed-syllables] on the chest with the Aghora mantra, and likewise on the back and the anus;
then on the penis, the two thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, and the region of the buttocks.
Then, the wise one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the sides of the hips with Vāmadeva;
likewise, [he should place] the feet, the two hands, the nose, the head, and the two arms with Sadyojāta. (78)
Having thus contemplated, "I am Śiva," hear now the internal sacrifice (antaryāga):
one should install the Lord, the Sovereign whose form is the Praṇava, within the lotus of the heart. (79)
One should worship, according to the prescribed rule, the one who is endowed with thirty-eight arts,
who is the size of a thumb, immovable, and joined with the limbs of Śiva’s Vidyā.
One should perform the fire-oblation at the navel and the "all-facing" [oblation] on the forehead;
there, one should properly meditate upon the Lord—this is the sequence for the internal sacrifice.
Or else there are five obstructions, or three, or even one;
likewise, it is fourfold: white, red, yellow, and black.
Droṇa, mandāra, punnāga, śvetārka, śvetapatraka,
nandyāvarta, śriyāvarta, and mahādroṇa are of the sāttvika nature.
One should designate the karavīra, the red lotus, the pāṭalī, the bṛhatī, and red water-lilies as flowers belonging to the rājasa quality. (84)
Campaka, āragvadha, karṇikā, dhūdhūma, and viṣṇukrānti stones are declared to be the mixed ones (miśrakāni). || 85 ||
The *vakula*, *śīrṣaketakī*, *karañja*, *bandhūka*, *karamuda*, *ḍāḍimī*, *kiṃśuka*, and others are declared to be *tāmasa*.
One should avoid the lāṅgalī, the bṛhatī, and japā flowers;
likewise, unripe fruits and the like, buds, and those entwined by spider-silk.
One should carefully avoid flowers that have fallen of their own accord, those gathered in a cloth, and those that have remained overnight. (88)
The purification of the flowers has been fully described; one should now commence the worship of the gateway.
One should worship the bull before Śiva with the Vṛṣabha-Gāyatrī mantra.
One should worship Gaṇeśa on the upper part of the door on the right side;
one should worship Sarasvatī on the upper part of the door on the left side. || 90 ||
One should worship Śrīdevī above the middle of the door;
on the right side of the door, one should worship Gaṅgānandin.
To the left of the door, one should worship Yamunā and Mahākāla;
one should honor them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using their respective name-mantras.
Then, the wise practitioner should perform the purification of the site; he should smear it with cow dung and, reciting the heart-mantra, draw a square mandala with three tiers.

Having worshipped the ground according to the prescribed rite and performed the binding of the directions with the Astra-mantra, one should prepare the vessels for the water for the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamana); this is known as the purification of the site (sthānaśuddhi). 94.
One should purify the arghya vessel, the shallow bowl, and the conch vessel;
one should place the water-pot at the heart and conceal it with the kavaca mantra. || 95 ||
One should fill the vardhanī vessel with water filtered through a cloth, using those waters along with the mantras of the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the [other] mantras for the vessel. 96.
Having formed the *surabhi-mudrā*, one should contemplate it as the water of Śiva;
[one should do this] with eight *droṇas* of water, and then successively with half and half again of those waters. 97.
One should perform the consecration endowed with all fragrances;
one should sprinkle all the vessels with auspicious water using the heart-mantra. (98)
One should especially prepare all the vessels, beginning with those for the water for the feet;
[the contents should include] barley, white mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, along with sandalwood and uśīra root. 99.
This water for the feet should consist of these ingredients combined with *nimbū* and *jātīphala*;
cardamom, cloves, and camphor shall constitute the sixfold water for sipping (*ācamana*). (100)
This is proclaimed as the *arghya* offering: consisting of sesame seeds, flowers, tips of *kuśa* grass, water, milk, barley, and rice mixed with mustard seeds. (101)
Through the renunciation of its previous form, by virtue of its nature as empowered Śakti, the substance becomes fit for Śiva; that process is the purification of the substance. (102)
Saffron, sandalwood, costus, mixed with camphor and agallochum—this is declared to be the fragrant substance; now the "enemy of cold" (śītāri) is being described.
Sandalwood is said to be three parts, resinous exudate (niryāsa) should be two parts, and agarwood should be one part, mixed with a small amount of camphor. || 104 ||
Now, the substance for cooling the enemy has indeed been described;
one should employ it when sprinkled during the invocation, at the end of the worship, and at the end of the dismissal.
One should properly apply fragrance in three instances: during the offering of water (arghya), the unguent (vilepana), and the bath (snāna);
likewise, it is used with the invocation (āvāhana), the water offering (arghya), the bath (snāna), the incense (dhūpa), and the unguent (vilepana).
One should employ eight flowers in the offering and the dismissal;
likewise in the invocation, as well as in the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and the bath.
In the rites of sipping water (ācamana), the food offering (naivedya), and the dismissal (visarjana), as well as seven times [during the ritual],
the invocation (āvāhana) was previously taught, and likewise the installation (sthāpana) and the respectful offering (arghya). (108)
Fragrance, flowers, incense, lamp, and food offering, as well as the dismissal and the water for sipping—these are remembered as the ten services (upacāras). || 109 ||
Having combined the flower with the fragrance, one should join the flower with the fragrance;
having combined the lamp with the incense, one should join the lamp with the incense. || 110 ||
The purification of substances has been fully explained; hereafter follows the purification of mantras:
[the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ending with Svāhā, [accompanied by] Namaḥ, Svāhā, Vaṣaṭ, and Vauṣaṭ. 111.
One should worship the expressive mantra by reciting it in a whisper during the rite of fire-offering;
however, in the case of internal recitation (japa) performed mentally, all mantras are said to be applicable.

The purification of the mantra has been fully described; hereafter follows the purification of the liṅga, [to be performed] during the consecration, the incense offering, the food offering, and the ritual acts pertaining to the liṅga.
Upon the completion of the dismissal, one should strike the great bell;
let it not be seen by the most wicked, those afflicted with leprosy, atheists, or those who bear ill names.
At that time, one should employ the supreme concealed cloth;
one should dismiss the flowers used in worship with the heart-mantra. || 115 ||
Having gathered that flower, the wise one should worship Caṇḍeśa after purifying the entire area of the liṅga-base with the water of Śiva.
One should purify everything with the Astra-mantra; the flower should always be placed upon the head.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should extract [the deity] from all parts of the linga.
(13) At the tip of the thread, the face [of the deity] should likewise be present; one should touch it with the *Vaktra* mantra.
Along the side of the thread, however, the side [of the deity] should be present; one should touch it with the *Aghora* mantra. || 118 ||
Having worshipped the *liṅga*, one should touch it for purification according to the sequence;
one should then touch the limbs of the Goddess, from the great pedestal down to the feet.
This is declared to be the purification of the seat (pīṭhaśuddhi); one should arrange the three seats and place Dharma and Jñāna in the corners beginning with the southeast.
By means of the very first letter of one's own name, one should visualize a lion-form with three eyes;
the forms of the lion are white, red, yellow, and black.
One should specifically place Adharma and the others in the four directions;
in their midst, one should cover the moon, which is attended by those with symmetrical limbs.
Having thus prepared the lion-throne, one should worship it with its own name-mantra;
[the mantra consists of] the fourfold: the Unmanifest, Niyati, Kāla, and Kalā. (123)
The wise one should arrange circles in all four corners;
having thus prepared the yogic seat (yogāsana), he should thereafter prepare the lotus seat (padmāsana).
The root, the stalk, the eight petals, the pericarp, and the filaments constitute the earthly [lotus];
its root is the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu, together with its own stalk.
The lotus has nine petals representing the eight powers (śaktis) and the pericarp as the solar disc;
its seed-syllable is like a conch shell, and its stalk resembles a lapis lazuli gem.
The petals are all the [other] jewels, while the pericarp is gold;
having joined each with its respective seed-syllable, this is the lotus posture (padmāsana) in due order. 127.
At the time of bathing and invocation, one should prepare a lion-throne;
but at the time of offering food and worship, one should prepare a lotus-throne. (128)
Thereafter, having prepared the yogic seat, the ritual dismissal (visarjana) is performed specifically;
likewise, the invocation of the fire upon a heap of wood and other materials is prescribed.
The turning away [of the deity] from that [liṅga] is then called its dismissal (udvāsana).
One should not perform either the invocation (āvāhana) or the dismissal (udvāsana) in the case of a Śiva-liṅga.
One should perform the placement with the mudrā called Āvāhana and with the Śānta mudrā;
one should effect the presence with the Dhvaja mudrā—thus one should employ these five mudrās.
One should worship with the Liṅga-mudrā and restrain with the Niṣṭhura-mudrā; having invoked with the Sadyojāta-mantra, one should establish the restraint with the Vāmadeva-mantra.

Having thus formed the mental resolve according to the prescribed rule, one should worship the Supreme Lord with the Aghora mantra, which is discerned as the Puruṣa, while maintaining His presence. 133.
Sadāśiva has five faces endowed with the fifteen organs,
possesses ten divine arms, and bears ten auspicious weapons.
The god resembles the pure moon, adorned with all ornaments, wearing divine garments, gentle, and anointed with divine perfumes. || 135 ||
The God, accompanied by Umā, beautiful in all his limbs, holds a trident, a thunderbolt, a sword, a spear, and the gesture of fearlessness in his right hands. (136)
Holding a noose, a goad, a serpent, a bell, and fire in his left [hands]—
having thus meditated upon him mentally, one should offer water for the feet at his feet.
One should offer water for rinsing the mouth at the faces and present the *arghya* offering upon the head.
First, there should be the form of Īśāna; likewise, the form of Īśvara is on the south. (138)
The form of Brahmā is in the west, and likewise the form of Śiva is in the north;
Sadāśiva is above that, and these are remembered as the five forms.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with the previously mentioned waters of Śiva;
the consecration is performed with the mantra of Īśāna and the Triyambaka mantra.
During the interval between consecrations, the preceptor should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya):
one kuḍuba of clarified butter, curd as prescribed, and twice or thrice that amount of milk. || 141 ||
The cow dung should be four times [the amount of water], and the cow urine should be six times;
or alternatively, one āḍhaka of each, one should bathe [the deity] with the water for the feet and so forth in due order.
One should offer perfumes, flowers, gold, and so forth, as well as water containing gems; likewise, garments, upper cloths, sacred threads, perfume, flowers, and excellent incense. (143)
One should cause the lamp, the food offering, and the betel leaf to be given together with milk;
likewise, the crown, earrings, necklace, armlets, and waist-band. (144)
The wise one should offer all the ornaments and the mirror with the heart-mantra;
having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, he should afterwards worship the surrounding deities (āvaraṇa).
At the conclusion of the sacrifice to the enclosure of the womb, one should worship the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa);
and one should likewise worship the permanent enclosure of the seat according to the prescribed rite.
At the base of the pericarp, one should worship the inner enclosure;
one should worship the face, which resembles the luster of saffron, with the Vaktra mantra. || 147 ||
One should know that the heart [mantra] resembles a conch shell; Aghora is like the color of collyrium; then Śikhā is dark-colored, and Sadyojāta has a white form. (148)
One should know the armor to be dark-green in luster and the left [face] to be red;
one should know the head to be smoke-colored and worship it with the Īśāna mantra. || 149 ||
Likewise, one should worship Īśāna, who resembles pure crystal, upon the pericarp;
and in the northeast (Īśāna), one should worship the Eye, which is like the rising sun.
In all directions, one should worship the Weapon (Astra), whose form resembles lightning;
they are all three-eyed and four-armed, possessing six limbs and five forms. || 151 ||
Adorned with all ornaments and joined with crested matted locks, they are radiant with tridents and axes, wearing garments of various colors corresponding to their respective hues. || 152 ||
In this very manner, having meditated in due order, one should perform worship:
the Māheśa [deity] and the stainless Śiva in the center, and the pericarp with the Heart [mantra]. (153)
The knower of mantras should know that the Śiva-tattva is in the center, the Ātman-tattva is in the south, and likewise the Vidyā-tattva is in the north, by means of the heart.
Having described the enclosure of the womb (garbhāvaraṇa), one should worship the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśāvaraṇa).
Ananta, who resembles a hibiscus flower, should be worshipped with perfumes and flowers. 155.
One should meditate upon Trimūrti, who is radiant with red splendor, subtle, and indeed possessing an orange glow;
Śrīkaṇṭha, who has the luster of a blue lotus; and that which is spoken of by Śiva, resembling the moon. (156)
Śikhaṇḍipuṣparāga has the reddish luster of the Ekanetra gem;
it has a form resembling a kunda flower, and Ekarudra follows in due order. 157.
In this way, all the Vidyeśvaras have three eyes and four arms;
they are adorned with all ornaments and graced with crowns of matted hair. (158)
All those bearing axes and spears should be worshipped with their respective mantras;
one should worship Nandin, who has the luster of collyrium, holds a staff in his hand, and possesses three eyes. (159)
Behind him is Mahākāla, possessing four arms and red in color;
he has three eyes, four arms, holds a trident in his hand, and is endowed with great strength. || 160 ||
The bull is blue in color, and Vighneśa is smoky-colored;
he has three eyes and four arms, and is equipped with a trident, a tusk, a noose, and a goad.
Bhṛṅgīśa has the luster of a jasmine flower, possesses four arms and three eyes;
Kumāra, however, is red in color, six-faced, and holds a spear in his hand.
[He has] twelve eyes and four arms, beautiful with all ornaments;
Umā has the luster of Jāmbūnada gold and holds a flower in her hand. 163.
Two-eyed and of beautiful form, with full and elevated breasts,
he beheld Caṇḍeśa, who resembled the luster of lapis lazuli and held a trident in his hand.
Having meditated thus according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the Gaṇeśas:
the dark-blue, the tawny, the smoky-grey, the black, the white, and the yellow. (165)
The white [fire] is indeed Dṛkopa, and the purifying [fire] resembles black;
Brahmā is at the head, and behind him is Myariti, presiding over the western direction.
One should worship Viṣṇu between Indra and Īśāna;
he is proclaimed as having four arms and three eyes, and is indeed Īśāna. 167.
Seven cubits in height, three-eyed, and two-faced, he is indeed like fire;
and Brahmā is four-faced, eight-eyed, and four-armed. (168)
Viṣṇu is manifest with four arms and endowed with two eyes;
having thus meditated upon him in this very sequence, one should then worship him.
It possesses great lightning of various colors, resembling a dark blue cloud;
it has the hue of blue fire, ruby, frost, and sapphire.
The color of weapons is said to be variegated and red;
having worshipped the lotus on one side, the discus [is placed] on the side of Viṣṇu.
One should know that the *jāyā* (wife) consists of the *śakti* and the *gadā*; the *pāśa* and the *padma* are neuter.
The remaining [weapons] are renowned as masculine; thus the ten weapons are said to be of three genders.
Having worshipped each of those with their respective mantras, beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*,
one should thus worship the enclosure and Kṣetrapāla in the temple of Śaṅkara.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should commence the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā). The plank should be square, and its height according to the prescribed measurement. || 174 ||
One should worship Śrīkaṇṭha with a moist glance, or the seed-syllable, or the seven seasons;
and for each of the four-armed [deities], one should perform the preliminary cutting according to the three divisions.
Having placed a level plank according to the extent of one's resources,
[one should place] the *nandī*, the *ānī*, the *balli*, and the *prakuṇī* upon the channel.
One should sprinkle the deity of the Gaurī-mantra and others with water from kuśa grass;
having worshipped them with the Gaurī-gāyatrī, one should proceed with the banyan and udumbara trees.
A vessel is said to be made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal;
however, in the absence [of these], one may use a bell-metal vessel for the flour and the *kausuma* ashes. (178)
That powder should be mixed in five parts with the lamp-powder itself;
every day at dusk, one should perform the rite while reciting auspicious benedictions.
The preceptor, surrounded by three [disciples], should lead [the image] with his own two hands;
afterwards, the liṅga, surrounded by three, should be led with a flower.
The wise preceptor should cast those flowers into the water with the Astra-mantra;
then, having brought the single-layered fragrant paste, he should place it in the lamp-vessel with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
One should touch the face with that ash while reciting the Vaktra-mantra;
having placed a flower upon the head, one should indeed apply it everywhere while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having lifted the vessel, one should set it aside on the outer seat;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented. || 183 ||
Unbroken, pure, and excellent śāli rice is declared the best;
rice from bamboo or nīvāra is said to be of middling quality. (184)
In this [calculation], one *kṛṣṇala* would be the lowest measure of rice;
one hundred *droṇas* would be the highest, and half of that would be the middle. || 185 ||
The lowest [measure] is half of that, and the lowest of the low is half of that again;
thus it may be twelve *droṇas* or even eight *droṇas*.
Four *droṇas* is indeed the highest of the high;
one should perform the occasional (*naimittika*) rite in this manner, and half of that for the daily (*nitya*) rite.
The wise man should cause an offering of food (naivedya) to be presented, measuring either a khārī or a droṇa;
or half a droṇa, or half of that again, while avoiding any other amount. (188)
One should offer an oblation of five colors, combined with balls, sugar-candy, and fruits,
along with various kinds of side-dishes soaked in tawny ghee and curd.
Alternatively, black cow products,
ghee, and curd are prescribed for the act of giving when one has transgressed [the rules regarding] the *nirmālya* and the *nivedya*.
In that case, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; one should scatter the cow-dung and clay (gonāga);
and one should perform the daily fire-ritual in the fire from the kitchen.
The square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has been described as adorned with girdles and other ornaments;
its opening is said to be one cubit (aratni) in width, and its depth is measured accordingly.
The one who establishes [the fire] should establish it, and he must guard it without interruption;
as long as the fundamental ritual service continues, he should worship the fire well. || 193 ||
Having purified it with the Aghora-weapon mantra, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers;
then, having covered it all around with *darbha* grass, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).
The consecration of the clarified butter (ājya) should be performed in this manner, followed by the Āghāra libations;
then, having specifically offered the oblation (havis) with the Ājyāhuti-dṛkṣa mantra.
Having empowered [the offering] with "svāhā," he should perform the sixteenth oblation according to the prescribed rule;
then, having offered the *praṇava* and *huṃ* into the sacrificial fire, he should offer the food in due order.

Afterwards, one should offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*, and then offer the limbs of Brahmā (*brahmāṅga*). One should then offer the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras, and finally perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering in the fire.
The wise man should always have the *caruhoma* performed with human [sacrificial substance];
one portion shall be the food offering (*naivedya*), and one portion shall be the oblation (*huta*). (198)
One should offer one part as the *bali* and the remainder as food for the preceptor;
however, if the time [for the rite] is missed through negligence, one hundred oblations should be performed with the *aghora* mantra.
Thereafter, the most excellent of teachers should perform the ritual service with the root-mantra,
having worshipped the eightfold retinue residing within the Lord Puruṣa.
Vṛṣabha, Pāvaka, the group of the seven Mothers, Vighna, Guha, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Sūrya—in this order. (201)
One should worship [the deity] in an image, on a pedestal, or even in a fire-pit;
if it is a pedestal, one should worship the head [of the deity] upon the middle girdle of the central part.
One should offer the bali-oblation, ending with "svāhā," in the size of a hen's egg;
the worship of the liṅga has been explained previously, followed by the worship of the sakala and other forms in due order.
Therefore, I shall explain that; one should perform it according to the previously mentioned procedure:
[the worship of] Sukhāsana, as well as Nandivāhana and Puraśāsana. (204)
Likewise, he saw the form of the Dancing One, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel;
he saw Śiva as Ardhanārīśvara, and likewise Hari as half of Śaṅkara.
And Caṇḍeśvaraprasāda, as well as Kāmanāśana, likewise Kālanāśa, and the twelfth Liṅga itself. || 206 ||
In the Purāṇa, he is proclaimed as Kalyāṇasundara; Hayardhanārīśa is dark-complexioned, while for others he is red in color. (207)
The form of the dancer, Kaṅkāla, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti—
these are all proclaimed as deities of knowledge (vidyādeva) and are white in color. || 208 ||
Likewise, Kṣetrapāla and Dhūmra have four arms and three eyes;
all of them have three eyes and four arms, and are adorned with all ornaments. (209)
Having meditated thus and worshipped with the mind, the twice-born devotee of Śiva should then perform the five purifications and subsequently begin the sacrifice.
One should perform all worship using vessels made of clay or metal, but never with those made of fresh materials;
the practitioner of mantras should likewise sprinkle the area with auspicious water using *kuśa* grass while reciting the Īśāna mantra.
One should offer the water for the feet with the Sadyojāta mantra, likewise the water for rinsing the mouth with the Vāmadeva mantra;
the arghya offering is prescribed with the Aghora mantra, and the fragrance with the Puruṣa mantra.
One should offer flowers with the Īśāna mantra, while incense and lamps are offered with the Vaktra mantra;
likewise, one should present the food offering (naivedya) and betel leaf with the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should offer the face with the *śiras* mantra, and the upper garment with the *kavaca*; likewise, the crown, earrings, necklace, and armlets. (214)
All [offerings] beginning with these should be presented with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra).
Therefore, the invocation (āvāhana) should always come first, and likewise the dismissal (udvāsana) at the end.
There is no covering for the seat, and the offering belongs to Caṇḍeśa;
Sūryakāma, the Lord of Nagas (Nāgendra), Guha, and Lakṣmī are red in color. (216)
Those with two arms and two eyes, as well as those with four arms and six faces—Śāstā, Durgā, Mahāmoṭī, Jyeṣṭhā, Kālī, and Surādhipa. (217)
These are said to have a dark-blue luster, with two arms and two eyes;
having thus described them, one should then worship them after meditating upon them.
One should perform each of those with the respective seed-syllables (bījas) and sprinkle them with the consecration (abhiṣecana);
in the mantras of their own names, there is the fivefold purification (śodhana).
At the time of worship, one should employ [the mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) with the *sadyojāta* mantra, and likewise the water for sipping (*ācamana*) with the *vāmadeva* mantra. (220)

The offering of water (arghya) is declared to be with the Aghora mantra, the flower with the Īśāna mantra, and likewise the incense with the Puruṣa mantra; one should not perform the worship at the conclusion of the lamp [with the Sadyojāta mantra].
One should offer the food offering with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and betel-leaf with the *śiras-mantra*;
one should cause garments, ornaments, and collyrium to be given here with the *kavaca-mantra*.
One should worship [the deity] on a pedestal, or in the heart, or in water, or in a mural painting, or in an image made of clay, metal, or stone. || 223 ||
One should worship the footstool on an earthen vessel or a mural painting;
one should worship the eighteen classes [of deities] using the first syllable of each of their respective names.
For women and kings who possess the grace of Śiva and have attained union with Śiva, as well as for devotees of Śiva by their own names, [this applies]. (225)
One should perform worship and consecration with devotion through the offering of oblations;
one should conduct the daily festival according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures.
A vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal is prescribed;
in its center, a wise man should fashion a pericarp occupying one-third of the area.

Having fashioned a mandala before Śiva and having offered [libations] there with the heart-mantra, the wise one should worship it with lotus-scented offerings and other articles, accompanied by the mantra "Obeisance to Śakti."
In the center of that, one should place a vessel and fashion a *bali-liṅga*;
one should perform this in the evening and the morning and worship a *puṣpa-liṅga*.
At midday, the food-liṅga should be twelve aṅgulas in length,
with a base of one prastha or double that, and a circumference of one aṅgula at the tip. (230)
He has four arms, belongs to the Kṣatriya caste, and is fierce; his hands grant boons and fearlessness, he resembles the tip of a flame, and he always holds a trident-staff.
Having thus meditated upon the mantra of the weapon, one should perform the invocation with the heart-mantra;
then, one should again perform worship in sequence with the [mantras] beginning with Īśāna, using fragrant substances and so forth.
Having worshipped the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) on all sides, one should worship the marriage-thread (kautuka), the sandals,
and [the deity] adorned with fragrant flowers, along with the turban, the head-ornament (uttasāyaka).
The wise one, recollecting all the deities, should carry [the vessel] upon his head;
having performed three circumambulations, he should then enter his home. || 234 ||
Having performed the washing of his feet, he stood facing Śiva;
the King of Weapons (the Trident) was to his right, and Candraśekhara was to his left.
One should perform the worship of the sandals while recollecting the *sadyo-mantra*,
having duly honored the world-protectors (*lokapāla*s), for this indeed constitutes the ritual procedure for the sandals.
Having placed the *arghya* on the head and likewise offered water for sipping (*ācamana*) to the faces,
and having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should thereafter enter the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*).
The preceptor should discharge the king of weapons with the heart-mantra alone, having caused the piśācas, rākṣasas, and asuras to fall silent amidst the sound of the bali-offering music.
Then, as a wise man would do, they quickly depart outside the village;
in this manner, one should perform a perpetual festival that brings about the attainment of desired prosperity for men. || 239 ||
If the lamp is extinguished at that time, one should provide two lamps. Bathing should take place for two *ghaṭikās*, and worship should last for one *ghaṭikā*. (240)
Three-quarters of the time should be for the offering, and three-quarters for the fire-ritual;
that which consists of one ghaṭikā or half a ghaṭikā is declared to be the daily festival (nityotsava).
Every day at the time of twilight, there should be a dance lasting for one ghaṭikā;
first, one should worship one's own guru, and then one should thoroughly worship Gaṇeśa.
Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, the wise man should satisfy his own self at the base of the [deity's] feet with handfuls of water.
The wise man, having performed the circumambulation, should cause [the image] to enter his own home.
He who acts thus for the sake of others, O Mādhava, acts for his own sake as well. (244)
Having reached the end of a parārdha, these two shall indeed remain eternally on earth;
fallen from the world of Rudra, they have come to the ground in human form.
Having attained the state of Rudra, he rejoices together with Rudra;
so too does he who, with devotion, offers a hundred thousand *bhavas* to the Supreme Lord. (246)
The fruit of that is multiplied ten millionfold through worship with devotion, passion, and qualities;
so too for one who worships Śiva even once during an eclipse or at the equinox.
One obtains the merit of six months by worshipping Śiva separately with devotion; one should worship and honor Śiva on the full moon and the new moon days.
One obtains the merit earned during the four-month period; there is no doubt about this.
Furthermore, one commits no sin whatsoever through the actions of mind, speech, or body. (249)
Bound by the noose of sin, he shall go to the hell of destruction;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship Śiva with devotion. (250)
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for worship in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra*, within the *Sūkṣmatantra* treatise.
Salutation to Subrahmaṇya. Salutation to Śiva.
Salutation to the Supreme Guru.
In the month of Māgha, one should indeed perform the "Ghee-Blanket" (ghṛtakambala) rite;
what is called the Ghee-Blanket shall be a source of great pleasure to Viṣṇu.
In the worship performed at the beginning of the year and so forth, this bestows the fruit of all worship;
it is especially so for each day, even when devoid of formal worship.
On that [day], which is to be honored as Śivarātri, worshipping [the deity] bestows the fruit of all worship;
by worshipping with curd in the month of Phālguna, one increases wealth and progeny.
One should worship Dadhi-saṃpūjya-vahni; this is called Puruhṛt-prīti.
This is indeed declared to be the Viṣuva; likewise, one should worship at midday.
In the month of Caitra, the offering of *damanaka* is said by the sages to bring about delight;
in Vaiśākha, by worshipping Vighneśa with the three fruits (*triphalā*), delight is said to arise.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, this milk-consecration (kṣīrābhiṣecana) should likewise be performed;
what is called the milk-consecration is indeed the Govardhana-pūjā for Vatsa. (6)
Therefore, the evening worship is prescribed during the solstices;
by worshipping the sacred ash in the month of Āṣāḍha, one will please Rudra.
By worshipping with sugar on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, the propitiation of the Moon is said to occur;
by worshipping with cakes on the full moon of Proṣṭhapada, it becomes a cause for the propitiation of Skanda.
Thus it is declared regarding the Viṣuva; one should worship during the half-watch (ardhayāma).
Having worshipped with food during the Āśvini [nakṣatra], it is said that this brings pleasure to Brahmā.
Born from the power of Śiva, it is the cause of the world's origin;
the sowing of seeds here is said to be for the purpose of providing relief to medicinal herbs in times of distress.
The giving of salt is declared to bring happiness that creates one's own prosperity;
the gift of clothing should be given to maidens, while the gift of gold should be given to a daughter.
Gold is for the sake of protecting the world and for the increase of clothing and progeny;
therefore, a vehicle drawn by a cow brings benefit to all living beings.
The month of Kṛttikā has indeed been declared as the time for the worship of lamps;
and one should worship Lord Hara, who bears a great flame, with devotion toward a Brāhmaṇa.
The offering of parched grain has been described, as well as the lamp of the Kṛttikās;
therefore, the ritual bath with clarified butter (ghṛtasnāna) is now being declared for the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
This is declared to be the "Ghee-Bath," which destroys all sins;
it is also called the "Swinging Rite" (Ḍolārohaṇa), following the sequence of Gaurī’s playful ceremony.
(28) Endowed with Śiva and Śakti, there is indeed the ritual of mounting the swing;
the worship beginning from the month of Puṣya and extending until the end of the month of Māgha. (16)
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for the worship of the Ghee-Kambaka in the section on occasional rites within the Sūkṣma-tantra.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure for the night worship; listen.
Having performed a dance at the beginning of the twilight, one should then commence the twilight dance.

That which is made of wood is said to be born of the earth; that which is made of conch-shell is called born of water. That which is made of metal is declared to be fiery (āgneya), while that which is made of bamboo belongs to the wind (vāyavya). || 2 ||
The Geya is born from space; therefore, it is considered to be of the nature of the elements.
One should first cause these five sounds to resound, and thereafter [proceed].
Listen to the method for protecting children from the forms such as Liṅgodbhava;
for one who is devoid of protection against these, there will be the destruction of the children.
The king shall attain invincibility; therefore, perform the *śāntihoma* sacrifice.
It should be performed at evening time, and thereafter one should worship Naṭeśa.
Having bathed according to the ritual for the root image, one should offer a gift with great joy;
having adorned it with white flowers and smeared it with white sandalwood paste.
Having adorned it with white garments and decorated it with all ornaments,
one should worship it at this time according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should perform the rite of the perpetual festival, and worship during the half-watch [of the night];
[the deity] whose limbs are anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine garlands and ornaments. (8)
Having adorned him with variegated garments and decorated him with all ornaments,
one should worship the eternal power (Ciraśakti) and perform the rites as prescribed for worship.
One should especially worship either the sandals or the image;
one should worship with the Śakti mantra and then cause the palanquin to be brought forth.
Then, at the edge of the palanquin, one should perform a circumambulation of the enclosure wall;
there, one should carry out a dance with nine rhythmic beats (tāla), using a number of gems [as ornaments].
From Indra to Īśāna, there is indeed pure dance (śuddhanṛtta) in the center;
from Indra to Īśāna, there should be the Ratnāka dance as well.
One should place [the vessel] upon a lotus-seat on the northern side of the liṅga;
having offered incense and a lamp with the heart-mantra, the wise one should then give water for sipping (ācamana).
A cake, a ball of mung beans, milk-rice, jaggery and sugar-candy, coconut and other such things, milk, plantain, and jackfruit—in this sequence. (14)
Mudga-rice, guḍa-rice, pure rice, milk-rice (pāyasa),
and kṛsara-rice— these constitute the fivefold food offering.
One should offer water mixed with fragrance, as well as powder for rubbing the hands, camphor for perfuming the mouth, and betel leaf. || 16 ||
Having offered all things such as incense and lamps, as well as the ashes from the night's fire,
and having then performed the purification of the doorway, one should worship the Great Liṅga.
Having worshipped in the middle of the door with the Prāsāda mantra,
[one should do so] with dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, purifiers, mirrors, umbrellas, and chowries. || 18 ||
One should perform recitation according to one's ability and always wash one's hands;
O Śambhu, one should also cause sacred ashes to be given to the king and to his devoted subjects.
One should especially worship Caṇḍeśa and Kṣetrapāla;
one should arrange the place for the bed in the western direction, the quarter of Soma.
Having placed [the deity] upon the couch, one should worship Śiva and Śakti;
or else, one should place the sandals or the image upon the couch. (21)
Having fully worshipped the form of Someśa, one should place a pair of sandals in his presence—
an image with three eyes and one face, holding a deer and an axe.
One should place the left and right hands in the gestures of fearlessness (abhaya) and boon-granting (varada);
he wears a tiger-skin garment and is adorned with all ornaments. || 23 ||
Having worshipped Gaurī according to the rules— she who is like pure crystal and seated upon a white lotus throne— one should then offer betel leaf.
Indeed, conduct toward him is said to be like that toward a king, affection like that for a son, devotion like that for a guru, and fear is said to be like that of a serpent. (25)
Thus, in this very order of daily rites, which includes the dance of Rudra,
one should then worship one's own guru according to this same daily sequence.
One should satisfy one's own self at the base of the feet with handfuls of water.
Now hear the procedure for the festival of Śiva known as Vijaya, Lalita, and Sūkṣma.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for nocturnal worship in the Sūkṣmatantra.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the sequence of the ritual for the festival of Śiva,
which is a manifestation for all people and has issued forth from the mouth of Śiva. (1)
First, there was the annual festival; second, the festival in the month [of Mārgaśīrṣa];
beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, there was a six-monthly festival lasting seven nights.
If, however, during the remaining month beginning with Jyeṣṭha, there is a three-night festival, it is beneficial for all beings, peaceful, and a warder-off of all defects. || 3 ||

Especially during the installation, the sprinkling, the sacrifice, and at the conclusion of initiation; as well as during the solstices, the transits of the sun, the vyatipāta yoga, and on one's own birthday.
In the event of excessive rain, drought, or likewise national unrest,
a wise man should cause a festival to be held at the conclusion of the king’s consecration or at the end of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
Sava is declared to be the cessation of utsava;
because sava has emerged [from it], it is therefore called utsava. || 6 ||
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, however, there is the Śivotsava ending with the constellation Śiva (Ārdrā);
in the month of Puṣya, it ends with Puṣya; and in the month of Māgha, it ends with Maghā.
All who perform [rites] directed toward the ancestors go forth uplifted;
and in the month of Phalguna, reaching the end of Uttarā, it is said that one is liberated for the sake of enjoyment from worldly existence.
In the month of Caitra, one should effect the destruction of enemies, and likewise in Vaiśākha;
in all other months, the wise man should do so under the respective lunar mansions.
The Śaiva, the Gauṇa, the Prabhūta, the Bhāvana, the Daivika,
the Paitṛka, the Kaumāra, and the Sāvitra— thus is the group of eight.
One day is called *śaiva*, three days is said to be *gauṇa*,
five days is declared to be *bhāvana*, and seven days and so forth [is *mukhya*]. (11)
The nine-day rite is declared to be divine; they know the fortnightly rite as pertaining to Sāvitrī;
the monthly festival is named the ancestral (paitṛka), so it is proclaimed.
That which is to be performed within six months is called the Kaumāra;
the various divisions of festivals and their names have indeed been declared. (13)
I shall state some specific details regarding the time for visiting sacred sites (tīrtha),
particularly concerning festivals and musical instruments, should there be a gathering due to negligence.
One should not cause [the ritual] to be performed for a day that is either increased or diminished;
the overnight consecration at a sacred ford (tīrtha) is known to be common to all.
The primary [rituals], beginning with the powder festival (cūrṇotsava) and ending with the pilgrimage site (tīrtha), have been correctly described;
and at that time, it is especially joined with the auspicious constellation of the pilgrimage site.

By that, one should know the sacred ford (tīrtha) to be auspicious, and it shall bring welfare to all. At night, the consecration at the ford and the worship of the asterisms of the ford cannot take place. || 17 ||
Therefore, while other holy places may lead to faults, the Great Holy Place (Mahātīrtha) does not cause fault;
for that reason, one should especially strive with every effort toward Mahātīrtha.
When the time for the gathering at a sacred ford (tīrtha) coincides with an auspicious lunar mansion (nakṣatra),
then that sacred ford shall exist for the sake of the abundance of all prosperity.
If, however, at the time of a great pilgrimage site (mahātīrtha), the astrological conjunction of the site (tīrtharkṣa) does not occur,
one should especially perform the rite of the site (tīrtha) on that particular festival day when the conjunction is present.
The power of the *parvan* [festival day] destroys all defects by its very nature.
If the *parvan* does not coincide with the day, a wise person should perform the rite at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) on the preceding day. (21)
One should perform the festival of the Kṛttikā-lamp in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa;
at the conclusion of this, one should undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords and carry out a journey through the forest.

In that [middle month], with the exception of the bali and homa offerings, everything else—from the raising of the flag (dhvaja) up to the ritual at the sacred ford (tīrtha)—is the same as before; this applies to the middle month.
When there was no festival for her at all upon the previous ascent of the ketu,
it became renowned as Adhamanta, and that very place became a sacred ford (tīrtha).
During that month of the festival, a sacred bathing rite (tīrthaka) must be performed according to this procedure; thus should the best of preceptors (deśikottama) cause it to be done.
Then, for those [altars] consisting of three units and those consisting of two units starting from that first one,
one should first raise the banner— whether it be of the highest, middle, or lowest grade.
But prior to the raising of the banner, on the seventh or ninth night,
the wise man should offer the ritual germination (aṅkura) according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
On the twenty-eighth day, following the eighteenth,
that day shall be the commencement, occurring on the tenth day.
On the twenty-first day during a divine festival,
one should perform the rite of sowing sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), especially for a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
On this day, at the time of the directional offering, the wise man should present the sprouts;
and on the fifteenth day during the occasion of a material festival.
On the eighteenth day, which is double [the number of days since the commencement], the wise one should offer the sprouts;
and on that same day, at the beginning of the rite, he should also offer a sprout for the sake of the [main] sprouts.
The best of teachers should also cause the commencement of festivals on other occasions;
indeed, whatever lunar mansion (nakṣatra) occurs in that month, he should have the festival performed under it.
In that month and under that asterism, one should always cause a festival to be held;
for if anyone causes it to be held otherwise, the king and the kingdom shall perish.

Therefore, with every effort, one should perform at the commencement of the rite the hoisting of the flag, the offering of oblations, the feeding of the assembly, and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana). || 34 ||

The bathing at the sacred ford (tīrtha), the sacrifice to Caṇḍeśa, the eight-limbed festival, the scattering of grain, the raising of banners, the germinating of seeds (aṅkura), and the offering of oblations (bali).
The bathing at sacred fords with powders for consecration and other substances is supreme;
first one should erect the banner, and secondly the offering of sprouts. || 36 ||
The fourth is the consecration of the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) along with the altar (vedikā);
the fifth is the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa); and the sixth is the grasping of the weapon-mantra (astraparigraha). || 37 ||

The seventh is the sacrifice of weapons (astrayāga), the eighth is the consecration (adhivāsana), the ninth is the powder festival (cūrṇotsava), and the tenth is the consecration (abhiṣecana). || 38 ||

The eleventh is the ritual bathing (snapana), the twelfth is the worship of the deities' forms (mūrtipūjana), the thirteenth is the sacrifice to the Gaṇas (gaṇayāga), and the fourteenth is the sacrifice to Caṇḍa (caṇḍayāga). || 39 ||
The ascent is proclaimed as the sacrifice [to be performed] on the fifteenth day;
thereafter follows the festival of the devotees, and after that, the flower-sacrifice.
Thus ends the chapter on the indication of festivals in the Sūkṣmatantra.
(35) Hereafter, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the time of the holy ford (tīrthakāla),
for the benefit of all the world and for the welfare of all living beings.
For the destruction of drought, for the increase of crops, for the eradication of smallpox, and for the happiness of the king and the kingdom. (2)
On that [day], as well as on the birth asterism of the king and the birth asterism of the kingdom, a wise man should cause a festival to be celebrated with every effort.
In a village, however, it should be under the birth asterism of the village; in a city and so forth, under the birth asterism of the city;
or under the birth asterism of the patron (yajamāna), or even at the end of those [asterisms]. || 4 ||
Then, during an eclipse or at the transit of the sun (saṅkrānti), one should perform worship;
or else, a wise man should cause a festival to be held on the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of his birth month.
On the full moon day of Kārttika when the moon is in the Kṛttikā constellation, it bestows all perfections;
in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, up to the end of Rudra, it indeed bestows wealth.
In the month of Puṣya, however, up to the end of Puṣya, it increases one's sons and grandsons;
in the month of Māgha, up to the end of Māgha, it always leads the ancestors to heaven.
In the month of Phālguna, under the asterism Uttarā, there is especially victory in battle;
and in the month of Caitra, until the end of Citrā, it causes the destruction of enemies.
In the month of Vaiśākha, up until the Viśākhā constellation, it increases the prosperity of three lineages;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the Mūla constellations, it fulfills the desires of kings day by day.

In the month of Āṣāḍha, by fasting until the end of the constellation Vaiśvānara (Jyeṣṭhā), one shall indeed attain victory through enjoyment; in the months of Śrāvaṇa, by fasting until the end of Śraviṣṭhā, one may attain the station of Brahmā.
(36) Ending with Proṣṭhapadā in the month of Bhādrapada, it increases enjoyment and noble birth;
ending with Aśvinī in the month of Āśvina, it destroys all diseases. || 11 ||
The festival of Śiva should be performed in all months up to Ārdrā;
however, in whichever month it falls within that year, one should perform it specifically in that lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
I shall state some specific details according to the distinctions of sacred sites and times:
Citrā and Svātī are in Aries, while Viśākhā and Anurādhā are in Taurus.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, during the constellation Aindrī (Jyeṣṭhā), there is the root-tuber; in the same month, during the constellation Vyāpī (Anurādhā), there is Vaiṣṇava.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, during the constellation Viṣṇuvasu (Śravaṇā), [there is the tuber]; and in the month of Bhādrapada, during the constellation Ajaikapāt (Pūrvabhādrapadā).
When the sun has entered Libra, during the asterism of Aśvinī, and specifically during the southern solstice, as well as during Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī, and especially on the day of Kṛttikā. || 15 ||
And likewise, Saumya and Dṛk [are worshipped] in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa;
Āditya and Pūṣan in Puṣya; and Sarpa and Pitṛ in Māgha.
Indeed, one should perform the rite at those sacred fords during the month of Phālguna under the asterisms of Uttarāphālgunī and Hastā,
as well as on the full moon, the new moon, the thirteenth, and the fourteenth lunar days.
And it has been said that if the three *tithis* are joined with the *tīrthabha*, at that time, during that conjunction, the best of preceptors should indeed perform [the rite]. (18)
As before, the asterism of the sacred ford (tīrtha) is the same; on that day, one should not perform the rite of the ford.
If one performs the ritual bath of conclusion (avabhṛtha), it should be done under another asterism.
One should perform [the rite] at night during a lunar mansion associated with a festival; by day, one incurs no fault even if it is not such a mansion.
The same applies when it is joined with a yoga, as well as during an eclipse.
If, however, on that very day or night, the [planets] such as Amṛta and others occur,
one should perform the *tīrtha* rite during the day when it is joined with a yoga, specifically under a *tīrtha* asterism.
Whether one is engaged in yoga during the day or even at night,
on whichever day one performs the pilgrimage (tīrtha), [the merit] accrues again from sunset. (22)
If it should coincide with a lunar mansion belonging to a heretical sect,
the wise man should not perform the avabhṛtha bath on that day, for it would result in a broken yoga.
Whether by means of the power of yoga or by means of previous power,
it should be performed on the very same day, and indeed it must be performed through the application of yoga.
In this very manner, one should perform [the rites] at the time of yoga;
for indeed, the respective sacrifices take place on the lunar days and under the asterisms previously mentioned. (25)
At those times, the best of teachers indeed perform the consecration of sacred sites (tīrtha);
yet, if even one among them is deficient, they should not perform the consecration of the sacred site at all.
In the same manner, having performed the festival and the yoga according to the prescribed method,
one should perform the Śiva-festival at a sacred site (tīrtha) on a time and day conjoined with yoga.
Or, even if [the planets] have entered a single asterism during the Amṛta-siddhi yoga, the best of preceptors should perform [the rite] during other times of auspicious omens. || 28 ||
What is the reason for this distinction arising from the power of yoga?
It is like how poison, when combined with honey and clarified butter, becomes harmless. || 29 ||
Indeed, those very [elements] become stainless through the immortal [nectar] when one is joined in yoga;
of this there is no doubt—such is the certainty of the scripture. (30)
In this very manner, one should first observe [the time] by means of the prescribed method,
provided that the birth-constellation of that person is conjoined with a yoga.
By that, one enjoys the fruit of a most auspicious and infinite sacred ford (tīrtha),
provided it occurs on the day of the initial commencement, even if that day is joined with an inauspicious conjunction (nāśayoga) or the like. (32)
On that day, nothing should be performed; if anything is performed, it is fruitless.
One should cause the excellent Tīrtha to be commenced on the previous day, under the asterism of Ārambha-tīrtha. || 33 ||

Having thus examined [the site] in many ways, the most excellent of preceptors should cause [the work] to be performed at an auspicious moment, in a favorable conjunction, during a period known as "stable," and under a propitious asterism.
At the time of the first undertaking, one should observe it in this very manner;
indeed, it is the supreme immersion together with the deities.
The middle [rite] is that with water from the heart-mantra, and another is the sprinkling;
at that time, one should take [water] in the water and sprinkle it upon elephants, horses, and so forth.

From the time the flagstaff is erected until the conclusion of the pilgrimage site, a wise man should not perform any auspicious human rites during the constellations that fall within that interval between those two events.
One should not undertake a journey to them, for it would cause distress to those who do so;
yet if a journey must inevitably take place, one should enter within the sacred precinct (tīrtha).
I shall explain specifically the sacred ford (tīrtha) for the Brāhmaṇa and the others:
for the Brāhmaṇa, it is during the months of Māgha, Phālguna, Caitra, and Vaiśākha.
In the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and likewise Jyeṣṭha,
as well as in the month of Puṣya, these [rites] belong specifically to the king and the Brāhmaṇa.
The month of Āśvayuja, Kṛttikā, and Mārgaśīrṣa are prescribed for the Vaiśya caste; and in the winter season, Mārgaśīrṣa alone is prescribed for the Śūdra. || 41 ||

In the manner thus described, the supreme preceptor should cause [the rite] to be performed during the month of Māgha under the asterism Uttarā, or also under the asterisms Proṣṭhapadā and Jyeṣṭhā (Aindrāgnika). (42)
The rite for a Brāhmaṇa should be performed under the three Aśravaṇas,
as well as under Mūla, Puṣya, the King (Pūrvaphalgunī), Kārttikā, and the two Aśvins.
For a Śūdra, it is ordained under the asterism of Ārdrā and Pūrvabhādra;
indeed, for all castes, the festival of Śiva should conclude with Ārdrā.
Likewise, on the asterisms of Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Punarvasu, and Hastā,
as well as on the seventh, thirteenth, and twelfth lunar days, it is auspicious for a Brāhmaṇa.
On Wednesday or Thursday, it is prescribed for a Brahmin; on Tuesday it is said to be for a king; and on Sunday or Friday for a Vaiśya. (46)
A Vaiśya and likewise a Śūdra should perform it on the full moon day,
the new moon day, the eighth day, and on other festival occasions.
In this very manner, one should cause it to be performed even at the first [conjunction],
especially during these aforementioned times when joined with a [lunar] yuga.
In this very manner, one should again perform the avabhṛtha bath;
however, at the time of the avabhṛtha, disturbances such as those affecting the kingdom may arise. (49)
If excessive rain or other such calamities occur, the pilgrimage tour is not undertaken;
instead, water should be taken from that very spot and filled into large jars.
One should perform the consecration of the sacred site (tīrtha) according to the prescribed rules for the ritual bathing;
at the time of hoisting the banner, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and the offering (bali) without [the full bathing rite].
When two asterisms of pilgrimage coincide within a single month, it is most excellent;
likewise, when two asterisms of pilgrimage fall on the same weekday, whether in a divine or a human [cycle], it is likewise so. (52)
The Brahma-rite (brāhmika) should be performed in the same manner; this is considered the prescribed procedure. For the eighteenth [day], it should be done on the twenty-eighth day, or even later.
On that very same undertaking, it should take place on the tenth day;
or, at the time of the proclaimed festival, on the nineteenth day.
One should perform the rite of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇaka), especially at a sacred site (tīrtha);
on the tenth day for a rite dedicated to the gods (daiva), the wise man should offer the sprouts.
During the festival of the sages (ārṣa), at the proper time, on the fifteenth day, the wise man should offer the sprouts; or, on the eighteenth day, which is double that [period].
On that day, at the commencement, one should plant the sprout of the sprout;
according to the previously mentioned time, one should immediately sow the sprouts.
In the case of Brahmī, it should be exactly the same; all else is likewise.
That day, being tripled, is proclaimed as the most excellent. || 58 ||
Twice that duration is the middling [time], and that same day is the lowest.
For rites of pacification (śāntika), it should be three times the time; for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), twice the day.
On that day, Kāmada is indeed said to have a threefold division;
likewise, at that time when it possesses the three qualities (triguṇa), it occurs on the eighteenth day.
On the fourteenth day, and likewise on the tenth day;
at the time of the middle [period], on the tenth and the eighth.
On that day, at the commencement, the sprout of the banner should be increased;
in this very manner, the most excellent of preceptors should cause it to be performed. (62)
In a Śaiva [temple], one should perform what is Śaiva; one should not cause anything else to be done. || 62½ ||
Thus ends the chapter on the determination of the time for visiting sacred sites in the Sūkṣmatantra.
I shall describe the festival of lights (Dīpāvali) according to the prescribed rule;
it should be performed during the month of Kṛttikā on an auspicious festival day.
The merit that brings about all peace, as well as the procedure for the monthly worship— whether it be joined with a festival day or not, or even joined with a specific lunar day.
A day joined with a festival (parvan) is declared to be excellent and highly praised;
the festival itself is said to be the primary element and is called the most excellent of all.
If the fourteenth day falls on a mixed conjunction of Kṛttikā and Bharaṇī,
there will be little rain, disease, and unrest within the kingdom.
On the night preceding that day, one should begin the consecration (adhivāsana) in the northeastern quarter of the pavilion,
or specifically in the southeast.
In the midst of that, the preceptor, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit,
should fill a small vessel with rice and draw a lotus in its center.
Having placed a tripod in the center of that, one should then prepare a lamp-stand;
having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should cause the declaration of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be recited there.
p. 42) Whether it be a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), that is called the rite of the fire (vahnikārya).
All [the rites] beginning with the installation of the fire (agnyādhāna) should be performed first according to the rules. || 8 ||
One should especially perform the binding of the protective thread for Maheśa during ritual acts,
adorning him with all ornaments and beautifying him with every auspicious rite.
Then, amidst the sounds of conchs and drums and the utterances of those proclaiming auspiciousness,
one should perform the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
The number of Rudras is nine; the number [of elements] is twenty-five;
the number of principles (tattvas) is thirty-six; and the number is one hundred and eight. || 11 ||
Or else, with the fivefold coverings according to the extent of one's means,
one should tie a packet there and apply it to the vessel.
One should prepare the Śiva-fire and then offer a lamp;
having offered incense and the lamp with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should maintain it without interruption. || 13 ||
It is declared that "sāyam" refers to the night, while "prātaḥ" is traditionally understood as the day; [the period] beginning from midday until ten nāḍikās [have passed]. (14)
Then, having performed the special ablution with the foremost parts of the root-mantra,
and having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should thereafter commence the sacrifice.
They were provided with garments, sacred threads, garlands, crowns, and earrings;
their limbs were anointed with all kinds of perfumes and they were adorned with every sort of floral wreath.
Having performed worship especially by means of the path of the five obstructions,
and having offered incense and a lamp with the heart-mantra, one should thereafter perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
Having likewise performed the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation, one should thereafter worship the lamp;
then, beginning from sunset, one should cause the lamp to be lit. (18)
Having summoned his attendants— who were well-bathed, dressed in white garments,
wearing turbans and upper robes, and were pure and holy— the merchant spoke.
One should place a lamp upon its summit and perform a circumambulation of the temple,
accompanied by the sound of hymns and the resonance of conch shells.
Thereafter, one should enter the inner sanctum (ālaya) before the primary image;
having paid homage to the God of gods, one should properly offer the eightfold flowers (aṣṭapuṣpa).
Having offered incense and lamps with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should engage the God of gods;
indeed, having thus performed the sequence for the inner enclosure, one should present the lamp of the mantra.
Taking the remaining lamp, one should insert it at the base of the staff;
then, having performed the purification of the staff, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited there.
O Maheśāna, after performing the inspection, one should then offer a lamp;
furthermore, one should offer a lamp from the shoes up to the end of the bedding.
One should cause all the lamps to be placed in the kitchen;
then, one should lead them again to the pavilion at the enclosure wall and the gate tower.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, he should enter his own abode;
having offered incense and a lamp with the heart-mantra, he should then apply the sacred ashes.
One should cause the God of Gods to be offered a mixture consisting of pieces of sugarcane combined with powdered black pepper, as well as parched grain, cakes, and fruit. (27)
Having offered abundant oblations, one should present betel;
there, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and finger-rings. (28)
The mortal who acts in this manner shall attain a meritorious state. || 28½ ||
Thus ends the chapter on the row of lamps in the Sūkṣmatantra.
To Indra, he spoke these words regarding the western gate, which is most excellent, concerning the God of gods, the Lord of the World, Umā’s consort, the Supreme Lord: || 1 ||
The Lord said: Now, I shall briefly describe the supreme procedure for worship,
according to the *Vijaya*, the *Sūkṣmatantra*, the *Kiraṇa*, and the *Parameśvara*.
The Raurava and Kāmika [Tantras] originate from that which faces west;
therefore, one who knows the Tantras and Saṃhitās should perform all ritual acts by means of them.
The *saṃhitā* of others is mixed and does not reach the gods;
here, the worship of creation for all those [deities] at the western door is described.
One should worship Brahmā, the presiding deity of the door, as the Supreme Lord;
to the south, a pure maternal uncle skilled in the scriptures should perform the worship.
One should worship the Lord of Gods daily, accompanied by the five preceptors;
likewise, one who performs the five-fold ritual times should worship all [the deities].
