Thus this conduct has been proclaimed; five types of teachers are celebrated:
the worshiper who should always honor the worshiper, and the practitioner who accomplishes with ritual substances.
One should perform the fivefold purification: the purification of the site, which is an ornament endowed with all ornaments, and the purification of the vessels for all [the deities]. (8)
The preceptor should cause [the disciple] to perform occasional rites, regular duties, and actions for the sake of others;
and the practitioner at the western door should possess wisdom regarding worship and other such acts.
Having first performed the purification of the body, the second is the purification of the site;
the third is the purification of the vessel, and the fourth is the purification of the *liṅga*.
The fifth is the purity of the mantra; thus the fivefold purity is proclaimed. The worshipper, endowed with celibacy, [should perform it] during the first part of the night. || 11 ||
When the Brāhma-muhūrta has arrived, being devoted to the meditation on the mantra,
[one should recite] the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva, which destroys all sins.

Having gone outside to the edge of the village, having performed purification according to the rule, and having sipped water (ācamana) and bathed according to the rite, one should perform the ritual placement of the deities upon the body (dehanyāsa). || 13 ||
Having performed three circumambulations, one should enter the temple of Śiva;
having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, one should mentally pray to Śiva.

Having meditated, one should fix the gaze on the tip of the nose at a distance of twelve finger-breadths; with the body, one should burn away the *āṇava* and other impurities from the feet up to the head.
Having reached the heart-lotus, which is Śiva, and having worshipped it again on the right side,
one should then dismiss it through the left nostril and likewise burn that [element] once more.
The wise man, situated upon a heap of ashes, should burn the body;
there he should meditate upon the lunar orb resting upon a white lotus. || 17 ||
One should perform the immersion in nectar within the body while remaining in the left nostril;
one should perform exhalation through the right [nostril], which is the cause for the arising of the body. (18)
The wise one should unite the self with the body of Sadāśiva and the establishment of the vital breath in truth; there, he should perform the concentrated *kumbhaka* breath-retention.
Having abandoned the mass of impurity, one should [place] the mass of mantras in due order;
thereafter, the placement situated above is the mass of mantras in due order.

Having first performed the placement of stability (sthitinyāsa), and thereafter the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa), you should perform the worship while setting aside the placement of reabsorption (saṃhāra). || 21 ||
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands, thereafter perform the ritual placement of the limbs:
place the limb of Śiva on the right hand and the limb of Vidyā on the left hand.
At the wrist, there are two [deities]; in Śivā, however, is the deity Brahmā;
and Śrī as well as Sarasvatī are proclaimed to be in the middle of the palm. (23)
Having placed Umā-Durgā at the base [of the thumb] and the left thumb like Indra at the right thumb, it is called the "well-pressed" (saṃpīḍita) when joined together. 24.
The ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) is proclaimed to extend from Indra up to Brahmā;
one should then sequentially perform the placement of the limbs of the Vidyā (vidyāṅganyāsa) from the navel down to the feet.

That which begins with the Praṇava and ends with the prostration, starting from the letter 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', is called the placement of syllables (akṣaranyāsa); it is here termed the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa).
One should assign the mantras beginning with Īśāna, conjoined with their respective divisions of the *kalās*;
thereafter, one should assign the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and perform the purification of the body.
Thereafter, one should purify the body and then perform the purification of the site;
having washed these [areas] all around, one should smear them with cow dung. (28)
One should perform the purification of the site by sprinkling it with water consecrated by mantras; likewise, one should prepare the six ancillary vessels, the shallow bowls, and various jars. (29)
The wise one should especially wash other water-vessels made of gold with the weapon-mantra, using the syllable *huṃ* according to the ritual injunctions.
The purification of the vessel has thus been declared; now hear the purification of the substances:
water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, as well as fragrance and flowers. (31)
The worshipper should purify the food offerings, the incense, the lamps, and the water substances;
he should also perform the purification of his own body and the purification of the linga.
Having entered the interior of the womb-chamber, one should worship the gatekeepers;
one should worship Daṇḍin and Muṇḍin, using their respective names preceded by "sva-".
Having entered the interior, the purification of the liṅga should then take place here;
one should discard all the flowers and offer them to Caṇḍeśa.
Having washed the Śiva-liṅga with water purified by mantras,
one should encircle the liṅga with a cord of darbha grass and fill it with eight types of earth.
One should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); thus, purification of the liṅga occurs here.
The wise man, standing facing north, should prepare a seat. (36)
One should meditate upon this lion-throne, which is said to be square, as being Vimala, Padma, and Ananta. (37)
On the exterior, there are twelve lines; on each side, there are two of them.
Each corner has one line, which should encircle the five moons.
Having visualized that lotus outside, the best of teachers should perform the beautiful yoga of the moon; without being saluted, he should cause it to be made.
One should always worship for the sake of others while standing facing north;
outside of that, there should be a lotus, upon which one should arrange the twelve weapons.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, and likewise the noose;
the goad, the mace, the arrow, and likewise the lotus and the wheel. || 41 ||
One should always place the deities from the west up to Ratna at the end, starting with Suvajra, Haṃsamūlī, and likewise Aṇḍatuṇḍa, within all the enclosures.
From the earth, there are seven kinds of essence: fire, wind, and space, as well as salt, milk, ghee, curd, and honey. || 43 ||
Having performed the enclosure of the elements (bhūtamāvaraṇa) starting from the west and proceeding clockwise,
one should worship with their respective names beginning with the first letter.
Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha, as well as Rāhu and Ketu;
Āditya, Śani, Śukra, Merusūnu, and Bṛhaspati. (45)
In this manner, one should worship the obstructions starting from the west;
here, the beauty of the digits (kalā) from Aries to Pisces is described.
One should worship two [deities] who know two or three Vedas, then two who know five or five [Vedas], and the sixth, the wise one, who knows the *bhagaṇa*, starting from the east. 47.
One should place the syllable *vyo* on the left side, which is the support for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
one should place the syllable *ma* in the position of the little finger, and the syllable *vyo* to the west.
Relying on the letter *vi* at the end, place the letter *na* in the domain of Vāyu;
having placed the letter *śi* for Soma, place the letter *vā* by its side. (49)
One should place the syllable *caṃ* on Īśāna and the syllable *na* in the east;
likewise, one should place the syllable *mā* based on Indra and the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) in the direction of Agni.
To the south is the lotus flower, and [the sequence] beginning with the support proceeds clockwise;
this is the enclosure of space—now hear of the lion and elephant enclosures.
One should worship Dharma-jñāna, Vairāgya, Aiśvarya, as well as Ailīkā, and Siṃhāvaraṇa; one should honor these [deities] with offerings. 52.
Having established Ananta in the east and Trimūrti as well as Agni;
having placed Sūkṣma in the south and likewise Śrīkaṇṭha in the southwest (Nirṛti).
Having assigned Śivottama in the west and Śikhaṇḍin in the region of the wind (northwest),
likewise Ekanetra in the north and Ekarudra in the northeast.
For these [deities], Anantavarana and the others are placed clockwise starting from the east;
Vama is assigned to the west, and Jyestha is likewise in the north.
One should place Raudrī in the southern part and Kali in the direction of Indra (the east);
having placed Kalavikaraṇa in the region of the southeast, one should assign them to their respective directions.
One should place Balavikaraṇa in the southwest, Balapramathana in the northwest,
and Sarvabhūtadamanī in the northeastern direction.
In the center, the goddess Manonmanī is said to be in the lotus posture (padmāsana).
Having placed the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the east and the letter *ā* in the southeast, [58]
The letter *ū* is in the southern part of the northeast; the letter *vyo* is situated in the direction of the Rākṣasas (the southwest);
and the letter *ṣa* is in the domain of Vāyu (the northwest).
One should place *vyo* in the northern direction, *kāraṃ* in the northeast, and *naikāraṃ* in the middle of those; this is here called the yogic posture (*yogāsana*).
In the palace at the western gate, however, there was a small door for the worship of Śiva.
O Bhārata, the Liṅga at the western gate is situated toward the south;
it is meritorious, removing all sins and destroying all calamities.
The attainment of all good fortune and prosperity, for the sake of being beloved by all the world, and the increase of sons and grandsons through Gaurī’s left hand. (63)
Just as a potter’s wheel appears in various forms through the clays [shaped] upon it, so too does [the world] appear according to the form conceived by the mind of the Teacher. 64.
Śiva is in the right hand, while Gaurī is in the right hand;
the Lord of Gods is in the left hand—this is the station of the twice-born Śiva. (65)
The region of the teacher’s hand is behind the right fingers;
for the sake of all that is dear, the hand is [placed] behind the back of the right hand.
"It is said that Śiva is pleased, and likewise by the mind of the Ācārya; this is declared to be the abode of Gaurī. Now hear about the food offering."
Just as an elephant, having eaten the fruit of the wood-apple (kapittha), extracts its inner essence, so too does the Supreme Lord grasp [the soul]. 68.

At the end of that [offering], one should perform the *bhūtabali* without distinction; there, one should cause the *digbali* to be offered, ending with the outer seats (*bāhyapīṭha*) of Indra and the other [deities]. (69)
One should likewise offer the remains of food, as well as the sacrificial oblation (bali) and the clarified butter (havis), to the Asuras, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and Brahmarākṣasas.
One should offer the bali-oblation upon the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) starting from the east and ending at the northeast;
one should offer perfume, flowers, incense, food offerings, and the bali-oblation. || 71 ||
One should cause the offering of incense with the Ghoramantra, flowers with the Īśanamantra, incense with the Astramantra, and a lamp with the Netramantra. || 72 ||
One should offer the oblation with the *puruṣa* mantra, the water for the feet (*pādya*) with the *sadyojāta* mantra;
the respectful offering (*arghya*) with the *puruṣa* mantra, and the water for sipping (*ācamana*) with the *vāmadeva* mantra. || 73 ||
By means of the utterance of all the mantras and specifically through the heart-mantra, one performs the western worship of these; now listen to [the procedure for] the northern gate.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Worship through the Western Door," in the Sūkṣma-śāstra.
The virtuous ought to forgive an offense committed by one who acts as an instrument.
Henceforth, I shall explain the supreme rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa),
which is likewise prescribed for festivals, ritual bathing, installation, and consecration by sprinkling.
At the beginning of all auspicious rites, one should offer the sprouts in sequence:
first the sprout [of the deity], and second the festive sprout.
The third is the sprout of the sacred ford (tīrtha), while the fourth is the sprout of the festival (utsava); the notion [of these] is proclaimed to extend from human beings up to the piśācas. (3)
On the ninth day one should perform the first [rite], on the seventh day the second, and on that same day the third; thus the wise man should sow the sprouts. (4)
The first and the second are called the sprouts of auspiciousness;
the third shall be the limb of the festival, which is appropriate for festivals.
In rites such as festivals and other ceremonies, one should first initiate the ritual germination (aṅkura).
Therefore, with every effort, one should then initiate the germination at a sacred site (tīrtha-aṅkura).
One should perform the auspicious rite of the sprout (maṅgalāṅkuraka) seven days, five days, three days, or even immediately before any undertaking, as it is suitable for all activities.
One should perform a special circumambulation of the weapon (astra) and the jar of Soma;
one should prepare auspicious sprouts and sow the sprouts of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
The *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva*—these are the threefold [vessels].
One should have the *pālikā* made with a height of one *ratna*, measured by the *mātrā-aṅgula*.
One should not calculate the width of the mouth of the *pālikā* for the sake of illusion;
its circumference is three times that, and the measurement of the base of the *pālikā* is the same.
The width of the jar-like vessel (ghaṭikāghaṭa) is declared to be six finger-breadths;
the width of the mouth of the shallow bowl (śarāva) is said to be twelve finger-breadths. || 11 ||
One should carefully avoid a drum that is cracked, hollow, split, or has a loose rim;
instead, one should employ one endowed with the proper characteristics.
The most excellent of preceptors should have [the vessel] made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or even earthenware, according to its availability and proper dimensions. (13)
One should make the hollow of the vessel seamless using the tips of *darbha* or *kuśa* grass;
then one should worship the *pālikā* and other vessels with sand, cow-dung, and clay. (14)
In front of the temple, one should prepare a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, along with sesame seeds and a surrounding layer of darbha grass.
There, the preceptor should place the *pālikā* with the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) alone;
he should place *aśvattha* leaves and *darbha* grass upon the base of the *pālikā*.
Having washed sesame, mung beans, black gram, horse gram, and even *aṅgu* with milk, one should sow them along with the ten seeds.
Thereafter, the wise one should offer milk-rice with the seed-syllable of Soma;
he should cause betel-leaf to be given there and have it placed in a well-concealed spot.
Having worshipped day after day with the Prāsāda mantra alone,
the wise man should subsequently observe what is auspicious and inauspicious, and then accept that which is auspicious.
If inauspicious signs should occur there, one should cause expiatory rites and the like to be performed. || 19½ ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Planting of Sprouts," in the Kriyāpāda of the Sūkṣmaśāstra, within the Mahotsava.
(54) Hereafter I shall explain the supreme ritual of raising the banner (dhvajārohaṇa).
The preceptor and the patron should contemplate [the procedure] according to the number of days. || 1 ||
Afterwards, having raised the banner— whether threefold or twofold—
it should be performed on that very day in the best, middling, or lowest manner.
One should indeed plant the banner in the forenoon for the benefit of Brāhmaṇas;
for a Kṣatriya, however, at midday, and for Vaiśyas in the afternoon.
For Śūdras, it should be at midnight, or it may be in the evening;
however, for the benefit of Brāhmaṇas, it should indeed be preceded by the hoisting of the flag. || 4 ||
For the prosperity of the Kṣatriyas, preceded by the beating of drums,
[the ceremony] should take place in the city or in a meritorious region, preceded by the rite of sowing seeds.
One should especially cause a drum to be beaten before entering a village.
In the city, at a meritorious site, one should first perform the hoisting of the banner and then,
preceded by the rite of sowing sprouts, have it carried out in all directions for the sake of the devotees.
A wise person should always perform an action in the same sequence as it was first begun;
however, he who performs it otherwise is said to cause a confusion of ritual actions (kriyā-saṅkara).
Therefore, with every effort, the auspicious first commencement [should be made] with *sarala*,
*candana*, as well as *dhātakī* and *campaka*.
The betel nut, the coconut, the wood-apple, and the bamboo are said to be made of cane;
the best should be one hundred cubits long, while the middling is half of that.
A wise man should have it made twenty-five cubits [in length] as the minimum;
or else eighteen cubits, with a width of twelve finger-breadths. (11)
Then, according to the measurement of the temple, one should have the flagstaff and its top-pendant constructed;
it must be straight, free from defects, and devoid of insect holes or hollows.
The preceptors should fashion the flagstaff according to their aesthetic preference;
its circumference at the base should be sixteen finger-breadths, and the top of the staff should be four finger-breadths wide.
There should be five, six, seven, or ten joints;
furthermore, there are three base-boards, each measuring one cubit in length.
Having forms resembling Vetālas, or [emerging] from the path of the womb—the best of preceptors should cause this to be performed according to this very procedure. || 15 ||
Either in front of the outer pedestal (bāhyapīṭha), or even in front of the gateway (gopura), or in front of the temple (vraṣālaya), or behind it, or again in front of the trident (śūla). || 16 ||
One should have the banner made either in front of the palace or in the northeast; for a Brāhmaṇa it should be white, but for a Kṣatriya it should be red.
For a Vaiśya it is yellow, while for Śūdras it is indeed dark;
[the material may be] silk, woven cloth, or even cotton fabric.
The twelfth [type] should be ten cubits, or nine cubits, or eight cubits;
its width should be one-fifth or even one-sixth [of its length]. || 19 ||
One should have the star at the top of the banner made thirty finger-breadths in measure;
its tail should be equal in width to that, and its crest should be half of that.
Alternatively, [the tail] may be made equal to the tail itself on both sides with finger-breadths;
that which is uncut is declared the best, while that which is cut possesses the [other] characteristics.
One should construct a great banner one hundred cubits long, or half of that (fifty), or half of that again (twenty-five), or sixteen, or twelve; it should be auspicious and eight cubits in width.
Having gathered whatever is available according to the requirements of place and time,
and having collected these for the sake of the festival, one should draw a bull in their midst.
During the three nights of the festival, a man should go to the sacrificial ground;
thereafter, the twice-born Śiva-worshipper should perform worship at the hall of the Lord of Sacrifice.
The cloth for the banner should be one-third [the size of the original]; in its center, one should draw a bull.
One should place a mirror, a full water-pot, and a fly-whisk between the two [ends].
One should cause a lamp and an auspicious [image] endowed with the proper characteristics to be made;
in this very manner, the most excellent of preceptors should cause it to be performed according to the prescribed rule. (26)
For the purification of the cloth, one should sprinkle the banner according to the prescribed measure;
thereafter, one should sprinkle the banner with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Śiva-mantra. || 27 ||

The wise one, a twice-born devotee of Śiva, should sprinkle the staff with water and kuśa grass while reciting the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra; he should then place the staff there during the first watch of the night.
Having dug a pit one cubit deep and sprinkled it with water mixed with *kuśa* grass,
one should place a golden bull or even a tortoise into the pit.
Thereafter, the preceptor should raise the staff with the Śiva-mantra and wrap it with a garland of *darbha* grass together with the *kūrca*. He should then encircle the flagstaff.
The altars should be made specifically according to the sequence starting with the Brāhmaṇas, measuring either seven, six, or five tālas, or even four tālas. (31)
Its height should be twice its width, or three-quarters, or half of that;
one should have it constructed with bricks, or with clay, or with lime-plaster.
A wise person should have it made square, octagonal, or circular;
above that, having drawn a lotus provided with eight petals.
Or the most excellent of teachers should make it with three girdles, beautifully adorned at the base, or he should make it as pleasing to the mind as possible.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the Vṛṣamantra,
the preceptor [should place] both the weapon [mantra] and the cloth either before the image or before Śiva.
One should worship with the ninefold mantra and offer oblations there, especially to the trident, the cloth-painting, and the image. || 36 ||
One should perform a circumambulation of the village while adorned with all ornaments;
having performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should then have it performed in the village, cities, and so forth.
Afterwards, having entered the palace, one should sprinkle the cloth with water;
it should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, offering a flower while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra. (38)

Having performed a circumambulation of the celestial palace (vimāna), one should plant it in the form of a mechanical device; or else, according to the method of binding, it should be provided with all ornaments.

The wise man should raise the banner specifically for the sake of the festival; there, the learned one should cause the ritual bathing to be performed and have the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited.
The wise man should offer an oblation of five colors and cause betel to be given;
afterwards, he should feed the Brahmins and always honor the preceptor. (41)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Hoisting of the Banner," in the Sūkṣmatantra.
Hereafter I shall describe the supreme beating of the drum.
On the night preceding the hoisting of the banner, the drum is to be beaten. (1)
One should cause all the materials for the food offering (naivedya) to be presented to the preceptor;
[specifically] one-eighth part of the rice and one-sixteenth part of the fan.
It is said that the portion for the cakes is one-eighth, and the same applies to the betel;
one should cause the fruits and other edible substances to be offered in sequence as a tenth part.
In this manner, one should cause [the rite] to be performed for occasional, regular, and optional purposes.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Sūkṣmatantra*, a scripture of Śiva.
One should strike the drum both by day and by night, preceded by the striking;
however, in the case of the ritual planting of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), one should strike it only at night. || 1 ||
Following the prescribed method for the characteristics of a drum, the wise one should have the drum fashioned;
he should then sprinkle it with the five products of the cow while reciting the Nandi-Gāyatrī mantra.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing there twenty-five times,
in the center of the pavilion and in the middle of the enclosure. (3)
Having smeared it with cow-dung and adorned it with the five powders,
one should sprinkle it with water and *kuśa* grass while reciting the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
One should prepare a sacrificial mound there, specifically two cubits in height and three cubits in width, [leveling it] with rice grains to a depth of four finger-breadths.

In the center, the wise one should visualize it as being endowed with eight petals and measuring a *tila* and a *daṇḍula*; he should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, according to the Dharma.
Having assigned the powers beginning with Vāmā, one should assign them during the first watch of the night;
one should place the trident in the pericarp, while others should cause the drum to be made.
Having prepared the sacrificial ground as before, one should place a drum in the center,
covered with a pair of cloths and encircled by *kuśa* and *darbha* grass.
The wise one should worship the tridents and other implements with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
having propitiated them in due order without effort, he should there offer the oblation.
Immediately thereafter, the preceptor should have the drum beaten by the musician;
in that place, he should offer the bali-oblation with the Nandigāyatrī mantra.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, fully adorned with all ornaments and equipped with a trident, one should strike the twilight with the twilight.
At the conclusion of that, one should specifically perform the invocation of the deities;
in this manner, the night-rite should be performed, especially during the nine nights.
Day and night, especially.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Beating the Drum," in the *Sūkṣmatantra*.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa).
One should construct it in front of the house, or in the northeast or the southeast.
One should cause it to be made in the south, the west, or the north;
having first performed the purification of the ground, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The best [size] is sixteen cubits, the middling likewise twelve,
and the inferior ten cubits, as well as nine and seven.
For all [the castes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇas in due order, [the height] shall be seven cubits;
the elevation shall be four finger-breadths, free from being either sunken or protruding.
One should have a pavilion or a peaked roof constructed, endowed with auspicious characteristics, joined with pairs of pillars and made of auspicious sacrificial trees.
One should fashion a four-gated palace with four doors,
having a height of one cubit and resembling the surface of a mirror.
The height, consisting of sixteen finger-breadths, should be made by the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes respectively with seven, six, five, or four tālas.
The wise one should thus visualize [the site] adorned with the five powders;
then, outside the altar, he should have nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) constructed all around.
One should cause [the sacrificial pit] to be made in its respective parts according to the method for circular pits;
or else, the pit should be one cubit in both width and depth. (9)
Having adorned it with three girdles extending four, three, and two finger-breadths [in width],
one should fashion squares in the cardinal directions and circles in the intermediate directions.
Between Indra and Īśāna, the wise one should fashion an octagon.
The procedure for nine oblations has been declared; now hear the procedure for five oblations.
One should fashion a circular pit (kuṇḍa) in the four directions beginning with Indra; between Indra and Īśāna, the wise man should fashion an eight-sided one.
One should arrange [the directions] starting from the northeast (aiśānī) in the east and the west;
the best of teachers should fashion it either circular or square. || 13 ||
Having made a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) in the northeastern direction, one should especially perform a single oblation;
one should have it constructed as either circular or square according to the prescribed characteristics.
I shall describe a certain distinction regarding the fire-oblation (homa) during the festival of Śiva:
on the ninth day there should be a ninefold oblation, and on the seventh day a sevenfold oblation.
A wise person, having performed the oblation, should perform five oblations over five days, three oblations over three days,
and one oblation on a single day.
One should offer oblations for the officiating priests all around, with the preceptor as the principal;
or else, the wise preceptor may perform it by means of a single oblation.
Having smeared the pavilion, especially with cow-dung,
it should be provided with four archways and adorned with the eight auspicious symbols.
Having consecrated the gate-pitchers and other elements, and having adorned it with canopies and banners,
the wise man should worship the pavilion with various parched grains and flowers. (19)
Afterwards, at the conclusion of the artisan's work, he should cause the proclamation of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be made.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sacrificial Pavilion," in the Kriyāpāda of the Pratiṣṭhātantra within the Śivāgama, the subtle scripture.
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme consecration (adhivāsana). Prior to the commencement of the festival, one should have the chariots and other [processional items] prepared in due order.
Having adorned the temple, its enclosure wall, and its surrounding area with various banners and the like, as well as with peacock feathers and various chowries; || 2 ||
Having consecrated all those [items] with the water of Śiva, one should sprinkle them;
then, on the first night of the festival, one should begin the rite of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Either in front of the temple or even before the image,
at the time of sunset or during the auspicious five-nāḍī period thereafter, [the rite should be performed].
Alternatively, one should perform the rite of sowing the seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) within seven nāḍīs;
specifically for the liṅga, the kautuka thread, and especially the trident.
One should tie the protective thread at night according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures;
having cleansed the pavilion, one should smear it with cow dung.
The teacher and the disciple alike, having become pure and having performed their ablutions according to the rite prescribed by rule, [should perform] the ritual placement (nyāsa). (7)
Then, having gone to the house for the sacrifice, one should wash the feet and hands;
one should not follow an improper sequence, especially regarding the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of stability (*sthiti*).
Wearing a turban of new cloth and golden finger-rings,
he was adorned with all ornaments and endowed with all the auspicious marks.
One should recite the mantra "Astrarāja" one hundred and eight times in succession;
then, on the sacrificial altar, one should prepare a ritual mound using eight *droṇas* of rice.
There one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) provided with a pericarp and filaments;
one should place a mixture of sesame seeds and rice at the tip of the filaments.
One should perform the strewing of darbha grass and worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
on the northeastern part of the paved floor, one should prepare a square area with śāli rice.
One should fashion a lotus seat with eight petals and a pericarp, measuring three *tālas* in width;
having deposited [the principles] such as Dharma and Jñāna, one performs the rite of worship for the seat.
A wise person should have a water-pot (kumbha), a pouring vessel (vardhanī), and a jar (kalaśa) made of silver, gold, copper, or even clay.
Having accepted [the invitation], one should perform the sacrifice especially during the night;
one should fill [the vessels] as desired with water filtered through a cloth. (15)
One should pour scented substances with water mixed with fragrant sandalwood;
one should place a tuft of grass and so forth therein, and one should deposit the five jewels and other such items. || 16 ||
Having wrapped [the image] in a pair of garments and adorned it upon a cloth band,
one should then worship Yageśa, who is seated together with the Goddess, in due order.
Having thus meditated upon him as three-eyed, four-armed, and adorned with all ornaments, one should mentally fashion [the image] within the sphere of the Lord.
Having placed [the image] upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), adorned with flowers and garlands,
one should [place] the *vaddhanī* joined with gold upon the jars in sequence to the north of the Lord. (19)
One should then assign the limbs of Śiva there, and subsequently assign those of Umā;
then [one should worship] with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and the ārātrika ceremony.
In the middle above the altar, or alternatively in the east or west,
[one should place it] adorned with all ornaments, accompanied by hymns and auspicious recitations.
Having fashioned a trident joined with the sound of a bell, one should circumambulate it and place it either in the center of the sacrificial pavilion or in the eastern direction.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and wrap [the image] in a new cloth;
having established the Astra-mantra right there, one should bind the protective thread (kautuka) with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having established eight jars starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, having wrapped each separately with a cloth, one should place gold within them.
One should worship Ananta and the other deities within those jars;
the best of preceptors should arrange the ten weapons around them.
Having honored the auspicious objects (maṅgalas), one should worship them with their respective mantras;
having worshipped the deities of the doors and so forth, one should fully honor all the gods.
There, he should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and sprinkle [the site] with water while reciting the *pavamāna* hymns.
On the southern side of the sacrificial fire, the wise man should worship the Lord of Sacrifice (*Yāgeśa*).
And one should place a water-pot there, provided with a cloth and a bunch of kuśa grass;
as well as sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame, mustard, and mung beans.
With cakes, unbroken grains, jujube fruits, milk, parched grain, and flour,
and with the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the ten-syllable Vyomavyāpin mantra. (29)
And with the primary seed-syllables of the *kṣurikā*, and especially with the *prāsāda* mantra,
one should offer oblations twenty-eight times according to the proper sequence.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) beginning with the Jaya and other Ābhyātāna offerings and ending with the Sviṣṭakṛt;
then, having taken the fire from the Śiva-fire, one should deposit it into all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
One should offer the bali-oblation at the beginning of the fire-sacrifice (homa), especially in villages and similar places;
it may also be performed at the end of the sacrifice, or even in the middle.
From Brahmā to Īśāna, and likewise from Indra to Īśāna,
the twice-born should offer a bali-oblation of pure food mixed with curd to Śiva.
The first is Gaṇarātra, the second is Bhūtarātraka;
the third should be Brahmarātra, and the fourth is Gāndharva.
The fifth should be Indrarātra, while the sixth is Ṛṣirātraka;
the seventh is declared to be Vaiṣṇava, and likewise the eighth is Rākṣasa.
The ninth is said to be Śaiva; these are proclaimed as the nights of the deities.
Within the week, it begins with the night of Brahmā and so forth, and on the fifth day, it begins with the night of Indra and so forth.
Over three days, the Vaiṣṇava and other rites should be performed; on a single day, the Śaiva Rātrika.
However, during the fortnightly festival (pakṣotsava), the lunar dates (tithis) are proclaimed as the deities of the night.
In the month of Dvātriṃśaddevatā, as well as in the sixth month, [the rites] are performed separately as before;
however, during the festival of the Āpta, that [rite] belongs to the deities of the night.
On the first day, one should cause pure food mixed with curd to be given,
along with lotus flowers, turmeric, and parched grain flour (lāja-saktu). (39)
In the second [offering] it should be given, and in the third one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) together with turmeric rice,
ghee, and coconut fruits.
On the fourth day, [food] should be given;
on the fifth, rice mixed with molasses and combined with ghee, together with plantain fruit.
On the sixth day, [the offering] should be given; on the seventh, however, food with savory juices;
on the eighth day, one should cause food made of mung beans mixed with ghee to be given.
On the ninth day, one should cause pure food mixed with curd to be offered;
one should present the bali-offering upon the banners and other objects with the respective mantras beginning with their names.
The wise one should collect [the deity] from the images of the trident, the seat, and so forth, using their respective [mantras].
One must not perform the rites of withdrawal; if they are performed, there will be great danger.
One should have the consecrated image made until the end of the month for the sake of the sacrifice;
if it must be done with another image, a great danger will arise.
During the festivals and auspicious times of Śiva, one should not, out of delusion, cause the festival of another deity to be held; if one does so, the king and his kingdom will perish.
Therefore, with every effort, one should have a Śaiva [image] made for a Śaiva [temple],
a Vaiṣṇava for a Vaiṣṇava, and likewise for those of the Buddhist and other traditions.
If there are many locations within a single city, and if their festivals should coincide at that same time and place; || 48 ||
The wise man should indeed hold a festival for them in separate streets;
he should establish a place for Brahmā at a crossroads or a triple-pathway. (49)
The preceptor should offer an oblation (bali) in the pathway surrounding it;
in that pathway, the festival should be performed according to the prescribed rite.
If, out of delusion, one should cause the festival to be held in other streets instead, there will undoubtedly be the destruction of the land for that ruler of the country. (51)
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause Bali to be performed on the street;
however, at the time of the festival, excessive rain may occur.
One should first perform the fire-oblation (homa) and offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) at dawn;
and upon that [image], one should conduct a festival adorned with every kind of ornament.
One should cause the supreme bali offering to be made with a trident as the emblem of the bali;
in the absence of a trident, there should be an image, and in its absence, a ball (golaka).
One should cause their appearance to be depicted on the limbs at the proper time;
one should perform the *bali* offering twice a day, and the divine rite (*daivika*) at the conclusion of the festival.
Or else, at one and the same time, [one may perform] the bali offering, the fire-oblation (homa), and likewise the festival;
therefore, with every effort, one should cause the supreme bali to be performed.
The male linga should be fashioned as before; the wise one should cause it to be made, and he should place it upon a pedestal for the sake of the bali offering while reciting the heart-mantra.

He has four arms and three eyes; in his right [hand] there should be a trident and an eye, and likewise in his left hand a noose, while the other right [hand] displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya).
Having thus meditated upon Pāśupata, who grants boons with his left hand and is endowed with a fierce gaze, one should worship him at the *baliliṅga*. 59.
One should place food accompanied by all ritual substances into the offering vessel;
in the first [vessel] are the banners, and likewise in the second are the musical instruments.
The preceptor should proceed to another place; at the fourth [stage] it is called the "spear" (śūla);
at the fifth, the "food-liṅga" (annaliṅga); and at the sixth, he should go to the "auspicious thread" (kautuka).
Adorned with all ornaments, the weapon and the eight auspicious symbols [should be placed] in the assembly hall,
in the royal palace, and likewise in the temple of the preceptor.
One should especially offer the bali-oblation in other auspicious places, using [the mantra] beginning with Oṃ, ending with Namaḥ, and containing one's own name in the middle. 63.
One should especially offer the bali-oblation, which brings auspiciousness to all the worlds.
Thus one should perform the circumambulation of the bali, and cast the bali upon the bali-pīṭha.
One should properly offer the oblation upon the sacrificial pedestal with the heart-mantra.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Consecration," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
Hereafter, I shall describe in due order the festival of the *kautuka*.
At the conclusion of the offering of the sacrificial victim (*bali*), one should perform the circumambulation of the village with the *kautuka*.
One should place [the deity] seated comfortably in a chariot or a palanquin,
equipped with various distinct mechanical parts in manifold ways. (2)
It was joined by people from various regions, endowed with various banners, possessed of various kinds [of goods], and filled with various peacock feathers. || 3 ||
Equipped with various swords and various white banners—
either one, or three, or four, or five as before.
The sacrificer should go in front, and the preceptor should follow after him;
[the procession] accompanied by various songs and accompanied by various dances.
Accompanied by hymns of praise and various auspicious recitations,
one should thus conduct the auspicious festival in this very manner.
A wise person should not construct an image in another village;
rather, it should be made in one's own village for the purpose of festivals along the road.
And in the assembly pavilion, one should duly install the deity;
the wise man should conduct the festival according to the prescribed form of the image.
For the purpose of purifying the feet of the deity, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) at the feet;
one should present the auspicious protective lamp and dismiss it upon the offering pedestal (balipīṭha).
One should perform the circumambulation of the site during the day while in the celestial chariot;
the consecration for the sacrifice and so forth, as well as the ritual of the sprouts and other rites, should be performed at night.
In a delightful village or region, the wise one should establish the end of the pilgrimage site;
on the following day, he should cause it to enter the temple for the new procession.

In this very manner, the most excellent of preceptors should cause [the rite] to be performed. On the day before the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), he should carry out the dance-image (nṛttabimba). (12)
The best of preceptors should bind the protective thread (kautuka) during the first part of the night;
he should perform a circumambulation of the village or [the circumambulation] of the temple.
One should worship the god and the goddess with their respective mantras on the right and the other hand.
There he should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and then feed the Brahmins.
The most excellent preceptor, being wise, should perform the rite of binding the protection on the right hand of the deity using thread and other materials. 15.
There, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and finger-rings;
having worshipped him at the morning hour, he should be brought into the auspicious pavilion.
The wise one should cause the ritual bathing to be performed according to his capacity and by means of the prescribed rite;
he should worship the dancing image with the *tryambaka* mantra.
Having beheld the golden vessel, the clarified butter, and Maheśvara,
one should subsequently cause them to be presented to the preceptor after they have likewise been beheld by the Goddess.
Thereafter, one should perform all [acts] beginning with giving according to one's capacity and in due order;
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there, and then feed the Brahmins.
One should offer five-colored oblations with the *Prāsāda* mantra itself;
one should prepare the supreme fragrance according to the prescribed rules for the application of perfumes.
Alternatively, having collected fragrant substances in a pure place, the wise one should sprinkle them with scented water while reciting the heart-mantra.
Afterwards, one should smear the deity as well as the goddess with those [substances] using their respective root mantras;
for one who has been initiated into the weapon-mantra, one should cause the root-liṅga to be given. || 22 ||
And afterwards, one should cause it to be given to Caṇḍeśvara himself and to his devotees,
provided with all ornaments and accompanied by all musical instruments.
Accompanied by various songs and joined with various dances,
one should perform the circumambulation slowly, neither too far nor too near.
One should return in the same direction as one entered the village;
when the [village] is united, one should act in a united manner, and when it is divided, one should act in a divided manner. (25)
There is no [homage] prior to midday, or else it may be performed twenty steps away;
afterwards, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and the offering (bali), and thereafter proceed with the festival.
The image consecrated for the sake of a sacrifice should likewise be [prepared] during the daytime;
at night, it should be performed in this manner after the sun has risen.
Afterwards, together with the devotees, one should bring the water for the consecration;
one should offer it to the deity, but one must avoid [using] such [impure] substances and indeed avoid [impure] perfumes. || 28 ||
The wise one should bathe the Lord of the Gods with the mantra "mahāvyoma," and likewise perform the same for the Goddess with the Śakti-mantra.
Having sprinkled [the object] with the Pāvamāna hymn, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
thereafter, one should perform the Nirañjana rite according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
At that time, one should offer cakes and other foods according to the extent of one's means;
and one should present abundant sacrificial offerings along with all kinds of side dishes.
Afterwards, one should indeed cause a dance to be performed, adorned with all ornaments;
and especially at evening, one should carry out the rite of circumambulation. || 32 ||
Having gone to Yāgeśa in the east, one should afterwards proceed to Nṛtteśaka;
thereafter, one should attend upon Śaṇḍeśaka, adorned with all ornaments. (33)
The wise dancer should perform circumambulation of the village at every twilight; he should enter the temple during the auspicious hour of Brāhma-muhūrta.
Having placed [the deity] in the pavilion of the inner chamber, one should indeed offer water for the feet;
afterwards, having removed the withered garlands, one should perform the consecration. || 35 ||
Having worshipped the God, especially each deity, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should afterwards perform the *nirañjana* rite and present abundant sacrificial oblations (*havis*).
Afterwards, the most excellent preceptor should feed the devotees;
in this very manner, the most excellent preceptor should cause the rite to be performed. (37)
The wise one should place the primary image, adorned with all ornaments, upon the throne; he should especially worship it according to the previously mentioned method. (38)
There, one should honor the teacher with garments, gold, and finger-rings. || 38½ ||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Festival of Wonder," in the *Sūkṣmaśāstra*.

Hereafter, I shall explain the preliminary consecration for the commencement of a sacred site (tīrtha). On the previous night, one should bind the auspicious thread (kautuka) upon the sacred site and so forth, using the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having first removed the preliminary auspicious thread (*kautuka*), and especially the [main] auspicious thread,
[one should perform the rite] with [threads] made of gold, or silver, or even of linen or cotton. (2)
In front of the Ālaya, one should prepare a site by smearing it with cow dung;
there, one should construct an altar four finger-breadths high using śāli rice.
One should fill a vessel with rice and place the *kautuka* (auspicious thread) in its center;
having performed the circumambulation of the temple (*vimāna*), the wise man should cause the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
One should bind the weapon-image with the Śivagāyatrī mantra;
thereafter, one should perform the preliminary consecration (ādhivāsana), especially that of Brāhmī.
Having swept the pavilion, apply a coating of cow dung;
having prepared it with a canopy above, adorn it with strings of pearls.
One should properly draw an eight-petalled lotus, provided with sprouts, incense, lamps, the eight auspicious symbols, rice grains, sesame seeds, and *darbha* grass.
In the center of that, one should place a water-pot (kumbha), and right there one should place a trident (śūla).
One should then set eight pots all around, representing the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti).
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, together with garments and scents,
one should thereafter install the image, especially the primary image.
Equipped with a trident, he should go to a river or a pond;
on level ground, the wise man should properly prepare a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila).
Having fully worshipped the Astra-mantra, one should place a water-pot before it,
provided with fragrant substances, a tuft of grass (kūrca), and a lid.
Having worshipped the seven Gaṅgās and others, one should bring forth the image with the Astra-mantra;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, by means of the Śūla-Gāyatrī mantra. || 12 ||
One should cause the trident, adorned with all ornaments, to be inserted during the sacrifice.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Holy Sites," in the Sūkṣmatantra.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the sequence of the ritual for the powder festival (cūrṇotsava).
According to the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) and prepare the image (bimba).
Afterwards, one should perform the festival of Śiva, adorned with all ornaments;
specifically, at the conclusion of the festival, one should begin the application of the Rajanī powder.
Either in front of the temple or even in front of the pavilion,
one should prepare a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) using eight droṇas of śāli rice.

Having strewn the sacrificial ground with sesame seeds and *darbha* grass, one should place three [vessels] upon it; having established the weapon-mantra (*astra*) in one, one should place the *tāla* in the center.
Having set aside the night, the preceptor should worship that pestle and mortar in due order with their respective mantras.
Having encircled both the mortar and the pestle with the Astra-mantra, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth; and especially the image and the weapon.
One should apply ghee to the head, especially for the sake of protective charms (kautuka);
having cast the turmeric with the Hṛdaya mantra, one should grind it with the Hṛdaya mantra as well.
(75) One should have [the enemy] crushed with pestles by three, two, or three courtesans,
and subsequently have him ground again and again by his own servants. || 8 ||
Then, having taken the powder, one should place it into three vessels;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should do so with a graceful demeanor and according to the mantra.
Afterwards, that same [substance] should be applied to the linga and to the images and so forth;
likewise, one should cause powder and oil to be offered to the sacrificial image.
The wise one should perform [the rite] for the attendants using their respective names and so forth;
afterwards, he should cause the devotees to receive the powder and the oil.
One should quickly perform the circumambulation of the village with the trident;
then, according to the prescribed sequence, one should cause the offering (bali) and the powder and oil to be given.
Afterwards, having entered the palace, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 12½ ||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Festival of Powder," in the *Sūkṣmatantra*.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme ritual bath in the ocean, which removes all sins and bestows the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 1 ||
Having taken nine jars, one should wrap them with thread;
one should fill them with scented water and place a tuft of grass within each. || 2 ||
In this manner, all the vases are adorned with mango sprouts;
having taken up the weapons such as the vajra and others, one addresses the vases.
Then, accompanied by the sounds of conchs and other instruments, perform songs and dances,
together with the resonance of drums, mṛdaṅgas, and paṭahas, joined with the rhythmic beat of the *tāla*. (4)
One should perform a circumambulation of the village, especially that of the trident-image;
whether at the ocean, a river, or a lake, the wise man should lead [the image] there.
Having gone to the water's edge, one should especially construct a water-shed (prapā);
having established the bridegroom facing the east, and especially the marriage-thread (kautuka).
One should place a trident behind him and likewise set down water-pots in front;
there, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) provided with sesame seeds and darbha grass.
One should place the water-pots (kalaśas) therein and arrange the weapons;
one should worship the pots and other items individually with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. || 8 ||
There, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and sprinkle with water consecrated by the *pāvamāna* hymns;
having invoked all the deities along with the assembly, one should conclude the rite.
The preceptor should worship all [the deities] mentally, but with the heart-mantra specifically for the image and the trident; he should then perform the consecration with water-pots.
Thereafter, at the edge of the water, the preceptor, together with [the disciple],
should perform a bath for the welfare of the world, having established the Trident-bearer (Śūlin) at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
The wise one should place the jars that have been consecrated overnight upon a trident;
with the ritual honors due to a universal monarch, the wise one should bathe the amulet.
Having cast the weapons and the eight auspicious symbols into the water,
he should thereafter worship the Lord of Gods and especially recite the mantra.
One should wrap the supreme cloth with fine silk, woven pattu, and divine garments;
it should be done for the trident as well as for the preceptor. (14)
There, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings, accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and provided with all ornaments. (15)
One should not establish the sacrificial site by circumambulating the village;
rather, one should place the auspicious thread (kautuka) for the sake of the sacrifice within the pavilion of the sacrificial enclosure.
The preceptor should perform the oblations in the sacrifice until the *sviṣṭakṛt* rite with their respective mantras;
he should especially offer abundant sacrificial food (*havis*) at the beginning of the sacrifice and other rites.
Afterwards, the wise man, having performed the circumambulation of the celestial chariot (vimāna), should place the back-plate, the water-pots, and all the ornaments before the liṅga.
Having propitiated Śiva with effort, the most excellent preceptor should cause [the rites] to be performed;
and on the following day, he should indeed commence the procession (yātrā). 19.

For the sake of visiting sacred fords, for curiosity, or for the purpose of a pilgrimage out of devotion, one should especially have the protective thread (kautuka) prepared; with a focused heart, one should bind the kautuka.
First, one should go to the forest retreat in the four directions during the day, moving from place to place or elsewhere as it pleases the mind. (21)
On the previous day, the preceptor should prepare for the forest procession;
and on that same prior day, he should consecrate the image intended for the sacrifice.
One should have images that have not yet been consecrated prepared at a sacred ford;
however, the image consecrated for the purpose of a sacrifice should be established outside the village.
If one should cause [the deity] to enter through delusion, indeed Rākṣasas and other malevolent beings will enter;
therefore, with every effort, one should first [establish] the sacrificial image. (24)
By the power of commencing the battle, one should especially anoint the God of gods with the finest of all weapons and with divine fragrance.
It was joined with various musical instruments, accompanied by various songs, provided with various drums, and equipped with various vehicles. || 26 ||
In this manner, one should perform circumambulation of the deity, and thereafter of the village and so forth;
then, in the forest, one should perform the water-rite with water from the "deer-pitcher" (mṛgakumbha).
In this very manner, the wise man should have [the pavilion] constructed in the forest;
then, in the center of the procession-pavilion, he should perform the *yātrā-homa*.
He should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and parched grain (*lāja*) for the sake of protection against Rākṣasas.
With the mantra "rākṣasāya," [he should offer oblations] twenty-eight times.
One should offer all kinds of meat as a sacrifice in the forest;
thereafter, having worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should present abundant oblations.
There, one should feed the Brahmins with extensive offerings according to one's means;
thereafter, the devoted person should feed all his followers with devotion. || 31 ||
Afterwards, let them especially adorn the god and the goddess,
who have mounted the back of a horse fashioned in the form of a mechanical device.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village while adorned with all ornaments,
he was stopped near the palace by the power of Śambhu.
Thereafter, however, one should cause [the disciple] to enter the temple in the form of the Goddess;
without the village offering (grāmabali), one should not perform the fire sacrifice (homa) therein. || 34 ||
One should dismiss the ritual procedure there and establish [the deity] in the primary location. || 34½ ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Bathing in the Ocean," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
On the fifth or even the seventh day after the concluding bath (avabhṛtha),
one should perform the hoisting of the banner (dhvajārohaṇa) accompanied by the Caṇḍayāga.
Furthermore, one should perform the forest procession and the ceremonial bathing there;
on the day prior to the Caṇḍayāga, one should have an auspicious pavilion constructed.
One should especially have it constructed at nine, eight, or seven cubits;
in its center, one should fashion a paved floor measuring five tālas.
Sixteen finger-breadths in height, resembling the surface of a mirror,
it is provided with four doors and adorned with four archways.
Having adorned it with ornaments and the like, one should decorate it with rice flour;
there, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) surrounded by offerings of sesame seeds and darbha grass.
The mantra-practitioner, recollecting the Caṇḍa-mantra, should place the jars;
the wise one should insert kūrca-grasses therein and cover them with cloths.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should install Caṇḍeśa there, accompanied by the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyā), while recollecting the Caṇḍa mantra.
Afterwards, one should offer the cooked rice and cause betel-leaf to be given there;
having become pure and observing celibacy, the practitioner should proceed like Caṇḍa. (8)
Having performed a circumambulation of the village and having especially offered the sacrificial oblation (bali),
one should perform the ritual dismissal of the deities and release the banner there.
One should cause the cloth-banner of the rope to be offered to the preceptor;
one should especially cut the staff with a chisel in the four directions.
The supreme preceptor should take the staff ending with the *anta* [mantra];
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), he should thereafter plant it with that very [mantra]. || 11 ||
Or even on a single day, one should perform the village offering (bali);
thereafter, having dismissed the banner, one should worship Caṇḍeśa.
One should first honor the teacher and afterwards dismiss the sacrifice;
one should cause all the implements of the sacrifice to be given to the teacher. (13)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Hoisting of the Banner," in the Sūkṣmatantra.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the auspicious ritual for the festival of the devotees;
as for you, however, the hoisting of the banner occurs on the third day or the fifth day.
On the fifth, the tenth, and the twelfth days, during the five-fold session,
one should especially prepare the image and the trident for the sake of the festival.
On the day prior to that [sixth] day, one should have the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha) performed;
having established [the deity] in the morning, one should perform the twenty-five-fold ablution (snapana).
In the absence of an ablution, however, having specially sprinkled the image and the trident,
one should offer the oblation there with the Prāsāda mantra.

In the case of the primary image, it should be the same; with the temple, there should be eighteen [offerings], specifically consisting of sacrificial wood, clarified butter, cooked rice, and parched grain, each one by one.
One should offer an oblation within it, or one should have it constructed with two stories;
and at its conclusion, one should perform the Savana sacrifice, provided with all ornaments.
One should feed the devotees and attendants according to the path of devotion;
this may be performed either in the evening or in the morning.
Having entered the temple, one should perform worship below according to the prescribed method;
thereafter, one should observe the night-vow (nakta), adorned with all ornaments.
Alternatively, one may perform the fire sacrifice (homa) and the offering (bali) even in a general manner;
in this very same procedure, one should perform them at the conclusion of the festival.
Thus, whatever a mortal performs, he enjoys infinite fruit;
indeed, being wealthy and glorious even in this world, he is glorified in the realm of Śiva.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Festival of Devotion," in the Sūkṣmatantra.
(p. 82) The Ritual for Flower Powder.
Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for flower powder.
One should also cause the concluding rites of the festival of devotion to be performed at the beginning of the month of Māgha.
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple;
one should have it made according to the procedure for a sacrificial pavilion, following the eastern path.
In the middle, one should construct a pedestal (vedikā) measuring five tālas;
it should be twelve aṅgulas in height and resemble the surface of a mirror.
To the east of that, one should have a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed right there;
and the wise man should place the weapon (astra) and the marriage-thread (kautuka) in the west.
The best of preceptors should place all white flowers there;
having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should sprinkle them again with the Pāvamāna hymns.
Afterwards, having gathered flowers specifically in a new vessel,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound on the altar and place nine jars upon it.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings ten jars filled with water, provided with lids, accompanied by cloths, and adorned with gold, one should place the ten weapons [therein].
Having envisioned the archways and adorned them with water-pots at the entrances,
the most excellent preceptor should cause this to be performed according to the very same procedure.
Thereafter, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed as a single offering for the festival;
this should be done at night, and one should worship Śiva in the morning.
Afterwards, having worshipped with flowers, one should place them above Śiva,
as well as the weapon (astra) and the protective thread (kautuka), according to availability and the prescribed measure.
The wise one should cause flowers to be offered with the Prāsāda mantra;
he should present abundant sacrificial food and cause it to be given to the devotees in due order. (11)
When the next day has arrived, one should offer fresh flowers;
one must not neglect the twilight worship (sandhyā), and one should perform worship upon the flowers.
Afterwards, having established the water-pots (kumbhas), one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with either the root mantra or the kautuka mantra, using the Prāsāda mantra.
And one should offer the oblation to Bhūpati with the mantra of grace on the ninth day,
or indeed on the seventh, the fifth, the third, or even the first day.
On a single day, the wise one should have the ritual powder of flowers prepared according to the prescribed characteristics.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Ritual for Flower-Powder," in the *Sūkṣmatantra*.
Expiation:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the sequence of the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*). *Prāya* is said to mean "casting away," and *citta* is said to mean "arising from joy. (1)
But because of the reconnection of what has been severed, it is traditionally taught that there is expiation;
thus, expiation is prescribed for the four [offenses], beginning with those against the teacher. (2)
However, if the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) is deficient in daily ablutions and other rites, the wise one should offer thirty oblations with the Āghora-weapon mantra.
If one is deficient in the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana), however, one should mutter the Sūrya-mantra a hundred times;
one should feed Brahmins there, and thereafter commence the ritual act. || 4 ||
If the fire-ritual (agnikārya) has been omitted, however, the preceptor should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times;
with the Śiva-mantra, he should likewise offer one hundred and eight oblations (āhuti).
Afterwards, having worshipped the fire, one should perform the daily rites;
[one should avoid] stepping over, giving away, falling upon, or defiling the remains of the offering (nirmālya) oneself.
One should recite the mantra Mahāvyomana one thousand times;
however, if one has consumed the remains of offerings (nirmālya), one hundred oblations should be made with the Hṛdaya mantra.
Afterwards, one should worship Sandhyā and recite the Prāsāda mantra a hundred times;
then, with flowers that have been kept overnight, one should worship Hara using the Prāsāda mantra.
The wise one should avoid that flower, especially during the six periods [of the day];
having established nine jars, he should again commence the worship.
One hundred and eight oblations should be offered with the primary seed-mantra;
the preceptor should always avoid [mantras] that have deficient or redundant syllables.
A Brahmin who is deficient in limbs, of evil conduct, devoid of initiation, blinded by intoxication, and a partaker of the sin of having a Śūdra wife—others should avoid even touching him. 11.
One should perform worship for one's own sake and never for the sake of others;
however, if by negligence at the time of sacrifice the ritual should become deficient in its constituent parts, [the following applies].
One should perform the ritual bath there using a thousand jars in sequence;
however, one must never perform it with the *mahāvyoman* mantra or with any part of the body [as a vessel]. || 13 ||
p.
85) However, in the case of one who lacks a limb, it should be joined again with particular care.
A defect in a limb is not a fault; rather, one should avoid the defect of the self. || 14 ||
Always on one foot; however,
if drinking liquor should occur through negligence at the time of a sacrifice,
one must specifically perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances until death.
Due to negligence or specifically from union with a *vṛṣalī* for even a single night,
one should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) therein, and especially the *brahmakūrca*.
Afterwards, he falls to the status of a Śūdra; for him, there is no expiation. || 17 ||
Especially for one night after consuming poison intentionally,
one should always go to the sacrificial pit and recite the mantra *aghora* alone.
In this manner, according to the prescribed method, one should cause [the rite] to be performed for three years;
having performed the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances, one should afterwards [proceed] with the mantra beginning with "vyoma."
There, a sesame-seed oblation (tilākṣa) should be offered with space (vyoman) and sacrificial porridge (caru);
there, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and afterwards give food worth one niṣka.
One should perform this especially for the slayer of a Brahmin and those equal to him;
likewise for the killer of a great sage, the killer of a father, and the stealer of the property of the gods. (21)
Having given three or two times the value of the stolen object as an excellent gift to Śiva,
and having then performed the rite of Śiva-dāna, one should ask forgiveness from the God of gods.
In the case of stealing a valuable object, one should give three times the value to the teacher;
one should perform the service due to a father for the teacher, and one should always chant the name of the teacher.
For the purpose of requesting the preceptor, one should perform a thousand oblations in sequence with ghee and sacrificial offerings, using the Aghora mantra alone. (24)
Afterwards, one should perform recitation; one is purified by the Brahmakūrca rite if one dies from thieves, in a vehicle, or by one's own weapon, or [if one touches] earth.
If there should be the death of both through mutual conflict, or if death should occur for one due to the cattle, it would happen solely through negligence. (26)
Whether it be a gift of cows, a gift of land, or a gift of gold, having offered that in the form of pure coins, one should present it to Śiva. || 27 ||
One should shake [the vessel] ten times in succession with the Mahāvyoman mantra;
likewise, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) and cooked rice (caru). || 28 ||
One should cause Śiva to be bathed with one hundred and eight jars;
thereafter, one should perform the rite of cremation according to the measurements prescribed in the Śiva-śāstra.
Then, one should cause the burning of the Moha-dvāra to be performed twice over,
so that the preceptor may especially proceed upon their backs.
Having performed a bath with one's clothes on, one should indeed fast for three nights;
afterwards, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Prāsāda mantra.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the Mahāvyoman mantra;
thereafter, one should feed one hundred and eight Brahmins in due order.
If death should occur while staying for the sake of cows, Brahmins, or kings, he is liberated from that burden by means of a path that is double [the previous]. || 33 ||
The supreme teacher should cause that [rite] to be performed for the aforementioned *kṛtyā*;
indeed, after [fulfilling] desires, perform the funeral rites (*pretakriyā*) afterwards. (34)
Even if it has been seen, it is declared that if it is not seen,
one should perform the Nārāyaṇa-bali and have a suitable image fashioned.
One should have [the rite] performed by kinsmen in due order according to the path described in the Darśana;
one should never [bind] with a stone-noose out of anger or fear, for that leads to death.
One should know that these are mortal sins (*pātaka*); one should have a pit dug outside [the village] and, having performed the Nārāyaṇa-bali rite, one should observe a vow of silence for a year.
Out of delusion, one might cause a fire to be lit; for this, one should perform an expiation.
Having quickly undergone the shaving of the head, one should practice the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances. || 38 ||
One should recite the mantra of the Aghora-weapon ten thousand times;
thereafter, the preceptor should cause the purification rite to be performed.
If he follows them even out of negligence,
having performed a bath with his clothes on, he shall dwell in a cow-pen for three nights.
Afterwards, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance according to the mantra of the Aghora-weapon;
having recited it ten thousand times, one should perform double that amount if the act was intentional.
For the sake of that [deceased], there may be the carrying of the burden and so forth;
and from the perspective of the purpose of weeping, when one is engaged in an action, it is accompanied by the loss of affection. (42)
However, he himself must not perform it; if it must be performed, there is great danger.
Therefore, he should have that rite for the newborn performed by one of the same lineage. (43)
At that time, when the two [measures] are separate in the *tamānī* [scale], the teacher from another region should cause [the ritual] to be performed by means of the mantra until its conclusion. (44)
If, at the time of the subsequent rites, the son, brother, or kinsman becomes distracted by negligence due to many worldly affairs, [the following applies].
If one should perform [the rite] on that day, one should complete the remainder with that;
provided one does not perform the action out of delusion regarding the connection to an evil death. (46)
One incurs the destruction of one's dwelling place and the destruction of villages and so forth;
for the purpose of removing that defect, [one should act] with the mantra of Mahāvyoman.
One should indeed cause an ablution to be performed with ghee from a hundred vessels, or one should perform a bath with a thousand jars for the Supreme Lord. 48.
Then, having performed a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should perform the rite once more;
in this very manner, one should cause it to be done with full awareness.
The supreme preceptor should bring about peace regarding the object of ignorance;
indeed, at the time of approaching that which is not to be approached, shaving is especially prescribed. 50.
Having performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, one should then perform the Kṛcchra-santāpana;
one should recite the mantra with the Aghora-weapon [mantra] twenty thousand times.
If one should consume the remains of an offering (nirmālya), whether intentionally or even unintentionally,
he shall shave his head including the top-knot and dwell for a night in a cow-pen.
One should follow the cows during the day and offer them fodder in the cow-pen;
afterwards, having performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance with the mantra beginning "mahāvyoma," [one is purified].
One should perform a thousandfold oblation with sacrificial offerings and clarified butter;
by performing a sacrifice to Caṇḍeśvara, he becomes purified. (54)
For one who has consumed food at an improper time, there should indeed be a ritual bath for Śaṅkara;
one should recite ten thousand times with the "Vyoma" mantra.
One should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) there and consume [the offerings] with cow products for a fortnight;
thereafter, becoming pure, the preceptor (deśika) should carry out the ritual action.
If, through negligence, a dog, a newborn animal, a cat, a cock, a vulture,
or even a crow should touch [the food], one should fast for three nights.
In that case, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and, being pure, feed Brahmins;
this applies equally to approaching a woman who has recently given birth, whether she be of the same or a different caste.
For that sin, one should perform penances such as the Kṛcchra; one should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa Kṛcchra and recite the Aghora weapon-mantra twenty thousand times.
One should perform a fire sacrifice there and feed the Brahmins with purity;
on uneven ground, one should perform it twice over and cause the gift for Śiva to be bestowed.
Therefore, in the case of approaching a maiden, one should perform half of that very penance;
however, no expiation is prescribed for union with one of the same lineage.
If [the rite] occurs through negligence at the time for bathing, one should perform the bath at the three periods of the day;
having performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, one should then perform the Kṛcchra-santāpana.
One should perform one hundred thousand oblations and recitations with the Prasāda mantra;
one should especially do this for all five, beginning with the Ādiśaiva.
At that time, there is no distinction between men and women, as they are equally possessed of faults.
In this very manner, the supreme instructor should cause [the rite] to be performed. (64)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Atonement for the Preceptor," in the *Sūkṣmaśāstra*.
The Atonement for the Preceptor:
I shall now declare the atonement specifically for the preceptor. "Prāya" is said to mean "perishing," and "citta" is said to mean "arising from joy. (1)
For one who is proficient, the reconnection [of the breath] is traditionally taught as the expiation;
it is the purification from sin when right knowledge arises. (2)
If there were no purification of sin for a person, all ritual actions would be fruitless;
therefore, the cleansing of sin must be performed with every effort.

If the sacrifice for one's own sake is deficient, it is doubled; and if it is deficient in other respects as well, the wise man should perform the sacrifice with double the effort, using both the temple and the mantra.
In the event of illness, one should perform an offering of handfuls of flowers with the Prāsāda mantra;
however, if immersion is not possible, one should indeed perform a ritual bath with a water-pot.
If one is unable to perform the bath with water from a jar, one should instead perform a bath with ashes;
or, in the absence of that, one should perform a cleansing with a wet cloth held at the heart.
O Mantrin, due to their absence, one should perform the ash-bath;
if one is unable to do so for them, even when ill, one should offer a handful of flowers in silence.
But in its absence, having seen him, or even upon seeing one who is intoxicated by [the sight of] virtues,
one should have a great ceremonial bath performed at the proper time for one who has been freed from disease. (8)
The root-mantra should be ten thousand, and the fire-oblation (homa) should likewise be the same;
the most excellent of teachers should perform it according to this very procedure.
