All those who are joined with the initiation of Śiva should be made to act according to that path; likewise, one of the four castes born in the reverse order (pratiloma) should practice in that same way.
Having touched something defiled by its own kind, one should perform a bath with ashes;
afterwards, being pure, one should indeed recite the root mantra fifty times.
But for those who have been initiated into their own caste, the wise man,
having become pure, should indeed recite the mantra of ten syllables fifty times with devotion.
If they eat the food of Śūdras out of desire, they should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
through these, they shall be purified according to the previously mentioned injunctions. (13)
Having eaten [food] in reverse order or even out of desire for meat,
a wise man should observe a fast and recite the Mahāvyoman mantra one hundred times.
One should recite the mantra a thousand times at will, using either the five-limbed or the six-limbed form;
one must avoid using floral remains from offerings, garlic, meat, and fish.
If one eats [forbidden food] unintentionally, one should recite the Īśāna mantra one hundred times;
if one eats it out of affection, one should perform the Santāpana Kṛcchra penance. || 16 ||
If one steps over or gives away the remains of offerings (nirmālya), one should perform two ablutions;
if one touches a Caṇḍāla at that time, one should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times.
If one touches something impure at an improper time through negligence, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
then, being purified, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Mahāvyoman mantra.
If one hears the censure of Śiva, the sacred fire, or the guru, or the censure of those who deserve censure,
one should plug the ears with the hands and perform a bath with one's clothes on.
One should observe a fast there and recite [the mantra] one hundred times with devotion;
one should perform the Santapana Krichchhra penance and then worship [the deity] twice as much.
Having touched the corpse of one initiated into his own caste, which grants or withholds desires,
one should perform a bath with one's clothes on and then consume ghee while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
With the Aghora mantra, one should recite it a thousand times while remaining pure;
one should perform the two types of ablution and recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times.
Even against one's will, having touched by mistake the corpse of an uninitiated Brahmin, [one should perform] thirty thousand [recitations] with the heart-mantra.
One should perform the ritual bath according to the Tantra and recite the Prāsāda mantra one hundred times;
having performed the bath as before, one should recite it one thousand times for the fulfillment of desires.
If one touches [the corpse] by sight, purification is through ashes; if out of desire, one should mutter the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times.
If it happens that one follows a corpse because of being uninitiated, [one must perform purification]. (25)
Having performed the bath as previously described, one should recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra one hundred times;
however, if it was done unintentionally, one who is pure should recite the Śiva-mantra one thousand times.
By the application of half of those [penances] for one who has been initiated, regarding a corpse:
having touched the corpse of one who has been initiated, he becomes pure by bathing in ashes. || 27 ||
If one has inadvertently touched the corpse of a consecrated king,
one should bathe in the ocean and observe a fast for one night. (28)
In the morning, one should drink cow's urine while reciting the Prāsāda mantra a thousand times;
being pure, one should then chant the Aghorāstra mantra three thousand times.
One should perform the two ablutions in sequence; with the Aghora mantra, one should recite it a thousand times.
The mantrin should then offer the *gotrāsa* oblation and practice the qualities beginning with the common [rites]. (30)

If one should follow after those two, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on, smear oneself with cow dung, and perform the recitation (japa) according to the previously mentioned method. || 31 ||
Having performed the ritual bath for the sake of desires, one should observe a fast for three nights;
being pure, one should recite the mantra "Prāsāda" exactly one hundred times.
If there should be a sighting of those two, one should perform the bath as before;
however, one should perform it twice or thrice with the heart mantra.
If one has, through negligence, touched the corpse of an uninitiated king,
one should perform a bath as previously prescribed and observe a fast for three nights.

The mantra-practitioner should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and recite the Prāsāda mantra one hundred times; having performed this unintentionally, he should do it twice over and give a morsel of food to a cow to become pure.
Whether it occurs unintentionally or intentionally, if following [the corpse] should happen,
the wise man should perform two ablutions, consume clarified butter, and recite the Hṛdaya-mantra.
One who is pure should recite the Aghora weapon mantra ten thousand times;
having performed the bath as before and having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, || 37 ||
One should perform the bath again and, being pure, recite [the mantra] a thousand times;
having touched the corpse of an uninitiated Vaiśya, one who grants desires [is purified]. (38)
One should perform the ritual bath in the ocean and the smearing with cow dung while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*; being pure, one should then recite the *aghorāstra-mantra* one thousand times.
For an uninitiated Vaiśya, this procedure is prescribed in due order;
and for an initiated Vaiśya, if he follows a corpse, [the following applies].
Having performed the bath as before, one who is pure should recite [the mantra] three times;
having committed an oversight through negligence, one should perform two baths.
Having intentionally touched the corpse of an uninitiated Vaiśya, one should perform a special bath and indeed consume clarified butter for purification. (42)
One should consume cow's products while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra* after a single night of fasting;
having performed the *taptakṛcchra* penance, one should always mutter the *sāvitrī*.
One who is pure should recite the Aghora weapon mantra three thousand times;
one should feed Brahmins there and perform the ritual bathing of Śiva.
Thereafter, once the purification of the body has been performed, one should then impose the religious observances (niyama);
this applies even after intentionally touching the corpse of an inner Śaiva.
Having consumed ghee while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should again perform the ritual bath in the ocean;
then, one should smear all the limbs with cow dung while reciting the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).
Afterwards, one should perform the ritual bath; one should recite the Īśāna mantra a hundred times, and being pure, one should properly recite the Aghora-astra mantra a hundred times.
Having unintentionally touched the corpse of an uninitiated Śūdra,
one should perform two ablutions and then consume clarified butter while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*. (48)
For the sake of a one-day fast, one should indeed consume the products of the cow while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra;
being pure, one should mutter the *sadyojāta* mantra a thousand times.
Having touched the corpse of one who has not been initiated, if it was through negligence, one should perform two ablutions;
thereafter, one should give a morsel of food to a cow and dwell outside the village until purified.
If that best of guides should follow those three in succession, he should perform the ritual bath as before and then undergo the Santapana Kṛcchra penance. (51)
There, one should feed the Brahmins with extensive offerings according to one's means;
moreover, one should recite the Aghora Śivāstra mantra one hundred times for each of them.
This is declared to be the method for those who act out of desire; for those who act without desire, it is the *kṛcchra* penance.
This is the manner for the uninitiated, while for those two [the initiated], it is half that measure.
If one sees the corpse of an initiated person, whether unintentionally or intentionally,
one should perform a bath there and, having become pure, recite the root mantra.
One who desires [merit] should perform two ablutions in the temple with a hundred recitations of the mantra;
having touched the corpse of one who has been initiated, one should perform twice that number.
If a Śūdra should touch the corpse of another Śūdra who has been initiated into the Śiva-dīkṣā,
he must perform a bath with his clothes on and recite the Prāsāda mantra one hundred times.
One should likewise follow [the corpse] and, being pure, recite the mantra twice as many times;
even if one touches a corpse in reverse order (pratiloma), whether intentionally or unintentionally.
One should perform two ablutions with the *prāsāda* mantra; having consumed clarified butter while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should perform the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances. (58)
The learned man should feed the Brahmins with extensive offerings according to his means;
and being pure, he should recite the mantra ten thousand times without the *araṇi* wood.
Following them and their superior bathing, O Śivā, are declared as Kāmadeva; there are two types of Akāma bathing.
One should indeed perform this with the heart alone; being pure, one should practice the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Likewise, following them [in death] is superior, O Śivā, as is the ritual bathing.
One should perform the practice of the tormenting of desires with the mantra known as Kāmadeva; being pure, one should recite the Vāmadeva mantra three thousand times. 62.
But for those who have been initiated, having intentionally touched a corpse,
one should perform a bath as previously described and must certainly consume the products of the cow (gavya).
Having fasted for one night, one should perform a bath at dawn;
being pure, one should recite the mantra of Aghora Astra three thousand times.
In that case, one should follow [the deity] and perform an additional recitation of mantras;
if one should go away due to negligence, one should perform a bath as previously described.
One should recite the Prāsāda mantra twenty thousand times if,
out of negligence, one has touched the corpse of a human being in reverse order.
One should have it made twice as large as the previously mentioned rule, being pure;
when one’s desires follow in succession, it is known as the *yoryadā*. 67.
Having performed the ritual bath as before, one should perform it twice or thrice;
having touched the corpse of one who has sons, one should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times. (68)
Afterwards, one should perform a bath; by consuming clarified butter (ghṛta), one becomes purified.
Having touched the corpse of a son initiated for a rite, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
Having performed a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should recite that [mantra] with the Prāsāda [mantra];
thereafter, those sons who are born indeed become united with Śiva.
All their remains, such as the corpse and so forth, should be placed upon the funeral pyre;
prior to that, one who has undergone the Śiva-consecration (śivasaṃskāra) should perform the rites according to his own lineage.
One who is engaged in the conduct of a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) should perform immediate purification;
having performed the bath as before, he should recite the Prāsāda mantra one hundred times.
The Ādiśaiva and the Mahāśaiva should practice the purification of women;
likewise, the Anuśaiva, the six [others], and the Aparakṣaiva Randhraka [should do so]. || 73 ||
The Bhānava and the Śaiva [mandalas], as well as the others with flickering radiance—
the best of teachers should cause these to be made in this very sequence.
In cases of birth-impurity (sūtaka), one should act in this manner; indeed, householders alone should perform these rites.
At those times, having beheld Śiva, they should worship the qualities of Śiva.
Otherwise, if one were to eat, one would incur a great fault;
therefore, with every effort, one should cause [the guest] to eat only after having beheld Śiva.

But one who is endowed with the conduct of a spiritual guide (deśika) and engaged in daily worship should also observe the impurity of birth (sūtaka) and death (pretaka) under the previously mentioned lunar mansion.
One born into a family that lacks a teacher, who does not understand the Śiva scriptures,
and who is devoid of daily worship, should perform the ten-day rite correctly. (78)
Those who are devoid of a connection to Śiva are all situated in the northern direction;
[this applies] on the tenth day, the fifth day, or even on the twentieth or thirtieth day after death.
During these very days, one should perform the rites for the Brāhmaṇas and others in their proper order; one should reside in a house occupied by a deceased person and perform the morning bath.
The mantra-practitioner should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the Prāsāda mantra;
for a king, a vaiśya, or a śūdra, the house should be inhabited by one joined with the *preta* [mantra]. 81.
Having performed the bath as before, one should recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra a hundred times;
by means of that mantra, one should perform it twice or thrice for the two [mantras].
When one has touched the birth-impurity (sūtaka) of a Brahmin, one should perform a bath;
likewise, having touched the birth-impurity of a king, one should indeed perform a bath.
One should touch the birth-impurity of a Vaiśya with the Mahāvyoman mantra;
having touched the birth-impurity of a Śūdra, one must perform the rite with that same mantra twice over.
For those other than Śūdras, upon touching [an impure person], one should bathe as before;
however, one should perform the purification by reciting that mantra twice. || 85 ||
If the preceptor should touch a woman who is menstruating,
he must immediately perform an ablution and recite the Aghora mantra one hundred times.
If the wise preceptor should touch a woman in her menses, or a second, or a third, or even a fourth such woman, he must perform a ritual bath and partake of the products of the cow (gavya).
Having recited the mantra twice as many times in sequence with the Aghora-weapon mantra,
the preceptor should properly show the food offerings at the time of the meal. (88)
Having discarded what remains of the meal, one should perform the bath as previously described;
one should observe a single fast and drink the products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the heart-mantra.
One who is pure should recite the Aghora weapon mantra one thousand times;
if, at the time of his meal, he hears their sound, [he shall succeed].
The practitioner should discard the remnants of the food and perform an ash-bath;
being pure, he should recite the Prāsāda mantra one hundred times.
A wise man should recite [the mantra] with a palace [visualization] twice the size of his birth;
indeed, at the end, when the loss and so forth occur, the wise man should discard what remains after consumption.
Then the wise one, having consumed ghee with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*);
thereafter, if he so desires, the best of teachers may take his meal. (93)
But if, at the time of the vessel [offering], a woman in her courses should appear, the preceptor, having discarded the remainder of the food, should perform a ritual bath. 94.
One who is pure should recite the mantra "Prāsāda" one hundred times;
at dawn, she should perform [the rite], and whoever hears their words [shall be purified].
Having performed the bath as before, he should indeed consume pure cow-products;
and if one hears the sound of a drum from a Caṇḍāla, one should feed [the person].
Having discarded the remnants of the food, one should perform an ablution with ashes;
or else, having placed his hand over the ear, the wise man should feed [the guest] at the conclusion of the sound.

If one should worship the gods while consuming food through negligence, or while in a state of ritual impurity, or while using impure substances, then one should recite the Aghora-weapon mantra a hundred times. (98)
He too should worship with devotion through burning, immersion in water, and other such rites;
at the conclusion of the worship, he attains purity when he is clean from contact with others. 99.
One should eat with the proper ingredients, especially at that time;
otherwise, one incurs fault, for destiny does not stand by in such a case.
Since it bestows defects upon one who has been born [in this world], one should therefore perform the worship of Mahādeva;
for that reason, one should by every effort cause [the offering] to be prepared with meat. 101.
One should indeed act in this very manner toward those who are devoted to the daily worship;
for just as a firefly [is no match] for the two suns, so too does the fault fall upon the protector.
A person associated with a corpse must not sprinkle liquids;
if he sprinkles them through negligence, he should perform the two types of ritual bathing for whatever [substances] he has sprinkled.
A thousand breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) are indeed the Aghora-weapon;
the best of teachers should perform it according to this very procedure. || 104 ||

During the time of performing a sacrifice for one's own sake, or for the sake of a servant, or for a preceptor, or when a death-impurity (śāva) occurs, one should sequentially avoid the following constellations: [the first] three, the ninth, and the twelfth.
Indeed, one who performs the daily worship by means of another teacher's path must perform the prescribed rite of atonement; now hear the procedure for the ritual bathing.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Atonement for the Preceptor," in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra* within the *Sūkṣmaśāstra*.
[Page 101] The Ritual Bath with All [Mantras].
I shall describe briefly the bathing of the entire liṅga,
which removes all sins and eliminates all defects.
The fruit of all giving is for the sake of purifying impurities alone—
whether during a festival, at a consecration, during an eclipse, or even at the passage of the sun into a new zodiacal sign.
If the day of the king's birth-star coincides with the day of his consecration,
he should perform [the rite] on another auspicious day, especially if the former is possessed of defects.
For all those made of stone, perform anointing with oil;
sesame oil should be used, but one should avoid castor oil.
One should apply ointments, unguents, and powders to the limbs and minor parts of the body;
one should massage it with those powders and then bathe it with pure water.
One should especially smear it with black powder made from that [substance],
and then one should bathe Maheśvara once again with fragrant water alone.
One should perform the wiping with a cloth very gently, especially;
thereafter, she should be adorned with garments and the like, endowed with all ornaments.
The procedure for [images] made of gold and other materials has been declared; now hear the rule for those made of clay.
No consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed; rather, one should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) with the heart-mantra.
One should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) upon the variegated cloth and install it according to the prescribed method for the sake of bringing about all prosperity.
Otherwise, one should establish [the deity] there for the purpose of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
At the conclusion of the bath, one should perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order. (10)
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering with extensive displays according to one's means. || 10½ ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Complete Bath," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
The Installation of the Liṅga.
Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme installation of the liṅga;
in cities and other celestial abodes, it is situated somewhat toward the northeast.
One should establish it in that center and cause it to be moved by means of the Sthāṇu [mantra];
one should lead the linga, which is immovable in the center, wherever it moves.
Having divided the womb (garbha) into nine parts according to the rule for each,
one should construct it either by the measurement of the door or again by the measurement of the cubit.
Or one may construct it according to the eighth measure, up to a maximum of nine cubits;
a length of thirty-three finger-breadths is declared to be the highest measurement.
Each being diminished by three finger-breadths (tryaṅgula) constitutes the middle and the lowest [sizes];
thus, the measurement is held to be ninefold, each step being reduced by three finger-breadths.
The nose should not be less than three finger-breadths, nor should it be deficient in its measurement from the ear;
one should especially ensure that everything is consistent with the proportions of income and expenditure.
(103) Furthermore, there should be no deficiency or excess in expenditure, especially regarding the surplus of income;
this should be in accordance with the treatises on architecture (śilpaśāstra), particularly following the specific instructions of the master craftsman. || 7 ||
A deficiency or excess of barley brings destruction to the patron of the sacrifice;
therefore, with every effort, one should not allow for deficiency or excess.
During the period of the northern course of the sun, it is considered day for the gods;
the six-month period beginning with Āṣāḍha is said to be night for the gods.
The rite of installing a *liṅga* should be performed during the daytime;
the installation of a *liṅga* is most excellent when done under the asterism Puṣya or in the month of Māgha.
In the months of Phālguna and Caitra, the middle period is desired;
likewise, in Vaiśākha and Jyeṣṭha, the lowest period is desired. || 11 ||
For the sake of the prosperity of Brahmins, it should be performed in the month of Puṣya;
for the sake of the increase of kings, one should have it performed in the month of Māgha.
For those of the Vaiśya caste, it is in Phālguna; for Śūdras, in the month of Caitra;
for those of the Paśu caste, in Vaiśākha; and for others, in the month of Jyeṣṭha. (13)
Thus has the fruit of each month been declared regarding the rite of installing a liṅga;
when the daytime has arrived, one should then install it at that time.
But when Jupiter and Venus are correctly visible at the wrong time, or when they appear in Maghā, Svātī, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Dṛś (Ārdrā), Śravaṇa, or Aśvayuj; || 15 ||
One should install [the image] under these lunar mansions: Punarvasū, Tiṣya, Uttarā-trayī, Maitra (Anurādhā), and Rohiṇī. || 16 ||
The days of Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, and the Sun are remembered as auspicious; likewise, the third, second, and fifth days of the bright fortnight [are auspicious]. (17)
The sixth and the seventh, as well as the tenth and the eleventh, and likewise the thirteenth, on both fortnights as well. (18)
On the third day of the dark fortnight, as well as on the first, the fifth, the sixth,
the seventh, and especially the tenth.
Especially during the Amṛta-yoga, Siddhi-yoga, and Parā-yoga,
as well as in the signs of Taurus, Gemini, Pisces, and likewise Leo.
In Scorpio, Aquarius, and likewise in Virgo,
the commencement of the consecration rite should be performed in accordance with what is favorable to the patron.
If the Moon should be in the fourth, seventh, fifth, or third house, and there is the rising of Jupiter, Venus, or Mercury; || 22 ||
In the twelfth, the third, the tenth, and likewise the eleventh—indeed, in these positions, the teaching of Mercury is especially distinguished. (23)
In the second, the fifth, the tenth, and likewise the seventh house—when Jupiter is situated in these positions, the scripture indeed [is effective]. (24)
Bhārgava (Venus) has declared that [the Moon] should not be situated in the sixth, seventh, or tenth house from both [the Lagna and the Moon];
likewise, malefic planets in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses [from either] cause harm to all. (25)
If all the planets are situated in the eighth house, ensure the stability of the performers;
therefore, with every effort, one should indeed avoid that which is inauspicious.
On the third [lunar day] joined with the Svāti constellation and Saturday,
conjoined with Mercury on the second, and likewise joined with Anurādhā. (27)

Especially on a Thursday coinciding with the fifth lunar day dedicated to Pūṣan, and during such conjunctions as these, one should perform auspicious rites under other favorable astrological configurations. (28)
Just as all defects are eliminated when the yogas are properly attained,
so too, having examined [the site] with effort, the preceptor should begin the consecration.
At the time of installing the *liṅga*, there should be no transgression of the proper time;
one should perform worship there for at least one day, which removes all defects for men.
Therefore, with every effort, having especially established the *liṅga*,
one should examine the time and the dissolution of the moving and other types of *liṅgas*.
Likewise, the temple, the pavilion, the enclosure wall, and the gate-tower may be constructed for the rites of other deities according to the desire of the patron. || 32 ||
The offering of *akura* grains should be performed on the ninth day, the seventh day, or the fifth day;
however, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) properly only after having offered the *akura* grains.
The first is the offering of the sprouts; the second is the purification of the liṅga; the third is the Brahma-thread, and the fourth is the circumambulation of the village. || 34 ||
The fifth [day] is for the water-rites in the midst of the water according to the rules;
on the sixth, the consecration of the pavilion; and on the seventh, the purchase of the bed.
In the eighth [chapter], the consecration of the jar; in the ninth, the rite of fire-offering (homa);
in the tenth, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is taught; and after that, the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
The twelfth is declared to be worship (arcana), while the thirteenth is the ritual bathing (snapana).
O eminent sages, I shall describe these in their proper sequence as they are. (37)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Sūkṣmaśāstra, titled "The Installation of the Liṅga."
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the daily bali offering;
in whatever village the sound of the bali is heard, there the spirits, rākṣasas, and others [will not dwell].
Having heard this, they go forth suddenly; it shall bring prosperity to the village.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the sequence of the daily bali offering.
At the conclusion of Śiva’s meal, and at the end of the daily fire-ritual,
a king who desires victory should always perform the *bali* offering according to the sequence.

The supreme [form] is the jewel-liṅga (maṇiliṅga), the middling is the image (pratimā), and the inferior is to be known as the sphere (golaka); or else, it may be made of flowers, food, or rice grains.
One should meditate upon the image or the liṅga; in its absence, however, upon a sphere (golaka).
In the absence of these, the wise person should always properly perform [meditation] on the mantras and so forth.
In the forenoon, the image of Brāhmaṇapriya is worshipped with a flower-liṅga;
and at midday, the Maṇiliṅga-Śivapriya is worshipped with a food-liṅga.
In the evening, one should offer balls of rice (*golaka*) shaped like grains of rice to Keśava;
these may be made of four kinds of materials: gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal vessels.
One should fashion an eight-petaled lotus in the center of the vessel, which has a width of eight finger-breadths and a height of four finger-breadths. (8)
On the southern side of the pavilion, having smeared a square mandala with cow dung, one should then place a vessel there.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra, Śiva shall bring him to auspiciousness;
having recited the Īśāna-mantra, one should place Śiva upon the *baliliṅga*.
One should worship in sequence with all kinds of perfumes, flowers, incenses, lamps, and water-offerings (arghya), using the mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra and ending with the Weapon-mantra.
Whether a student or a householder, with his body smeared with ashes,
he should wear a linga upon his head together with a turban and an upper garment.
Having recited the Sadyojāta mantra, one should proceed together with the image and other [ritual objects],
or else [proceed] as the embodiment of the Pāśupata weapon or indeed as Candraśekhara.
One should go before all [the others], and they should follow him with jewels;
the flower, the food, the rice, and the linga should follow his linga.
It was provided with canopies and banners, equipped with parasols and chowries,
accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, and adorned by courtesans and others.
One should perform the first circumambulation together with the pedestal of the temple;
one should proceed from the front of the gatehouse accompanied by the sound of conchs.
The place for the sandals is desired on both sides of the entrance of the *citīrī*;
however, the place for the image is said to be in its western part. || 17 ||
In the west, the location for the image is said to be in front [of the central deity];
the location for the *golaka* is desired behind the *maṇiliṅga*. (18)
At the rear of the three [central deities], however, the location for the attendants (anta) is desired;
one should install the images and so forth in a clockwise sequence. || 19 ||
One should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of images and so forth, and install the *baliliṅga*.
By "images and so forth" is meant [the various forms], and "prati" refers to the jeweled globes (*maṇigolaka*). 20.
The *puṣpānna-taṇḍula-liṅga* and the *bali-liṅga* are thus remembered;
having placed them facing east, one should install the sandals at the front of the image.
Having placed the pair of sandals upon a small stand, one should worship them with vessels,
perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and water for the arghya offering.
Having worshipped with the six limbs in due order and having offered the *arghya* according to sequence, one should place the *arghya* of the four—beginning with the first—upon the head. (23)
Having performed the washing of the feet, one should cause [the image] to enter the temple;
having established it in its own place, one should worship it with the five Brahmans beginning with the day of the week.
The preceptor, having established the *baliliṅga* in the eastern maṇḍala,
should worship it with the five Brahmans in sequence, beginning with the door.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra, one should place the Lord residing in the *bali-liṅga* into the root-liṅga, and then recite the Śiva-mantra once more.
One should place all the offering-liṅgas and other items within the inner sanctum;
then, after dismissing the offering-liṅga, the wise practitioner should worship the sandals (pādukās).
Having performed the washing of the feet, he should enter the interior of the temple;
the most excellent of teachers should cause everything to be done according to the previously stated procedure. (28)
It may be the Saṃsthāna-liṅga, the Pāśupata-liṅga, or an image of Candraśekhara; in the absence of these, a Maṇiśiva-liṅga, and especially a Golaka-liṅga.
Or else, one should offer them food, a flower, or even an arghya offering;
therefore, with every effort, one should always act with the desire for the fruit.
Having worshipped the six-limbed form with the six mantras in sequence,
and having thus worshipped according to the rule, one should cause [the deity] to enter its own place.
One should offer the sacrificial oblation (caru) with the *hṛdaya* mantra and then cause betel-leaf to be presented;
thereafter, one should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) with the *prāsāda* mantra.
One should offer abundant oblations and worship all the devotees;
one must not perform the rite deficient in a *droṇa* measure, but rather follow the sequence prescribed for the temple.
At the conclusion of the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), one should perform an oblation for the sake of the bali offering with the heart-mantra;
one should offer fifty, twenty-five, and nine oblations smeared with clarified butter.
Thus it should be on Wednesday and likewise on Saturday;
one should perform an oil massage with the heart mantra and carry out the remainder as previously described. (35)
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) during the first part of the night, especially with fragrant oil;
and at the time of dawn, one should perform the anointing (abhyaṅga), the root-rite (mūla), and the offering (bali) before the image.
Having bathed with royal honors using fragrant *āmalaka* and other substances,
the wise man should thereafter offer the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) to each [deity] individually while reciting the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
(110) Afterwards, one should construct the gateway adorned with all ornaments;
for if anyone should cause it to be made otherwise, that rite shall become fruitless. || 38 ||
This is declared to be the Vāra festival; in that mantra, it is especially so. || 38½ ||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Festival of the Days of the Week," in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra*, a subtle treatise.
The Characteristics of the Teacher.
Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme characteristics of the teacher: he is one who abides in the sphere [of truth], speaks the truth, and is knowledgeable in the application of former conduct. (1)
One who knows the scriptures, knows the Śiva-mantras, and has been consecrated by the initiation of Śiva;
one who knows the mantras, knows the distinctions of words, and worships the Guru, the deity, and the sacrificial fire. || 2 ||
He was a master of established tenets, skillful and dexterous, illustrious and dear to his devotees;
he ate only at night, had conquered his senses, was knowledgeable, followed manifest conduct, and spoke kindly.
One who has been initiated into the pure Self by a true preceptor is not fallen;
he should be constantly devoted to the five great sacrifices and should strictly avoid the food of a Śūdra.
O knower of the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas, O knower of the Śiva-śāstras, you who possess subtlety;
just as the manifest (sakala) was born from the partless (niṣkala), so too is the disciple born from the teacher. || 5 ||
Especially the son of the teacher, or his grandson, or his daughter’s son;
in their absence, it is as if performed by the teacher’s son himself.
When the flower has perished, there is no fruit; as with grain in saline soil, there is no fruit.
One should not take another's property, even for the sake of favoring one's devotees. (7)
One should avoid the teachings of other scriptures that are difficult to comprehend and shun the initiations of others; among all four castes, the Brahmins are distinguished as superior.
In the absence of Brāhmaṇas, however, especially among Kṣatriyas,
those born from a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya maiden are indeed superior Kṣatriyas.
He is slightly inferior to a Brāhmaṇa and slightly superior to Kṣatriyas;
indeed, in the absence of Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, he is especially [qualified] among Vaiśyas. || 10 ||
In this very manner, the sequence for the ritual arrangement of the Śiva-worship has been declared;
it follows the direct order (ānuloma), while the reverse order (pratiloma) is to be avoided.
One born from a Vaiśya woman by a Vaiśya is indeed a Vaiśya-Śūdra, yet he is superior;
even one born from a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya woman is somewhat superior to that [Vaiśya-Śūdra].

One who is endowed with all auspicious marks, born from a Kṣatriya woman by a Vaiśya father through the initiation of Śiva-consecration (pratiṣṭhā-śivadīkṣā), becomes a most excellent Vaiśya. || 13 ||
But one born of a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra maiden is the most excellent among Śūdras;
endowed with all auspicious marks, he is initiated and has Śiva as his sphere of concern.
In this very way, by virtue of his qualities alone, he became the preeminent leader of the Śaiva lineage;
thus, there are three divisions of the Siddhānta: Śaiva, Pāśupata, and Soma.
O you who delight in the eightfold vision, the Śaiva Siddhānta alone is preeminent among the eight systems of philosophy by virtue of its connection with the divine play of Śiva. (16)
He was preeminent, a knower of the heroes of others, and a reciter of all the scriptures;
his limbs were smooth and graceful, and he was adorned with the beauty of every member. (17)

Whether possessing a topknot or bound with a thread, one who wears ashes and rudrākṣas, who has abandoned the sacred thread and the topknot, yet remains auspicious through the mastery of mantras and other such means. || 18 ||
One who is proficient in all the scriptures and free from all attachments is indeed called the "naiṣṭhika," the best of teachers. || 19 ||
His son, who is learned in the scriptures, should also be worthy of the ritual;
he should be endowed with such an appearance and adorned with garments and ornaments. (20)
This pure form of Śiva is prescribed for the teacher; it consists of long-limbed, short-limbed, deceitful, curd-like, virtuous, and flowing [qualities]. 21.
Vimala, Kṛpaṇa, Ahanākulodbhava, Viṭapa, Dhūrta, Dṛta, Matta, and Pramatta. (22)
Gulma, Rogikuṣṭha, Śipiviṣṭa, Muṣṭivān, Andhaka, Tanuka, Aṅgahīna, and Kopavān. || 23 ||

One who sells the Vedas, one who is deceitful, one who does not abandon [impurity], one who is covered in ash [without cause], one who is impure in eight ways, one who is devoid of vows—he is a Brahmin in name only. || 28 ||
One who is constantly a servant to others, one who reviles the gods, the sacred fires, or his guru, or the son of one who lacks a teacher—such a deluded person has his heart stolen away. (25)

One whose limbs are afflicted by the decline and transformation of the elements, who has lost his sense of being a living being, who is devoid of intelligence, who is distracted by worldly affairs, who is enslaved by the gods, and who has lost his knowledge—such a person is truly lost. (26)
A wicked person is one who is joined with faults and likewise adorned yet fallen;
he is one who, in matters such as consecrations and the like, reaps the fruit of his own actions. (27)
In this very manner, being properly prepared, one should perform the dismissal (visarjana) starting from the installation (sthāpanā);
the rites beginning with the installation are to be performed according to the Ādiśaiva tradition.

All [the systems], beginning with Anuśaiva and the others, proceed respectively regarding the domain of the self's purpose; the Sakala [system] is determined by its coming and going throughout all locations. (29)
The characteristics of the teacher have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the disciple and others.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Master," in the *Sūkṣmatantra*.
The Characteristics of the Disciple and Others. Hereafter, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the disciple and others; listen.
He who bears the form of one's own deity, who is diligent and a devoted attendant—(1).
The *hodaka*, the *bodhaka*, the *hotṛ*, and the *adhvaryu*—these must be born into the lineage of the primordial Śaivas and consecrated by the initiation of Śiva. || 2 ||
Endowed with all auspicious marks, a devotee of Śiva, and possessed of great fame,
he was perfected in the Śaiva Āgamas and had reached the truth of the meaning of all scriptures.
One who is learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas and possesses fitness for all ritual acts is known as a Mahāśaiva; in his absence, the king may likewise [be appointed].
In their absence, however, a Vaiśya may act in due order, as well as a Cāhika,
a Samayin, a Putraka, a Sādhaka, and a Mūrtidhāraka. (5)
If one is situated in another country, one should carry out [the rites] under the authority of the guru's command;
in this very manner, by means of the prescribed procedure, one should cause the consecration and other rituals to be performed.
First, one should carry out everything by that very same method by which the undertaking was begun—
from the initial plowing until the final consecration— following the path of a single continuous sequence.

In the case of an action as well, it is prescribed in this very same way as both distinct and non-distinct; for instance, the construction of a temple, as well as the installation of the *liṅga* and so forth. (8)
Whatever building work and so forth is devoid of restoration for what has become dilapidated, or any other [activity], such as the annual festival held over a long period of time; (9)
Thus, all these rites have been correctly proclaimed in their entirety:
worship, the fire-ritual, the ceremonial bathing, and the work concerning the site.
The path of the procedure for initiation, as well as the cold water jars and so forth, and the rule regarding the number of days, is proclaimed as being indivisible [from the preceding]. (11)

At the time when all [the disciples] have departed for their respective tasks, as long as there is no one remaining with the instructor—if there is a desire to go inevitably, one must certainly stay for that night. (12)
At the conclusion of the daily rites, however, one should go everywhere to the preceptor;
according to the procedure for those of undivided [status], the number and so forth were previously prescribed.
One should not go outside; however, if one must go, it is considered a fault.
This same rule is prescribed for the four [classes], beginning with the teacher (ācārya). || 14 ||
He who first constructs the abodes of the *liṅgas* such as Sāyambhuva and all their complete retinues, as well as other [structures], [attains the fruit]. (15)
When those [previous] times have passed away, one should perform [the rite] through the lineage of that [deity], provided there is a specific distinction made by a change in form. (16)
Or would one act through another lineage, or by means of the cause of a previous continuum? What specific reason is there for the efficacy of the connection with mantras? (17)
Therefore, with every effort and in accordance with the command established by the ancients, one should perform the rites of installation and so forth, exactly as they are prescribed. || 18 ||
But for one whose lineage is unknown, one should always write it on cloth;
and for her sake, one should perform it through that very favor, or else by means of another lineage.
If one should perform even the head-rite with those mantras according to the previous path, that performance for the ancestors would be as if performed by his own son.
In the absence of a son, however, the daughter's son [performs it]; in his absence, the maternal uncle;
and in his absence, his son shall perform the various rites after a long time.
And at the clear time, it should be thus when clearly manifest by the command of the deity;
in this very manner, one should indeed cause everything to be performed. || 22 ||
Otherwise, if it is performed incorrectly, it will bring destruction to the king and the kingdom;
there is no doubt that it leads to the ruin of villages and the like, as well as the destruction of enemies. (23)
The characteristics of the disciple and others have been declared; now hear the procedure for the ritual placement of the embryo (garbhanyāsa).
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Disciple and Others," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
(116) The Characteristics of an Image. Hereafter, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the image.
For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, and for the sake of bringing peace to all. || 1 ||
Because the form of the deities is distinct, it is called a "pratima" (image). It is said to be of two kinds: with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala). || 2 ||
The *niṣkala* is formless, while the *sakala* possesses its own essential form;
the *sakala*, moreover, is complete with thirty-two limbs according to its divisions.
Thereafter, one should have an image made according to the extent of one's wealth:
a golden one for those desiring a kingdom, and one adorned with jewels bestows prosperity upon Vaiśyas.
Copper is for the sake of the prosperity of Brahmins, while gold shall be for the Śūdras;
a wise man should have an image fashioned according to his means and wealth.
It is of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Each one has three further subdivisions; thus, nine types of divisions are taught.
The festival, the image, Umā, Skanda, and Maheśvara—
these constitute twenty-one divisions, or sixteen according to another classification.
The twelvefold division is said to be of three kinds;
the measurement of the Lord (Īśa) should be fashioned, which is called the "best of the best" (uttamottama).
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall be of that same measure, and its pillar-height likewise;
a measurement of eighty fingers is prescribed as the best.
Having divided that measurement into nine parts, one should perform each division according to its specific distinctions;
thus one should carry out the classification of measurements as declared in the treatises of the artisans.
The first is said to be the *sukhāsana* (easy posture); the second is the *vaivāhya* (wedding posture); the third is joined with Umā; and the fourth is the one mounted upon the bull. (11)
The fifth is indeed Tripurāntaka, while the sixth is in the form of a dancer;
the seventh is specifically said to be Candraśekhara.
The eighth is Ardhanārīśa, the ninth is Hari-ardhaka,
and the tenth is proclaimed to be Caṇḍeśvaraprasāda.
The eleventh is declared to be Kāmāri; the twelfth is Kālanāśana;
the thirteenth is Dakṣāṇamūrti; and after that is Bhikṣāṭana. (114)
Sadāśiva is the fifteenth, while the origin of the Liṅga is the sixteenth;
thus, the distinction between these sixteen forms will now be explained. (15)
Sukhāsana, Mahāśānta, Kalyāṇa, Somadhārin,
and Gaṅgādhara— these five are here called the forms of creation (sṛṣṭimūrti).
Ardhanārī, Trirātra, Vireśa, Vṛṣavāhana,
and Bhikṣāṭana— these five are declared to be the Sthitimūrtis.
The burning of Kāla, the burning of Ākāma, the destruction of the great Tripura, the charming story of Gajodbhava, and likewise the slaying of Jalandhara. (18)
And Caṇḍeśa—these eight are said to be the forms of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
They have three eyes and four arms, with the crescent moon as their crest-ornament. || 19 ||
Clad in tiger-skin garments, adorned with necklaces and armlets,
they were invested with sacred threads and decorated with two earrings.
(118) They are endowed with matted locks and crowns, adorned with all kinds of flowers;
with their two hands they grant boons and fearlessness, and they hold a black axe. || 21 ||
Thus has this common [characteristic] of the sixteen forms been declared;
now I shall explain the specific [details] regarding Umā, Skanda, and Maheśvara.
It is said to have three types of divisions— gentle, fierce, and mixed—
and is endowed with five seats according to the previously mentioned measurement.

The wise man, having thoroughly examined the asterisms, weekdays, degrees, and birth-constellations (yoni) of both income and expenditure, should specifically observe their auspicious and inauspicious nature. 24.
The measurement of Skanda is said to be equal to the arm-span of Īśa;
the measurement of Skanda is declared to be equal to the arm-span of Mumā. (25)
O Skanda, between Umā and Śaṅkara, there should especially be a seat for the deity in the form of a child, according to his original proportions.
One should cause the middle [type of] seat to be made with five parts or three parts;
one should know the lowest to be with three parts; thus the seat is remembered as being of three kinds.
It should be provided with a single seat according to the previously mentioned proportions;
having determined the frontal portion to be two hundred and forty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) [in length]. || 28 ||
One should have the form of the Goddess made with ten *tāla*s as the medium size;
one should have the form of Skanda made according to the measure of eleven *tāla*s.
For the goddesses, it should be likewise; one should join them with the teeth.
He has one face, mighty arms, and the great luster of blue Śiva. (30)
Adorned with a crown of matted locks and accompanied by Pāśupatī on his left side,
he has three eyes and four arms; gentle in appearance, he is the supreme Lord clad in a tiger skin.
Kṛṣṇa has his right hand in the boon-granting gesture (*varada*) and his left hand holding an axe;
his right foot is extended downward while his left foot rests firmly on the seat.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament, his hand holds a flower and displays the gesture of granting boons, especially in the case of Gaurī.
This has been taught specifically for the sake of Skandadeva; in this very manner, it is auspicious and brings about all accomplishments through its gentle nature. (34)
Joined with a black axe, it should be a bracelet that grants fearlessness;
it should be endowed with various ornaments and adorned with diverse jewels.
Raudra should have a bracelet in his hand, or Skanda should have flowers in his hand;
Raudra alone is declared [to be worshipped] in the form of Pāśupata and others. (36)
The mixed posture (miśra) is inferior, with the left leg hanging down and the right leg seated; it is likewise [applied] to the goddess Umā. (37)
The sixth face is said to be the very peak, with hands granting boons and fearlessness;
this is declared to be the "Mixed" (miśra) type, which one should certainly not perform in the Lākula tradition.
The gentle Śūla-Śaiva [initiation] consists of twenty-eight varieties according to its three divisions;
thereafter, one should perform the rites beginning with the "foot of the bound soul" (paśupada) according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
If the builder or the patron should cause even a single instance of confusion [in the proportions], he shall perish;
therefore, with every effort, one should have it constructed according to the prescribed characteristics.
Thus, one should effect that threefold division there by means of the path.
The characteristics of the image have been declared; now hear the procedure for Manonmanī. (41)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Images," in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra* within the *Sūkṣmaśāstra*.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme characteristics of the halls (sālās):
first is the Bhūta-hall, and second is the Mūrti-hall. || 1 ||
The third was the assembly hall, the fourth the hall of the world-protectors,
the fifth the hall of scriptures, and the sixth the hall of ponds.
The seven Gaṅgās and the seven Tālana trees are its presiding deities;
for the purpose of worshipping them, the wise man should construct a rampart.
For the purpose of protecting the palace and for the sake of auspiciousness,
the wise man should divide the width of the palace into four parts.
First, one should construct [the structure] entirely on one side, provided with a *sālaka*;
then, using two parts of that [measurement] in their entirety, one should cause two [other structures] to be made separately.
Thus, the wise one should first have [the mandala] made in three ways; then, according to the sequence of two and a half [units], he should have the supreme [mandala] made in three kinds.
It should be made with a length of two and a half, three, or four times [the width],
and its directional divisions should likewise be fourfold or threefold.
One should perform it according to the sequence of the courtesans by means of that very [number] multiplied by five; beyond that... (8)
The pavilion for the worship-image was pure, like a divine grove of the five spring flowers.
Mahendra, Svastivṛtta, Māya, Bāhuvikāraka, Utpala, Paṅkalagna, Śrīsvasti, and Niveśana. || 10 ||
Vāpībrahmasabhā, likewise utpalapatraka, mahāpadma, mahācchanda, and likewise devavṛtta; || 11 ||
By Candra, who was afflicted by suffering, these celestial chariots were fashioned as auspicious signs:
Somacchanda, Somavṛtta, Bahupatra, and Suveṣṭika.
The Śrīvatsa-shaped, the Ghoṇacchandavṛtta, the Vedika, the Siddhayoga, the Caturvṛtta, the Kūṭākāra, and the Vilokana.
The kūṭākāra, the gāndhāra, the svastika, and likewise the tilaka; the śaśivṛtti, the viśāla, and furthermore the kulenduka. || 14 ||
These celestial chariots were indeed fashioned by the Moon:
the Vedika, the Vedivṛtta, the Somaveṇu, and the Caturmukha.
The Āhika, Kīñcika, Yāna, Agni, Chando-raka, Hasti-pṛṣṭha, Ne-vṛtta, Pramadā, Lata, Vibeka, and Trivṛt; 16.
The Vṛṣabha, the Mādhūvṛtta, the Trikūṭa which deals with the arts, the Goyāga, the Maṇḍūka, and the excellent Pariprādaka; || 17 ||
The *pāśika*, the *paṅkalagna*, and likewise the *gaganeśvara*; the *śābhikārasavṛtta*, the *nivuṣa*, and the *paribrahmaka*. (18)
The palace of Caṇḍeśa is shaped like a cloud, possesses the sky as its very substance, extends to the ends of the horizon, and is endowed with the form of a living being. || 19 ||
These nine and six celestial chariots (vimānas), fashioned by sages such as Kanaka and others, have indeed been described by the ancients.
The Vahnīpatra, the Cūrṇa, and the Cūlikā—
these are all nine distinct types of celestial chariots (vimānas).
A wise man should cause a rampart to be constructed in accordance with the principles of income and expenditure;
however, in the expansion of forms such as the *liṅga*, one should not apply the rules of income and so forth.
The measurement of the ear-projections for the *liṅgas* of Svāyambhuva and others will now be described;
one should divide the circumference of whichever *liṅga* is to be worshipped into eight equal parts. (23)
Within those parts of the liṅga, the wise and learned man should fashion the head and other features using twenty-four hundred finger-breadths (aṅgulas). || 24 ||
Therefore, the most excellent of instructors should fashion the face and other features upon that portion.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, named "The Temple," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra consisting of ninety-six [verses].
(123) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the *ghṛtakambala* (the ghee-blanket),
for the benefit of all the world and for the welfare of all living beings. || 1 ||
Those who cause harm to cows, Brahmins, kings, and others during the summer, especially on the full moon day of the month of Māgha under the Maghā asterism, [suffer the consequences]. || 2 ||
One should prepare a "ghee-blanket" (ghṛtakambalaka) on a Sunday or a Monday,
during the day on a festival day associated with a lunar conjunction, or at night when joined with a [lunar] mansion.
On that very day, it should be performed because of its connection with the sacred festival (parvan);
it brings about the destruction of all sins for men and is the means for accomplishing all goals and purposes.
For the sake of nourishment with oily substances and other offerings, one should perform worship in due order during the month of Māgha;
this is the manifest emblem of Śiva, which destroys untimely death.
The wise man, having collected the ghee from white and other such cows, should smear it with cow’s ghee from the feet up to the head.

Having placed a *kambala* upon two *liṅgas*, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; for rites performed for oneself as well as for others, one should place the *golaka* and then perform the ritual installation (*vinyāsa*).
One should collect pure cow’s milk from all four castes, provided it is free from fire, devoid of insects or hollows, and obtained from a celibate woman.
In vessels made of gold and other materials, the wise man, using water filtered through a cloth,
should perform the rites of fire and so forth with the mantra alone within his heart.
While it is still joined with moisture until it reaches a state of solidity,
one should worship it in the vessels with the Prāsāda mantra.
In the kitchen area, or in another pleasant place,
one should establish the site of worship for one's own sake in the eastern direction. (11)
One should have a mandala made there, either circular or square;
in its center, one should place a vessel with the heart mantra itself.
Therefore, the preceptor, having collected curd into other vessels, should fill them with auspicious water while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra. || 13 ||
A man should rub it with his two hands using only a cloth;
the process of churning continues until it reaches the state of being broken.
The wise man, having brought fresh butter into other vessels, should cause it to be heated in the kitchen area with the fire-mantra. || 15 ||
The wise man should collect [the ingredients] into a pure vessel with his heart;
the primary measure is one thousand *prasthas*, decreasing in sequence down to one hundred *prasthas*.
One should have each [measure] made ninefold, according to one's wealth;
or else, it may be of lesser measure, ranging up to ten *prasthas* in sequence.
Then, in the case of its existence, there is ten *prasthas* at the end of the *prastha*;
thus, in many ways, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others.
A wise man, having worshipped each [deity] individually with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, should establish a firm path for his own purposes in an abundant manner within the temple. (19)
Adorned with all ornaments, accompanied by the sound of conchs, joined with various musical instruments, and accompanied by various songs. || 20 ||
Having performed a circumambulation of the village or a circumambulation of the temple,
one should install [the deity] in a well-concealed pavilion by means of the mantra of the temple. (21)
In front of the temple, one should construct a square pavilion measuring twelve cubits, or nine cubits, or eight cubits.
The wise man should cause a water-shed (prapā) to be constructed according to the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇas;
it should be provided with four doors and adorned with four arches (toraṇas).
Having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass and adorned it with canopies and banners,
one should prepare an altar in the middle of one-third of the pavilion.
The height should be one *ratni* or even one *tāla*;
indeed, one should have a sacrificial pit (*homakuṇḍa*) constructed on the eastern side of the altar.
Whether it be circular or square and adorned with three girdles,
the preceptor should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the four directions for a fixed (sthāvara) rite.
For one's own sake, there should be a single oblation, beginning with the Brahmā;
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there and sprinkle [the site] with the *pāvamāna* hymns.
To the east of the Ghṛtakambalaka, in the ninth [section], specifically in the seventh and fifth [sub-sections],
the wise man should offer sprouts according to the ritual procedure seen in the scriptures.
On the previous day, the preceptor, having taken hold of clarified butter, should offer the seed-syllable (aṅkura) and fill the vessels with water on the night of the consecration ceremony.
Combined with all types of perfumes and the five Brahmans and six ancillaries,
or else one should fill a large water-jar or a small pitcher in due order.
(126) There should be ten vessels, five vessels, or even three vessels;
however, when the [guests] are few, there should be one vessel for oneself, and three together for the others. 31.
In ten vessels, one should worship the tenfold form; in five vessels, the fivefold form;
in three vessels, the threefold form; and likewise, Śiva in a single vessel.
Provided with tufts of thread, accompanied by cloths, and joined with lead,
one should likewise place them in this very sequence outside the altar.
Having wrapped the vessels with a new cloth,
O Teacher, one should treat them as Śiva in the water and then pour clarified butter into that water.
The wise preceptor should there draw [the design] with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood, combined with powder, while reciting the Īśāna mantra.
Thereafter, the wise one should gradually extract the state of fullness and the rest from the Prāsāda mantra and collect them individually in golden vessels.
Following the path of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), the wise one should have an altar constructed,
surrounded by the ten weapons and endowed with the eight auspicious symbols.
As before, one should place consecrated jars upon the altar;
one should then worship the eight lords of the worlds within those jars in their proper sequence.
In their midst, one should place balls of ghee;
having wrapped them in a new cloth, the wise man should worship them with the Prāsāda mantra. || 39 ||
There, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas;
and at the conclusion of that, having performed a fire-oblation with the five Brahmans and the six ancillary limbs.

(127) Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, cow dung, milk, curd, barley, mustard seeds, mung beans, and black gram are the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) in their respective order. || 41 ||
One should perform a homa for each of the four types of stationary beings with abundant pieces of food, following the instructions of the preceptor.
If one is unable [to perform] these oblations, then only a single one is prescribed;
likewise, for one's own sake, a single oblation is ordained for Śūdras as well. (43)
In this manner, according to the prescribed method, one should have [the rite] performed;
indeed, one should offer the bali-oblation there, casting the bali outside the altar.
Thereafter, one should worship the God and the Goddess in sequence according to the prescribed method of worship;
one should perform the offering of clarified butter upon the head with the Prāsāda mantra.
There, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (havis) accompanied by side dishes;
then one should cause betel-leaf to be given and feed the Brāhmaṇas. || 46 ||
One should let it remain there overnight together with the nectar of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
At dawn, having bathed the preceptor, one should thereafter commence the sacrifice.
Having adorned and worshipped [the deity] with the ten-syllable mantra that pervades the sky, the best of teachers should perform [the rite] in this manner according to the prescribed procedure. (48)
One should worship the Ghṛtakambalaka with the Heart-mantra, having duly honored the world-protectors individually by their respective names. (49)
One should perform the ritual procedure for the fire oblation (homakarma) together with the previously mentioned rules;
at the conclusion, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Prāsāda mantra.
There, one should worship the teacher and worship the embodiments of the deities;
having performed the circumambulation of the village, the wise man [should offer] a blanket of ghee. (51)
Afterwards, one should place the form of the Liṅga, adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by dance and song, upon a woolen blanket smeared with ghee, while reciting the Heart-mantra.
One should place the *kambala* (woolen cloth) in sequence from the crown of the head down to the feet;
and all the *sakalas* (embellishments) should also be placed in sequence during the rite of installation.
One should place all the retinues upon the stationary [seat],
and by means of the Mahāvyoma mantra, one should in every way place the kambala.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, with the mantra of the temple (prāsāda), one should offer abundant oblations with the mantra of the heart (hṛdaya). || 55 ||
It should be performed at the end of every period, especially during the twilight; for a whole day, for half a day, for a watch, or even for half a watch. (56)
And having performed the *pātaka* rite and likewise the sprinkling (*snapana*) as before,
one should perform it with the *mahāvyoman* mantra and similarly with the ten-syllable mantra.
The wise one should worship according to the path of the scriptures with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
he should then perform the ceremonial bathing for all the retinues in due order.
One should give them sacrificial food (haviṣya), but cause it to be given with the tantra-mantra;
one should cause a blanket to be presented to Caṇḍeśa, the god of gods.
Having recollected the fierce mantra, one should abandon the blanket;
all the ghee-blankets should be cast away among cows and into the waters.
One should cause [the body] to be cremated by fire there, while recollecting the Caṇḍa-mantra;
in whatever rite whatever mantra [is prescribed], in that case [one should act] from the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra). (61)
One should especially perform it with the mantra itself, particularly so;
for if it is maintained for even a single night on a mere "butter-blanket" (ghṛtakambala), [the result is attained]. 62.
Each of these three and seven products of the cow should be prepared separately;
beyond this, one should not perform it for one's own sake, though it may be done for the sake of others.
For one's own sake, having placed a cloth of ghee upon a crystal or similar substance, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), on a mandala and so forth, or on a painted wall or in a mirror; 64.

In the first stage as well, that same procedure should be performed; the wise one should purify the "blanket" (kambala) of the sky, beginning with the solar orb, by means of oblations into the fire. 65.
Having placed [the seed] in water within a watery place with their respective roots, the wise man should not move the seed as long as it has not reached the stage of the *kambalaka*.
In this way, one should act for one's own benefit, but not perform that action for the sake of others;
in this very manner, according to the prescribed rule, one should cause it to be done following the stated path.
There, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings;
a woolen blanket with ghee is prescribed. Now hear about the offering of *damanaka* flowers. (68)
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Butter-Blanket," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
(130) I shall proclaim the Śaiva conduct, both the general worship and the specific [rites]:
one should commence the rite of shaving when the sun is in its northern course.
Indeed, in the eighth year from conception, one should begin the study of the Vedas for the twice-born;
thereafter, after fifteen years have passed, perform the matter of marriage.
For the sake of purification, one should perform a ritual bath according to the procedure prescribed by the rules;
thereafter, having commenced worship while wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,
one should contemplate the Śiva-āgamas at the time of his [the deity’s] presence.
Subsequently, one should establish the connection with Nirvāṇa through the investigation of the Vāgvara,
as taught by Śiva to the pure self who has transcended the five objects of sense.
Afterwards, the wise initiate should indeed perform the ritual acts;
or he may perform them at another location, according to the requirements of the site.
He too, due to the injunction of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), should not cause [the disciple] to act otherwise;
for the Guru belongs to the same prior continuum (*pūrvasantāna*) as the beginningless object. (7)
A Guru who follows the Ādiśaiva tradition and others should perform the rites for the village and so forth;
whatever was previously performed by the father is thereby considered performed by the son.
At the time of its consecration, one should bring everything for it;
otherwise, if it is done differently, there will undoubtedly be the destruction of the site.
In the absence of those two, the wise man should properly perform [the rite] for them through their kinsmen; if these are not available, he should do so through their friends and others.
One should perform this specifically here according to the tantras of that Vaktra;
if one were to perform it with another [deity] who is not Vaktra, great fault would arise.
What is the reason for the distinction arising from the cause of connection with the mantra?
It is because of our two lineages being perfectly pure and belonging to the same clan. (12)
Just as the ritual of the *garbha* is distinct, so too the nature of the *garbha* has two purposes;
one should perform the sacrifice for one's own sake, but never for the sake of others. (13)
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform all of that during the month of Muktakālaka;
if one should do it in another month, its fruit will become fruitless.
In a linga or an image, on a wall-painting or even on a cloth-scroll;
on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or a mandala, in fire, in water, or in the solar orb. || 15 ||
A wise person should have [the deity] fashioned for his own sake in these various locations:
specifically in a linga, an image, on a wall, or even on a cloth. (16)
The wise man should cause [the image] to be installed for the sake of others in the four positions;
prior to the ascent and so forth, in the ninth or seventh direction.
At an auspicious moment and a favorable lagna, the wise man should offer the ritual sprouts;
he should prepare a maṇḍala in front of the temple in the direction of Śaṅkara.
It should be sixteen cubits, or ten, nine, or eight cubits in size;
it must be provided with sixteen pillars and endowed with four doors.
One should fashion the central altar (madhyavedī) as one part out of nine parts;
alternatively, make its width five, six, or seven tālas.
One should construct it with a height of two tālas, resembling the surface of a mirror;
having adorned it with five types of colored powders, it should be beautified with canopies and banners.
Adorned with a garland of *darbha* grass and decorated with arches (*toraṇa*),
and provided with the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgala*), one should arrange the ten weapons there. (22)
One should have the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) recited there and sprinkle [the area] with water consecrated by mantras;
one should worship in the center of the altar using six or five droṇas [of grain].
For that purpose, [one should prepare a vessel] filled with rice and also half as much sesame;
having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp in its center.
One should cause fire-pits (agni-kuṇḍa) to be made in the four directions beginning with the east;
or else three pits, or even a single fire.
In accordance with the dimensions of the pavilion, or even merely the measure of a weapon,
it should be adorned with three tiers of girdles, or even with a single tier.

In this very manner, the wise one should perform the construction of the pavilion in due order; on the preceding day, he should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of the *damana* plant with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).

Having collected [the materials] in nine vessels, the preceptor and the image-makers should place them in a well-concealed location; then they should perform the ritual bath for the [deity] along with the śikhā.
Having adorned [the deity] with the five-fold ornaments and anointed him with divine perfumes,
one should place the Śiva-kumbha and the Vardhanī pitcher in the center of the altar.
On all sides, eight water-filled jars adorned with gold should be placed;
from the fourteenth day up to the sixth, and on the fifteenth day and thereafter, [the same applies].
On the eighth lunar day itself, beginning with the preparatory rites, one should consecrate the ram;
having wrapped each one individually in cloth, one should worship them with perfumes and flowers.
Having separately purified the *damana* plant, one should sprinkle it with water from *kuśa* grass;
one should divide the flower into five parts and place each portion into a vessel.

One should worship with the five Brahmans and the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga), using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; one should then place [the vessels] around the Śiva-pitcher while reciting the Heart-mantra.

One should offer sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds with the five Brahma-mantras, the Śiva-aṅga-mantras, and the ten-syllable mantra.
The wise one should offer oblations with the *kūrma* mantra twenty-five times for each [deity];
specifically, he should do so at every sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the instruction of the preceptor.
At the conclusion of the materials, having offered two *āhuti*s, the wise one should touch [the deity] with the *Prāsāda* mantra;

he should fashion the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the prescribed rule, whether for Śiva or for another, and the best of preceptors (*deśikottama*) should cause it to be performed in this very manner.
One should touch the *damana* plants and the vessels, as well as those beginning with the fourteenth day;
one should then place the *kāraka* jar between Indra and Īśāna.
Beside them, one should place a jar of nectar, each wrapped in cloth;
they are to be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using their respective names and the heart-mantra. (39)
Adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by every kind of musical instrument,
one should offer a garland of fragrant flowers upon the head of the God of gods.
One should worship all [the attendants], beginning with Sakala, by their respective names;
one should provide for the devotees and servants according to what is available. (41)
Afterwards, one should present the sacrificial offering with the mantra *prāsāda*.
One should perform this in the same manner at night, and in the morning, one should perform the ritual bath.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa especially for the preceptor,
he should sprinkle him with the Pāvamāna hymns and with the Mahāvyoman mantra.
Then, accompanied by the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, and by songs and musical instruments,
he should take up the *kāmakumbha* and especially the *ratikumbha*.
Having circumambulated the village, one should install Nandin and Mahākāla at the side of the entrance, performing the consecration in due order.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting one's own name, one should then go to the interior of the womb and discard the used floral remains (nirmālya). || 46 ||
The wise man should place the Śiva-kumbha and other jars before the Liṅga;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he should sprinkle them while reciting the Pāvamāna hymns.
One should perform the consecration in sequence with the Mahāvyoman mantra,
and then perform the pure ablution with the Prāsāda mantra.
Then, having removed the dāmanaka [garlands] and performed a circumambulation of the temple,
one should especially place the two vessels separately.
O Lord of Gods, with the mantra Mahāvyoman,
one should deposit it upon the pedestal, especially that which is supreme.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the Gaurī-Gāyatrī mantra;
one should also worship Śeṣa, Aśa, Sakala, and the others by their respective names.
When he causes [the offering] to be given through the acquisition of devotees and their attendants,
he should subsequently present the sacrificial food (havis) and feed the devotees of Śiva. || 52 ||
One should worship the preceptor afterwards, and then worship the guardians of the image;
one may worship for oneself at the proper time, but assign the portion as before.
One part is prescribed for Bhāskara, then one for Vighneśa;
the third part is prescribed for Śiva, and the fourth for the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
One should properly divide the remaining portion into five parts;
one part should be given to the preceptor, and another part to the officiating priest.
One should give the third portion to Agni, and the fourth portion to the Bhūtas;
one should likewise give the fiftieth [portion] to the ancestors and others in this very order.
The fire-oblation (homa) for one's own sake should be performed according to one's capacity, and likewise for the sake of others;
for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, it should be as prescribed for the installation for one's own sake.
Alternatively, one may perform a single oblation according to one's means, for three nights, two nights, or even for a single night. || 58 ||
One should begin during the day, specifically before midday;
on the first day of the undertaking, it is called the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana). || 59 ||
As for the time of descent, one should observe the time of the lunar day (tithi).
Indeed, in the ascent, the lunar day is primary; in the descent, however, there is no fault [in disregarding it].
Having placed [the materials] in nine vessels, one should sprinkle them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
one should then sprinkle them with the water of Śiva using the Mahāvyoman mantra.
p.

136) At the conclusion of the twilight rites, one should always perform the mounting of the restraint (*damana*) by means of the mantra of the Great Void (*mahāvyoma*), according to the remainder of the ritual procedure. 62.
"It shall not be considered *nirmālya* (remnant offering) there"—this is the certainty of the scripture.
If it is to be dismissed with a mantra, then it is certainly *nirmālya* there. (63)
Thus, for a long duration, a wise man should indeed perform the rite for an immovable image;
however, for his own sake, a wise man should perform it for a single night and then dismiss the deity.
The wise one should avoid [the ritual] when counted by means of the Aghora weapon mantra;
rather, it should be offered to Caṇḍeśvara while recollecting the Caṇḍa mantra. 65.
The wise one should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) with the mantra of the temple;
he should perform the ablution with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) during the pure bathing rite.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the mantra of Mahāvyoman;
then, having dismissed the barley and other items, one should thereafter speak to the fire.
With the mantra *mahāvyomana*, one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) every day, offering one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
At the time of the descent, however, the wise one should offer a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with Śiva and present abundant sacrificial food (havir) to the God of gods.
Likewise, at dawn, he should offer oblations to all others,
as well as to his devotees and their attendants, according to his means and following the prescribed path.
There, one should honor the teacher with garments, gold, and rings;
or [one may worship] the image on a wall-painting, on a cloth, or even in a mirror. 71.
A wise person should especially have the *āmanaka* made according to the measure of one cubit, in accordance with the primary temple. (72)
Upon the completion of the ritual action, however, one should show the mirror to Śivā;
in this manner, according to the prescribed method, the wise man should indeed perform the rite upon the painting.
The preceptor should fashion a diagram on the sacrificial mound according to the method of the yantra;
having prepared the *damanaka* plant over the fire, he should cast it into the water there.
