The wise one should offer the *damanaka* flower through the space of the solar disc;
for one's own sake and for the sake of others, one should indeed perform it in this very manner. (75)
If one should perform what has not been prescribed, there is no doubt that the performer will be destroyed;
therefore, with every effort, one should have it performed according to the stated path.
Regarding the matter of one's own welfare, perform [the rite] at the proper time by way of devotion;
briefly, [determine] the month, the fortnight, the lunar day, the zodiac sign, and the portion. || 77 ||
It is not at the time of the fire-oblation, nor when there is a division, nor for one's own sake, nor among those of low birth;
rather, it is equal in all other respects for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, in their respective order.
One should perform a great festival beforehand, especially for the sake of others;
whatever may be unmentioned, one should perform it in accordance with the *pavitra* rite.
The Dama, the Pavitra, the Pukraṇa, and likewise the Utsava;
the Śivakumbha, as well as the Śānti, the Ghṛtasnāna, and the Kambala. (80)
Furthermore, whatever has been performed for a long time that is common to all of them,
both the worshipper and the preceptor should practice celibacy (brahmacarya) therein.
(138) The disciple, [maintaining] the purity of the syllables, should observe the vow for as long as it lasts.
One must not go to another village; one should not sleep facing the direction [of travel]. || 82 ||
However, at any other time, going and coming involves fault;
therefore, the best of preceptors established in the vow should first offer the sprouts. (83)
Regarding the purpose, the object, the time, the worshipper, and the preceptor—thus, the wise one should proceed in this very sequence when undertaking [the rite]. (84)
"One who has fallen away from heedfulness should perform the fire sacrifice and the food offering;
he should recite the Mahāvyomam mantra ten thousand times. (85)
One should perform it either with the ten-syllable mantra or again with the Prāsāda mantra;
in this very manner, one should act during the commencement of the ritual site (vīthi).
If one should act otherwise, it would bring about the destruction of the king and the kingdom; by performing rites for one's own sake, the certain ruin of the ritual follows.
The offering of the *damanaka* flower has been declared; now listen to the conduct of the Śaivas.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Planting of the Damanaka," in the Sūkṣma-śāstra.
I shall describe the sacrifice for one's own benefit; listen to it, O Prabhāñjanas!
It bestows health, long life, fame, and victory as its fruit.
(139) It serves to destroy the loss of Brahmins and to eliminate the slaughter of heroes;
it serves to destroy the loss of cattle and is supreme for increasing progeny. (2)
For the sake of accomplishing all desires and bestowing the fruit of all sacrifices,
there has never been, nor will there ever be, one who performs sacrifice so perfectly as he does for his own sake.
It is remembered as being threefold: pure, solitary, and mixed, for the sake of the self.
The pure is devoid of power (śakti), while the solitary is endowed with power.
That which extends from Saura to Caṇḍa is proclaimed as the mixed [type].
Having risen in the morning, one should mentally apply ashes to the forehead.
One should contemplate the ancient Purāṇa of Śiva’s meditation and reflect upon the speech of Śiva;
then, having gone outside that village, one should void feces and urine.
Perform purification, ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and the cleansing of the teeth and palate;
having performed the bath and the mirror-cleansing, face the east and proceed with the rites upon the altar.
Having discarded his wet garment, he should wrap himself in a clean cloth;
facing north, he should perform the ritual sequence of the Śaiva sandhyā.
Holding water in the right hand, one should sprinkle it and write the syllable;
then, having performed the purification of the cloth with the mantra "Ekākṣarī," [one should proceed].
With the *āpośana* and *arghya* mantras, and with the three *tatva* mantras,
one should consecrate the sacred ash (*vibhūti*) in the right hand using the left hand.
The wise one should abandon the thirty-two [deities] and the single portion belonging to the Rākṣasa;
then, having performed the binding of the directions while recollecting the mantra of the weapon (astra), [he should proceed].
Having taken water in the left hand, one should rub it and apply it with the fingers:
on the head, on the forehead, and likewise on each ear. (12)
In the heart, the two arms, the navel, the two ears, and the head,
[one should apply] one *niṣka* for the purpose of the *niṣka*, and two and a half *niṣkas* respectively.
One should perform the ash-bath for the castes beginning with the Brahmins;
during the Rudra-sandhyās and at the junctions of time (sandhyās), one should assign the limbs of Brahmā.

Having performed three breath-retentions (prāṇāyāma) and the binding of the directions (digbandha) with the Astra-mantra, one should first perform the assignment of the fingers (aṅgulinyāsa) and the assignment of the limbs (aṅganyāsa). || 15 ||
Holding water in the right hand, or that which is situated in the left hand,
one should place it first with the three mantras using the *āpośana* and *arghya* mantras.
Holding water at a height of two cubits while reciting the *antarāghya* mantra,
one should take water in the left hand and circumambulate with the *astra* mantra.
The libation (tarpaṇa) is performed eleven times with the mantra consisting of the limbs of Brahmā.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to both Vedic and Śaiva rites, and having washed one's feet at a garden of the planets or in a temple of Śiva; 18.
On the bank of a river, by a pond, on a mountain, or at a royal assembly, [the temple] should be nine cubits, seven cubits, five cubits, or three cubits [in size]. || 19 ||
One should construct a pavilion that is square, oblong, or circular as desired;
it should be swept, sprinkled with water, and smeared with cow dung.
Having worshipped the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), one should place the seat (kheṭaka) in its center;
above that, the Nirmikā [seat], and first, the western upper seat upon the pedestal.
Above that should be the lotus pedestal, joined with a halo;
it should be provided with a cloth-holding support, a cloth, and a flower-receptacle.
(141) Iron, silver, gold combined with gems,
rudrākṣa beads, coral, and accompanied by strings of pearls. || 23 ||
Adorned with various garlands and ornaments made of the nine precious gems,
it was covered with fine garments and beautified by diverse decorations.
It should be provided with a piece of cloth, joined with the purification of the liṅga, accompanied by a vessel for fragrance, and endowed with a vessel for flowers. || 25 ||
The conch-holder and the conch, the bowl-stand and the bowl, the small vessel and the small-vessel holder, and the water-receptacle bowl. || 26 ||
A water-vessel filled with a droṇa of water, a vessel for drawing out water, perfume, incense, a lamp, and the ārātrika rite performed first above and then below. (27)
The bathing altar, the footstool, together with a standing lamp,
joined with the vessel for the holy water (tīrtha), as well as the vessel for clarified butter and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
A cooking vessel together with its lid, a side-dish tray joined with its receptacle, rice, a hide, a ladle, and a wooden tripod stand. || 29 ||
A fan joined with a coconut and equipped with a sharp blade, along with a vessel, is said to be prepared; this is called "preparation by means of materials. || 30 ||
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, red sandalwood, Himalayan water, black fragrant substance, and the two types of gorocana. (31)
A flower, the fivefold flower, the eightfold flower, and the alms-bowl; a bracelet, a hanging garland, as well as bilva fruit, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice grains. || 32 ||
Thus, it should be filled with water and provided with the substance of water;
it should be joined with the substances for the *pādya* offering and so forth, and joined with the substances for incense and so forth. (33)
Kapila ghee, pure oil, powdered head-hair paste,
the nectar of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and coconut should be prepared with great care.
It should be provided with plantain fruit, accompanied by bathing materials, and various garments and cloths should be diligently offered. (35)
It may have five, three, or one thread, or be measured by the number of Rudras (eleven);
it may be encircled by seven tubes, five tubes, or a single tube.
Cow’s ghee combined with the flame of a lamp, or the oil of vasu;
whatever is desired may be used, as well as cow’s ghee or the oil from the seeds of trees.
Two *prasthas* and so on up to four *droṇas* of pure rice, along with salt in the prescribed proportion, and accompanied by various side dishes and condiments. || 38 ||
Marīci, salt, cumin, mustard seeds, as well as the fruit and leaf of the betel nut, and white powder (śvetacūrṇaka). || 39 ||
Ashes, a mirror, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a palm-leaf fan, a seat, kusha grass, wood, and even the skin of a spotted deer; || 40 ||
The wise one should prepare a seat consisting of a tiger skin, hair, and a garment of precious woolen cloth; this is declared to be the sequence of worship. (41)
Facing north and seated upon a beautiful seat,
he should then perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
The binding of the directions is said to be the striking of the head; therefore, perform it.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one should carry out the sequence of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). (43)
One should sever the five knots and perform [the ritual] from the head to the end of the feet;
having performed the immersion in nectar, one should place the hand-gestures (karanyāsa) upon the fingers.
One should perform the placement of the thirty-eight syllables beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha upon the limbs;
then, having consecrated the Hand of Śiva, one should worship Śiva within the lotus of the heart.
One should perform the oblation at the navel and meditate on Śiva in the center of the heart;
this is declared to be the purification of the self. Now hear about the worshiper of the Sun and others.
Whether on a small mound or upon the ground, one should perform the worship of the Sun in due order;
facing the eastern direction, one should draw the solar disc.
Then, those two having been drawn within the circle according to the desired mandala,
[the disciple] should rise with the mantra while the vessel is filled with water.
One should worship with red sandalwood, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the heart-mantra;
then, one should sprinkle the water of the respectful offering (arghya) upon the palm of the right hand for the purpose of beholding the Noble One.
Having mentally established Daṇḍin, Piṅgala, Gaṇeśa, and the Guru, as well as Prabhūtāsana, Vimala, and Saura; || 50 ||
Having propitiated the Supreme One, one should place the lotus in the center;
[the mantras] Dīptā, Sarvatomukhī, Arkāsana, and Khaṣolkā.
Joined with the *nāda* and the *visarga*, doubled and conjoined with the *rasa* (the letter *sa*), it is joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, and conjoined with Ananta and Rudra. || 52 ||
Having uttered the mantra joined with the third vowel, beginning with *nnāda*, conjoined with *śiva*, and ending with *namaḥ*, recite *sūryam* and perform the worship of the Sun. (53)
The Sun, resembling saffron in hue, adorned with all ornaments, having two eyes and a beautiful face, and anointed with red garlands and unguents. || 54 ||
Endowed with four arms, with two hands holding lotuses, possessing the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and adorned by a halo of light. || 55 ||
He should be depicted as wearing the sacred thread, joined with the dawn and the early morning light, seated upon a lotus, or mounted on a chariot accompanied by Aruṇa. || 56 ||
Having meditated upon and worshipped [the deity] together with his retinue by means of the six-limbed rite, [one should worship] Soma,
Aṅgāraka, Saumya, Guru, Śukra, and Śanaiścara.
One should worship the eight planets, beginning with Rāhu and Ketu, starting from the east and ending in the northeast;
thereafter, one should offer milk-rice and present incense, lamps, and other offerings.
Having worshipped Tejaścaṇḍeśvara and prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness;
having performed the washing of the feet, draw a maṇḍala before the deity.
Having prepared the general offering (sāmānyārghya) and having sprinkled the ground with that very water,
[one should prepare an area] sixteen fingers in length and endowed with a square shape.
Having wiped [the hands] with the Vāmadeva mantra using the palm of the left hand,
one should perform the purification of the place (sthānaśuddhi) with the mantra "bhūmirbhūmnā."
One should arrange the materials for the bath, including the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the nectar (amṛta), along with the arghya;
one may place them on the right side of the deity or as desired in the mind.
Facing north and seated upon a beautiful seat,
one should perform the placement of ashes, the placement of the hands (karanyāsa), and the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa). (63)
Then, one should worship the vessel containing the substances for the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth;
or alternatively, there may be a single vessel for the water for the feet, the water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya).
Having washed the vessel, one should examine it with the Weapon-mantra and the Heart-mantra;
then, having placed the conch above the tripod, one should perform the avakuṇḍana rite.
One should fill the vessel with water while recollecting the limbs of Brahmā;
with the mantra of the left hand, one should mutter the Śiva-gāyatrī.
Having touched the Surabhimudrā, one should sprinkle the vessel according to the rule;
O Goddess, the base of the conch is the earth, and its deity is Viṣṇu. (67)
One should wear the Ghoradeva amulet, which has the Sun as its deity;
and one should cause the seven sacred fords (tīrthas) to enter the mouth, which has the Moon as its deity.
The three quarters [of the Veda] have the deities as their presiding powers (adhidevatya): Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
the metre and the foundational power (ādhāraśakti)—these are the presiding deities.
Then, having performed the purification of the pedestal (pīṭhaśuddhi), one should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
Likewise, Vṛṣeśvara is in the east, while Bhāskara is on the left side of the bull.
One should worship Maheśa in the south-eastern quarter, Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the south,
Gaṇeśa in the south-western quarter, and Kamalodbhava to his left.
One should place Ṣaṇmukha in the region of the wind (the northwest), Vidyāpīṭha in the south, Nṛttamūrti in the north, and Kṣetrapālaka in the northeast.
Between Kubera and Anila, one should install the Liṅgodbhava;
between Soma and Śaṅkara, one should install the Bhakta and the others in due order. (73)
One should place the Ekākṣarī on the left side of the devotees;
and to the left of the Ekākṣarī, one should place Lakulīśa.
Having placed a flower upon the head, one should thereafter worship the door;
one should sprinkle the western door with the weapon-mantra and with the auspicious water of Śiva.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa on the right and Vāgdevī on the left side,
one should worship Mahālakṣmī in the center, and Nandin and Gaṅgā on the right.
One should especially worship Mahākāla and Yamunā on the left side;
having worshipped them above and below, one should then thoroughly worship the Śiva-weapon.
One should worship the Gaṇeśas up to the Kṣetrapālas with their respective mantras;
thus, at the western door, the food offering (naivedya) is placed at the eastern face.
Having grasped the *liṅga* with his hand, he should place it upon the sacrificial altar for bathing;
having sprinkled it with the water of the *arghya* offering, he should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the faces.
One should assign the mantras of the five Brahmans to the fingers from the thumb to the little finger;
then, one should collect nine flowers between the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger.
One should discard the flower offerings (nirmālya) with the thumb and forefinger;
at the time of dismissal, one should place that flower upon the head.
Having discarded the floral remains (nirmālya), one should offer them to Caṇḍeśa;
then, having performed the consecration with pure water, one should mutter the Pāśupata weapon-mantra (astra).
Having taken [the breath] from the *mūlādhāra*, one should deposit it into the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
This, which is to be understood as the instruction of the Guru, is declared to be the purification of the mantra. (83)
Having mentally conceived the moving seat (calāsana), one should place it upon the flower at the crown;
then, having performed an anointing, there follows consecration with pure water.
One should rub the body, as well as the linga and its pedestal, with powdered flour;
then perform the consecration with pure water and place a flower upon the head.
Having bathed [the image] in the nectar of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should consecrate it with water;
then, recollecting the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should place a flower upon its head.
Milk, curd, ghee, honey, as well as coconut water, sugarcane juice, pure water, and an ablution with scented water [should be offered]. (87)
Then, having offered the mantra-flower (mantrapuṣpa), one should present the mantra-food (mantrānna).
Having wiped [the deity] with a white cloth, one should place a flower upon the head.
Having established [the deity] upon the lotus-seat while recollecting the Śiva-mantra,
one should worship the five seats and arrange them one above the other.

Having worshipped the lotus-seat (kamalāsana), one should worship the petals, the filaments, and the pericarp with the mantra "namaḥ" (obeisance); likewise, one should worship the seed-syllables with "saḥ".
One should worship [the deities] from Śakti up to Śaktiparyanta on the tips of the petals;
having placed Manonmanī upon the pedestal, she who resembles pure crystal.
Having invoked Śiva in the center of that, one should worship him with five enclosures:
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna.
Ambigaṇā, Ambikā, Bhāginī, Gaurī, and Umā likewise [are situated] in the west, north, south, east, and the northeast. (93)
The Heart, the Head, the Topknot, the Armor, the Eye, and likewise the Weapon;
Vāmī, Nīlī, Pāśāṅgī, Khaḍginī, and likewise Jambinī.
One should worship the obstruction born of disease located in the southeast;
[and likewise] Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, and Ekanetra. (95)
Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin;
Bhūmi, Svāhā, Svadhā, Kānta, Puṣṭi, Kīrti, and Ameya. (96)
The enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) has been declared; one should worship them starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna, as well as Vṛṣa, Nandin, Gaṇeśa, Mahākāla, and Guha.
One should worship Bhṛṅgin, Gaurī, and Caṇḍeśa, from Indra to Īśāna;
likewise Bhadrā, Kuṇḍalī, and the consort of Bhṛṅgin.
Devayānī, Caṣṭādī, Rūpiṇī, and Caṇḍikīśaka are declared to be the enclosure of Gaṇeśa; one should worship them in sequence by their own names.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, Īśa, Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha, and Īśāna. (100)
And with Svāhā and Śānti, give [protection], O Kālakarṇī, O Dehinī!
And with Bhoginī, Ghoṣaśakti, Gambhīṇī, and likewise Harṣaṇī! 101.
Then Lakṣmī and Vārī, followed by the selection of the guardians of the directions in order:
the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, and likewise the banner. (102)
Holding a mace, a trident, a discus, and a lotus—thus possessing ten weapons; with a serene soul and yet the essence of wrath, O you whose nature is both gentle and fierce! (103)
Vṛṣātmikā, Vṛkatātmikā, Mahātmi, and Maṅgalātmi—this is declared to be the enclosure of the Lord of Weapons (Astreśa); one should worship them in this sequence.
A garment, a neck-ornament accompanied by ghee and water, scented flowers, a crown, and a dangling bracelet with a garland; 105.
A sacred thread of rudrākṣa beads, a necklace of coral, a garland of pearls,
and an ornamented golden girdle variegated with gold and gems.
In the eastern region is the Unmanifest (Avyakta), in the southern region of the sphere of Niyati is [the principle] called Kāla,
and in the northern region is that called Kalā.
One should place the moon above and Mādhava below;
this is declared to be the yogic posture (yogāsana), and one should worship Śiva in its center.
Having offered incense, banners, lamps, and food offerings,
and having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should place a mandala before the deity.
One should strictly avoid food that is overcooked, undercooked, or stale;
having prepared the vessel, one should fill it with the food offering (naivedya). || 110 ||
Salt covered with fans and wrapped in cooked leaves, along with milk mixed with sugar and fruits, and curd, should be placed in the middle [of the row]. (111)
Perform the sweeping and sprinkling on the path for the raising of the food offering, which is accompanied by the vow of clarified butter and consists of garments and the like. 112.
One should place water for the feet (pādya) above each of the images individually;
then, one should perform the sprinkling with the Astra-mantra and likewise the triple-clapping of the hands (tālatraya).
Then, having performed the binding of the directions (digbandhana), one should display the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā).
Having offered the water for sipping (āpośana) and the respectful offering (arghya), perform the washing of the hands.
Having taken fresh flowers, one should offer them to Gaṇeśa;
then, after discarding those flowers, one should perform the washing of the hands and other such rites.
Having offered abundant sacrificial oblations, one should present drinking water;
however, the food offering for the images of Maheśa and others should be presented with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
The remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of Sadāśiva should be placed near Caṇḍeśa;
all the remaining offerings should be discarded in the northeast (aiśānya).

Then, having performed the purification of the *liṅga*, one should again offer the *arghya* water; the rubbing of the hands has been prescribed, and one should apply the mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*). 118.
Afterward, one should offer betel-leaf after having presented the daily purifying thread (pavitraka);
then, having performed the daily fire-sacrifice (agniyajana), one should perform the internal bali offering.
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, after that, one should offer the *ārātrika* ceremony,
as well as sacred ash, a mirror, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, and a palm-leaf fan.
Accompanied by Vedic hymns, dance, song, and instrumental music, the wise man,
having taken a flower between his little finger, ring finger, and middle finger, [should perform the rite].
The rosary should be made of *nakṣatranāyaka* (pearls), and the moon should be its central bead;
having covered it with a clean cloth while recollecting the root mantra.
At the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should place [the flower] upon the head at that very moment.
Having worshipped the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), one should perform circumambulation and prostration. (123)
Having announced the completion of the worship, he should perform the adoration with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and the name-mantras (nāma).
Then, having taken water in his cupped palms, the Guru should offer the final libation (arghya) for dismissal.
One should perform the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) and unite all the deities within oneself;
having performed the seating as before, one should collect the primary liṅga and other items.
Having covered each of the images individually with flowers and cloth,
he should worship Caṇḍeśa with the materials remaining from the previous worship.
Having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings with the weapon-mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ" addressed to Dhvanicaṇḍeśvara, the Guru should perform the dismissal (visarjana) of the arghya.
Śiva is in the head, the throat, the two breasts, and the two elbows of the hands;
thus, day by day, having worshipped him, one should perform the ritual as before in the proper sequence. || 128 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Worship for One's Own Benefit," in the *Sūkṣmatantra*.
I shall describe the installation of Gaurī; listen to the two distinct types of yoga.
One should perform the rite with the Lord joined by Umā, seated together upon a single throne.
The form of the Goddess was indeed in union (yogarūpa), namely Ardhanārīśvara;
however, the Lord was established separately, and I too was established separately. || 2 ||
Viṣṇu is not joined with the gift of water from the auspicious path;
whether she is seated on the same seat or seated on a different seat. (3)
The two types of Kṛtayoga are declared to be on the right side of the one mounted upon the bull (Śiva),
while for all other forms, they are arranged on the left side.
In the case of the primary, partless, and exalted [liṅga], the portion for worship shall be tenfold;
O Goddess, it is fashioned according to the logic of the deity's height measured by its own arms.
And thus, in the eleventh [chapter], the rule for the height of the Goddess is set forth;
having invoked the Niṣkala deity as the root, one whose abode is momentary [should proceed].
Having joined the Goddess, who has been brought to rest by Viṣṇu, with Kalyāṇa at the base once the rite is completed, O Goddess, one should enter after the bath.
Whether the temple is constructed at the edge of the enclosure wall or outside it,
the Goddess is installed within the inner sanctum (garbha), having been placed upon a couch and other such furnishings.
One should offer perfumes and other oblations, as well as food and betel;
by means of this ritual service at the conclusion of the worship at night.
Having performed a circumambulation of the watchtower, especially that of Śiva himself,
[the procession] was adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by every kind of musical instrument.
One should worship the Goddess at the door of the temple with various offerings, accompanied by songs of victory and auspiciousness, using perfumes, flowers, and other such items.
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and entered the inner chamber,
one should prepare a seat for the Goddess on the right side of the God.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and offer milk-rice (*pāyasānna*) while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Afterwards, having performed the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), [the image] should be adorned with all ornaments. (13)
Afterwards, one should perform the sacrifice properly; one should not arrange it otherwise here.
At the time of dawn, one should carry out the installation of the Goddess.
Adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by shouts of victory and other sounds,
perform the consecration in the temple according to the path that has the *yap* as its primary element.
One should worship each deity individually, excluding the [central] deity;
thus has the method of the path been declared—now hear of its many varieties. (16)
The Viśaṃ, Krama, Yoga, Saṅkara, and Raudra [steps]—these five should be known; one should cause them to be performed according to their defining characteristics.
In a temple or a pavilion, or even in the form of a garland,
it should be constructed according to the sequence prescribed by the technical characteristics, specifically starting from three cubits and so forth.
Wherever the stūpa is joined, one should have it constructed in five ways:
in the northeast, southeast, and likewise the west of the temple.
And just as in other delightful directions within, one should not construct the fundamental object by way of a path of five enclosures. || 20 ||

The procedure for the self-manifested linga (svayambhuva) is properly prescribed in twenty ways; likewise, the sequence for those of divine origin (daivika) and those of sage origin (ārṣaka) is correctly ordained.
One should prescribe the yoga for both the human and the arrow-liṅga;
however, outside of villages and the like, one should perform the mixed-saṅkara rite.
One should perform all the rites, such as the preparation of the bed, and worship the Vīra correctly;
one should especially fashion the Vīra according to the proportions of the root-liṅga.
One should specifically construct the pedestal according to the measurement of the base; the union with the *liṅga* is properly performed by means of the measurement of the *liṅga* itself. (24)
The Miśra-śakti is prescribed according to the measurement of the Hero’s neck, or else by the measurements of the womb, the primary abode, and so forth. (25)
Or one may perform it with a *virāj* measure or even with a finger-measure;
beginning from nine fingers and increasing by two or three fingers at a time.
O Goddess, the height (tuṅgaka) is ninefold, ending at twenty-five units;
beyond that, the height is said to be ninefold, increasing by two units at each stage.
Four, six, eight, ten, twelve, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, and twenty units—thus the height is ninefold, according to the divisions of the best (uttama) and so forth. (28)
Two cubits in height, with a beautiful face and especially holding flowers in her hands;
she has full and elevated breasts, a neck marked by three folds like a conch shell, and lovely eyes. (29)
She wears garments of two colors, stands upon a lotus seat, or sits upon a lion throne, adorned with all ornaments. || 30 ||
It is joined with a northern face or even a western face;
the face is said to be of the same nature as the original image.
One should especially fashion the Goddess with a medium height of ten tālas;
for images such as those in a comfortable posture (sukhāsana), the proportions should be according to their respective measurements.

The wise one should make [the nose] ending at the tip of the nose, or ending at the middle of the eyebrows, according to the measurement of the ear, or by means of the *mātrā*-finger, using the same number as previously stated. (33)
In this same manner, the wise one should perform the rites for the *mūla-mantras* and so forth.
Now I shall describe the *saṅkara*, the *raudra*, and especially the *svatantra* [rites].
To the east of the temple, or to the south, or in another pleasant location, there should be a pond or similar feature on the side. (35)
One should construct either a temple or a pavilion together with surrounding walls,
specifically starting from three cubits in size for those consisting of one story and so forth.
Whether it be of Brahmā, of the gods, of humans, or of the Piśācas,
one should install the fierce Saṅkara, either two-armed or four-armed.
Having established [the image] facing east, or indeed facing north, or even facing west—but never facing south. (38)
If the seat is well-established or even associated with the rite of the trident, one should especially fashion it from stone, metal, or painted materials. (39)
One should especially fashion the primary image of Śambhu as Śakti;
the wise man should place Śambhu on her right side. (40)
He may have two arms or four arms, with a form corresponding to that of the Goddess;
he should be placed either in the fire-altar of the Goddess, or in front of her, or even to her right.
One should especially place that very pure [image] in front of him;
it may face west, east, or likewise north.
Whether standing, or reclining, or even ready to depart,
or situated at the sides of Śaṅkara during his installation (pratiṣṭhā). || 43 ||
To the east of Śaṅkara, the ascetic should install Vighneśa,
either in a standing posture, a seated posture, or even upon a mouse.
To the north of that goddess, or likewise in the northeast;
or in the region of Śaṅkara belonging to the goddess, either to the east or even to the north.
Regarding the installation of Durgā, it is prescribed that [the site] should be neither too far nor too near;
rather, it should be at the edge of the enclosure wall, either to the east or in the northeast.
One should perform the installation of the Teacher, whether he be standing or seated;
or one may install Kṣetrapāla, either outside or inside [the shrine]. (47)
In the inner area, one should fashion a sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) according to the same method as for Śiva, either in front of the temple or elsewhere.
Whether without attendants or with an extensive display according to one's means, [one should perform worship] upon images using comfortable seats and so forth, both externally and internally. (49)
One, two, or three [of these], or indeed all of them, one should especially fashion from metals and the like, or from paints and so forth. || 50 ||
Thus the *saṅkara* [type] has been described; now the *raudraka* is being discussed:
the establishment of a village and so forth, either on a mountain or even in a forest. (51)
Whether at the edge of a village, under a tree, or even within a *krośa* of the village,
you should act so that the faces of the village robbers are turned away, just as their backs are.
One should especially perform the fierce [rite] facing toward the city;
one should perform everything specifically in accordance with the patron. (53)
In the temple, in the pavilion, in the middle of the temple,
or indeed in the pavilion of the temple, one should perform the installation of Śambhu as Sakala, Miśra, or Niṣkala.
Having first installed the Liṅga, one should place Cāmuṇḍī to its south,
whether she has four arms, six arms, or eight or ten arms.
One should likewise fashion the arm as twelve or sixteen units,
if [the image includes] Vināyaka, Durgā, and Śaṅkara with his bull.
Or else, the Great Teacher [established] Skanda in that place;
or again, the distinction regarding Gaurī will be explained in another manner.
Whether in the middle or even in the other [postures], it is two-armed and embodies power (śakti);
with the ankles placed in the ūrdhvajānu position, the hands rest upon the knees.
To his front, on the right side, there should be the bull of Śaṅkara, either standing nearby or lying down. (59)
One should [place] Vighneśa or Kumāra in the eastern direction of Śaṅkara;
and directly in front of those two, one should place Durgā or Sarasvatī.
Or else, having fashioned a great moṭikā or a great weapon by others, one should place the kṣetrapāla either inside or outside, or near or far. || 61 ||
One should especially construct a pedestal for offerings (balipīṭha) to the east of the goddesses;
one should fashion the festival image with two arms and its natural form.
Adorned with the emblems of Śiva, having installed [the image] facing east in a beautiful temple or pavilion, whether it has two arms or four arms.
With his knees raised and joined, his feet and back are pressed against the ground.
In the portion of the Brāhmī [quarter] or in the Paiśāca [quarter], or alternatively in the Brāhmī [quarter],
one should properly install Kṛttikā and meditate upon her by the name Ambikā.
To its left, or to the east, or even to the south, or likewise to the west— one should perform [the rite] and the wise should arrange everything accordingly.
He may have two arms or four arms, with the intention of moving backward;
these are described as the characteristics of the Aṣṭhanaka [Aṣṭanāga] image.
To his front, Durgā should be neither too far nor too near;
likewise, Vighneśa may be situated in a direction of the Goddess, if it is possible.
Or else, it is known as the "Five-Formed" (pañcamūrti) when there is a single thread on the outside;
specifically, it should be in front of the Goddess, or on both sides.
They likewise gaze upon Śaṅkara, Vighneśa, and the Blessed One Śāstṛ,
as well as others, or they look toward the movement of animals.
Within an area of three daṇḍas, or otherwise within five daṇḍas,
one should [place] the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa), the great seat (Mahāpīṭha), and the retinue all around.
The seat, the months, the power (śakti), and the limbs of the power beginning with Śiva—
one should perform these in this very manner in many various ways.
(159) One should especially place the earth [element] conjoined with the base of the trident;
first, however, one should perform the deposition of jewels (ratnanyāsa) at each of the locations of the base.
At the time of the installation of an image made of stone, one should first place a jewel in the east;
however, in the case of images made of metal and other materials, this is preceded by the ritual of opening the eyes.
In the performance of the rite for producing variegated effects,
one should place the nine gems and so forth either at the root of the tree mentioned above, or upon the ground.
The wise one should perform the consecration according to the procedure for installing Durgā;
likewise, perform the installation of the Teacher (Śāstṛ) according to the procedure for installing the Teacher.
In the installation of Vighneśa, one should install Vighneśa in due order;
and according to the procedure for the mixed-liṅga, one should install Miśreśa in due order.
One should measure their respective forms individually by means of the *mūladhāma* and other units;
here, one should specifically [measure] the Lord of the Field (*kṣetreśa*) according to his own path.
One should perform all the attendant rites there according to the prescribed rule;
one should perform those for Saṃkara and Raudra according to the previously mentioned rule. (79)

In this very manner, one should perform [the rite] according to the rules of craftsmanship during the period of the sun's northern course (uttarāyaṇa), in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day. || 80 ||
Or during stable *mṛta-yogas*, or likewise during other auspicious ones;
on an auspicious weekday, in a stable ascendant, in an auspicious division (*aṃśa*), and at a favorable moment (*sumuhūrta*). || 81 ||

The installation of the Śakti should be auspiciously performed under a lunar mansion favorable to the patron; one should construct the measurement of the Śakti according to the form of the temple and so forth. (82)
According to the prescribed rule for their respective powers, one should fashion Śaṅkara and the others,
as well as their various mounts, seats, and so forth, along with the wise ones. (83)
One should perform the calculations of income, expenditure, and so forth according to the rules of their respective systems.
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
It should be fifteen cubits in measure, or sixteen, or twelve;
or it may be six, seven, eight, or even nine cubits.
It should be ten cubits in extent and provided with four doors;
one should construct an altar in the center, occupying one part out of nine parts.
One should arrange nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) all around the altar;
having smeared it with cow dung, one should place them upon the leveled ground.

The "platform for the site" (sthānavedikā) consists of an unenclosed area outside the altar, joined with four archways and adorned with garlands of darbha grass, established according to one's capacity.
The width of the altar is three cubits and five cubits;
its height is eight cubits, and it has fourteen tiers.
One should fashion the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) as either circular or square;
however, for the principal Śakti Durgā, one should have them made in the shape of a womb (yoni).
At the time of the installation of the immovable [image],
one should perform the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) together with the tuft of grass and the mirror, concluding with the rite of liberation (mokṣa).
p. 161) Or, by a river, a pond, or in the middle of water, construct a water-shed (*prapā*).
Having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass, one should install the Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā. || 92 ||
The wise person should perform the purification of each individual image in particular, including those on vehicles and so forth, provided they are adorned with all ornaments. 93.
Having wrapped each of the images, especially the central one, with cloth,
one should place them specifically within the water together with *kūrca* grass.
For five nights, or three nights, or even for one night;
or for half a day, or half of that, or even half of that again. || 95 ||
Having emerged from the water onto the altar, one should specifically bathe each [deity] individually with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The wise one should place all the items, beginning with the bed, individually according to the prescribed rite;
the wise one should then install the *vardhanīs* from the center up to the northeast.
One should worship [the deity] provided with garments and other offerings, using perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
one should then sequentially place all the Śaktis, beginning with Āryā, within the Vardhanīs.
In the procedure for the Great Liṅga, however, once a separate mirror has been fashioned,
one should construct it entirely from sacrificial trees, especially with great care.
Sacrificial grass, clarified butter, milk, mung beans, mudga beans, and *prayaṅgu* seeds;
sesame, mustard, and *nīṣpāva*—the pulse cake is the eleventh. (100)
One should perform the homa separately with the respective mantras for each limb of Brahman;
having offered the *vyāhṛtis* at the end of the substances, one should touch the image with the *kūrca*.
And the wise preceptor, having become separate, should, at an auspicious moment,
perform the rite with the Śakti-kūṭas, and all the preceptors should likewise grant their authorization.
One should perform meditation in each of the directions, extending to every quarter;
at the beginning and the end of all [these rites], the wise man should cause the proclamation of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be made. (103)
Having sprinkled [the image] with the Pavamāna hymns accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas (brahmaghoṣa),
one should thus keep a vigil at night and perform the ritual bath in the morning.
Having become pure, one should offer [the image] to the teacher individually and especially;
having removed the image from its bed, it is offered as something distinct from the original image.

Having worshipped thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, one should first perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa); then, specifically for each [deity], one should perform the offering of clarified butter upon the head.
The wise one should perform the consecration with the central and other jars; he should indeed place [the deities] beginning with Āryā and ending with Bhagavatī within that [vessel]. 107.
One should perform this very same procedure for Śaṅkara and the others by means of the central region of that [channel], using the root mantra of Manonmanī. (108)
O Great Mother, having performed the sprinkling and especially the consecration for the great image,
the consecration should take place in mirrors at its base.
There, one should honor the teacher with garments, gold, and rings; one should also honor him separately with cows, land, and food. 110.
One should offer oblations to the Hotṛ priest and especially betel-leaf;
at the conclusion, one should perform a great festival, and especially a procession.
At the time of installing the immovable image, and especially in the case of a mirror,
one should perform all the rites not explicitly mentioned here according to their respective injunctions.
Among all the systems of commitment (samayas), the Śaiva alone is the most preeminent.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are said to constitute the triple form (trimūrti). (113)
From him, Indra and Vighneśa are remembered as the fivefold form; from that, Skanda and likewise Durgā are remembered as the sevenfold form. || 114 ||
And she who is seated upon a throne, Gaurī together with Śaṅkara in his entirety, as well as Vighneśa, and especially Āryā and the Teacher (Śāstṛ). || 115 ||
It should be known as the "Mixed Power" (Miśraśakti), which brings about all accomplishments;
it should be known as the "Fivefold Form" (Pañcamūrti), which constantly increases victory.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, along with Jyeṣṭhā, Gaurī, and Sarasvatī—all these abide within a single form; thus she is called the Sixfold Form (Ṣaṇmūrti). || 117 ||
If, in front of them, there is a field-lord (Kṣetreśa) or a Nāga, according to their availability—this is known as the *saṅkara* [arrangement], which is beneficial for all living beings. || 118 ||
In each of these various divisions, one should perform [the rite] by way of the corpse;
otherwise, if one should act differently, one will certainly not obtain food from the village. (119)
Therefore, with every effort, one should indeed perform [the rite] according to the Kāmika and other [Tantras],
whether Hari or anyone else may be present within those various specific divisions.
One should have that which is known as Śaiva performed according to the Śaiva Tantra;
and in the remaining divisions, such as the Buddhist and others, the forms of Āsna and the rest [should be used]. (121)
In a single possible location, that is remembered as belonging to Śiva;
it is the region of Viṣṇu facing west, and of the Śaktis and others.
That western face is Śakti; it is then called Vaiṣṇava.
One should perform this especially according to the Vaikhānasa Pāñcarātra. (123)
If, however, a bull is present in every respect within that region, it is declared to be a division of Śaivism; indeed, the Tāṇḍava is the pure Śaiva.
Thus, the most excellent knower of signs should observe in many ways;
for [a woman] who is worshipped out of ignorance comes from other than the Śaiva [tradition]. 125.
Furthermore, after the consecration, it removes all defects for men, especially if worship and sacrifice have been neglected for a long time. (126)
Furthermore, through delusion regarding the nature of other paths,
there arises specifically the fear of undesirable things in villages, which increases all calamities.
Therefore, with every effort, one should establish [the disciple] on the path of Śiva;
for after ten years have passed, it is possible that he might become devoid of worship.
One should perform the re-invocation or commence the sprinkling;
then, one should properly undertake the consecration according to the sequence prescribed for installation.
According to the path prescribed for atonement, one should surround [the area] with a single [line];
whether it be a pustule, or something decayed, or affecting a single limb, or the entire body. (130)
Having observed the decay of all the limbs, one should perform [the rite] according to the previously mentioned path;
that body would then become a temple, and therefore it does not remain as a mere pillar (sthāṇu).
Furthermore, one should especially perform [the rite] by way of re-establishment;
alternatively, some may make Gaurī the primary deity, or Vighneśa the primary one.
In the case of the Blessed One, the primary element is *pradhāna*; for Śaṅkara, it is *pradhānaka*.
For the Teacher (*śāstṛ*), it is primarily something [else], while for another, it is primarily light (*jyotis*). (133)
One [school] holds Skanda to be supreme, another holds Kārttikeya to be supreme; one holds Viṣṇu to be supreme, while another holds Śaṅkara to be supreme. (134)
The two-formed, the three and three-formed, and beyond that the five-formed;
the seven-formed in seven ways, the eighth, and indeed the nine-formed and the ten-formed. (135)
One should worship Gaurī, Āryā, and others, as well as Bhāskara, the principal [deities], the vehicles, the principal [deity] near the feet, and the previously mentioned deities. 136.
If one should perform such an installation among the worlds, one should especially perform all these various types within this [rite]. || 137 ||
The installation of Gaurī has been declared; now listen attentively to the division concerning Śiva.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Installation of Gaurī," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme characteristics of Pārvatī,
for the benefit of all the world and for the destruction of all calamities.
For the benefit of women, as a cause for all auspiciousness, and especially for the sake of beautifying the primary linga or for the sake of its graceful play. || 2 ||

Just as the *mastu* (curd-whey) is for the limbs of the bed, so the wise man should fashion the *vesara* (hybrid) style for the primary temple of Śaṅkara, as well as for the temples of Pāvaka and Nairṛta.
Outside the inner circle, however, there is an inner necklace on the two excellent sides;
one should not cause the end of the middle necklace to extend outside.
It may indeed be in the form of a palace, a pavilion, or a gateway;
likewise, it may be in the shape of a garland, according to the sequence starting with the Brāhmaṇas.
For all castes indeed, the Drāviḍa style is said to be the proper abode,
whether specifically on the exterior or interior of the walls and enclosures.
Whether outside the main temple or within the interior of the temple,
the binding of the ritual cord (sūtrabandha) must be performed for the destruction of enemies.

The shaking of the enclosure wall is not desired; yet this [shaking] is desired [only when it occurs elsewhere], for it bestows all virtues upon the patron. However, one should never cause this defect to occur in that [enclosure wall] under any circumstances.
One should construct palaces and other such structures according to the measurement of an arrow's length;
beginning from nine cubits, that very measure extends up to twenty cubits.
One should increase the three [measures] by three each, starting from five cubits and ending at fifteen cubits, following the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
But for the intermediate castes, it has been stated that [the height] is from three cubits up to eleven cubits (rudra-hasta). 11.
If all [the parts] are endowed with the same proportions, the measurement is indeed proclaimed as follows:
the height is twice the width, but the base (pāda) is not half of that.
One should construct a pavilion in front, according to the dimensions of the temple;
likewise, one should construct it around the temple and also in close proximity to it. (13)
A wise man should not perform the *sāla-karman* (the ritual of the enclosure) in the vicinity [of the main shrine];
rather, the dance pavilion (*nṛtta-maṇḍapa*) is said to be located outside the front pavilion (*agra-maṇḍapa*).
In front of that, one should then construct an offering pedestal (balipīṭha) complete with its five constituent parts;
the pedestal should be made according to the path prescribed in the treatises on architecture (śilpaśāstra) and endowed with the proper characteristics.
O Hero, this has been correctly explained; one should arrange it according to the sequence of yoga for a self-manifested linga, as well as for those made of stone or metal.
One should cause the palaces of the Asura Bāṇa and the abode of the Liṅga of Pauruṣa to be constructed by means of a pit.
The height of the spire (tāra) should be made equal to the temple, or three-quarters, or half, or even one-quarter; its elevation should be as previously described.
In this very manner, a wise man should construct a temple;
he should cause the abode of the Pauruṣa-liṅga to be built according to that [same] method.
The temple of the same height as the palace is in the southern direction;
and there is also the temple of the self-manifested liṅga in all eight directions.
A wise man should especially cause [the image] to be made, and he should fashion it with its consort;
he should especially have the bed and the woman fashioned out of gold and other precious materials.
In their absence, one should do so with pure stone or wood;
and in the absence of those, one should have the power of sleep depicted upon a wall.
On a cloth or on a wooden board, the wise one should have an image of Pārvatī made;
therefore, with every effort, for the sake of rest, [one should do so] within the state of Manonmanī. (23)
A wise man should have the measurement of the thread-mark made according to the *mānāṅgula*; he should have the best [liṅga] made at fifty [units], doubled [to one hundred]. 24.
Therefore, starting from thirty-one finger-breadths and decreasing by one finger-breadth at each step, there are nine individual offerings, beginning with five finger-breadths. || 25 ||
Each [mandala] should be nine measures, ending with fifteen in sequence;
one may construct it using either the *mātrā*-finger or the finger-measure of the patron (*yajamāna*).
Thus, by the measurement of finger-breadths, the length of the nine [types of] liṅgas is one more than ten;
this is considered the best measurement, equal to the length of the root-liṅga.
For that purpose, the smallest [measurement] is declared; when those two are divided by eight, each part shall be nine units, constituting the three triads beginning with the best (uttama).
One should divide the length of the linga equally into nine parts; each part shall be the measure of one unit, and make the portion for worship equal to that.
The highest [measurement] should be thus for the face, while the lowest is for the purpose of worship;
between those two, at the eighth part, there is a measurement of nine for each.
The height of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be equal to its length, or twice or thrice as long;
this is described as being of three types: superior, middling, and inferior. || 31 ||
One should then divide the measurement of the width of the pedestal into five parts;
the length exceeding by one part is said to be the best.

One should know the smaller [measurement] to consist of five parts; when these two are divided by eight in their midst, each shall be the measurement for the *narma* (the base) as well as the measurement for the *karṇa* (the ear). || 33 ||
O Goddess, one should construct that [pedestal] for the male organ (puruṣaliṅga) according to its height,
using measurements such as the dimensions of the liṅga itself.
One should then divide the width of the temple into nine parts;
furthermore, these are of three types: superior, middling, and inferior. (35)
One should divide the width of the palace into seven parts;
five parts should be known as the best, and three parts shall be the smallest.
One should distribute the best portion to the eldest and the lowest to the youngest; the middlemost should receive an equal share.
Each individual's portion should be nine measures, especially so for the door-pillar.

If one should divide the garbhagṛha (sanctum) into nine equal parts, with the *tāra* (width) being one part, this is said to be the ninefold classification for the measurement of the height (*tuṅga*). || 38 ||

One should know that half a *garbha* is the smallest [measurement], while five parts and four parts constitute the superior measurement; between these two, when divided into eight, the intermediate measurements are declared. (39)
Each of those should be one cubit in length and likewise one cubit in width;
for the liṅgas of Svāyambhuva and the others, the portion for worship should have a height double that.
The measurement exceeding three times the portion for worship is called the best;
the middle [measurement] is twice the length, and that which is equal to it is called the [standard] length. || 41 ||
It is described as being of three kinds: middling, excellent, and inferior;
having divided the portion for worship into nine parts, each one is called a measure.
p.
170) That linga whose worship consists of ten equal parts is called "excellent" (uttama); that which possesses three parts more than that is called "most excellent" (uttamottama). || 43 ||
The medium measurement is twelve parts, while that which is one part less than that is declared to be the inferior measurement for a small liṅga. || 44 ||
When the length of the linga is divided into sixteen parts,
among those, nine parts constitute the primary [size], while the remaining parts constitute the three smaller sizes.
The circumference of the liṅga should be equal to its height, O Goddess;
the middle size is twice that, and the best is remembered as three times that. || 46 ||
The wise man should divide the portion among them as before and perform the work in sequence;
the width should be three times the height, or twice, or equal to it. (47)
It should be of three kinds—superior, middling, and inferior;
the wise one should begin as before according to the measurement of the ear of the *liṅga*.
One should have the male linga made according to the measurement of the thread;
one should lead the auspiciousness of the womb through the eight divisions of income, expenditure, and breath.
Endowed with a lunar mansion favorable to the sacrificer,
and accompanied by all prosperity according to one's capacity, may the king and the kingdom flourish.
Therefore, with every effort, perform [the rite] together with the *āya* and other factors;
having ascertained the height of the mountain, one should divide it by means of the *māna-śūla*. || 51 ||

A wise man should effect an increase by means of the qualities of Vasunanda (eighteen) measured in *mānāṅgulas*; when divided correctly by twelve (*bhānu*), the remainder shall be the *āyā* and so forth. (52)
Therefore, the wise one should first have the pedestal (pīṭha) or seat (pītha) made with its full width.
That [mandala] is increased by eight and adorned with twenty-seven. || 53 ||
In this manner, the remaining asterism would serve as the cause for the continuity of the world;
the wise one should increase it by nine and divide it by seven.
The remainder is declared to be the day (vāra), and the asterism (nakṣatra) is multiplied by four;
having divided that by nine, one should indicate the remaining portion as the degrees (aṃśaka). || 55 ||
The remaining planets, drawn by the Sun, Mars, and Saturn, are indeed considered auspicious;
one should know that an excess of income is auspicious, while an excess of expenditure is inauspicious.
For those desiring smoke, dogs, donkeys, crows, and ungraspable,
pure luster, the elevation of the *pīṭha* on the right side should be in this manner.
The protection of the seat and the protection of the power (śakti) should be mutually auspicious;
one should not act contrary to the family tradition, for from what is favorable, auspiciousness arises. || 58 ||
In this very manner, at the time of commencing the image, one should correctly observe the six auspicious signs so that no [inauspicious] action is performed therein. || 59 ||

And the host of Rakṣasas, Mahendra, the womb, the three-eyed one (Tryakṣa), piercing (Vedha), the cord (Rajju), the zodiac sign (Rāśi), subjugation (Vaśya), and likewise the lord of the zodiac sign (Rāśyādhipa). || 60 ||
One should know their auspicious and inauspicious [results] by examining the reflection;
one should examine the auspicious and inauspicious [results] for the patron by examining his protection.
O Gaurī, that [yoga] in which there is an excess of auspicious [planets] over expenditure bestows all prosperity;
that in which there is an excess of expenditure over auspicious [planets] bestows all defects.
In this very manner the best of teachers should have [the image] made;
otherwise, if he should have the image made differently, the king will perish along with his kingdom. (63)
Because the presence of the deity arises from that [visualization], one should always observe them in this way.
Furthermore, another specific method is now being stated by me. (64)
One should divide the measurement of the Pārvatī-festival by thirty-one;
having multiplied those parts, one should then multiply them by twelve. (65)
The remainder is produced by eight; therein, the procedure is prescribed as follows:
having multiplied those [units] by sixteen, they are to be divided as before.
When there is an excess, it shall be the height of the *tuṅga*; therein, an auspicious measurement is prescribed.
The measurement for the attained height (*utsedha*), however, is twenty-nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
Having performed this correctly and specifically, one should calculate by means of the ten winds;
having subtracted all of those, the remainder is the expenditure by means of the seven.
Multiply those [results] by nine and divide them correctly by six again;
the remainder is known as the expenditure (vyaya), and that which is free from expenditure will be auspicious. || 69 ||
A wise person should specifically calculate those portions by means of the [planetary] day, either as the original number or multiplied by twenty-seven. (70)
Having divided by twenty-seven, one should determine the remaining asterism;
one should count those [remainders] by tens and divide them by twenty-seven.
One should know the remaining asterisms and observe the previously mentioned characteristics;
the height should be calculated by means of the earth-measures, and those [measures] should be increased by eight.
The sages should divide the remainder by seven; that is prescribed as the day of the week.
Having counted those [quotients] obtained through division, one should specifically divide them by twelve. (73)
One should divide by seven; the remainder is said to be the day of the week, starting from the Sun.
One should multiply the measure of the *āvarta* by four in due order. (74)
One should fashion the *hāsaka* with eight [parts]; the remainder is traditionally known as the *yoni*. The portions of the *sedha* should be multiplied by three, according to the rule. (75)
One should divide by eight; the remainder is prescribed here as the *yoni*.
According to the method previously described, one should indeed discern the auspicious and inauspicious. (76)
In this very manner, the supreme instructor should cause it to be made; when there is an excess of income and a deficiency of expenditure, that measurement is the state of equilibrium.
Income that is inferior and expenditure that is primary brings pride, which gives rise to all faults; therefore, with every effort, one should arrange matters so that income exceeds expenditure. (78)
Among them, the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) is preeminent, bringing benefit to all;
the Moon is the lord of the lunar mansions, and therefore its excellence is auspicious. (79)
Likewise, the two portions (aṃśavārau) should consist of the deity; such is the fruit thereof.
In this manner, the best of preceptors should cause it to be performed in many ways.
One should perform the ritual of emanation with whatever measure [is prescribed];
however, at the time of commencing the primary undertaking, one should deliberate upon what is auspicious or inauspicious.
For one whose embryo has been established, one should cause it to be made in this manner:
having taken the measurement of the height, one should then divide it into five parts.
The height of the pedestal (pīṭhaka) is one part; [the plinth] is one part out of four parts;
and the height of the base (pīṭhikā) is one part out of three parts—thus the height of the pedestal is of six kinds. 83.
One should make the height three times the width, or twice the interval,
or even fourfold; and furthermore, it should be provided with five limbs.
At the commencement of an incomparable auspicious rite, one should observe the auspicious and inauspicious signs;
having established them by way of that form and method, the wise man should cause them to be gathered.

One should remove that [old] form there and not interrupt the purification of the mind; at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, the wise one should begin the construction of the image. (86)
The womb [of the mandala] should be established with mantra and accompanied by the Brahma-thread;
one should cause it to be constructed using the same materials as those used for its creation. 87.
An image made of iron and other such metals that is devoid of the [proper] marks—if one installs such an image out of delusion, one shall incur the destruction of worship. (88)
The consecration and worship should be performed; one should install [the image] in another location.
By means of the procedure for another location, the wise man should transfer the image. (89)
One should perform the consecration there and worship right there with devotion;
for among the gods, an image made of metal is especially meritorious when complete with its primary and secondary limbs.
A wise person should establish only that which is endowed with some characteristic; one should not create a name for a substance, nor should one smear a name upon a substance. 91.
Therefore, with every effort, one should arrange [the offerings] at the beginning of the rite;
likewise for the Dānavas and others, as well as for the parasols and other such items. (92)
The act of omission must not be committed; if it were committed, there would be great danger.
If, however, in this world, a quarrel arises and confusion is produced even once— || 93 ||
By that causal path, there is the relinquishing of form everywhere;
in this world, one may assume a human form if there are kinsmen through [the power of] rite and conduct. (94)
Why indeed should this divine form ever be subject to diminution?
One should perform the reconnection of one's own image with the ancient [form] once again. (95)
A wise person should have the images of Brahmakāya and the others fashioned according to the prescribed rite;
they must not be made in the form of stone, for doing so would result in faults.
Having thus examined [the site] according to the rule, the most excellent preceptor should have [the image] fashioned;
indeed, he should have the form of Indra made with a middle measurement of ten tālas.
The uṣṇīṣa is said to be one aṅgula; the head is said to be three aṅgulas.
The face is thirteen aṅgulas, and the neck is recorded as half an aṅgula. || 98 ||
Therefore, [the space] from the end of the *kākameḍhra* up to half a finger-breadth is declared to be the two faces;
the measurement of the thighs constitutes the two faces.
The shank is said to be two mukhas in length, measured by two kolas and one jānu;
the sole of the foot is declared to be one bhāga, while its width is as previously stated.

At the crown of the head, between the eyebrows, in the middle of the nose, at the top of the head, in the middle of the jaw, at one finger-breadth to the left of the navel, and two finger-breadths at the left ankle. || 101 ||
The corner of the eye should likewise be formed by the three units of the fifth [line];
in its center, two types are prescribed, the tip of which is said to be half a barley-corn.
It should be made of two barley-corns in height from the upper and lower skin;
the pupil should likewise be one barley-corn in both length and width.
By means of which the middle black circle (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala) shall constitute one-third of the watch (yāma);
[this is done] on the back between the two ears, extending twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula). (104)
From the tip of the beak to the base of the crest, the measurement is four barley-corns;
from there to the end of the hair (the crown), it is two finger-breadths plus two barley-corns. || 105 ||
The youthfulness of his vision is equal [to that of others], and likewise he bears the name of a sage;
they say his eyelashes and body hairs are black and number ninety. (106)
The region resembling a bow, a lotus, or a fish is said to be distant from the eyes;
however, O best of sages, the two points between the eyebrows are called the *pada*. 107.
From the root of the nose to the tip of the nose, it is said to be six parts of a barley-corn;
its width is three finger-breadths, while the height of the eyebrows is two barley-corns.
The height of the *padapañca* [pedestal] should be known as five [units], and the height of the *puṣkara* [lotus] as six barleycorns;
in this very same way one should make the height, and likewise the width.
Furthermore, the measure of two *ūrṇas* is six *yavas*; that is so stated.
The measure of a sesame flower (*tilaprasūna*) would be half, one, two, three, or four [of those]. || 110 ||
One should gradually imagine the nose-tip as the limit of the support; the thread of the fold extends from the base to the end, measuring two finger-widths plus one barley-corn.
Its length is declared to be four mātrās;
the width of its upper lip is desired to be three barley-corns.
The *pālikā* should be made of barley-corns; likewise, it is desired to have three faces.
Half a barley-corn should be the space for the cow, the lotus, and the nimba tree, while the height should be four barley-corns.
The width of the root of the chin is two barleycorns or half of that;
the width of the lower lip is one barleycorn more than the measure of a lightning-flash.
The width of the *pravāta* [frieze] is desired to be seven barley-corns (*yava*);
however, the *pālikā* of the *madhara* is said to be one and a half barley-corns.

One should know the height of that Hari to be six *aṅgulas*, measured from the sprout-like joint of the forearms to the tip of the excellent *bimba* fruit [of the chin]; however, it is not visible to the eye.
Their height is thirty-two [finger-breadths] plus three barley-corns;
below the teeth, it is one-eighth of that, but at the top of the head, it is sixteen.

The tongue should be six barley-corns in width, one cubit in length, and three finger-breadths in thickness; its elevation should be made in sequence, measuring two barley-corns and three [finger-breadths].
From the lowest point of the barley grain upwards, there is an emergence and movement of three measures;
it should follow the beautiful path for one measure and proceed for two.
Then, his face should be known as having a single uniform luster, resembling the full moon;
above the two lotus-like eyebrows, there should be three barley-grains (yava) plus a half-barley-grain.
The cavity of the ear should be one mātrā in depth and four yavas in width;
the lobe of the ear should be two yavas, and the ear-flap should be equal to that.
The earlobe should be half a mātrā, while the ear-stalk should be one mātrā;
the ear should be shaped like the letter *la*, as taught by the former teachers. (122)
The height of the *picchiṣṭi* should be four finger-breadths above the half-measure mark;
the two front and back tubes, however, should hang down by themselves.
There should be a hanging [measurement] of one finger-breadth from the ear;
from the outer corner of the eye to the root of the ear, there are seven mātras and three yavas. (124)
The distance from the forehead to the hairline should be stated as nine and a half mātrās;
from the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa) to the front hairline, it should be eight aṅgulas.
From the teeth to the end of the side-hair, thirteen finger-breadths are prescribed; likewise, from the back of the head to the hair, it is recorded as being twelve and a half [finger-breadths].
On the surface of the eyebrows, it is intended to be four mātras in length and shaped like a winnowing basket;
at the joint of the hips, it should be twenty-seven mātras.

They say that in the middle it is one-fifth of the side-length, and at the center of the yoni it is one barley-corn; the width of the maṇḍala is ten finger-breadths, while the upastha is likewise ten finger-breadths.
It should be thirteen and a half mātrās in length from the middle of the hip to the end of the back;
its width should be nine and a half mātrās, and its projection [the part rising above] should be four aṅgulas. || 129 ||
Situated in the middle of the circle on the back is that wind [element], half the size [of the previous];
it has the width of the root and tip of the eyebrows and is endowed with three lines. || 130 ||
The width of the outer border should be sixteen finger-breadths; from the line of the collarbone to the armpit, it is desired to be five finger-breadths. (131)
The rule for the arm is that it measures four mātrās, then two mātrās,
and then one and a half mātrās respectively above the root of the shoulder and neck, over the line of the hiccups.
From the sutra onwards, the hikkā should be twenty-seven mātras;
likewise, the bhujayāma is one mātrā, and the korpara is three mātras.
The forearm is twenty-one finger-breadths; the [span] of the palm is seven units. Half, half, half a unit, and half again is held to be the measure of the middle finger. (134)
The index finger is six sūtras [long], the ring finger exceeds a barley-corn,
and it is known that the little finger and the thumb exceed four measures by half [a measure] each.
The length of the arm should be nine cubits, and the width of the thighs of the Nāga should be one cubit;
the wise man should likewise cause the width [of other parts] to be made one cubit.
The wise know that the width of the elbow (korpara) is eight finger-breadths (mātra);
the base of the forearm (prakoṣṭha), however, should be half a mātra plus one barley-corn (yava). || 137 ||
In the middle of that, the middle width is six barley-corns (yava) or five or six finger-breadths (aṅgula);
at the wrist, however, the width is four mātras or six barley-corns.
The circumference of that base is known by the wise to be three times its width increased by one-fifth, plus an additional half [of that fifth]. (139)
The width of its base is like one and a half [units];
one should know the width at the tip of the ring finger to be equal to the root of the little finger.
The tip of that [finger] consists of eight parts; the joint of the thumb and so forth is half the length of the tip-joint, while its width is desired to be nine [parts]. 141.
The base, the top, and the middle [of the staff] should be three units and two units [respectively];
by means of the joining of the lines of the base, there should indeed be a lotus and a conch in the middle.
The other section to be described is stated by two [verses] to be twenty-one and a half measures;
the space between the heart and the hiccough is seen to be thirteen and a half finger-breadths.
At that time, the breast is desired to be two barley-corns [in height] and fourteen finger-breadths [in circumference];
the width of the breast-circle is proclaimed to be nine mātras. (144)
Half of that [measurement] is the height of the breasts, which should be well-rounded and beautiful;
the nipples should be two barley-corns high, shaped like a snake’s hood or a cluster of *kolaka* fruits. (145)
The middle part should be broad at eleven aṅgulas;
likewise, the lower portions are proclaimed to be two and a half yavas and five and a half [aṅgulas].
The navel, turning clockwise and provided with horizontal lines,
should be broad in the region of the hips and measure seventeen finger-breadths.
The width of the region of the hips is traditionally remembered as being twenty finger-breadths;
the width of the root of the womb is traditionally remembered as being five finger-breadths. (148)
The back should be shaped like an aśvattha leaf, gradually tapering from the base;
from the armpit to the end of the spine, it measures fifteen finger-breadths.
The width of the middle of the belly is seventeen great finger-breadths (mahā-aṅgula), and the width of the region of the hips should be eighteen [great finger-breadths]. 150.
The width of the middle of the thighs should be twenty-one units;
the middle of the knees should be five and a half units, plus one barleycorn.
The width at the base of the shank should be ten mātrās;
its width at the tip should be nine mātrās, increased by three parts. || 152 ||
The *nālaka* is desired to be four *mātrās* with an addition of six barley-corns; its width, height, and elevation are known to be equal to that. || 153 ||

The widths of the ankles should be known as seven and five *yava*s respectively. Whatever has not been mentioned here should be understood according to the methods taught in the treatises of the artisans (*śilpiśāstra*). (154)
A wise man should fashion the goddess from iron for a stone linga;
however, one should not make an iron linga for an iron [base], nor likewise one made of iron for an iron [base].
One should employ [images] made of gold and other materials upon lingas made of wood and the like;
however, in the case of those made of clay or painted on a wall, one should have them fashioned from gold and other such substances.
Having two arms and two eyes, with a dark complexion and lotus-like eyes,
she holds a blue lotus in her right hand while her left hand hangs down.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with every kind of jewelry,
it should be four finger-breadths wide at its best and eight finger-breadths in length.

One should [visualize] the goddess Sustanā, who has a beautiful face, whose feet are adorned with anklets, who is seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), and who is graced by the splendor of the crescent moon. || 159 ||
One should likewise have the Śayana-Ambikā fashioned according to this very procedure, whether it be slightly three-fold or properly mounted upon a pedestal.
O Pārvatī, one should have the auspicious Umā and Caṇḍikā made with two faces, measuring five mānas in height. (161)
A deficiency or excess of even two finger-breadths or two barley-corns brings about defects;
therefore, one should carefully avoid both excess and deficiency. ||162||
If one should have Umā made with the same proportions as the principal image,
one should correctly perform the six auspicious measures, such as length and so forth, according to the measurement of the Goddess.
One should always observe the other mental states as well, such as illusion (māyā) and so forth;
however, that which is free from defects is the defining characteristic of all signs, beginning with the primary sign. (164)
If there is no performance of the rite for them because of the lack of a horse,
then at the time of their commencement, one should observe the constellations and other such factors.
At the commencement of the month of Pauṣa, one should examine the six auspicious factors; in this very manner, according to the prescribed rule, one should arrange everything for all months.
O Pārvatī, having installed [the image] in the eastern direction, it bestows all prosperity upon men;
in the south-eastern direction, one should place it so that it grants sons; and in the southern direction, it grants the attainment of good fortune.
In the northeast (Ishana), one should perform the Jayaka rite; in the west (Varuna), the Shatrunashana; in the northwest (Vayu), the Dhanada; and in the north (Soma), the Sūnuvivardhana. || 168 ||
In the northeast, for the sake of increasing wealth, the fruit for each is stated;
however, in the western courtyard or in the southeast, along with Śaṅkara. (169)
Alternatively, one should establish Vāyu as part of the bedding in the southern portion of that linga which faces the east.
The arrangement of the bedchamber and the courtyards should be made in the eight directions;
or else, like the main temple, the entrance should face north.
The installation of the deity should take place within the space between the base of the Śakti-pillar and the inner sanctum; likewise, if there is a temple for the son of Iṣa (Śiva). || 172 ||
One should have the Puṣyadraṃ constructed according to the measurement of the root-liṅga;
it is made for the purpose of increasing the subjects, according to the measurement of the temple.
