The life-span [of the image] for the sake of strength should be according to the measurement of the inner sanctum;
it should be increased for women according to the measurement of the principal image. (174)
By means of the authority of the *Mūlasūtra*, the increase of cattle, elephants, and so forth occurs;
by the application of the measurement of finger-breadths (*mātrāṅgula*), there is the prosperity of the king and the kingdom. (175)
Having thus examined it according to the prescribed rule, the wise man should have the supreme [image] fashioned;
in the manner thus described, he should likewise have others fashioned as well. || 176 ||
One should undertake the commencement with this substance, having it performed with the substance for the eyes;
at the conclusion, however, it should be equal to that [initial] ritual. || 177 ||
One should perform this procedure in such a manner, especially with metals and the like;
with stones and other materials, it may be done as desired, but one should not apply a coating of paste.
But at the conclusion of the artistic work, the preceptor and the architect, together observing that [the image] is auspicious, should afterwards install the image. || 179 ||
In this very manner the supreme guide should cause [the rite] to be performed;
in such a way, he should cause it to be performed by many paths. || 180 ||
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Goddess," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme ritual of consecration and worship, for the sake of dharma, wealth, desire, and liberation, as well as for pacification and nourishment. (1)
Longevity, glory, victory over death, the destruction of disease, and the subjugation of enemies are proclaimed; it brings about the prosperity of the village, and all calamities perish. (2)
Preceded by the rite of offering the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), it lasts for seven days in five stages;
the three-day ritual pertaining to the Bhuvana is proclaimed as the most excellent, beginning with Śiva.
The Rohiṇī constellation is well-yoked with Puṣya, which is called Vaiṣṇava;
Āditya is said to be Hasta, while the eighth and fourteenth lunar days are [auspicious].
One should perform it especially at the end of a month on the full moon day;
a nine-day period is declared the best, while a seven-day period is middling.
A five-day rite is declared for pacification (śāntika), while a three-day rite is dear to Śiva;
a one-day rite is for the purpose of destroying disease—having understood this, the wise man [should act accordingly].
During the first part of the night, one should perform the rite of Nirvāṇa and offer a lamp;
having performed the consecration with milk, one should then bind the protective thread (kautuka).
The food offering (naivedya) should consist of milk-rice (pāyasa); this is highly praised.
Having bathed in the morning and become pure, [one should honor] both the preceptor and the disciple.
Having performed the smearing with cow-dung and likewise the sprinkling on an auspicious day,
[one should prepare] water-vessels, a vardhanī-pitcher, a water-jar, and a flower-vessel.
The vessels for water for the feet and for sipping, as well as the jars for the consecration,
should be shaped like the *pāṭālī* flower and endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Then, having made [the vessel] a universal receptacle, one should wash it with the Astra-mantra;
standing upon a seat of Darbha grass, one should envelop it with the Kavaca-mantra. || 11 ||
One should gaze with the heart-mantra alone and sprinkle with the Puruṣa-mantra;
the striking is done with the *huṃ phaṭ* syllables, and the touching with the Sadyojāta mantras. (12)
The opening rite (unmīlana) should be performed with the eye-mantra for the pavilion situated to the north;
one should collect water in the water-vessels using water filtered through a cloth.
One should perform [the ritual] at sunrise; one should take water even from the end of the night.
One should take water along with cardamom, nutmeg, camphor, fragrance, and flowers.

Adorned with the five ornaments, the preceptor, together with the image-makers, should perform the ritual of internal sacrifice (antaryāga), including the placement of mantras on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the hands (karanyāsa). || 15 ||
Having understood through yoga that which is superior to the vital breath (prāṇa), one should perform everything accordingly;
then, one should wind both the water-pot (kumbha) and the pitcher (vardhanī) with a thread.
The preceptor [should fashion] the three machines with their respective mantras; likewise, that which is born of jewels, elephant flesh, hair, and sinews [should be prepared] with thread.
One should perform the ablution with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and place the five nectars (pañcāmṛta);
in the center of the bathing pavilion, prepare a mound of rice with śāli grains.
The eastern thread should be the eight-thread [line], and likewise the northern thread;
from one thread to the next thread is a *tāla*, and in the center, one should take nine squares.
On the outside of that, all around, one should leave out one foot;
one should abandon [that area] joined with two doors using cow-dung water.
Prepare either two measures or one measure of rice-grains into polished rice;
polished rice is said to be for the sake of rice-grains, and likewise, sesame seeds are for its sake.
p.
186) Or, with pairs of *droṇa* measures of rice, or with sesame and rice grains, one should perform the drawing of the lines;
then, one should strew *darbha* grass and flowers around it.
It is praised that one should use nine, eight, five, four, three, or two darbha blades; for each step, the blade should be placed with its tip pointing eastward and then northward.
In the center, however, is the Śiva-pitcher; in the middle of the ritual arrangement is the Vardhanī vessel.
[One should offer] water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), and camphor-scented oil.
Nivāra, saffron, sesame, and likewise ājimura,
as well as a water-pot, [should be placed] in the first enclosure in the eight directions.
And on the second enclosure, one should arrange sixteen jars;
likewise, [one should place] madhuka, kṣamāṅgula, uśīra, and sandalwood.
Takola, all kinds of fragrant substances, jasmine and campaka, as well as kalhāra, śatapatra, mālatī, and droṇa. || 27 ||
Parched grain and the three myrobalans, as well as coconut; plantain and jackfruit, and likewise castor seed and mustard. (28)
Gorakṣa, Candana, and Bilva, numbering twenty-five;
likewise Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Hṛṣīkeśa. (29)
Sūryasoma, Mahāsena, Śarvaradra, and Jvareśvara—
one should place these in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa) upon the surface of the deity's hand.
Having worshipped the deity of the second caste as the Grandfather (Brahmā), as well as Indra and the other world-protectors, and Soma, Aṅgāraka, and Bṛhaspati; 31.
Pīṭhala, Manuja, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Iṣi, as well as Vasiṣṭha and Kāśyapa— these, together with the sages, constitute the sixteen. (32)
Having placed [the vessel] upon the palm of the hand seven times, the wise one should perform the ceremonial bathing;
and with eleven *darbha* blades, the preceptor should fashion a brush for the hand.
The knot should be one finger-breadth [in height], and the space [between knots] should be one finger-breadth;
the vardhanī should have nine knots, with a width of one palm-span.
Having worshipped with flowers and perfumes all the jars on the twelve-finger span of the tip of the thumb, while reciting their respective mantras; || 35 ||
Then, one should have a bath performed for each [deity] with a new cloth;
thereafter, one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the western direction of that [area].
One should prepare a sacrificial mound with rice grains and arrange nine squares;
three squares in the middle, five in the east, and [five] in the south. (37)
And likewise on the northwestern side, having first performed the strewing of grass,
one should join parched grain, flowers, and sesame seeds to the openings of the threads.
Having washed the jar, especially its three legs,
one should place the *kṣara* (salt) in the middle and the cow's urine in the eastern direction.
Cow dung is to be placed in the south, and curd is said to be in the west;
ghee is to be placed in the north, and honey is situated in the forest (the northeast).
In the southwest, Phalasāra; in the northwest, Gulūsāraka; and in the northeast, Nālikera—these nine substances are prescribed. || 41 ||
p.
188) It is said that one *prastha* of milk, two *kuḍupas* of cow urine, one *kuḍupa* of cow dung, and three *kuḍupas* of curd [are required]. || 42 ||
Clarified butter is said to be one *guḍupa*; three *guḍupas* make two *prasthas*.
Honey is one *guḍupa*, and fruit juice is two *kuḍupas*.
Then, one *prastha* of the essence of molasses (*gulāsāra*) and a fourth part of coconut;
listen now to the enumeration of the nine substances and their presiding deities.
Mudgala [honored] Agastya, Pulastya, Viśvāmitra, Kāśyapa, Bhārgava, and Mura, along with Bhāradvāja. (45)
Likewise, the preceptor, having worshipped the water-pot held in his hand—along with the Ṛṣi, the Brahma-pada, and the flower-tuft—with their respective mantras, [should proceed]. (46)
Having performed [the worship] with incense, lamps, and so forth, and having worshipped the Liṅga with its respective mantra using the Surabhi-mudrā, one should display the ten mudrās.
The wise one should place the primary pitcher in the center everywhere;
the intelligent one should also place it with its lid everywhere while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Having sprinkled the door with water from the Astra-mantra, one should worship the gatekeepers;
then the preceptor, having entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), should face the north.
Having understood [the process] through the yoga of the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), one should perform the ritual action;
having worshipped the root-liṅga, one should perform the purification of the liṅga with the weapons of Śiva.
One should rub the liṅga and its pedestal with tulasī and bilva leaves; then the wise man should apply ground āmalaka and dāruharidrā, each individually.
One should bathe [the deity] with the root mantra and perform the yoga of the vital breaths (prāṇayoga).
One should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās, beginning with the crown (makuṭa), in their proper sequence. 52.
Having abandoned the state of material nature, one should worship Sadāśiva, who resides in the liṅga, and Maheśvara, who resides in the water-pot, with a single-minded heart.

One should perform the ritual bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as prescribed for worship; one should worship with fragrant waters using the root mantra, the Brahma-mantras, and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 54 ||
They know that water from the moonstone is worthy of all worship;
the study of the Vedas by Brahmins takes place in the middle of the half-pavilion. (55)
The Camaka, the Namaka, and likewise the Puruṣasūkta—
these belong to the Brahmins and others who are great Śaivas well-initiated and masters of the four Vedas.
Even at the very beginning, one who is devoid of devotion or lacking in mantra should not touch [the deity];
this is the same regarding the *liṅga* as well, yet the teacher (*ācārya*) should perform it.
One who is engaged in the study of the Vedas should worship with fragrant water;
one should likewise offer the five products of the cow (pañcāmṛta) while reciting the Vyomavyāpin mantra.
One should worship Maheśvara with the ten-syllable mantra,
accompanied by the hanging beard (*lambakūrca*), using the root-mantra and the six limbs of Brahmā.
One should offer eight flowers and three fragrant substances into a vessel filled with scented water mixed with camphor and agallochum, using seven recitations.
One should cause the consecration to be performed with twenty-five jars, accompanied by dance and song, and by hymns of praise and auspicious recitations.
Having adorned [the deity] with various garments and provided it with various perfumes,
and having adorned it with various flowers, one should worship according to the prescribed method of worship. || 62 ||
Mudgānna, pāyasānna, gulānna, kṛsarānna,
and śuddhānna— these five types of food are highly praised.
One should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented to Śambhu, followed again by water for sipping (ācamanīyaka);
then one should show the betel leaf, a mirror, an umbrella, and mouth-perfume.
One should cause it to be performed with the sound of the Vedas by Brahmins who are pure through mantras and penance;
and I shall now describe the Śaiva fire according to the path taught for the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
One should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge from the *brahmavṛkṣa* trees; all the materials for the oblation should be offered with the *sadyojāta* mantra. (66)
One should perform the rites beginning with the Jaya offerings and ending with the Sviṣṭakṛt, concluding with the Pūrṇāhuti,
for the purpose of removing all diseases and bestowing the fruits of all desires.
Having honored the teacher, the wise man should then honor the astrologer;
for the intelligent one who honors them in this manner shall obtain the fruit of all desires. || 68 ||
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Great Consecration," in the *Sūkṣmaśāstra*.
I shall now describe the procedure for the measurement and the ritual sprinkling with water,
specifically regarding images made of stone, clay, wood, and metal.
The supreme preceptor should sprinkle [the image] on a cloth or on a mural painting; however,
if the daily worship has been omitted, the rite must be performed twice as much, as well as at any other juncture.
If the worship is omitted for one day, a ritual bath (snapana) is prescribed;
if it is omitted for a month, then one should perform the rite of oblation (homa) following the ritual bath.
If [the period] is deficient by one month, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma);
if it is deficient by six months, one should perform a ceremonial bath (snapana) with one hundred and eight [offerings].
Then, having performed the Vāstuhoma, one should perform the Mūrtihoma following the ceremonial bathing;
however, if a year has elapsed, one should indeed perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
If [the period] is less than a year, one should begin the re-installation;
having installed [the deity] according to the previously mentioned procedure and sequence.
One should bathe the Lord of the Gods with one hundred and eight jars in due order;
there, one should feed eight thousand Brāhmaṇas.

One should perform the offering of food (naivedya), the ceremonial bathing (snapana), and the feeding of Brahmins; for if these are omitted for a year, it is said that one enters the abode of the Dānavas.

In a two-year-old house there is the dwelling of Kṣa; in a three-year-old house, the dwelling of Bhūtas; in a four-year-old house, that of Piśācas; and in a five-year-old house, it is the refuge of Rākṣasas.
For one less than five years, it is the abode of Brahma-rākṣasas;
up to thirty-three years, it is as stated; and beyond that, it is progressively like iron.
Having fashioned [the image] out of stone like a mountain, or likewise from clay or wood,
one should perform the rites beginning with the installation (sthāpana), as well as the placement of gems and so forth, and the ritual of the arrow (śarakriyā), according to the prescribed sequence.
If [the image] is less than five years old, however, the ritual of sprinkling with water (*jalasaṃprokṣaṇa*) is prescribed.
These twelve types of images are subject to the ritual of sprinkling with water. (12)
Now I shall fully proclaim this auspicious rite which brings about all peace, destroys all misfortunes, and increases sons and grandsons. (13)
It brings wealth, grain, and happiness to the king and the kingdom;
however, one should avoid it when the sun is in its northern course during the month of Māgha.
When the sun is in its southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), one should avoid the first two months;
beginning from the remaining months, it increases longevity, prosperity, and fame. (15)
In the bright fortnight, it is declared auspicious; in the dark fortnight, it is so except for the final [day]. The three Uttaras and Puṣya are indeed for the benefit of Brāhmaṇas.
An Āditya sacrifice under the asterisms Maitra, Maghā, or Svāti is prescribed for a Kṣatriya; and an Āditya sacrifice under Rohiṇī or Pauṣṇa is prescribed for a Vaiśya. || 17 ||
The Aṣṭaśravaṇarudra is indeed proclaimed for the Śūdra alone;
likewise, the third, fifth, seventh, and tenth [lunar days]. || 18 ||
The second, the eleventh, the thirteenth, and likewise the first [tithis], as well as the signs of the zodiac beginning with Aries—both of these would be middling. (19)
One should perform [the rite] when situated in an excellent lagna, and avoid it when not so situated; the days of Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, and the Moon are prescribed as most excellent. (20)
The days of Mars, Saturn, and the Sun, as well as the middle [period], will be declared; however, an auspicious planet is especially held in high regard during the Drakkaṇa. || 21 ||
One should prepare a sacrificial ground (daiśonya) in front of the temple, or likewise to the southeast;
it should measure twelve cubits, or nine cubits, or eight cubits on each side.
It is provided with sixteen pillars and adorned with four archways;
the height of the pillars is prescribed as ten or eight tālas.
The height of the archway (toraṇa) should be five cubits for the Aśvattha tree, three cubits for the Udumbara, Plakṣa, Vaṭa, Śakra, and so forth, respectively.
The width for the purpose of height should be joined with a trident;
the height of the trident shall be ten or eight finger-breadths in measure.
In the center of that pavilion, one should especially construct an altar occupying one part out of nine parts; its height should be two or three tālas.
One may begin with separate altars or even with a single altar;
one should construct it as pleasing to the mind, resembling the surface of a mirror.
Around the altar, there should be nine or five fires;
or else, only one, according to the extent of one's means.
One should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rules in the sequence beginning with the best [size];
starting separately from the eastern pit, one should commence the fire-offerings (homa) separately.
Whether circular or square, measuring one cubit (ratni) in size,
it should be adorned with three girdles (mekhala) measuring four, three, and two finger-breadths (aṅgula) respectively.
The navel is joined with the yoni; its width is exactly the same, and the yoni is like half a leaf, measuring five, four, and three finger-breadths respectively.
The width of the stalk shall be one-fifth of that measurement;
in the center of the pit, there should be three finger-breadths [in height], joined with eight-petaled filaments.
Regarding the procedure for the nine pits, starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna:
between Indra and Īśāna, construct a circular primary pit.
One should arrange [the sacrificial pits] according to the procedure for the five *kuṇḍas* in the four directions;
specifically, there is a circular *kuṇḍa* between the directions of Cakra and Īśāna.
In the fire of the qualities (guṇāgni), one should first perform the rite in the eastern [direction] and then in the north-eastern (aiśaka) direction;
this is the procedure for the nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), beginning with the triangle and ending with the octagon.

In the ritual procedure for the five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), a triangular shape is prescribed for those in the cardinal directions; however, in the ritual procedure for the three-fold pit, a square shape is prescribed.
In the principal pit, the preceptor should perform all the rites, or even just the essential ones;
however, when there is only one pit, [the rites] may be performed for either Indra or Śaṅkara.
One should perform the oblation in the eastern and western fire-pits facing north;
in the others, one should specifically perform the oblation while facing east.
Having thus established the fire either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should smear it with cow dung and decorate it with the five powders.
The eighth [image] should be endowed with ten weapons and joined with the syllable *ga*; it should be one cubit in height, and one should fashion the weapons accordingly.
The height should be sixteen finger-breadths, and the width eight finger-breadths;
or else, the width should be half the height, which is four finger-breadths.
Among all [objects] such as mirrors and the like, the wise man should especially [observe] the characteristic of the wheel within them, specifically in those made of red chalk and coral. (42)
One should perform [the rites] up to that point according to the prescribed rules;
in this manner, the most excellent of teachers should cause [the ritual] to be performed.
One should perform the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) on the day before the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), at nine days, seven days, five days, or even three days prior. || 44 ||
The most excellent preceptor should cause [the rite] to be performed by way of the "offering of the sprout" (aṅkurārpaṇa);
then, he should cause an altar (sthaṇḍila) to be prepared in the center of the pavilion.

Having strewn around the sacrificial fire, which is the wing of the Droṇa vessel, rice and sesame seeds as its half-measure, along with Darbha grass and flowers, one should likewise install the deity.
There, he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made by those who utter words of well-being and blessings;
[the ritual] should be accompanied by all ornaments and provided with all musical instruments. (47)
Together with various classes of devotees, one should perform the supreme circumambulation;
then, having reached a body of water, construct a water-shed (prapā) in the midst of the water. 48.
Adorned with canopies and banners, and encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass,
one should wrap the deity in cloth and provide it with a long hanging beard.
One should lay down the Lord of the Gods with his head toward the east and his face turned downward,
surrounded on all sides by eight jars and encircled by the eight Vidyeśvaras.
A wise person should especially worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
having kept it immersed in water for one night, two nights, or three nights.
Alternatively, by this method, one should cause [the object] to remain in water for a watch (yāma), or ten nāḍīs,
or even fourteen nāḍīs. || 52 ||
At the conclusion of the preliminary consecration of the waters, the wise one should lead [the ritual] to the water's edge;
having placed the jars with water, he should then perform the consecration.

One should worship [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, according to the mantra and with the Prāsāda hymn; having brought [the image] adorned with all ornaments, one should place it in the sacrificial pavilion.
One should install the God of gods on the northern side of the pavilion;
there, reciting the Pāvamānī verses, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made.
Having worshipped the *kautuka* separately, one should wrap it individually with a cloth;
the wise man should then bind the *kautuka* according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Upon the altar, having been thoroughly purified, [he should place] eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice,
half as much (*catur-droṇa*) of *taṇḍula* rice, and half as much again (*dvi-droṇa*) of sesame seeds.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound there and spread it with *kuśa* and *darbha* grass;
one should arrange a bed for Prajāpati [Brahmā] in due order, beginning with those born from eggs.
One should prepare five types of bedding, consisting of those born from eggs, those born from sprouts, those born from wool, and even those born from hair, all provided with coverlets. || 59 ||
The wise one should lay down the image of the dancing form with the Vāmadeva mantra,
having wrapped it in a cloth along with its beard, with the head facing east and the face turned upward.
Above that, the best of preceptors should wrap it with a red cloth,
having worshipped it thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should place the primary pitcher at the very top portion of that [altar];
and one should place the *vardhanī* pitcher in the northern direction of it. (62)
Having taken up each of those forms, one should place them into their respective pitchers;
having taken up each of those powers, one should perform the ritual for each respective goddess.
It should be provided with a beard, a lid, and cloth, adorned with gold and gems,
joined with fruits and sprouts, and endowed with all fragrances.
One should place the seed-syllable within the pitcher; fashion it according to the proportions of the thread.
It has three eyes and four arms, and is radiant with a crown of the crescent moon.

And [one should meditate on] Kṛṣṇa, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who is equipped with an axe, adorned with all ornaments, and seated in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana). || 66 ||
In this manner, one should meditate upon such a form in the center while recollecting the Śiva-mantra;
and having visualized the seed-syllable of Vardhanī and Manonmanī within the Vardhanī vessel.
She has two arms and a beautiful face, with full and elevated breasts;
she is adorned with all ornaments, and her two hands are joined with lotuses.
In this manner, the wise one should place the goddess Manonmanī upon the *vardhanī*;
she who has great luster, with arms both manifest and unmanifest, and a blue throat. 69.
Adorned with ornaments consisting of matted locks, a crown, rubies, and the crescent moon;
three-eyed and four-armed; the Lord clothed in a tiger skin. (70)
And [he saw] Kṛṣṇa, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who wields an axe, who is endowed with all auspicious marks, and adorned with every ornament. || 71 ||
The god Indraśaṅkara, the creation of Umā, and the causal principle;
the goddess wearing divine garments, with two eyes and radiant with two arms. (72)
Adorned with a tilaka on her forehead, possessing full and elevated breasts, she was graceful with a slender waist and held beautiful, red, blossoming lotuses in her hands. 73.
Adorned with a crown endowed with all kinds of jewels, with an auspicious thread around her neck, and decorated with every ornament; || 74 ||
On the left side of the cart, one should fashion the goddess endowed with auspicious marks,
and the youth Manonmanya, endowed with all auspicious marks.
Facing toward Īśvara, together with Umā, he was seated upon a single throne, possessing two arms and two eyes. (76)
One should fashion the form of Bāla as Mausala, who is pleasing to behold;
likewise, one should fashion Kumāra, the commander of the divine army, accompanied by his playthings.
Having meditated upon the god Caṇḍeśvara, who has two arms and a peaceful form,
and who is equipped with a chisel in his hand, one should place him in the center of the water-pot.
Kuṇḍodara, of massive body, wearing excellent red garlands, resembling a dark blue cloud, with a staff in hand and three eyes. (79)
One should fashion Vighnanāyaka with an elephant's face and three eyes;
one should worship each respective seed-syllable with its corresponding mantra. (80)
On both sides of the jars, there should be eight lords of the sciences (vidyeśvaras), together with golden [ornaments],
filled with water to the capacity of a droṇa, and wrapped in cloth.
(199) One should worship the Supreme Lord with vessels provided with strainers, covered lids, and filled with fruits and sprouts, using various mantras. 82.
Thereafter, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented, and then cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla) to be offered.
One should then place eight auspicious objects (aṣṭamaṅgala) all around the exterior of the altar.
One should worship the mirrors and other items from Indra up to Īśāna;
one should then place the ten weapons in their respective locations.
One should worship from the east up to the northeast, ending with the vajra and the other [emblems].
One should worship the archways (toraṇas) and so forth from the east up to the north. || 85 ||
Having established eight jars, provided with cloths and joined with gold, [one should worship] Nandin, Mahākāla, Daṇḍin, and Muṇḍin as well. (86)
One should place Vaijayantī, Bhṛṅgī, and Kirīṭa in the pitchers at the doors in the four directions starting from the east. (87)
One should especially adorn [the deity] from the day of the *pālikā* until the end of the festival. || 88 ||
The wise one should have two ladles made, measuring one cubit in length;
thereafter, having established the Śiva-fire, the twice-born Śaiva priest should perform the rites.
The Ādiśaiva Brāhmaṇa is established as the Ādiśaiva; the Śivadvija is likewise an Ādiśaiva. One should have both the festival and the consecration performed by an Ādiśaiva.
All [the rites] beginning with the conception (garbhādāna) are performed with the five Brahmans and the six ancillaries;
by means of the first [mantra], each of the nine purificatory rites (saṃskāra) is performed twenty-five times.
One should offer oblations in due order and thereafter perform the fire sacrifice (homa),
using sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds. (92)
Mudga, māṣa, and jujube—these are said here to be the ten substances.
The Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees are located in the directions beginning with the East.
The Palāśa wood is prescribed for the primary fire of all [fires];
one should perform the oblation with Palāśa wood alone, whether for the elemental fire (bhūtāgni) or the qualitative fire (guṇāgni).
One should perform the oblations in due order with the five Brahmans and the six limbs;
then, specifically with the Astra-mantra, one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
The wise one should offer oblations one hundred and eight, or fifty, or twenty-five times for each; and while they are burning, he should touch them.
The most excellent preceptor should cause the principal oblation to be offered into the Śiva-fire;
therefore, he should cast [the materials] into all the fire-pits while reciting the Heart-mantra.
The bearer of the form should perform the rite with fuel-sticks using the previously mentioned mantras;
he should offer oblations into the five sacrificial pits for the five forms beginning with Sadyojāta.
Īśāna, Bhava, Śarva, Viṣṇu, and Sadyojāta—these five forms reside in the five fires, beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna. || 99 ||
Having specifically worshipped Bhava, Śiva, and Civa— the presiding deities within the fires of the qualities— with their respective mantras, || 100 ||
With the mantra of the *deśikāstra*, one should offer all the *pūrṇāhuti* oblations;
at night, it should be performed in this manner, and one should perform the bath during the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*).
There, one should honor the teacher with garments, gold, and rings;
or, before a cloth painting or a mural painting, one should perform a single fire-oblation. 102.
A wise man should have [the consecration] performed by a single preceptor;
for images of many forms, there should be a preceptor who is versatile in form.
One should worship each [deity] there with garments, gold, and rings;
the best [offering] should consist of one hundred niṣkas, while the middling should be half of that.
Twenty-five niṣkas is declared to be the lowest [fee];
starting from twenty niṣkas down to ten niṣkas. || 105 ||
The three middle [grades] have thus been described; now hear about the lowest grade, which begins at nine niṣkas and ends at nine times that number (ninety-nine niṣkas). || 106 ||
The fee for the preceptor (deśika) is said to be three times the lowest amount; however, the fee for the practitioner (sādhaka) is half that of the teacher (ācārya). 107.
The fee for the image-protectors (mūrtipas) is merely the amount required for the practitioner;
half of that for the reciters of the mantras, and half of that for the attendants.
The preceptor, having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* rite and especially completed the remaining rites,
should perform the circumambulation of the village, and especially that of the ritual jars.
Alternatively, one should place the sanctum, adorned with all ornaments,
in front of the bathing pit and install it according to the prescribed sequence.
The most excellent preceptor, being wise, should perform the ritual placement of mantras at an auspicious hour and a favorable moment, accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (111)
Then, having performed the consecration according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures,
one should offer abundant oblations and present betel-leaf while reciting the heart-mantra. (112)
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, adorned with all ornaments. || 112½ ||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Sprinkling of All [Vessels]," in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra*, a subtle treatise.
I shall describe the sacrifice to the lunar mansions (nakṣatrayajana); listen to it, O Prabhāñjanas!
It pacifies the great elements and causes the enemy army to flee. || 1 ||
It causes the destruction of all enemies, grants desired success at the proper time, pacifies untimely death, and destroys the influence of the nine planets. || 2 ||
At the time of his royal consecration, on his birthday, and also on the fourteenth and eighth days of both fortnights; || 3 ||
One should perform the sacrifice to the constellations for the sake of accomplishing all desired goals.
One should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva, endowed with all ornaments;
in its center, one should construct an altar measuring one part from the portion of the qualities (nine parts).
Its height should be half its width, resembling the interior of a mirror;
it should be adorned with night-blooming lotuses (niśibhadra) and be free from depressions or elevations.
One should fashion a horse or a bull on the front and sides, adorned like a palace and provided with twelve pillars.
Having adorned it especially with garments, flowers, unguents, and so forth,
one should fashion Kailāsa in the center out of rice-flour paste.
Then, having constructed the secondary altar (upavedī) with a measurement equal to half the width of that [main altar],
it should be four finger-breadths in height and free from depressions or elevations.
Having fashioned a circular mandala, one should draw a lotus in its center;
the great lotus has twelve petals, and the wise know there to be ninety-six lingas.
One should prepare saffron of black color, red, and the color of cow’s milk,
following the sequence of white colors according to the previous method.
Then, one should construct the pavilion for the sacrifice according to the previously mentioned procedure,
having determined it on the ninth or seventh day prior to the day of the ceremony.
In the fifth [rite], one should likewise resort to a bilva tree with what remains; having cleared away the grass and other coverings from the east and all sides of it.
The learned man should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and should sprinkle [the site] with the *Śiva-mantra*.
At sunset, he should construct a square area all around the base of that [tree].
One should excavate it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and fill it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
having worshipped it thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings using the root-mantra (mūlamantra), O observer of good vows.
The rite of the protective amulet (*pratisara*) is performed with the *trayambaka* mantra;
having offered a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) of curd-rice to the forest deity for his satisfaction. (16)
Having recited the mantra over the dried cow-products while taking Rudra as the presiding deity,
the wise practitioner, at the conclusion of the recitation, should collect a bilva tree together with its roots.
One should divide that [mantra] individually using the five-limbed *praṇava* alone;
having conjoined it with the *sadyojāta* [face], it is endowed with the ritual actions of the primary form (*mūlamūrti*). (18)
Holding the tree with the left hand, one should grasp the vessel with the heart-mantra;
holding the fruit with the face-mantra, one should take the flower in the northeast.
Then, having wrapped it in a clean cloth, one should carry it on the head,
adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by the recitation of the Svasti-sūkta.
Having performed a circumambulation of the sacred abode, either before the image of Śiva or in the pavilion,
one should smear it with cow dung and decorate it with various powders of flour.
The wise one should prepare a sacrificial mound with pure and auspicious rice grains;
he should then place a bilva leaf upon it, reciting the respective mantra in the proper sequence.
To the east, west, or especially to the north of that,
having cut three [pieces] measuring eight finger-breadths each with an axe, || 26 ||
One should soak bilva wood and its root in pure water;
[then apply] yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron (kuṅkuma), costus (koṣṭha), sandalwood (candana), and yellow sandalwood (haricandana).
One should grind uśīra, camphor,
and ash mixed with agaru, together with hirivera, using cold water.
Having dried the footprints in the shade and taken fruit and other offerings for his son,
he should place them in a new vessel and bind its mouth with a cloth.
Having meditated and worshipped with the six-limbed rite, perform the act of attaining supernatural powers;
having recited one thousand and eight times the mantra that consumes sins.
On that day, or on the preceding day, one should begin the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Then, having entered the pavilion (maṇḍapa), with one's body purified by the ritual of the *sakalīkaraṇa*, [one should proceed]. (28)
Having worshipped Vighneśvara, the preceptor should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
the learned man should always worship the pavilion according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the center of the altar using eight droṇas of śāli rice;
it should then be strewn with rice grains, sesame seeds, parched grain, and darbha grass.
Having sprinkled it with the Bahurūpa mantra, one should worship the bull-throne,
specifically in the north, east, or west of the pavilion.
One should perform the ceremonial bath with eight *droṇas* of milk;
the wise one should prepare the *arghya* offering and carry out the purification of the vessel.
The most excellent of teachers should divide the five parts of the *bilva* fruit into eight portions;
O Pārvatī, two portions shall be the form of Śiva, and one portion [shall be for] Pārvatī.
One should fashion [the offerings] from the constellation in five parts according to the sequence;
having touched them with perfume, flowers, and so forth, one should recite the previously mentioned mantra. || 34 ||
Having grasped it with the syllable Om alone, one should place it upon the pedestal;
O Pārvatī, one should worship the Supreme Lord and Goddess in the center of the pericarp.
The wise one should assign the constellations in their proper order in the four directions:
from Aśvinī up to Āśleṣā, he should place seven groups in the region of Indra (the East).
The seven constellations beginning with Anurādhā and ending with Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa) are in the western direction;
the seven beginning with Māgha and ending with Sūrpa (Pūrvabhādrapadā) are in the southern region.

206) Having mentally conceived [the deities] from Śraviṣṭhā to the end of Bharaṇī within the region of the seven [Mṛgaśiras], one should worship them with perfumes and other offerings, each by means of its own name-mantra. || 38 ||
Then, having gone into the inner sanctum, one should perform the purification of the *liṅga*;
one should offer mung-bean rice and smear it with sandalwood paste.
Having worshipped with incense and lamps, the preceptor should pray for his desired object;
then, having entered the pavilion, he should perform the ritual offering to the presiding deity of the pavilion.
Having reached the fire-sanctuary, one should duly establish the Śiva-fire;
[one should offer] a plantain fruit joined with the three sweets, with its tip pointing eastward.
One should perform the fire-oblation with coconut fruit, milk, and cooked rice—
either one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five times— using the root mantra itself.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should dismiss the Śiva-fire;
thereafter, one should worship the Lord of Gods together with the Goddess Umā.
Having offered the oblation, one should then cause betel to be given;
having summoned the attendant, who is wearing a turban and an upper garment, [one should give it to him]. (44)
Having lifted the jars and carried them upon his head, he should perform a circumambulation of the temple; then, having entered the inner sanctum, he should bathe the deity worthy of the ritual bath.
Having offered the oblation, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
then, having entered the pavilion, which is adorned with all ornaments.
Having gathered the five powders with the *praṇava* (syllable Om) into a sweetmeat (*laḍḍuka*),
one should carry it on the head and then perform a circumambulation.
Having arranged [the materials] in front of the pavilion, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited;
then, having worshipped Mount Kailāsa, one should worship Vṛṣadevatā.
Above that, one should place the five-limbed Bilva tree together with its presiding deity;
having heated it all around with the constellations, one should worship it in sequence as before.
Paṭṭikā, paṭalivyāghrī, red agastya,
dhātaki, lakṣmī, and red lotus— these seven [are the deities] in the asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā.
O Earth, one should place the *vakula*, *droṇapuṣpa*, *dhūdhūra*, *karavīra*, *pradoṣa*, *padma*, and *bhūpāṭala* flowers on the right side.
Tulasi, Jāti, Punnāga, Śvetārka, Bilva leaves, Rudraparṇī, and Dūrvā grass [should be offered] during the seven asterisms beginning with Anurādhā. (52)
Śrīyāvarta, mandāra, raktārka, caturaṅgula,
viṣṇukrānti, sahasrābha, and śraviṣṭhā— these seven [are to be used] in the [seven constellations] beginning with Śraviṣṭhā.

One should offer food of mung beans during the asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā; rice mixed with sesame (kṛsarānna) during those beginning with Maghā; and milk-rice (pāyasa) should be offered during the seven asterisms beginning with Anurādhā.
During the asterisms beginning with Śraviṣṭhā, one should worship the Lord with devotion and all ritual offerings, including a māṣa bean mixed with molasses, for the attainment of one's desired goal.
A mortal who acts in this manner shall be born in all worlds;
there he should honor the teacher with garments, gold, and rings.
He should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to his ability to the devotees and attendants,
and he should provide food, drink, and other necessities to the twice-born and the other devotees.
At the end of the twilight rite, or else at another time, the Guru, holding a handful of flowers,
should take up Śiva with the root mantra and unite him within his own self.
Having taken the five powders into a pure vessel,
the Guru should cause that powder to be given to the patron according to the prescribed ritual.
Having taken five powders and combined them with sandalwood,
or else having mixed them with ashes, a person should wear them constantly.
One shall be liberated from all sins and become victorious everywhere.
The worship of the lunar mansions has been declared; now hear the procedure for the worship with flowers.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the *Sūkṣmaśāstra*, titled "The Worship of the Lunar Mansions."
I shall proclaim the Great Peace; listen to it, O Dispeller! It is eternally bestowing the world of Śiva, auspicious, and pleasing to Śiva. (1)
It causes the destruction of all enemies, destroys all sins, increases progeny, is meritorious, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 2 ||
In the month of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism Śravaṇā, in the rainy season under Pūrvabhādrapadā;
in the month of Āśvina under the asterism Aśvinī, and in the month of Kārttika under the asterism Kārttika.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, under the Puṣya asterism, it is praised for the Puṣya rite;
in the month of Māgha, under the Maghā asterism, and in the month of Phālguna, under the Uttarā asterism.
In the month of Caitra, under the asterism Citrā; in the month of Vaiśākha, under the asterism Śravaṇa;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, under the asterism Mūla; and in the month of Āṣāḍha, under the asterism Uttarāṣāḍhā. (5)
Alternatively, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight, one should observe the vow month after month,
either by a river, at the ocean, in a sacred family lineage, on a mountain peak, or in a great forest.
In the middle of the village, in the assembly hall or near a temple,
having purified the ground according to the rules, one should construct a beautiful water-shed (prapā).
Having approached the vicinity of the Śivaliṅga, [one should perform this] a thousand times,
or half of that, or a hundred, or even half of that again.
One should fashion [an image] for the purpose of worship using wood, stone, metal, or alloys, or even from ephemeral materials, and especially from precious gems.
Starting from three barley grains and increasing by one barley grain at a time,
up to a count of twenty barley grains, the emergence of the earthen linga occurs.
Regarding the characteristic of momentariness:
one should fashion a wooden liṅga beginning at one finger-breadth and increasing by half a finger-breadth each time, up to twenty-four finger-breadths. || 11 ||
The measurement of the jewel-liṅga is proclaimed according to what is available,
beginning with three māṣas and increasing by one māṣa at a time.
Up to a maximum of eight thousand [aṅgulas], the emergence of the stone liṅga may occur;
one should fashion the momentary liṅga according to one's desire as its measurement.
Indeed, there is some distinction among clay, stone, and metal;
however, in the case of a liṅga made of wood, one part out of four parts shall be the width of the liṅga.
Alternatively, [the base] may consist of one part of the qualities (three parts) with a width of two parts out of five;
at the length of the *liṅga*, it should be one part of the qualities (three parts), and its base should be square. (15)
This [umbrella] may have an arched portion for its increase, or it may be entirely of a well-rounded form;
it may be provided with or devoid of a central cord, and it should be topped by a small parasol.
One should bring forth each individual linga endowed with these characteristics, or one may fashion them all within a single linga according to their specific distinctions. || 17 ||
Having thus made the liṅga one yāma, the portion of the sky (the upper part) shall be situated on the ground;
one part shall be the pedestal-base (pīṭhabandha), and one part shall be fit for worship.
Alternatively, in a five-part division, one should place two parts on the pedestal;
the worship portion shall be three parts, and in a seven-part division, there is a triple-columned structure.
This [calculation] consists of the arc-portion, the remainder of the increase, and the entry into the aggregate;
it arises from twenty-five degrees when the exaltation of the worship-portion has dawned.
The wise one should divide each [liṅga] into forty parts; such is the rule for the thousand liṅgas. Now hear the procedure for ten thousand.
When the linga is raised, the wise one should divide it into fifty parts;
having made forty parts and five parts, it shall be joined with the linga.
When the height of the pedestal (pūjāṃśa) is divided into ten parts, the pinnacle (tuṅga) is one part;
with fifteen [parts] for the base, there shall be five hundred lingas.
In the Śivodaya, within the Veda-section, one should contemplate a single asterism;
one should then fashion one hundred and eight liṅgas all around it.
But when the emergence of Śiva occurs in the portion of worship divided into five, there are twenty-five [units] for the liṅga; when it is divided into fifty, [the same applies]. (25)
One-fifth of five hundred parts of the linga is prescribed for the pedestal;
for a small linga, it should be half a tārā, or a quarter, or even one-eighth.
Having joined the width of the great liṅga at its upper part on both sides,
that measurement belongs to the small liṅga which has emerged from the great liṅga.
A linga should never be placed upon another linga;
rather, there should be an interval between them, and one should arrange the sequence of lingas in the middle accordingly.
The wise one should fashion it either with the head-circumference included or excluding it;
he should then determine the measurement of the top of the great liṅga in due order.
One should sequentially determine the measurement of the head of the jewel-liṅga;
for all liṅgas as well, one should fashion them without [excess] thread.
A wise man should acquire a Śiva-liṅga that possesses these characteristics, including a stone pedestal in the form of a Nandyāvarta, according to the prescribed rules.
Having thus made the arrangements on the previous day— whether on the ninth or the seventh—
the wise man should finalize them during the evening mealtime on the day before the ceremony.
Having performed the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules together with the patron,
one should enter the pavilion of the water-stall and perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa rite, one should then perform circumambulation;
one should recite the root mantra as many times as there are liṅgas, together with the patron.
At the conclusion of the recitation, facing eastward and having consumed milk while keeping his senses subdued,
he should cause [the image] to lie upon sand on the northern side of the pavilion. (35)
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, perform the washing of your feet;
then, having purified your mouth and sipped water (*ācamana*), the best of teachers [should proceed]. (36)
Then, having applied a tilaka with ashes, one should mutter the root mantra;
thereafter, accompanied by the patron, one should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rule.
Having performed the salutation at the junctions of the day (saṃdhyā) and completed his daily obligatory rites,
he entered the pavilion of the water-station with his body consecrated by the ritual of *kalaśa*.
The wise man should worship the pavilion, or indeed construct it within the pavilion;
having worshipped its four doors according to the prescribed rite beginning with the east.
Then, for the sake of protection, the wise one should worship the King of Mantras together with his Śakti,
either in the middle of the water-shed pavilion or in the western part.
One should install [the deities] with the great mantras, or else with wooden [images];
then, one should prepare a covering on top with pure cloths and other such materials as appropriate.
One should fashion the seat of Śiva above that and determine the number of liṅgas;
there, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) as well as the offering of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and nectar.
Having taken [the deity] by means of the mark of intention (saṅkalpa), one should place it upon the sacrificial altar for bathing;
then, having washed it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), nectar, and so forth.
Having bathed [the image] with the Liṅga-mantra, one should install it upon the Śiva-seat;
then, having worshipped it with its respective mantra, one should offer perfume, flowers, and excellent incense.
Immediately after that, one should cause a lamp, food offerings, and betel to be presented,
along with blue lotuses, white water-lilies, or leaves of white lotuses. (45)
The wise man should [construct it] with Arka flowers, or Āragvadha, or Campaka;
or with jewels, or gold, or even with a fragment of coral.
Alternatively, one should worship the Liṅga with Bilva leaves while reciting the mantra;
having gathered the flowers intended for worship in a pure vessel.
Having purified [the vessel] by means of inspection and other rites, one should offer incense and a lamp;
then, having approached the patron, one should sprinkle him with consecrated water.
Having fashioned a tilaka with ashes using the Śiva-mantra,
the preceptor should then consecrate the "Śiva-hand" upon the head of the patron.
Having placed that [flower] in the water one hundred and eight times at the root of a lotus,
he should offer the flowers collected for worship accompanied by the sound of a conch.
Having worshipped them, the wise one should place [the flowers] in the hand of the sacrificer;
he should apply each flower to the respective limb while reciting its corresponding mantra.
There is a specific single-liṅga [shrine] on the outside of the pedestal all around;
having cleared away a space measuring three cubits or half of that, || 52 ||
The extent of that [mandala] which is to be pervaded is equal to the measure of the rising of the worship;
outside of that, the measure of the altar (vedikā) is seven tālas in height.
Its height and width should be equal, or even half of that, or half of that again;
it may be provided with three tiers (mekhalās) or even two tiers.
One should gradually fashion it as either square or perfectly circular;
there, one should fill it with lime, gravel, and pure water.
Having seen a thousand lingas within that circle of water,
the wise and learned man should worship them as before, proceeding in order around the [central] linga.
From the tip down to the root, it bestows devotion and liberation;
from the root up to the tip, it bestows the fruit of worship and liberation. (57)
And the best of teachers, having worshipped the *liṅga* and the enclosure (*varaṇa*) in due order upon the water-mandala by the patron, as before; 58.
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) to the Liṅga with half an Āḍhaka measure;
then, having offered incense and a lamp, one should proceed along the path of the Liṅga’s enclosure.
The wise man should perform the concluding worship of the liṅga,
including all such acts as singing and dancing, proceeding in order around the liṅga.
Having made the formal resolve at the conclusion of the Linga worship, one should mutter the Śiva-mantra one hundred times together with beloved kinsmen and accompanied by the patron.
Having bathed in that circle of water with the mantra of the God of Gods,
and having bathed in that circle of water according to this ritual procedure.
He too, being liberated from all sins, shall attain union with Śiva after beholding and bowing to the thousand Liṅgas at Mahāśāntivrata.
He who, performing [this], rejoices even in the world of Śiva together with Śiva—
there one should honor that teacher with cows, land, gold, and other such gifts.
For this vow and its auxiliary rites, one should cause a new garment to be given.
This is declared to be the Mahāśānti-vrata; now hear the Gaurī-vrata. (65)
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Vow of Great Peace," in the Kriyāpāda of the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
O Prabhāñjanā, listen as I describe the Gaurī-saṃkocana rite,
which bestows long life, health, and victory, and grants the prosperity of sons and grandsons.
The first and the second are thus the two types of *taruṇālaya*; the collection of rites for the *taruṇālaya* begins with the plowing of the ground and ends with the worship.
When a temple has fallen or been shattered, and likewise when the *liṅga* has moved, all other ritual acts are declared to be equal [in their required remediation]. (3)
Having determined the root-position (mūlasthāna), one should establish the child-position (bālasthāna);
above that is the state of childhood (bālabālyatva), therefore one should cause it to enter the root.
It should be constructed at the front of the temple, either to the south or to the north;
the pavilion should be twenty cubits in width and of the highest quality.
The middle [maṇḍapa] should be twelve cubits, while the smallest is ten cubits;
the best maṇḍapa is recorded as being joined with thirty-six pillars.
The middle pavilion, which is the lowest [grade], is provided with sixteen pillars;
it is without gaps in the cardinal and intermediate directions and arises from the sky.
It was provided with four gates, adorned with four archways,
equipped with canopies and banners, and encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass.
Together with lamps, flowers, and fruits, the auspicious Māṣa [vessel] should be worshipped;
one should wrap pillars there, each individually encircled with cloth. (9)
Having divided the pavilion into three parts, there shall be an altar in the middle section,
one cubit in height and resembling the surface of a mirror.
One should construct a secondary altar (upavedī) all around the base of the main altar;
its height is said to be one yuga-aṅgula, and its width is double that.
One should construct fire-pits around [the central one], with specific distinctions as appropriate;
one may perform the rite with nine fires, five fires, or a single fire.
One should not construct all the *yonikuṇḍas* within one another;
the field [of the kuṇḍa] is five parts, while the *śrotra* is half a part, measured by the *śocya*. 13.
From that, the peacock [of the fire] becomes nourished like a leaf of the Pippala tree;
then, having fashioned the Yoni-pit, one should properly perform the ritual characteristics.
After removing the clay, one should subsequently smear [the ground] with cow-dung;
there, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited and then feed the Brahmins. || 15 ||
Afterward, having disposed of the remnants of the food, one should again perform the *puṇyāha* rite;
then, as prescribed for the *maryāda* [boundary] ceremony, one should duly cause the *vāstu-homa* to be performed.
One should perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) and again observe the auspicious day (puṇyāha).
Having performed this according to the rite, one should bathe and smear the image with white sandalwood paste. || 17 ||
Wearing white garments and a white turban, adorned with white garlands,
the wise one should offer sprouts and perform the purification of the site.
Facing north, perform the ritual of dismemberment (*sakalikaraṇa*).
Then, having entered the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*), perform the purification of the site (*sthānaśuddhi*). (19)
Then, having performed the purification of Gaurī, one should bathe her with water mixed with turmeric;
then, having performed the rite for a "holy day," one should consecrate her with pure waters.
Having bathed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should rub it with a bilva leaf;
then, having taken earth from an anthill at the root of a darbha grass in a sacred field, one should smear it [with that].
Having bathed [the image] with scented water, one should worship it with the heart-mantra,
using sandalwood, agallochum, costus, saffron, and kesara flowers.
O Gaurī, one should smear the pedestal with *lālya*, enriched with saffron, leaves, and camphor;
having thus anointed the lotus of the pedestal, one should sprinkle the seed-syllable of Śakti.
Having honored with eight flowers the left hand placed upon the head, as well as the golden thread and the auspicious amulet, one should offer a vessel filled with flowers.
Having wrapped [the image] in a new cloth according to the procedure for the pedestal of Gaurī,
one should thereafter worship the Child’s chamber together with Gaurī.
A journey-homa must be performed; one should perform that homa in front of it. The sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) should be one cubit in size, made of flawless sand.

One should perform all the rites beginning with the taking up of the fire as prescribed for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*). One should offer fuel sticks with the *Sadyojāta* mantra and clarified butter with the *Īśāna* mantra. (27)
Having offered twenty-five oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) with each of the Aghora mantras,
one should offer oblations with the Prāsāda mantra, the Śakti-bījas, and the ten-syllable Vyomavyāpin mantra.
One should offer sixteen oblations each with Śakti and the others, as well as Vāmā and the others;
having touched [the object], one should perform the homa while recollecting the Gaurī-bīja mantra. (29)
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before him with pure and auspicious śāli rice,
one should place either a water-pot (kumbha) or a small vessel (karaka) upon that mound.
Together with their threads and covers, joined with golden shoots, provided with coconut fruits, and endowed with hanging tufts of hair. (31)
Having invoked the pitcher situated within Gaurī, one should place it in the center of the [main] pitcher;
one should establish it with the Vāma mantra and conceal it with the Aghora mantra. || 32 ||
One should worship the presence [of the deity] in sequence with the fifth mantra, the Śakti-mantra;
one should display the Śakti-mudrā, the Mukali, and the Padma-mudrikā.
Having bound the mudrā called namaskāra, one should direct the weapon-mantra toward the quarters; then, one should place eight jars all around, provided with threads and other requisites.
Having invoked the eight powers, beginning with Vāmā, and those starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna into the center of the pitcher, while recollecting their respective seed-syllables (bīja).
One should worship with the Gaurī-mantra using perfumes, flowers, and so forth in due order;
one should also present the food offering, incense, a lamp, and betel-leaf.
One should then perform the Jaya and other oblations, as well as the Abhyādhāna and Rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings in sequence;
and with one's head, one should lift up the jar containing the Pūrṇāhuti.
One should cover the image with a mantra and cast it into a pond;
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should enter the sacrificial pavilion.
One should prepare a sacrificial ground with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice,
as well as with rice grains, sesame seeds, parched grain, flowers, and *darbha* grass. (39)
In the center of that, one should draw a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp;
then, having carried it around with the head, one should perform circumambulation.
Accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments and endowed with the chanting of the Veda,
one should slowly perform circumambulation while reciting the Umāsūkta in sequence.
Then, having entered the pavilion, one should place [the vessel] upon the altar;
recollecting the seed-syllable of Gaurī, one should worship the water-pot right there.
Having placed the water-pots all around, beginning from the left, one should worship the Śaktis in sequence with their respective name-mantras, offering perfumes, flowers, and other articles.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as having assumed each respective form, one should worship with their own respective seed-syllables during the breath-retentions (kumbhaka),
and likewise offer oblations such as perfumes, flowers, and the food offering (naivedya).
Having performed the study of the Rigveda, one should recite the Umāsūkta in sequence, as well as the Śrīsūkta, the Rudrasūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Tryambaka hymn. (45)
The wise one should recite the two *śāntis*, especially on the right side;
then the preceptor, together with the image-makers (*mūrtipas*), should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
All rites beginning with the taking of fire should be performed according to the path prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya),
using sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.
One should indeed offer these seven sacrificial substances in their proper sequence:
Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Bilva, and likewise Khadira.
One should offer clarified butter with the *mūla-mantra* and offer the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *aghora-mantra*.
One should offer parched grain (*lāja*) with the *vāma-mantra* and mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*) with the *kavaca-mantra*.
Having offered barley with the *śikhā* mantra, one should then offer sesame seeds with the *astra* mantra,
either one hundred and eight times, or three times that number, or half of that, or even half of that again.
The wise one should offer each substance individually; at the end of the substances, he should offer the *vyāhṛtis*.
He should cause the oblation combined with all the substances to be offered into the fire.
Having thus remained awake during the night, perform the ritual sprinkling at dawn;
the preceptor, together with the image-keepers, should perform the bath according to the prescribed rite.
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with his head bowed and having dismissed the fire,
he should lift up the jar containing the Śakti and perform a circumambulation of the temple.
Equipped with all musical instruments and adorned with every ornament,
it brings about all prosperity and happiness for sons, servants, and wives.

Then, having entered the inner sanctum (garbhageha), one should place [the deity] upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila); having observed an auspicious moment, one should then establish the command of the God.
In that very place, one should perform the placement; O Gaurī, one should place the thirty-eight kalās.
Then, having offered the mantra-flowers, one should present the mantra-food.
Having wrapped [the image] in a new cloth and honored it with perfumes, flowers, garlands, and so forth,
one should offer oblations at dawn and present betel leaf.
The wise one should offer mouth-freshener accompanied by water in a handful;
he should perform the recitation of the Nṛga chapter, as well as hymns, dances, and instrumental music.
At the conclusion of the sprinkling, one should especially perform consecrations with ritual baths;
at the conclusion of the sprinkling, one should properly carry out the *utsava* (festive procession) in a special manner. (59)
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the *Sūkṣmaśāstra*, titled "The Procedure for the Contraction of Gaurī."
Now, for the benefit of the king and the kingdom, I shall explain the pacification of portents.
Portents are said to be of two kinds: the common and the great portent. (1)
While ordinary [remedies] yield fruit over a long period, a great fruit is obtained immediately;
therefore, the respective counter-measures must be properly applied for the destruction of the humors (doṣas).
But that [false] instruction regarding what ought not to be done brings all manner of faults upon men;
it is especially a source of great fault for Brāhmaṇas and kings. (3)
Therefore, when a king thus delays, an immediate counter-measure must be taken by him,
just as one acts at sunrise upon seeing the new moon on the night of the amāvāsyā.
During an earthquake, the agitation of a river, the churning of a well, or in a small pond;
likewise during the weeping of an image, and then during a rain of blood.
Likewise, during a rain of stones and dust, as well as a rain of honey, and during rains of milk and blood, or when blood flows from the trees; || 6 ||
If the temple, from its crest down to its pedestal, falls down without cause, or if that which stands within its chamber moves from its place to another location; || 7 ||
When a tree has moved to another location, or when another fruit arises on the tree, or when other flowers are produced, or when a different fragrance arises; (8)
And likewise, in that which is born from heat, as well as in an image, [the deity resides];
so too in those born from eggs, those born from sweat, quadrupeds, and humans. (9)
Likewise, when one's own kind gives birth to another, or when there is wandering upon a temple,
or when white crows appear, or when two mountains engage in combat.
When a tree that provides water is burnt by itself, or likewise when an image trembles, or when the Śiva-vardhanī or the liṅga and the image are broken; || 11 ||
Likewise, in the case of the breaking of an image, as well as the breaking of a *liṅga*,
[the rite is performed] while observing the image and the *liṅga* joined with the rut of a female elephant.
When smoke arises without fire, when there is a change in color, when it appears in excess on the limbs, and likewise when it appears on all four feet; || 13 ||
When these most wonderful sounds were uttered by you from the resonance of the drum—
namely, the sight of a reflected sun and the sight of a reflected moon— 14.
When a rainbow is seen at night, when there is a sight of stars during the day, when a star falls upon one's house, and during the seven-day period of Saturn's turbulence; 15.
For seven days continuously during the eclipses of the moon and sun, and when there is a great outbreak of heat or the occurrence of a conflagration of the quarters; 16.
When the flower offered to the *liṅga* has changed its color, or when the flower has fallen unexpectedly—even if it was a white flower that was originally white—[the worship must be redone]. (17)
Likewise, when there is an outbreak of excessive locusts, or when there is madness and pestilence, parrots will be born from mice, and there will be venomous serpents and the like. (18)
In a palace, in an assembly hall, at a city gate, in a pavilion, as well as in the residence of attendants, and in that which arises from a honeycomb— (19)
In the event of excessive rain, drought, or when a king prepares for war—
especially if it occurs during the half of the month presided over by the sign of Taurus (Vṛṣa)— [the following applies].
When the chief queen or the preeminent elephant has died, there is blood; and the three crows, the owl, the jambu, the vulture, and the tawny one [are also seen]. (21)
When [the sun] has entered the king's palace, or when it has touched a temple of the gods, or when it is above a temple of the gods or above the king's residence. || 22 ||
When a dog mounts [a woman] and she cries out there, the ritual actions for that specific species [are performed];
likewise, when a firefly mounts Rohiṇī, [the same applies] to the linga or the image.
In some cases, however, the Teacher [perceives] through various forms from the two comets;
when there is a linga at the base and a bimba at the point of ascent.
The extraordinary powers (siddhis) are traditionally held to be the effects of actions distinct from [ordinary] generalities;
I shall now declare the remedies for the purpose of removing their defects.
O King, if the sun enters [the sign] at night, there will be the destruction of living beings and fear from the ruler;
therefore, having performed the Diśāhoma, one should perform the supreme Mahāsnapana.
Having performed the rites and worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should offer abundant sacrificial oblations;
there, one should feed the Brahmins and likewise feed the observer of the vow.
In this very manner, for seven days, day after day, at the rising of the moon on the new moon day, there shall be the destruction of cattle and the destruction of crops. (28)
One should perform everything as before for the pacification of those defects. Furthermore, an earthquake may arise as a cause of misfortune for the king and the kingdom. (29)
Having bathed [the image] with thousands of prasthas of milk and thousands of portions of honey and clarified butter, while being focused on Śiva, with the mantra "mahāvyoma" (the Great Ether).
One should perform a hundred oblations with fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood and should constantly feed Brahmins until the end of twenty-one days.
Likewise, when rivers are agitated, as well as when wells and ponds are disturbed,
famine arises in the world and thereafter a great pestilence shall occur.
Having constructed a pavilion on its bank measuring nine cubits in size,
properly prepare a mandala within that pavilion and a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in its center.
There, the preceptor should perform the fivefold fire-ritual according to the path prescribed for the fire-ritual,
having prepared the *vyāghāta* fuel-sticks with the *astra-mantra*.
Having offered clarified butter with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *pāśupata-mantra*,
one should offer one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five oblations for each, in due order.
One should perform the *mindāhuti* offering and offer the *vyāhṛtis* in sequence;
then one should perform the *jayādi* offerings, the *abhyādhāna*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings in due order. (36)
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rules, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
having performed this for five days, one should finally perform the concluding rite (udvāsana).
If there is weeping at an image, it portends the destruction of cattle and the ruin of grain;
the king who is the lord of that mandala will perish along with his village and kingdom. (38)
Having performed the purification of the image, one should then carry out the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa),
[repeating it] for one fortnight or two fortnights, with pacifying oblations (śānti-homa) for the sake of subduing obstacles. (39)
One should always perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) accompanied by the fire-oblation for the quarters (diśāhoma);
one should always feed the Brāhmaṇas and likewise feed the husbands.
Then there shall be a rain of blood and the destruction of living beings;
thereafter, one should wash the palaces, pavilions, and other structures with water.
One should smear the entire floor of the ālaya with cow dung;
having performed the rite of circumambulation with fire, one should again perform the auspicious day ceremony (puṇyāha).

Having bathed [the image] according to the rules with a thousand *prasthas* of milk and a thousand measures each of honey and clarified butter, while reciting the mantra "Mahāvyoma" along with the *mūlamantra*.
One should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) using fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood;
one should do this for seven days and then conduct a festival with mantras.

During the showers of honey and the showers of milk, the best of preceptors, having removed the three defects of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, should bathe [the deity] with thousands of prasthas of those respective substances.
One should perform worship especially with great offerings of oblations;
one should also cause a peace-offering (śāntihoma) to be performed with fuel-sticks of the Aśoka tree.
One should perform this for seven days; afterwards, a meal for Brahmins should be provided.
If blood is produced from a tree, there will be fear of an enemy army.
At the foot of a tree, the best of those skilled in the directions should perform the Diśā-homa;
he should feed the Brāhmaṇas there and worship the deities of the site (Vāstu-devas).
One should worship Śiva and thereafter perform the great ceremonial bath;
one should worship him especially and offer abundant sacrificial oblations. (49)
If a sandal falls down for no reason from the edge of the temple, it portends the destruction of women, children, and the fields. (50)
Having restored the temple as before, the preceptor should also rebuild what is dilapidated; then, having prepared a new image, he should install it as previously described.
Having performed a special worship, one should conduct a festival at the end;
however, if there is a relocation to another place, it results in the displacement of the king from his position.
Having established the locus as before, one should properly perform the emanation; the installation of the deity should be performed as previously described, but with particular care. || 53 ||
Having performed the consecration with cow products, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
furthermore, if the Vardhanī vessel or the Śiva-kumbha should be broken or cracked, [one should perform atonement] in their presence.
The king should cause the bathing and consecration of the deities of that kingdom to be performed according to the rules with devotion on the bank for the sake of peace. (55)
If another Brahma-abode is reached, other fruits will arise;
if it is produced from a different flower, a different taste and fragrance will occur.
And for all mortals dwelling in that kingdom, there is suffering; it affects the entire tree of that lineage, especially in its former location. (57)
Then one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) using peacock fuel-sticks;
having worshipped Śiva according to the rules, perform the ceremonial bathing for seven days.
Having performed the consecration with milk, one should worship the deities of the site (vāstudeva).
Then, one should worship Śiva with all kinds of fruits and flowers. (59)
One should especially worship with all kinds of perfumes when [the deity] has entered the lingas and the images;
otherwise, various diseases arise for all mortals.
And famine and the destruction of cattle will certainly arise in that kingdom. || 61 ||
A wise person should bathe Śiva with thousands of prasthas of milk, thousands of measures of honey and clarified butter, and even with coconut water.
There, the ritual bathing (snapana) should be performed with the mantra "mahāvyoma";
one should worship especially with saffron, camphor, and sandalwood.
Having mixed it with powdered agaru and camphor, one should smear Śiva with it;
the great oblation (mahāhavis) should be offered, and one should perform the offering to the quarters (diśāhoma).
One should perform this for seven days, and at its conclusion, a jar of cold water;
[by this,] those born from eggs, those born from sweat, quadrupeds, and likewise humans [are purified]. 65.
If offspring other than one's own caste is born, the death of the king is certain;
therefore, one should diligently perform gifts of cows, land, gold, and so forth. (66)
One should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and a pacifying fire-oblation (śāntihoma) with a single fuel-stick (samidh).
One should continue doing this for seven days, and at the conclusion, one should perform a festival (utsava).
If a circumambulation of the temple is performed, there shall be no calamity in the kingdom;
and one should likewise [construct] a temple with a thousand *prastha*s of cow-products for each [circumambulation]. (68)
The wise one should bathe the Supreme Lord with the five Brahmans and the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga),
and sprinkle the temple according to the previously mentioned procedure. (69)
In that case, a wise person should perform a ceremonial bath and feed Brāhmaṇas;
for when a comet has arisen, there will always be turmoil in the kingdom.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing there and worship especially;
one should have a propitiatory fire-oblation performed with fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood.
One should sprinkle the mountain with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Prāsāda mantra;
then, having installed a linga near that mountain, one should worship it.
