One should perform the ceremonial bathing of the deities of that kingdom and offer sacrificial oblations;
one should perform special worship and, at its conclusion, conduct a festival.
If a tree that has been watered is itself consumed by fire, it will bring about the destruction of children;
moreover, a disturbance of fire will certainly occur in that kingdom immediately. (74)
A monk should especially perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the village itself;
he should carry out the oblation with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), and mustard seeds.
Then, with fuel-sticks of that tree, one should shake [the fire] according to the sequence of the five Brahmas;
one should offer oblations one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five times for each, in due order.
One should offer oblations, in sequence, one thousand times for each of the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the Prāsāda mantra, or half of that number.
Then, having offered the oblation for atonement (mindāhuti), one should subsequently offer the Jaya and other oblations;
after performing the ceremonial bath (snapana), one should worship with special excellence.
One should perform a propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*) with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *udumbara* wood;
however, if trembling occurs in the image, the king will meet his death. (79)
Having performed the purification of the image with the products of the cow (gavya),
one should then perform the oblation to the quarters (diśāhoma) and thereafter cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
One should perform this for seven days, and at the conclusion of that period, hold a festival;
likewise, when the Śiva-vardhanī and the liṅga or the image have been broken.
There will be fear from enemy armies on the earth, and a great pestilence shall prevail;
therefore, having performed the *bālātāna* rite, construct the temple as before.
Having performed the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the temple according to the previously mentioned procedure,
if the linga is broken, one should remove it and install a new one using that very same method.
The supreme guide, being wise, may have it constructed even by another means; he should perform the consecration in accordance with the previously stated procedure.
If the primary or secondary limbs are missing, or if the image is devoid of garments and ornaments,
one should perform the reconstitution (*sandhānaka*) and then carry out the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*).

Then, having performed the oblation to the quarters (diśāhoma), one should carry out the great ablution (mahāsnāna) and likewise cause the consecration (abhiṣeka) to be performed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the nectars (amṛta). || 86 ||
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with thousands of prasthas of milk and thousands of prasthas of honey, using the mantra "mahāvyoma."
Having caused the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed, one should then feed the Brahmins;
furthermore, one should have a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma) performed with fuel-sticks made of khadira wood.
Having performed it in this manner, one should conduct a festival at the end of seven days;
having performed the opening of the image, [the destruction] of the kingdom or village occurs [wherever it is done]. (89)

For one fortnight or two fortnights, one should daily perform the pacifying oblation with the "Speech-fuel" (vāk-samidh), as well as the ceremonial bathing and the oblation of the quarters (diśā-homa).
One should constantly feed the Brāhmaṇas and provide food for the poor and the blind;
[this should be done] when an elephant is in rut and during the onset of a great windstorm.
There shall indeed be a destruction of vehicles and a destruction of women.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rites, perform his ritual bathing daily.
One should perform the fire-oblation with the Śivāṅgas, the Vidyāṅgas, and the Śiva-mantras;
having thus passed seven days, one should present the great sacrificial offering.
If fire is absent or smoke has been extinguished, there will be the destruction of vehicles;
in that case, danger from a foreign army will certainly arise on the earth. (94)
Having dug up that spot, one should fill it with the five types of earth;
having explained [the procedure for] the sacrificial fuel, one should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma). || 95 ||
One should feed the Brahmins there and also feed the poor;
one should bathe the Supreme Lord with thousands of prasthas of milk.

At the end of that, one should perform a ceremonial bath; at the conclusion of that, when the [proper] color has been attained, one should apply a jar of water to the linga to remedy any defect in its caste.
Then, having ground cardamom, cloves, camphor, jasmine, jambu fruit, and nutmeg according to the mantra, one should smear the liṅga with it.

At the conclusion, one should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed, followed by a peace-offering (śāntihoma) for seven days; the preceptor, having offered oblations with *aśoka* wood, should do so while reciting the *tryambaka* mantra. (99)
O Brahmin, if after performing a special worship one feeds the brahmins at its conclusion,
and the sound of the drum arises spontaneously, a great pestilence breaks out.

One should cause the ceremonial bathing to be performed with *bilva* fuel-sticks and perform a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*); one should practice in this very manner for a fortnight or even for two fortnights. (101)
Thus has the great marvel been described; now hear of the common marvel:
when the sun is rising, if a secondary sun (pratisūrya) is seen.
When there is fear from an enemy army on earth, or when men are seized by fever,
one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) using horse-dung fuel-sticks.
At the conclusion of that, one should perform the ceremonial bath and worship especially with abundant offerings; in this manner, one should practice for seven days.
Just as when the moon rises, if a secondary moon (praticandra) is seen, famine arises in the world and a great pestilence breaks out. (105)
One should practice according to the very path taught for the vision of the Inner Self, whether during the sight of a flash of lightning, or the sight of fire and stars. (106)
During a planetary conjunction with a lunar mansion (graha-nakṣatra-pāta), there will undoubtedly be drought;
all men will be seized by fever, and there will be a depletion of mounts. 107.
Having worshipped Śiva there, one should perform the great ablution (mahāsnāna);
then, having performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should offer fuel-sticks (samidh) into the fire.
Having performed it in this manner for seven days, hold a festival at its conclusion;
[this should be done] continuously for seven days, day and night, once [the deity] has descended. (109)
Excessive rain will surely bring disease upon men;
at the end [of the period], however, there will be thousands of vessels filled with ghee and milk.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord and worship him especially;
at the conclusion of that, one should perform a ceremonial bath and offer abundant sacrificial oblations.
Likewise, if the sun or the moon is surrounded by a halo for seven days,
the king who is the lord of that region shall meet his death in battle.
Having likewise performed the gift of land, the gift of sesame and cows, and the gift of gold,
one should worship Maheśvara with a thousand *prasthas* of milk.
One should perform the bathing especially at that time;
then, having performed the *diśāhoma* (offering to the directions), one should practice in this manner for seven days.

But when the phallic emblem (liṅga) has been worshipped, when flowers have been obtained, and when another caste has arrived, one should likewise prescribe clothing, ointments, and the non-defilement of the cow. 115.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite, one should offer abundant oblations when locusts have appeared in great numbers or when the vehicle has become uncontrollable.
Parrots and mice will become more virulent than venomous serpents;
there will be the destruction of living beings and drought, without a doubt. (117)
In front of the temple, one should construct a square pavilion measuring ten or twelve cubits, resembling the surface of a mirror.
(233) Equipped with sixteen pillars and adorned with all ornaments,
the circular pit (vṛttakuṇḍa) in the center should measure two cubits in size. 119.
The best of teachers should cause each [lotus] to be joined with the *meghalātrīya* [pattern] and six finger-breadths in size, provided with a navel and a womb. 120.
Having prepared the fire of Śiva— square in the cardinal directions and lotus-shaped in the corners— with a mind focused as prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya), [he should proceed].
The most excellent preceptor should offer into the fire sacrificial fuel, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seed, salt, and likewise the seeds of cotton.
Palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, and vaṭa are to be planted in the east and the other cardinal directions in order;
and śamī, bilva, aśoka, and mayūra are to be placed in the intermediate directions.

Palāśa wood should be the primary substance; one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the Sadyojāta mantra, as well as with the five Brahmans, the six limbs, the limbs of the Vidyā, and the root mantra.
With the Pāśupata weapon and the Aghora weapon,
the wise one should offer oblations one thousand times or half of that for each, in due order.
One should perform the Jaya and other rites, as well as the Abhyādhāna and the Rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings in sequence;
at the conclusion of that, one should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) and worship with special care.
Then a great oblation (mahāhavis) should be offered and Brahmins should be fed;
in this very manner, at midday, the wise man, having performed the recitation, should cause [the rite] to be performed. 127.
And likewise in a palace, in an assembly hall, at a city gate, in a pavilion, in a residence for attendants, and in a place where honey-bees have built their nest. (128)
O King, the destruction of the village and certain death [will follow];
therefore, having removed the honeycomb, one should sprinkle it with pure water. (129)
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rules, the wise one should perform the oblation for the quarters;
he should bathe the Supreme Lord with honey, ghee, and milk.
One should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) using fuel-sticks produced from the interior of a nest;
at its conclusion, one should perform an ablution for the deity and carry out this rite for seven days.
At the conclusion, one should hold a festival for seven days or three days;
when drought occurs, there is the destruction of cattle and the destruction of crops.
One should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) using fuel-sticks made of khādira wood;
having performed the sprinkling with milk, perform the ceremonial bath at its conclusion.
One should perform the rite for the deity for seven days; thereafter, fashion a white water-pot.
When excessive rain occurs, famine will certainly arise. (134)
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with thousands of measures of honey and thousands of measures of ghee; at the conclusion of that, perform the ceremonial bath.
Having stirred it at night and subsequently mixed it with camphor,
one should encircle the pedestal of the liṅga with a width of six finger-breadths.
It should have the circumference of the little finger, be free from camphor, be combined with cow's ghee, and measure four tālas in height. || 137 ||
One should gradually offer a thousand lamps or half of that number,
accompanied by split mung beans and an abundance of sacrificial oblations.
Having performed the pacifying *homa* at the end, [using] fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *pālāśa* wood,
or even the primary lotus, death shall indeed occur for the ascetic. (139)
One should perform special worship and conduct the rite for three nights, except in the case of a king engaged in battle or when there is a danger of a fall from a tree. 140.
Likewise, if the chief queen falls to the ground due to some cause,
or if the chief elephant should die, death will surely occur.
O King, death shall certainly occur right here and immediately;
therefore, one should perform great gifts, especially for the Brāhmaṇas. (142)
Having worshipped the Great Lords, one should begin the great ablution;
then, having offered the great sacrificial oblation, one should fully worship the deities of the site (Vāstu).
Whether in the abode of the gods, or in the house of a king, or in a hall of learning, in an assembly hall, or at a crossroads; || 144 ||
Whether in a monastery, on the bank of a pond, or near a well, a remedial rite must be performed if blood appears from a woman. 145.
Then it releases that village, and likewise even its foundation;
when this occurs in the assembly hall, the destruction of the village will then take place.
When the [asterism] Catvāra arises, the destruction of living beings occurs;
when Maṭha arises, one should predict the ruin of the village. (146)
If these two appear on the bank of a pond, then one should eat them;
however, if they arise on a street, there will be the destruction of women and children. (148)

When a well has been dug on the edge [of a sacred site], suffering arises for the inhabitants of that village; therefore, one should fill that spot by digging it out again or by filling it with sacrificial bricks (*yuga*) and the like. (149)
Having caused the Brahmins to recite the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) formula, he should then feed them;
having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), while chanting the Pavamāna hymns.
Then, having performed the *śānti* oblation with *palāśa* fuel-sticks, and having performed the ceremonial bathing at its conclusion, one should perform the *śānti* oblation once again. (151)
If cows, tawny-colored creatures, vultures, owls, or crows enter the interior of the king's residence or his inner apartments, [it portends misfortune]. (152)
One should prescribe [remedies] for children, groups of women, and those who have perished;
then, having prepared a jar of cold water, one should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma). || 153 ||
Having fed the Brahmins, perform the ceremonial bath at the conclusion;
it should take place atop the temple or above the king's palace.
If a dog should howl there while it is being barked at, the king shall meet his death;
therefore, having killed that [dog] and abandoned three goats, one should then have the Puṇyāha recited.
One should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) with horse dung and sacrificial fuel;
thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins and perform the great ceremonial bath (snapana). || 156 ||
At the conclusion of that, one should perform a festival and worship the Vāstu deities;
likewise, when there is the mounting of a living being upon a liṅga or an image, [the same should be done]. || 157 ||
It would bring about an increase in disease for all kings;
having killed that [image], one should immediately bathe the gods here below, and then [proceed] from there.
Having performed the pacification oblation (śāntihoma) with fuel sticks (samidh) during the first half [of the rite],
one should then perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and present the great sacrificial offering (mahāhavi). || 159 ||
If a comet endowed with various forms should appear in the sky,
one should observe it there with certainty and perform an expiation.
If one ascertains that an insect has ascended the base of the *liṅga*, there will undoubtedly arise turmoil in the kingdom and famine; of this there is no doubt. (161)
One should worship the Lord of the Gods of gods and perform the eightfold binding;
then, having performed a peace-offering (śāntihoma) with fuel-sticks of khadira wood.
Then, having prepared a jar of cool water, one should present the great oblation;
whatever ritual remains deficient shall be pacified by a rite of propitiation through fire-offerings.
In that case, a counter-measure should be performed by a Guru who has witnessed the ritual action;
having done so, he should spend a month each month, for otherwise the rite becomes fruitless. (164)
There, one should honor the preceptor in accordance with the prescribed rite of recompense, with garments, finger-rings, cattle, land, wealth, and grain. (165)
A fee of one niṣka of unrighteous wealth is known as the middling;
however, the fee for the preceptor should be understood as three times that amount for the highest grade. 166.
One should cause the materials required for the sacrifice to be presented to the preceptor.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Portents," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
(238) I shall describe the ritual for pacifying a village; listen, O you who possess such splendor!
Whether in a village, a city, a town, or a capital— || 1 ||
If the Kubjaka, the Kheṭaka, and the Bahurūpa are likewise devoid of their proper positions in the east or even in the south; || 2 ||
In the west or the north, or even in the intermediate directions,
[the site] should be one-fourth or one-eighth of the size of the village.
Having determined the portion of the *kalā* and the *daśā* among those [elements] by means of the *kalpavāstu*,
the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) should be performed thus, whether externally or internally.
One should apply the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā) all around the palace,
proceeding in order from Brahmā to Īśāna, and from Indra to Īśāna.
Having taken refuge in the village, one should offer the bali-oblation to the gods in the middle of the village;
this offering, joined with the beginning and the end, should be performed every day.
Brahmarākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, and indeed night-stalkers—
all these deities dwell in an empty village.
If [the sun] makes its transit through the eastern and western auspicious sites (suvāstu),
all the inhabitants of that village will experience disease, grief, and fear.
If one constructs a mound in that village, that kingdom will perish;
therefore, to pacify that evil, one should offer a bali-oblation to the Rākṣasas and other spirits.
Having gone out to the gateway situated facing the village,
the Rākṣasas and other deities who occupy the gateway should be [propitiated].
(239) The deity residing in this place should perform the bali offering for the sake of satisfaction.
Having prepared the materials for the bali, the preceptor should perform his ritual bath. (11)
Having wrapped [the image] in very clean cloth, one should discard the wet cloth;
then, having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, one should prepare the ordinary *arghya* offering.
Having first prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship Vighneśa;
then, having offered a coconut fruit divided into two halves, which bestows all accomplishments (sarvasiddhi).
Laxity is a slackness in one's duty; therefore, one should abandon that fault.
O Vighnarāja, having made this petition to the Supreme Lord, salutations be unto you. (14)
O God of gods, Lord of the world, destroyer of the forms of the worlds, you who have initiated the sacrifice of Śiva—fulfill my command always. (15)
O Blessed One, whatever was performed by him and by me in the sacrificial hall, and the offerings to the spirits, I perform through your grace. (16)
"Indeed, let a betel nut and a single flower of the coconut tree be accepted individually; let a coconut fruit be accepted according to the number of months. (17)
For that purpose, there should be one drona of rice and four times as much of its flower;
the flower, resembling a yellow gem, bestows the abundance of lotus flowers.
One should place loose flowers— such as jasmine, white water-lilies, and ketaka— as well as other fragrant flowers, into the flower-vessel for the deity.
With one [part] of cotton wick, there should be five [parts] of a great wick;
and black musk from elephants and deer, combined with fragrance and camphor.
p.
240) Incense made from *kunduruṣka* and *garu*, five red garments, and a wooden seat—these five, or the fourth [item] combined with them. || 21 ||
A sword, a trident, a bow, arrows, a small knife, a mallet, and a shield;
a coconut, oil, and a bountiful plantain fruit. || 22 ||
Milk with five types of powders and pieces of plantain leaf, betel nut combined with oil, and betel leaf bestow prosperity. (23)
The wise one should cook śuddhodana with two āḍhakas of rice, and pāyasa with one āḍhaka, along with an equal amount of white unbroken grains of sugar.
One should place it in a pure vessel mixed with grape juice;
having thus prepared the substance, one should then worship the Lord of the Astra-mantra.
Having taken up the auspicious sword, one should place it in the presence of Śiva;
having informed the Supreme Lord, one should collect the materials for the offering.
The disciple, having grasped the lord of weapons, the sword of Śiva, with his hand amidst the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, and the ḍamaru, paṭaha, and mardala drums; 27.

It was filled with other sounds as well, joined by the voices of women of ill-favored appearance; it was always broken, accompanied by its own [internal] noise, and endowed with the flickering of lamp flames. || 28 ||
One should take refuge at the gateway adorned with parasols and chowries;
having duly worshipped the gatekeepers, [one should perform] the rites beginning with the bath and ending with the offering of food (naivedya).
One should thoroughly worship the enclosure, whether it be external or internal;
having washed the door with water, one should offer the bali-oblation to Nandin and Kāla.
One should worship the bull in the center and strike the great *khaṇṭā* [gong];
thereafter, having made the door on the outside with a measurement of five cubits. (31)
One should discard grass, roots, and so forth, and prepare a square area equal to that; in its center, one should construct an altar and perform a smearing with cow dung.

One should sprinkle the sacrificial materials for the bali offering with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and collect them; then, one should place the Lord of Weapons (astranātha) above the altar and install the sword of Śiva (śivakhaḍga).
In the center, in the east, in the south, in the west, and in the northern direction;
in the center is an eight-petaled lotus, while in the northeast is an eight-cornered [figure].
One should draw a ninefold womb (navayoni) in the south, a hexagon in the western direction,
and an eight-pronged trident in the north, using red pigment.
Outside of that, one should fashion a square with white color;
its inner corner should be adorned with five colors.
One should place four seats on the outer edge of the mandala’s base;
having placed a seat in the center, one should [place another] in the middle of the western part of the mandala.
Having spread a cloth upon the pedestal, it is covered with red silk;
there is a circular mound of rice exceeding a *kuḍupa* in measure placed upon the pedestal.
Above that, there should be a coconut; one should place it on the fourteenth day.
Having arranged a sword in the east, one should place a bow and an arrow in the south. (39)
Having placed the *kṣurikā* in the west and the *piṇḍipāla* in the north,
one should place the trident in the center, with the five arrows upon the cooked rice.
One should cause a prastha measure of rice, combined with kunda flowers, to be placed;
one should have that rice placed in a bronze vessel upon its top. (41)
One should place coconut water filled with ghee,
and within that, one should set a great wick prepared according to the prescribed rules.
A svastika, adorned with five powders, should be placed in the direction of the wind;
above that, or alternatively, a pure vessel filled with coconut water.
In front of him, he should place a plantain leaf, complete with its base and tip,
upon white unbroken rice (akṣata), and atop it, a plantain fruit.

One should worship the Teacher (Śiva), Caṇḍikā, Aghora, and likewise Bhairava; in the center of that [space], one should worship the Lord of the Masters of Beings (Bhūtanātheśa) in the directions starting from the east. || 45 ||
In the southeast pavilion,
one should place [the deity] adorned with five powders to the east of the lotus-form, or alternatively, in the eight directions.
One should place a single *piṇḍa* made from wood-apple fruit smeared with ghee upon a plantain leaf, accompanied by a wick-lamp. || 47 ||
One should offer the *bali* to Ananta and others, performing a sprinkling with water;
and having drawn a hexagon in the southwest using five types of powder.
Having prepared the maṇḍala in the northeast, provided with four corners, one should offer the sixfold oblation (*bali*) to the great elements in their proper sequence. (49)
Accompanied by the six sūtras and adorned with the five powders,
one should suspend the *padārthaka* with coconut water alone.
One should suspend betel nuts and the flowers of the coconut tree; at the crossroads, one should offer a bali-oblation to the piśācas, and at the triple-junctions, to the rākṣasas. (51)
Having worshipped Kūṣmāṇḍa at the triple-path (tripatha), one should sacrifice to the Nāgas at the triple-path;
having worshipped Bhairava at the triple-path, one should perform the worship of the Asuras at the double-path (dvipatha).
Having offered this *nandabali*, one should perform the *pātrādīpa* (the lamp of the vessel).
Having thus worshipped in due order, one should take up a flower and scatter it.
Then, having scattered white [flowers] over the wound, perform the "dwelling" (vāsana) while feeling aversion [to the enemy].
Having purified it with the Śiva-sword and released the blood-water, [proceed].
In the northeast, at the tip of another [blade of grass], one should withdraw Aja according to the scripture:
"Obeisance to you, Lord of the lords of beings; may this offering be accepted for the sake of your pleasure. (55)
"I have initiated this sacrifice which bestows all desired objects;
therefore, with contented minds, go as you please for your own happiness. (56)
In the midst of empty dwellings, one should afterwards cast the propitiatory offering (śānti-bali);
in that village, one should perform the bali for the sake of satisfying Bhadrakālī.
By giving food, one causes all the gods to attain satisfaction;
having performed the washing of the feet, one should afterwards lead [the deity] into the sacrificial site (vāstu).
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) at the place of Brahmā, in front of the deity, in the middle of the ritual procedure,
on the pedestal of the spirits, in the center of the tree, or in the center of the site, one should perform the rite.

One should cast the offering to the gods in the directions of fire (East), Yama (South), Nirṛti (Southwest), Varuṇa (West), Vāyu (Northwest), Kubera (North), and Īśa (Northeast) respectively. || 60 ||
(244) In the place of strength, I [should perform] that; one should avoid it in other places.
Hunting expeditions and the like, as well as sacred fords (tīrtha), should be outside the site (vāstu), as should the vehicle. 61.
One should offer the Artharātri bali at midday or in the evening;
one should perform the grāmaśānti bali, which bestows all desired fruits.
All the inhabitants of that village should offer the *balida* known as *balirucya*;
for if the *grāmaśāntibalih* is omitted, there will be the destruction of the dwellings in that kingdom.
The king shall conquer his kingdom and overcome the fear of enemy armies;
all those dwelling in that region shall be afflicted by fever and other maladies. (64)
Therefore, with every effort, one should offer the village-peace oblation (grāmaśānti-bali);
at its conclusion, one should perform a festival that bestows the fruit of all desires. || 65 ||
The mortal who acts in this manner shall attain a meritorious destination.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Rule for Atonement for the Community," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
I shall describe the ritual of the Fish Incarnation; listen to it, O Prabhāñjanā!
In this way, there shall be enjoyment for all beings, and happiness shall come to you all.
The play of the fish is praised from the sign of Pisces up to Virgo;
thus, it is declared to be of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling.
Whether in the ocean, a river, a lake, or even a small well—for one who is equal [to all], the ocean is best; and for one who is middling, the middle of a river is best.
A fish [image] in a pond or tank is proclaimed to be the lowest;
however, an image that has undergone consecration (abhiṣeka) is praised as the highest. (4)
The ancient image of the deity is proclaimed as the middling type;
however, the image made for immediate purification is called the inferior by me.
In this manner, the vision of the ocean is considered appropriate for the supreme image (bera);
likewise, the vision of rivers and the like is considered appropriate for the medium-sized image.

Now, in this case, for a *bera* [temple], a tank, or a step-well (*vāpī*), the procedure extends up to one hundred *krośas*; however, for the highest [type of temple], the *darśana* [ceremony] is prescribed.
Thus, the vision in the intermediate [level] is considered to be fifty cubits;
the vision in the inferior [level] is considered to be twelve cubits. || 8 ||
Thus the Kṛtayuga has been described; one should consider it with every effort to be devoid of the portions belonging to the gods and demons, and should conceive of it in its proper sequence.
Another [type] would be for six days, the middling would be for three days,
and the excellent would indeed be for seven days, according to the sequence of the number of days.
One should perform all this together with the locations such as villages and so forth;
that [practice] is said to be of two kinds, namely the *līlā* and the *sāyana*. || 11 ||
If the vehicle is the Ālayavijñāna, one should lead it to the pavilion of the ritual site,
which is endowed with all ornaments, and decorate the pavilion.
On an auspicious morning and a favorable day, at the conclusion of the night’s worship, [he said]:
"O God of gods, Lord of the World, O dispeller of the world's afflictions! (13)
p.

246) Having made the formal request, "O Lord, surely the weapons have been taken up," one should then, in due order, take up the golden thread and so forth, and perform the binding of the protection as previously described. || 14 ||
On the following day at midday, he should lead [the image] to the assembly pavilion;
and at the conclusion of the morning twilight, it is attended by hosts of gods.
One should satisfy the Supreme Lord with all the royal services;
one should worship him at midday, adorned with every ornament.
Having adorned it with all kinds of musical instruments and embellished it with all manner of sounds,
one should proceed with the vehicle as before, dedicated to the deceased.
At that time, however, the king, together with his preceptors,
[should especially prepare] a powder of camphor and turmeric, as well as the leaves of the *rāgavallī*.
Having entered that place with all the various colors and forms,
it may be in the north, the west, the east, or even the south.
Having constructed a water-stall at that place, adorned with canopies and other ornaments,
one should install the deity in the center and perform the worship of Matsya in front of it.
Having arranged the rice and other offerings, one should worship with the words "of the rice";
one should properly honor the fish with rice, sesame seeds, and parched grain.
Having thus recited the mantra, "O Great Fish, you are the lamp within the belly of Malika," one should lead the fish to their food.
Having observed the play of the fish, one should first perform the *sayāna*;
at the conclusion of that, for the task of sailing, one should perform the *limlāgana* and the *gādhaka*.
Accompanied by music for diversion, one should cause [the deity] to enter the previous location;
then, having performed the ablution and the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*), one should bathe the Supreme Lord.
At the end of that, however, there is protection from the evening until the morning worship;
and as before, one should perform the daily worship, with special worship at its conclusion.
At the conclusion of that, having performed the ceremonial bath and released the protective thread,
meditation is thus prescribed in the vicinity of the temple.
Thus has the vehicle been fully described; now hear concerning the residence as well.
At the conclusion of the worship at night, one should perform [the ritual] together with the preceptor.
The wise one, having made a request before Maheśa, should arrange the single form of the deity into five aspects. (28)
O Prahbañjanā, listen to this for the sake of protecting the world:
the Lord, accompanied by Ambikā, is the cause of the origin of the universe. (29)
"Let us go toward Matsyalīla," Śaṅkarā said;
thus at that time he requested permission from the Blessed One.
Having bound the *pratisara* as before, one should lead it toward the mount;
then, at dawn, it should be adorned with all ornaments.
Adorned with all kinds of musical instruments and accompanied by shouts of victory,
the vehicle, along with royal honors, proceeded slowly.
One should scatter camphor, turmeric, and parched grain over the well-decorated area;
in another delightful spot, one should present various kinds of food offerings.
One should cause various kinds of betel-leaves to be offered in the presence of Śiva;
especially every day, one should perform ritual bathing and the fire-oblation for peace (śāntihoma). (34)
One should always perform [the rite] in this manner according to the rules for daily worship;
having constructed a well-characterized water-shed (prapā) at the site of the sacred place, one should dedicate it to that purpose.
In the center, provided with a pedestal, one should place a lion-throne above;
having installed Maheśa there, listen now to the playful song below. (36)
Having performed the spring festival (Vasantalīlā), which is attended by hosts of wise men,
there should first be a meal of fish, followed by rice and other foods served individually.
One should place the cooked rice and other items with the mantra "oṃ danasya";
having observed the playful movements of the fish, one should offer the food for the fish. (38)
One should perform this every day, having resolved upon it until the end of the day;
if one is deprived of the daily worship, one should likewise perform the expiation.
Whether due to an unknown oblation or because an expiation was not performed—if an expiation is omitted, it brings harm to the king and the kingdom. (40)
Therefore, one should perform the daily worship with every effort;
at the conclusion of the play, the rite called Vimukhayāna should be performed.
The king, by way of showing honor, should re-establish [the image] in its former place;
he should provide a ritual bath, a fire-offering for peace, and abundant sacrificial oblations.
The king and the queen, together with the guide,
should recite the melā-mantra and cause the flower to be placed upon the head.
Having reflected with the mind upon whatever task is to be done and having made his request, the wise man should carry out the "sport of the fish" (matsyalīlā) in this very manner. (44)
Listen now to the method for catching pearls as proclaimed by Matsyalīlā.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Fish’s Play," in the Sūkṣma-śāstra.
I shall describe the collection of pearls; listen to that, O Prabhāñjanā!
[It should be done] in the month of Phālguna, Caitra, Kārttika, or even others.
For it is proclaimed that [the practice] is auspicious during the first half of the month (pūrvapakṣa), or alternatively, during the other;
likewise, if it is undertaken during the eighth or ninth [lunar days] of the first half of the month.
The second, third, and fourth lunar days, or even the festival day itself,
the wise man should avoid with great effort, while accepting the remaining days.
If it is undertaken during the dark fortnight on the fourth or the fifth day as well; || 3 ||
One should diligently avoid the eighth, the ninth, the thirteenth, and the tenth lunar days; as for other lunar days, they may be used. || 4 ||
Alternatively, capture by means of a constellation is considered to be of another kind:
namely, Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, and Maghā. (5)
In the triad beginning with Āḍhaka, as well as in Hasta and Śravaṇa—
having taken these constellations, all other constellations are considered inferior.
One should avoid Friday and Saturday, and the Sun [day] in sequence;
likewise, one should avoid Vajra, Siddhi, Parigha, and Śiva.
Siddha, Sādhya, Śubha, Brāhma, Mahendra, Pratirāyuṣman, Saubhāgya, and likewise Śobhana. || 8 ||
A "staff of fortitude" (dhṛtiśūla) should also be performed; here, an increase [of the lunar day] in the cheek is mentioned.
These are declared to be auspicious; one should avoid other configurations. || 9 ||
Aries, Cancer, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius are to be known as auspicious; one should avoid the other zodiac signs.
Thus, one who knows the rules of time should commence this at that specific time;
having determined it on the day prior, at the conclusion of the morning twilight.
The wise one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of the consecrated image;
above that, he should sequentially place all the royal insignia.
Having paid homage to the God of gods, he should then make this request,
taking up a highly esteemed jewel for the purpose of obtaining pearls.

Therefore, with every effort, together with the people of those respective regions, [one should perform the rite] beginning with the banner and ending with the parasol, accompanied by the sounding of drums and other instruments. (14)
Having taken all this—equipped with thunderbolt-like instruments and accompanied by loud-sounding drums—the vehicle is described as before. (15)
Especially on the bank of a river, construct either a peak-shaped structure or a water-shed;
in its center, it should be provided with an altar and endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
It should be provided with four gates, adorned with four archways, and beautified with banners, canopies, betel nuts, and other such items. || 17 ||
Having thus caused [the deity] to enter the pavilion, seated upon the lion-throne,
perform the daily worship with diligence as a regular rite.
On that day, at the time of dawn, one should worship the gods together with the ocean,
and [worship] Amburāśi for the sake of obtaining pearls. (19)
Having bowed down to the milks for the sake of obtaining pearls, O Ocean of Curds, salutations to you for the sake of obtaining pearls. (20)
Salutations to you who have begun to produce pearls, and salutations to you for the gathering of pearls;
salutations to you who have produced pearls, and salutations to you for the gathering of pearls. || 21 ||
Salutations to you when the ocean of sugarcane was being churned for the sake of obtaining pearls;
salutations to you when the ocean of milk was being churned for the sake of obtaining pearls. || 22 ||
When the [beads] have been treated with alkali, one should say, "Salutations to you for the grasping of pearls," and in this very manner, the most excellent preceptor should perform the worship.
Having brought a boat or similar vessel, and having properly placed the deity— adorned with all ornaments— upon it, one should hoist the banner-cloth.
The teacher, wearing a garland, should stand to the right or left of the deity;
in front of the deity, he should perform playful singing accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments. || 25 ||
One should enter every place where pearls are located with all the royal honors; the extraction of pearls is considered to be performed through the path of all musical instruments.
Having filled it with grain and other such items, he should place it in its former location—either in the west, the southwest, the northeast, or the north. (27)
The best of teachers should prepare the hall for the taking up of the pearls;
having placed jewels within that hall, he should perform the ritual according to the rule until the end of the day.
At the time of evening, one should diligently and correctly perform the ritual bathing, the peace-offering fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*),
and the daily worship as if they were regular rites. (29)
In this manner, the rite should be performed every day; on that [specific] day, perform the sacrifice. In this very sequence, one should carry it out until the end of the fortnight.
Having brought together a multitude of riches and returned once more toward his home,
he reached the assembly pavilion, which was attended by throngs of eminent scholars.

Then, the ceremonial bathing (snapana), the pacificatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma), and the occasional worship (naimittikārcana) should be performed in the main sanctuary; one should conduct the worship as previously described.
If the daily rite is neglected, it brings about the destruction of the kingdom and the king;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the daily worship as previously described. (33)
Then, having offered the great oblation, one should satisfy the Supreme Lord;
specifically, perform a smearing with cow dung in front of Maheśa.
Having adorned it everywhere with flour-dust and burning lamps, one should place jewels before the deity; that substance shall be eightfold.
One share belongs to the preceptor alone, one share to the king, one share to Āditya, and likewise one share to the Sun (Sūrya). || 36 ||
The worship was performed as prescribed, and one should cause the mortals to offer a single portion;
the divine portion shall be the sixteenth, according to the sequence of the divine portion.
In this very way, one should gradually proceed with the acquisition of pearls;
it is meritorious, beneficial to all the world, and a source of prayer for all the gods. (38)
p.
253) The method for catching pearls has been explained; now hear the method for catching deer.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Catching of Pearls," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
I shall proclaim the wheel of worship; listen to it, O Prabhajana!
[It consists of] the master of the site, the master of the ritual, the serpent-worker, the initiate, and the lord of the assembly. (1)
The ruler of the country, the ruler of one's own land, and these seven are the leaders of the circle;
they are seated on the broken royal seats in the front pavilion of the preceptor.
The serpent stands on three or four feet in the Īśāna pavilion of the deity,
or in the southwest, the northeast, or the north, as the lord of the ritual observance (samayādhipa).
Sugrīva, the lord of the land, [should sit] in the pavilion for hearing the Dharma;
or in the north-western direction, or in the pavilion of jewels where the ritual acts are performed.
Sugrīva, the lord of the region, was in the pavilion for hearing the Dharma;
at the door of the pavilion known as Sthāna, he is said to have attained his station. (6)
The lords of the time-periods were on the northern side of the staircase,
while Sugrīva, the lord of the region, was in the pavilion for hearing the Dharma.
The place situated near the gate of Hamra is said to be my own domain, where I am to be slain. || 7 ||
Thus the location has been fully described; now hear, O observer of excellent vows, about the conduct, the ritual for bestowing the wheel-mark, and the yoga itself.
The collection of materials, the preservation of those materials, the production of flowers from the materials, and the accomplishment of the portion for the wheel. || 9 ||
The production of substances, their application, and the honoring of the preceptor and others—thus has conduct been described; now hear about the form of the wheel.
The bull, the serpent-seal, the mechanical device, the Caṇḍa-seal, the axe,
the golden seal, the momentary [seal], and the Phiṇḍi-plow. (11)
The Lord of the Samaya [holds] a serpent and a mace worthy of the Dharma-mudrā, a scepter worthy of the Mitra [mudrā], and an axe worthy of the Mudrā-samīcaṇḍa. || 12 ||
The king, who is worthy of receiving the *phiṇḍiphālā* offering, should hold a golden cane while standing in his own country;
the preceptor should bestow the *dharmamudrā* and other signs, such as the two serpents and so forth, upon the hand. (13)
The mark of the wheel has been fully described; now hear about the impeller of worship.
The materials for the articles of worship consist of the vessels and receptacles for each respective substance.
Having gathered [the offerings] at midday and presented them in the presence of Śiva, one's own duty as a teacher has been declared; now hear the conduct of the *samayin*.
Then, from that substance until the conclusion of the worship, the presiding deities of the substances should be dismissed at that time; having urged them to depart, one must not cause confusion.
The conduct of the initiate has been declared; O Lord of the Samaya, listen [now] to the sacrificial implements and the various materials required for their preparation. (17)
Having summoned all [the deities], one should place the Lord of Causes at the conclusion of the worship.
This is declared to be the duty regarding the *samaya*; O Lord of the *samaya* lineage, listen! (18)
Having rejoined the lords of the senses—who had fallen away due to contact with the wheel of Śiva’s command—to their respective wheels once more, he praised them according to their capacity. (19)
The duties of the ruler of one's own country are indeed the office of action (*karmakośa*) belonging to the lord of the [relevant] planet;
this is declared to be the duty of the agent. Now listen to that which has been proclaimed as the duty of the planets. (20)
(255) Endowed with the fivefold action and possessing the sevenfold self-experience,
one should relinquish the five offices at the conclusion of each respective task.
Having informed the presiding teacher (sthānācārya) of one's own spiritual experience, [one should proceed]. || 21 ||
At the conclusion of the offering of worship, one should perform the rite with the mantra "Cāhne ni cāhare";
then, while reciting the respective mantras, one should place [the offerings] into the hand of the officiating priest (sthānācārya).
Thus should the rite for the serpent be performed; now hear the procedure for the presiding teacher (sthānācārya).
Prior to the commencement of the ritual observance (samaya), one should worship the various marks of the maṇḍala (cakracihnāni).
Having worshipped with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should request permission from the wheel [of deities].
One should cause the names of the five authorities (*pañcādhikāra*) and the various wheels (*cakracihnāni*) to be bestowed.
The duties performed by the Sthānācārya have been declared; now listen to the qualities of those presiding over the mandalas:
the reciter, the worshiper, one who performs the twilight rituals, one who is all-pervading, and one who is adorned. (25)
And the practitioner, following the preceptor at these six locations, [should be] one who offers ashes, one who offers incense, and one who holds the lamp and the mirror. (26)
The water-bearer, the incense-collector, the holders of the parasol and the fly-whisk, the one holding the lute and the flute, and the bearer of the palm-leaf fan; || 27 ||

The leader of those performing the ritual duties should offer betel-leaf and pronounce "Svasti. The leader of the purification rite should wash the perpetual lamp and the water-vessel in the temple. || 28 ||
O you who purify the remains of offerings, O you with beautiful hair, you who cook the milk of the ocean;
having washed away the impurities with water, [apply] the fragrant ointment and the foot-ornament.
p.
256) These various types arose as leaders in the performance of tasks:
the cleaners, the plasterers, the washers of vessels, and those who carry lamps in their hands. (30)
To the spinner, the one who husks rice, the flute-player, the entertainer, the actress, the lute-player, and likewise the passionate woman. (31)

O Leader, having established these and other external ones as practitioners of the pledge (samayin), the conduct of their ritual activity has been proclaimed; thus the practitioner of the pledge performs the ritual activity.
O giver of gifts, O giver of light, you who grasp the flowers, you who bind the buds;
O you who remove the thorns of the assembly, you who sing the hymn in the Dravidian tongue! 33.

O Lord of the Samaya, you who perform the rites of purification; you are the ash that removes all impurity, the sandy bank that receives the sprinkling of water, and the one who bestows knowledge, dispassion, and contentment.
The village-dweller, the guest, the kinsman, the king, the forest-dweller, the attendant, the seeker of progeny, the native of one's own land, and the leader—these are [the types of persons]. 35.

He praised those who knew the proper times for the service of the gods, who were most devoted to dharma, protectors of justice, and eloquent in speech, as well as the sovereign of his own country in his ritual duties.
The priest, the celibate student, the water-carrier, and the sweeper;
the food-preparer, the cook, the singer of hymns, and the one who knows the Dravidian songs. (37)
The Dāmavidyā and others, including the Preṣyaka and Lekhakandhana,
are declared to consist of twelve divisions, preceded by the Cakra of Śiva’s command.
The sequence of the Cakrarāja has been declared; now hear the sequence of enjoyment and non-enjoyment.
One should divide the *nirmālya* intended for specific desires into eight equal parts. (39)
The priest shall indeed receive one-eighth part, while the assistants (pariyaṣṭins) shall receive one-sixteenth part; the musician shall receive one-sixth part, and the scribe one-fourth part. (40)
One-sixth of the Drāviḍa style, two parts for the *dāma* (string-cornice) in the *bhogaka* style, two parts for the wooden section, and four parts for the *prekṣyaka* (theatrical) style. || 41 ||
The Śodhaka shall receive one part; the Śuśrūṣaka, two parts;
the Pātraśodhi, two parts; and the Sthānācārya, one part. (42)
One part for the serpent [the Guru], one part for the ritualist (karmī), likewise one part for the initiate (samayin), and one part for the Lord of the Rule (samayādhipati). || 43 ||
One part for the lord of the region is indeed the regional share;
the remainder, consisting of four parts, one should designate as the portion for the guest and the cook.
In this very way, the enjoyment of desired objects is obtained equally through this gradual sequence;
thus has the order of portions been declared. Now hear the ritual arrangement for the *nirmālya*.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship Circle," in the *Sūkṣmaśāstra*.
Now I shall describe the festival of Śakti; let it be heard, O Prabhāñjanā!
This festival is to be known as fivefold, and its divisions are here explained. (1)
A nine-day [observance] is declared to bestow prosperity; a seven-day one would be rajasic;
a five-day one is declared to be sattvic; and a three-day one is called secondary (gauṇa). || 2 ||
The one-day rite is declared to be of a tamasic nature and is proclaimed to be fivefold;
the festival from the beginning of the month until the end of the month is described according to the prescribed rule.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the supreme festival ending with Āṣāḍhī;
at the conclusion of the ritual bath (avabhṛtha), one should observe the vow, and at the end, the descent ceremony (avarohaṇa).
It should likewise be performed in the month of Puṣya on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight (bhūtāṣṭamī);
and in the month of Māgha, it is traditionally held that it should be performed on the day of Āśleṣā as well as on the two new moon days (darśa).
One should perform the first [observance] ending with the full moon of Phālguna,
and the second should be performed in the month of Caitra, ending with the Citrā constellation.
In the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, under the asterisms of Viśākhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā,
Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla, this should be performed on the fourteenth day.
It should occur on the thirteenth day of the months of Uttaraṣāḍhā or Āṣāḍha, or specifically on the twelfth day of Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada.
O auspicious lady, that lunar mansion of the month shall be [Puṣya], and the eleventh day is considered [auspicious].
When Aśvinī is joined with a horse-like [day], it is considered Kṛttikā in the month of Kārttika.
There are two white [days] for each principal [deity] during the bright and dark fortnights;
or else, in another manner, that specific day of the image (berādina) is considered [the time for worship].
Whether it be a Sāmadāyika rite or a festival lasting ten days,
one should perform the pilgrimage there for three days according to the will of the patron.
Having thus resolved, one should begin the consecration at the sacred site;
on either the ninth or the seventh day, one should perform the hoisting of the banner.
One should perform all other rites up to the sounding of the drum and the bathing at the sacred ford;
beginning from three or four cubits, they should increase in sequence up to double that size.
For that purpose, the width of the cloth is said to be either three-quarters [of the length] or three feet; it should be provided with two tails and equipped with two bamboo poles. (14)
Dividing that cloth into eight parts, one part is considered for the head;
two parts are prescribed for the tail, and one part is for the lotus pedestal.
Having drawn the vehicle in two parts, one part should be joined with a parasol;
furthermore, the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) should be depicted on the sides of the pedestal.
On both sides of the two vehicles, one should place a lamp along with a self-manifested [image];
and on both sides of the parasol, two chowries should likewise be made.
Having drawn all of this together, one should arrange the auspicious Āyā and so forth,
endowed with five colors, in the place of liberation.
In the center of that, one should draw a bull or likewise fashion a lion; one should also depict it as standing, or reclining, or even as a vehicle.
That which is half-painted is called *ābhāsa*;
it is hollow and equipped with a mechanism, upon which one should fasten the rope well. (20)
Having thus prepared the cloth, the flagstaff is now described here:
it may be made from stone, wood, or from the heartwood of trees such as the *dhvaja*, *sāra*, or *kramuka*. (21)
Starting from nine cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time,
the measurement of the cubit is ninefold, ending at twenty-seven cubits.
Thus, the threefold [rite] ending with the *trivilā* has been explained as previously stated.
Thus, the inferior [rite] has been explained; everything else is as previously stated. (23)
Having prepared everything, including the banners and so forth, one should begin the consecration (*adhivāsana*).
At the end of half a watch (*ardhayāma*), the wise practitioner should worship Vighneśa. (24)
In front of the Goddess, or in the pavilion, one should prepare a fourth sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
having placed the cloth-painting (paṭa) in the west, one should place the nine [deities] to its east.
To the east of that, [he should perform] the form of the weapon (astramūrti), and to the east of that, the fire-oblation (homa) itself;
then the preceptor should perform the opening of the eyes with the Netra-mantra.
Then one should perform the purification of the bull (vṛṣaśuddhi); perform the ritual of the kalās;
the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) must be performed, as well as the binding of protection (rakṣābandha), as previously described.

The satiation of the mantra has thus been described; one should place the sequence of the breaking of the staff (daṇḍabhaṅga) and meditate upon the supreme Guru, beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti.
Having worshipped the bull in the central pitcher, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) around it;
facing west, having worshipped the bull, one should worship [the deities] beginning with Varuṇa in the eight directions.
Having worshipped each with its own mantra, one should place the bull and the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras).
Thus, having worshipped the jars, [one offers] the food offering, incense, and lamps.
Having worshipped the weapon according to the prescribed rule, one should then commence with gold;
one should perform the fire-ritual according to the path described for the fire-ritual.
One should perform the oblation with the respective Brahmins together with the retinue beginning with Vṛṣa;
one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and perform the rite of atonement (prāyaścitta).
Having taken [the fire] from the hearth, one should place it into those respective jars.
The site for the banner was previously described; one should then smear that location with [sacred substances].
Having adorned it with flour-dust and accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments,
one should place the vehicle there during the circumambulation of the village.
Having placed the Astra-mantra in the west, one should install Utsaveśī;
having placed that pitcher in the north, one should then worship Vighneśa.
Then, having made a formal resolve as before, the preceptor should worship Bṛhaspati;
thereafter, he should hoist the banner with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra.
In this manner, if one must perform [the rite] for a bull, or especially for a lion, one should carry out the preliminary consecration (ativāsa) with the root-mantra of the lion. || 37 ||
White, golden, with large tusks, and possessing fierce rain-like claws;
his body was like that of a faceless one, with a head and tail, and a curved form.
The characteristics have been declared as before; one should fashion the form of a lion, including the heart, the head, the crest-lock, and the armor.
The wise one should, however, arrange [the deities] starting from the western direction and so forth. || 39 ||
Having thus established them in sequence, one should worship each by its own name;
all the others as well should be caused to be performed as described by Vṛṣabha.
In this manner, the purification of the ritual procedure is said to be performed step by step;
one should especially adorn the goddess who wears the remains of the offerings.
O Leader, at the time of the ritual for the food offering, the purification of the rite is performed;
this very purification of the rite is called the "beating of the drum. (42)
At night, the sounding of the drum should be conducted according to the previously mentioned procedure; the preceptor and the disciple alike should summon the eight groups [of spirits]. (43)
Having thus invoked the gods, one should worship them with perfumes and flowers;
having worshipped the drum according to the rules, one should strike it once, twice, or thrice.
One should strike with the *sarvatāla* rhythm using the *pañcatpāraśiva*;
one should offer the invocation-oblation (*āvāhana-bali*) consisting of pure rice or rice mixed with molasses. (45)
From Brahmā to Īśāna, and likewise from Indra to Īśāna;
from the banner (dhvaja) to the end of the offering (bali), this constitutes the day, excluding the quarrel with the gods.
Then, having commenced the festival preceded by the auspicious rite of the sprouts (maṅgalāṅkura), one should bind the thread of protection upon Vighnarāja, Gaurī, and [the other deities]. || 47 ||
Having purified the sacrificial hall for the sake of the sacrifice, the wise one should especially adorn the altar and the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the center of the vedi.
The Guru should place a water-pot or a small jar in the central pot, which is the Manonmanī;
he should then establish the eight Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā, in the directions starting from the east.
One should deposit half a niṣka, or half of that, or a fiftieth part;
for the superior and other classes, it should be richly adorned with cloth, while the remainder is declared to be as previously described.
Recalling each respective meditation, one should worship within each of those pitchers;
or else, one may perform the rite with nine fires, five fires, or even a single fire.
Having thus meditated upon the powers beginning with Vāmā, as well as the five forms and Manonmani, one should worship them according to the rules with their respective presiding mantras.
Beginning with the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), it should be performed as previously described;
however, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityāgnihoma) or practice the constant offering (nityahoma).
Having struck the drum according to the rules, one should begin the offering of the *bali* sacrifice;
from the door up to the *balipīṭha*, one should offer the *bali* of rice mixed with jaggery (*gulānna*).
One should perform all those rites for the deities of the day and so forth in sequence, just as one does for Śiva.
After the conclusion of the offering of the bali-oblation, one should properly perform the ritual of departure (yāna):
first, the sweeping of the path, and second, the sprinkling with water.

The third [day] should be adorned with banners and the like, while the fourth is adorned with mechanical devices and the like; having thus decorated the lords of the festival, accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments, || 56 ||
Having performed a circumambulation slowly, accompanied by various playful gestures,
there were lamps burning everywhere and the place was crowded with people of various castes.
That which is not surrounded by halos at its edges and is frequented by hosts of enemies;
wherein the meaning [is established]— the characteristics such as height and so forth are proclaimed as before.
That measurement of the interval between them is traditionally taught to be one finger-breadth. || 59 ||
The ritual for the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) was previously declared in the procedure for the attendant;
having completed all of this, one should perform the rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
The installation on the door and the pedestal should be performed in the first and second [sections];
one should carry out the installation of the Bhadrapīṭha according to the Samatantra.
Or one may perform the four-limbed rite according to the rules either separately or through a single tantra;
it must be performed by a single preceptor at one time, not by many [preceptors] simultaneously.
One should perform the rites for the seed-syllable (aṅkura), the sacrifice to the site (vāstuyāga), and so forth, according to a single unified ritual manual;
then, one should construct a pavilion (maṇḍapa) in the eastern direction of the temple according to the prescribed rules.
In the middle of that, having constructed an altar (vedikā) measuring one cubit in size, it is called the Rudra-altar; its pinnacle is as high as the Tārā [image].
One should prepare the ritual altar (vedi) in the four directions starting from the east;
by this method, one should construct the dwelling according to its prescribed procedure. (65)
In this very manner, one should properly prepare the pavilion;
or else, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkura) on the ninth day, the fifth day, or the third day.
Having discarded a worn-out pedestal, one who makes and installs a new one is said to have performed the "forefinger" rite three times; [the same applies to] crystal that is broken or cracked.
The auspicious pedestal (bhadrapīṭha) is especially endowed with great primary and secondary limbs, as well as the base-molding (upāna),
the ground-covering (jagati), the kumuda, and the ear-plate (karṇapaṭṭikā).
The lotus, the pericarp, and the great limb (mahāṅga) are proclaimed [as the primary parts];
the petals, sub-petals, faces, and so forth are proclaimed as the subsidiary limbs (upāṅga). || 69 ||
One should avoid [defects] such as cracking, being split, or breaking in the major parts;
likewise, one should avoid all small seats and those that are unevenly carved.
I shall describe the sequence for the extraction of the grain in the southern maṇḍala-pīṭha;
having mentally conceived the seat and invoked [the deity], one should perform the worship mantra. (71)
Having prepared an entire sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with pure and auspicious śāli rice,
one should draw a lotus in its center, complete with eight petals and a pericarp.
The wise one should place the *droṇa* vessel within the midst of the water-filled jars;
having invoked the deities from their seats, he should then install them within the center of the jar.

Having completed the offerings and so forth, and having performed the rites from the laying of the fires (ādhāna) up to the marriage ceremony according to the path known as Adhika, using honey and clarified butter as well; 74.

Reciting the mantra of each respective deity, one should perform the fire offering (homa) separately with dūrvā grass and rice grains, either one hundred times, fifty times, or twenty-five times for each. || 75 ||
Then, with the primary seed-mantra of the *kṣurikā*, one should perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*);
thereafter, having offered the *jayā* and other oblations, one should sequentially offer the oblation for the kingdom (*rāṣṭrāhuti*).
One should likewise invoke those situated in fire, those situated in the mandala, and those within the pitcher; one may lead them into the ground or into the oceans.
If this [rite] should be performed using a worn-out pedestal or similar materials,
then one should perform the purification of the pedestal with the five earths, the products of the cow, and bilva leaves.
There is a special procedure regarding the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) and the mirror placed before it;
one should perform the consecration with streams of water while reciting the "Uddhṛ" mantra.
First, one should perform the Vāstuhoma and the Bali offering from the pavilion;
then, having performed the binding of the protective thread (rakṣābandha), [one should place it] upon the pericarp of the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha).
Or one may perform that rite for other seats as well;
on the altars, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with eight droṇas of rice.
It was joined with half as much rice, and half of that with sesame seeds;
it was beautifully adorned with parched grain, flowers, and scattered sesamum seeds.
To the east of that, one should worship Nandin, Mahākāla, and the Bull in sequence upon the pitchers on the altar, from south to north to the center.
Then, on all sides upon the altar-pots produced in the south,
one should worship Durgā, Mātra, Vighneśa, Varaskanda, and Mādhava.
(266) One should worship Śaṇḍeśa, Agni and the others, and Śānta in front; Bhūteśa in the center;
and Siṃha and Bhujageśvara in the directions, on the altar, and in the jars. 85.
Likewise, one should worship Dharma in the west, and in the middle [of the directions] in sequence;
and in the northern altar-pots, Indra, Vaiśvānara, and Yama.
One should worship Nīti, Pāśivāddhin, the Great Lord known as Vaṭuka, and Viṣṇu-Pitāmaha, beginning from the east.
In the center, within the sacrificial jars (vedikumbhas), [one should worship] Āmoda, Pramodaka, Sumukha, Durmukha, Avighna, and Vighnanāyaka.

One should worship those [deities] together with the root-mantra and the root-vidyā, seated upon the moon at the eastern-southern petal and above the pericarp of the Rudra direction (the north). || 89 ||
In a location to the north of that [central] altar, one should perform the preliminary consecration (vāsana) for the minor seats and so forth;
however, if there is a special auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), one should perform the consecration at that very spot.
One should perform the complete study of the Vedas preceded by the ritual of the water-pot (kumbha-sthāna);
one should carry out all the rites beginning with the taking up of the fire (agny-ādāna) as prescribed for the fire-sacrifice (agni-kārya). || 91 ||
One should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds,
using the respective root-mantras, the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅga), the Pāvamāna hymns, and the Tryambaka mantras.
Having touched [the materials] again and again, one should offer them into the fire while recollecting their respective root mantras.
Thus, one should keep vigil at night and perform the ritual bath at dawn.
One should worship all the vessels, such as the archways and so forth, with perfumes and flowers.
I shall now describe the location for the consecration of the small pedestal; listen to that.
Having taken his place in the center of the palace, within the middle maṇḍala,
he should worship [the deities] beginning with Durgā and ending with Caṇḍapīṭha, extending to the other directions.
In front of it is Vṛṣasthala, where that sacred seat (pīṭha) is located; behind that, at a distance equal to the length of the staff of the Lord of Beings (Bhūtanātha), is the site. || 96 ||
One should especially worship the Lord of the Door (Dvāreśa) at each door in the location of the pedestal;
[one should also worship] the half-mouth of the Maṇḍaleśa within the inner maṇḍala, in front of the bull.
In the Indra-pīṭhas, the extent of the site is measured from the tip of the Padra-pīṭha;
the boundary of its location is connected according to the measurement of the inner maṇḍala. || 98 ||
One should install the deities beginning with Agni in the seven directions from the center between Soma and Īśa;
one should consecrate the Viṣṇupīṭha in the southwest according to the measurement of the staff.
In the northeast, one should install the Brahma-pīṭha measuring one cubit;
one should likewise arrange it on the second enclosure (varaṇa) pīṭha in this very same manner.
The consecration of the auspicious throne has been explained in the description of the enclosure wall;
thereafter, one should worship the preceptor with garments, gold, and finger-rings. (101)
And they should be accompanied by their respective retinues according to their means,
adorned with upper garments, parasols, and so forth, as well as with the uṣṇīṣa.
Having carried on his head the jars previously established, which are provided with all musical instruments, and having performed a circumambulation of the temple, || 103 ||

Having recited each of those [mantras] at their respective roots and having consecrated them upon their respective seats, there is a special procedure for the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha); one should perform the extraction of the mantra-deposition (mantranyāsa).
268) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the worship of the Gaurīs;
it is threefold: namely Gaurī, Manonmanī, and Bhavānī. (105)
Dark-complexioned, with two eyes and two arms, she stands in the *tribhaṅga* posture with her feet bent to the right and left;
she holds a blue lotus in her right hand, and her body is adorned with beautiful bracelets.
She should be the supreme Goddess, providing a hand to hold. || 106 ||
The equal bending of Śambhu’s power is described as having two eyes and being well-established in Prakṛti;
it has one hand hanging down on the right, with a face that follows the curve of the brow.
May the wielder of the Pināka bow grant you auspiciousness—
he whose limbs were addressed by the bracelets on his arms at the time of marriage, and who, with a glance from within the assembly, suddenly brings about the fulfillment of what was spoken.
Sumukha is in Ambikā. || 108 ||
She has two eyes and two arms, is dark-complexioned, and possesses a white lotus in her right hand; she is adorned with a jeweled casket in her crown and endowed with all auspicious marks.

The characteristic of Gaurī has been described; the essential form of Manonmanī is dark-complexioned, possessing four arms and three eyes, and is said to hold a lotus, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a rosary of *japā* beads.
He is endowed with a crown of matted locks gathered by a yellow cloth, seated upon a red lotus, and is the very embodiment of Manonmani. || 110 ||
He should have four eyes, resembling the moon and possessing the fire of the sun;
his four hands should hold a lotus, a banner, the gesture of granting boons, and a blue lotus;
he should possess limbs adorned with cool ornaments and a face of wondrous beauty.
The essential nature [of the Self] shines within the supreme consciousness of the lofty peak of Kuṭa.
The hand [of the deity] should display the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhayavarada*) and hold a rosary and a lotus; on the other ear, however, the goddesses should be placed in due order.
One who bears matted hair and a serpent like the moon, whose crest is dark with smoke, would become entirely dark-complexioned, even if he were fair. 112.
Holding a lotus, an eye-garland, and the gesture of granting fearlessness in her hands, she is adorned with beautiful dark limbs and three eyes;
she wears a crown, has a moon-like face, and a mass of matted locks bound at the top.
Śrī Kāmakoṭi, who is the embodiment of Śiva and Śakti. || 113 ||
His body is like a conch shell, his limbs are ruddy, and he has the face of a bull;
his hands are long like outstretched lotuses and his arms are tall like serpents;
his belly is dark and sunken, and his eye is exceedingly smoky.
On the left side of the Veda, in the portion to the north or south, or even within the enclosure (prakāra), it is especially recommended in the northeast.
Having conceived the independent Ālaya in Vāyu, Soma, and Īśaka,
or else in another manner in Dakṣa, Nairṛta, and Pāvaka.
In the temple itself, the wise man should install the Śakti;
having conceived it as independent, he should establish it within his own mind.
Facing east, O Gaurī, one should worship for the sake of peace;
likewise, facing south, one should perform the rite that brings about all prosperity.
Facing west, O Goddess, it bestows abundance of wealth and grain;
facing north, O Goddess, it grants supreme happiness thereafter. (119)
Whether situated on a circular seat (*vṛttapīṭha*) or on the auspicious seat of Gaurī (*gauribhadrapīṭha*),
the bed shall be upon a lotus-seat (*padmapīṭha*); this is here called the power of the seat (*pīṭhaśakti*).
Having conceived the mouth as the gateway, one should then conceive the ramparts and other features.
Yoga, Bhoga, and Vīra—Śakti herself becomes threefold.
In Yoga, she is joined with the Liṅga; in Bhoga, she is associated with the left. (121)
The Hero is said to be independent; thus, Śakti becomes threefold.
Furthermore, one should worship Gaurī in the north and Manonmanī in the region of the wind.
One should install Bhavānī in the north-eastern direction according to the prescribed rite;
Gaurī in the southern direction, and Manonmanī in the south-east.
Or the wise man should arrange it in the south-western quarter;
he should establish it in a place joined with a heap of ashes, or in a spot where the images of the Śaktis have become worn out or destroyed.
Then, having abandoned the *ālaya* (the storehouse-consciousness) and the abode described by its characteristics,
one should [establish] the devotees and their retinues with devotion in a place favorable for the performance of rites.
That which is joined with favor toward people should be performed quickly and well;
one must not make it deficient or excessive, but should arrange it as before.

Furthermore, having conceived the intention independently, one should install and then worship the auspicious [deities] who bring peace to the village and possess the power to re-establish them. (127)
The wise one should visualize Bhūmadevī before those Śaktis;
she has two arms and two eyes, wears yellow garments, and is in the full bloom of youth.
She is endowed with one face, her hands joined in the gesture of reverence (añjali),
adorned with a basket-shaped crown (karaṇḍa-mukuṭa), the goddess of the earth, possessing all auspicious marks.
Having worshipped the tip of the door in that manner, the procedure for the worship of the door is performed;
then, one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā on the right side of the door. (130)
Having worshipped the Yoginī on his left, he is enjoined to worship Yamunā likewise on the left side of the door. || 131 ||
Having worshipped the Ḍākinī on the right and honored her in due order,
one should worship Mahālakṣmī above, in the center of the sun.
On its right side, one should likewise worship Narmadā;
on the left side, one should worship Sarasvatī above the sun (pataṅga).
One should worship Pataṅga and Bhuvaṅga above;
one should worship Vimala and Subāhu on the two door-panels.
Having worshipped the bull before him, one should worship the deity of the weapon;
the ritual for the worship of the door as prescribed by rule, and especially the worship of Gaurī, [should be performed]. 135.
Then, having entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should worship Gaurī;
after discarding the remains of the previous offering (nirmālya), one should then worship Caṇḍeśvara.
Since Maheśvara is the very form of the power of the Guide (deśika), and because he is the essential nature of Śiva and Śakti, one should worship Śiva-Śakti. || 137 ||
O Pārvatī, the Supreme Lord, born from the earth among the Śaivas, is *niṣkala* (partless) as the daughter of the mountain (*śailajā*), yet he assumes a *sakala* (manifested) form as his consort.
This relationship, which is the very nature of existence, is composed of metal and joined with stone. 139.

Having performed the bathing of Gaurī, one should carry out the rites as prescribed for all perfumes; one should worship her with the limbs, sub-limbs, and minor limbs—this is remembered as the threefold [worship]. (140)
The water for bathing, water for the feet, as well as water for rinsing the mouth, clothing, ornaments, and likewise fragrant unguents; || 141 ||
The *arghya* offering, the *mantrapuṣpa*, and the primary limbs (*aṅga*) are proclaimed as three;
the secondary limbs (*upāṅga*) consist of incense and the lamp, while protection at evening is performed with ashes.
The parasol, the fly-whisk, the mirror, as well as that accompanied by dance and song, is proclaimed as the subsidiary limb (upāṅga). || 143 ||

Having performed the offering of food (naivedya), the presentation of oblations (balidāna), and the fire-sacrifice (homa), one should carry out the daily festival; this is proclaimed as consisting of the water-offering in the hollowed palms (culukodaka) and the ritual for each limb (pratyaṅga). || 144 ||
One should worship Vāmā in the eastern quarter, Jyeṣṭhā in the southeast,
Raudrī in the southern region, and likewise Kālī in the southwest.
*Kalavikaraṇī* in the west, *Balavikaraṇī* in the north, *Balapramathanī* in the north-east, and *Sarvabhūtadamanī* in the north-west. (146)
Having worshipped [the deities] beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ* in the center of the mind-mandala,
one should worship each [deity] in its respective location with its own specific name-mantra.
The first enclosure has been described; now hear of the second enclosure.
Having worshipped Brāhmī in the east and Maheśī in the southeast (the domain of Agni), [one should worship the others]. 148.
Having worshipped Kaumāri in the south, as well as Rākṣasi and Vaiṣṇavī;
having worshipped Vārāhī in the west, and Indrāṇī in the region of the wind (the northwest).
