One should worship Cāmuṇḍī in the north, Durgā in the direction of Īśa (the northeast),
Vīrabhadra and Vighneśa in the northeast and southwest respectively, and one should perform sacrifice [to them]. || 150 ||
The second enclosure has been described; now hear about the third enclosure.
One should worship Vṛṣabha in the east and Gaṇeśa in the southeast. (151)
Having worshipped Skanda in the south and Mahāśasta in the southwest,
one should worship Śanaiścara in the west and Vīra in the northwest.
One should worship Kṣetrapāla in the north and Bhāskara in the northeast;
this is declared as the third enclosure. Now hear about the fourth enclosure.
Jambhinī is in the eastern direction; Stambhinī is in the domain of fire; Śānti and Mohinī are in the south; and Bhedinī is likewise in the southwest.
Ramaṇī is on the western side, Bhadrakāminī on the northern;
Durgā is in the direction of the north, and Caṇḍīśamiśā is in the northwest. (155)
Likewise, on the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) and in front, she who consists of all powers;
and likewise on the sacrificial pedestal in the eastern direction, in the Mother of Space (ākāśamātṛ). || 156 ||
The Bhūtamātṛs are in the south; the Lokamātṛs are in the west; the Devamātṛs are in the north; and the Matṛmātṛs are above. || 157 ||
The seat (pīṭha) consisting of all powers is proclaimed as the Baladevīs;
it extends from Vṛṣādi to Balipīṭha, measuring the size of a hen's egg.
At the times of morning, midday, and evening, one should offer the bali-oblation;
for it is there, in a place devoid of all beings, that the bali-offerings find their satisfaction.
If one worships without an offering (*bali*), the worship becomes fruitless.
Therefore, one should perform the offering of the *bali* with every possible effort. (160)
It increases longevity, prosperity, strength, sovereignty, and health. || 160½ ||
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Daily Worship of Gaurī," in the Sūkṣma-śāstra.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme procedure for sprinkling (prokṣaṇa);
likewise, the second sprinkling is declared, as well as the auspicious conjunction (bhadrayoga). || 1 ||
In the construction of a temple, as well as in the rite of laying the foundation,
having likewise established the site for the child, the sprinkling [of water] is called "Auspicious" (Bhadra).
If, while you were looking on, your linga fell and was likewise [picked up] by Caṇḍālas, artisans, dogs and the like, or even by cocks and monkeys; (3)
In a month devoid of worship, sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is said to be the yoga;
one should construct a square pavilion in front of the prasāda.
It was provided with four gates, adorned with four archways,
decorated with canopies, garlands of darbha grass, and hanging festoons.
Having fashioned a nine-square grid adorned with the eight auspicious symbols and graced by the sprouts of fortune, one square in the center shall serve as the altar.
One should construct sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) all around— in the cardinal and intermediate directions— with a height of one fathom, or even just one fist-breadth.
In the cardinal directions, one should fashion squares, and in the intermediate directions, circles; between Indra (East) and Īśāna (North), one should arrange the principal [mandala]. (8)
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and likewise performed the ritual of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa),
[one should offer oblations] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, kuṣṭha, and cakrakesara.
Having smeared the liṅga with cloth and having covered the pedestal and other items with the finest [cloth],
one should sprinkle them with the five products of the cow while reciting the Pāvamāna hymns.
The wise one, having wrapped the linga with darbha grass,
should tie a golden auspicious thread upon the head of Śiva while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Then, having gone to the Bālasthāna and having performed worship there especially,
one should perform the Yātrā-homa sacrifice in front of the Bālasthāna.
There, a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) should be prepared with pure and auspicious sand;
then, having performed the rites beginning with the taking of fire, one should prepare the Śiva-fire.
Then, for each of the six limbs of Brahman, one should offer a hundred oblations; touching [the limbs] repeatedly, one should likewise offer them in groups of one hundred and fifty.
Having offered the sacrificial oblation (caru) with the Īśāna mantra and having touched the entire linga,
one should place the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha) upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of it.
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva as being endowed with the five jewels, possessing a beard, and clothed in garments, one should then invoke him therein with the Sadyojāta mantra.
Then, having formed the seed-gesture (bījamudrā) and the bud-lotus gesture (mukulapadmamudrikā), one should bathe and worship Gaṇāmbikā with the mantra. || 17 ||
Having sprinkled the altar with the five products of the cow while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra,
one should place a vessel for increasing the mantras, containing gold, to its north.
One should place eight water-pots all around the Nala pillar,
having performed the ritual recitation at night according to the rules by those who protect the Vedas.
Then, having covered it with a large cloth, one should begin the fire-oblation (homa),
[offering] sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, rice-mixture (caru), parched grain (lāja), mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.
These seven sacrificial substances are to be prepared according to the prescribed ritual;
[the ladles] should be made of Palāśa, Udumbara, Dhava, and Plakṣa wood, or else from [wood native to] the various directions.
Likewise, for the sacrificial posts made of Śamī, Khadira, and Bilva wood,
one should [offer] a thousand, or half of that, or even half of that again, respectively.
One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times for each [deity] in sequence:
ghee with the Īśāna mantra, and likewise the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Puruṣa mantra.
He should offer parched grain with the Ghora mantra, mustard seeds with the Sadyojāta mantra,
sesame seeds with the Pāśupata-astra mantra, and barley with the Kavaca mantra.
Having offered oblations at the end of each substance with the *vyāhṛtis* while touching the heart, one should touch the *liṅga* with its own mantra;
for each substance, there should be a concluding full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with its respective mantra.
Having performed worship at dawn and having removed the thread-bindings,
one should perform the consecration with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using the [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta.
Having performed purification with pure water upon the liṅga, the pedestal, and the ground in sequence,
one should place a golden flower, joined with other flowers, upon the head [of the deity].
First, one should honor the teacher with garments, gold, and rings,
as well as bracelets, earrings, and a golden sacrificial thread. (28)
When one has the capacity, however, land together with wealth should be given;
then, at an auspicious moment, having meditated upon Tryambaka, the God of gods.
Having consecrated one's own body with fragrant substances for worship and other offerings,
and having joined the *liṅga* to the crown of the head, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *kalās* upon the limbs.
Then, having brought the auspicious water-pot and having set aside the ritual procedure,
one should bathe that [linga] and meditate upon the temple of the linga.
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva, one should fashion Brahmā along with his attendants;
[one should place] the deity in the water of the Śiva-pitcher, and the pedestal (piṇḍikā) in the Vardhanī vessel.
Having consecrated the water-pots with their respective mantras according to the ritual procedure,
one should worship the Deity with perfumes and other offerings, preceded by the fivefold enclosure (pañcāvaraṇa).
Offering food (naivedya) and the presentation of oblations (balidāna), accompanied by dance and song, one should satisfy Śiva directly; this is proclaimed as the auspicious (bhadra) method. || 34 ||
One should thus satisfy Śiva directly; this is proclaimed as truly auspicious. || 34½ ||
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Sprinkling," in the Sūkṣma-śāstra.
I shall declare the sequence of the rules for expiation when the daily worship is omitted.
"Prāya" is said to mean destruction, and "citta" is called restoration. (1)
The rejoining of a severed member is recorded in the Smṛti as an expiation;
however, the material used for that initial restoration does not, in fact, cause any fault. (2)
To pacify those faults, one should perform an expiation;
however, there is no fault in using an unprepared substance when [the recipient] is of inferior status. (3)
Likewise, the laborer is not fit for the rites of sweeping and sprinkling;
and the day of merit is not fit for one who omits the worship of the Sun or who lacks the products of the cow.

If the worship of Lambodara is deficient, if the worship of the apertures is omitted, and if indeed the water for the feet, the water for sipping, and the respectful offering are lacking, as well as the bath; || 5 ||
Devoid of garments and ornaments, lacking perfumes and flowers,
and deficient in food offerings, side dishes, and drinking water.
Nor should one use mouth-perfume when food is deficient, nor during a funeral rite or a festival.
When it is devoid of incense and lamps, when it lacks the *ārātrika* ceremony, when it is lacking ashes and betel-leaf, and when it is devoid of the mirror and the umbrella; || 7 ||

When the fly-whisk is absent and the sword is missing, when the Vedic hymns are lacking, when the hearing of the Purāṇas is omitted, and even when the hearing of the five ancillary limbs [of the Purāṇas] is neglected; || 8 ||
When dancing, singing, and instrumental music occur during a rite devoid of the worship of Caṇḍa,
I shall now declare the expiation for such occurrences as these.
In the absence of sprinkling and cleansing, there is the destruction of the cow and the bull;
therefore, one should perform cleansing and sprinkling using cow-products after having sprinkled the ground.
For the purpose of overcoming the lapse of time, one should perform the consecration with the Peace Vessel (*śāntikumbha*);
for the sake of pacifying that fault, one should recite the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra a hundred times.
One should diligently avoid that very substance which has been touched. || 12 ||
Alternatively, if the image of the Liṅga is especially touched [by an impurity],
one should discard earthen vessels and then perform consecration with ritual baths.
(279) O King, when the worship of the Sun is neglected, disease arises;
therefore, having performed a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma), one should consecrate [the image] with ritual ablutions (snapanas). || 14 ||
Having recited the mantra of the Sun a thousand times or half of that,
if the daily rites and the *puṇyāha* ceremony are omitted, the prosperity of that kingdom shall perish.
For the sake of pacifying those defects, one should perform an ablution with the five products of the cow;
for if the five products of the cow are lacking, a great pestilence breaks out.
One should bathe Śambhu with ghee and recite the Brahma-mantra a hundred times;
if the worship of Vighneśvara is omitted, there is the destruction of the life-force and the breath.
One should have Gaṇeśvara perform the ceremonial bathing and the propitiatory fire-offering;
having offered edible foods, cakes, and so forth, one should recite the Vighna-mantra one hundred times.
If the worship of the apertures (randhra) is omitted, famine arises on earth;
therefore, one should consecrate the Lord of Gods with the water from the peace-vessel (śāntikumbha). || 19 ||
One should recite the hundred mantras of the deities stationed at the gates;
if the materials for the foot-washing (pādya) are always deficient, there will be the destruction of the kingdom.
One should give that substance doubled at other junctions (saṃdhyās) and cause it to be offered;
by means of this, one should bathe the Supreme Lord while He is stationed within the image-vessel (mūrtikumbha).
If one performs the ritual sipping (ācamana) but omits the arghya offering, or if one fails to provide the materials for the foot-washing, that kingdom will be deprived of water.
If the materials for the bath are omitted, that kingdom likewise becomes devoid of water.
One should give that substance two or three times over and bathe the Supreme Lord with the waters of fifty jars while reciting the *vyomavyāpin* mantra. (23)
If the gift of clothing is omitted, a great disease arises;
one should bathe the Supreme Lord with water infused with the dye of bark garments. (24)
One should give a pair of garments to Śambhu with the mantra "yuvam vāsā," and having recited it one hundred and eight times, one should cause them to be offered during other periods of twilight.
If the ornaments and the sacred thread have become inferior due to poverty,
one should bathe him with the water from the *śānti*-vessel and recite the *aghora* mantra one hundred times.
If it is devoid of fragrant substances, that kingdom will encounter danger;
however, by bathing that object with weapon-water, the substance shall become twofold [in value].
If the [trees] are devoid of flowers and leaves, there will be drought;
having bathed the water-pitcher of the direction with the *sadyas-mantra*, one should recite it a hundred times.
If the food offering (naivedya) and the side dishes (upadaṃśa) are of inferior quality or originate from a time of famine,
one should bathe the deity with water infused with bark-fiber (valkala) in order to pacify that defect.
Having recited the hundred limb-mantras, one should offer that substance doubled;
however, for a deficient [offering], it is waterless, consisting only of water for drinking and mouth-rinsing.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with the waters of fifty jars;
one should give double the quantity of those substances and recite the root mantra one hundred times.
If the daily fire-oblation is neglected, there will be the destruction of the king;
therefore, having performed a propitiatory oblation, perform the sixteen-fold ceremonial bathing.
Afterwards, one should perform the daily fire-ritual and offer a hundred oblations with the Aghora mantra;
if the ritual is deficient in the offering of the *prakāra* bali, that kingdom will be deprived of strength.
Then, having performed the *śānti*-oblation, one should bathe [the deity] with water from the *mārjana* vessel;
after reciting the hundred-fold ten-syllable mantra (*daśabīja*), one should subsequently perform the *bali* offering. (34)
If there is an absence of constant festivals, there will be fear of an enemy army;
therefore, having performed a peace-offering (śānti-homa), one should consecrate [the deity] with ritual ablutions.
Having recited the *trayambaka* mantra, one should thereafter recite the hundred [mantras].
Then, having performed the daily festival (*nityotsava*), I shall speak something further. (36)
Having been touched by dogs, crows, and the like, or likewise by those of low caste (pratiloma) and so forth,
one should offer an oblation (bali) at that spot and the like, and then recite the Astra-mantra one hundred times.
This applies even to whatever place remains situated where there has been a lack of offerings and lamps.
Having again offered the lamp, one should conclude with the remainder of the bali offering;
for if the ashes and betel are omitted, a great pestilence will prevail. (39)
Then, having performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should bathe [the image] with the primary waters;
even if the ārātrika rite is omitted, it destroys the dance and the covering.
Having bathed [the deity] with the waters from the peace-pitcher (śāntikumbha), one should conclude with the remainder of the offering (bali).
Having bathed [the deity] with the waters from the peace-pitcher, one should recite the Bahurūpa mantra a hundred times.
If the ashes and betel are lacking, the king shall become invincible;
having recited a hundred times the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should [purify] with water for wiping.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord and provide double the quantity of those materials;
if a mirror or an umbrella is missing, one should provide a fly-whisk, and if a sword is missing, [the same].
A king shall obtain invincibility on the earth even against the armies of enemies;
having then performed a peace-offering (śāntihoma), he should consecrate himself with ritual ablutions (snapanas). || 44 ||

Having recited the Kṣurikā mantra a thousand times or half of that, one should perform the study of the Ṛgveda and other Vedas; however, if these are deficient, one should offer oblations and the like, even if devoid of hymns of praise.
Having bathed [the deity] with water from a peace-pitcher (śāntikumbha), one should recite the principal seed-mantra one hundred times;
likewise during the hearing of the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Purāṇas, even when they are deficient.
It causes the destruction of wives and the destruction of children;
having bathed [the image] with water containing sandalwood paste (mānya), one should recite the hundredfold mantra of the ten seeds.
If dance, song, and instrumental music are deficient, that kingdom will perish;
therefore, having performed a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma), one should consecrate the image with the water from the ritual pitcher.
Having recited the hundred-fold mantra of Nandin, perform the dancing and other rites thereafter;
for if the worship of Caṇḍa is omitted, there will be the destruction of the king and his army.
Then, having performed the *mūrtihoma*, one should consecrate [the image] with perfumed waters;
having recited the Caṇḍa-mantra a hundred times, one should subsequently worship Caṇḍa.

If the evening twilight rite is omitted, the penance is doubled; likewise for the omission of any other twilight rite. In such cases, one should perform expiation as previously described for the sake of satisfying the deity.
And when it is devoid of the two joints, one should then perform the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
The mortal who acts in this manner shall attain a meritorious state.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the *Sūkṣmaśāstra*, titled "The Daily Rites and Expiatory Rites."
Henceforth, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
it is taught for the purpose of destroying all sins and for the sake of universal pacification. (1)

One should conceive of three types [of disciples] in order: the superior, the mediocre, and the inferior; the mediocre is for that purpose, and the inferior should be known as being for that same purpose. || 2 ||
Clarified butter is indeed one *prastha*, while curd is two *prasthas*;
milk is said to be three *prasthas*, and cow dung four *prasthas*.
Three prasthas of cow urine are recommended as the middle measure;
there should be one kuḍupa of ghee and two kuḍupas of curd.
Three *kuḍupas* of milk and one *prastha* of cow dung are prescribed. || 4 ||
Half a *prastha* of cow urine is prescribed for the *pañcagavya*;
likewise, the ghee from a *kapilā* cow is called the "white-limbed ocean. (5)
The milk should be yellow in color, the cow dung red in color, and the cow urine black in color; thus the wise one should collect them.
Clarified butter indeed has Rudra as its deity; curd has Soma as its deity;
milk has Śukra as its deity, and cow dung has Arka as its deity.
Cow’s urine has Agni as its presiding deity; the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) have the Supreme Deity as their presiding deity.
Cow’s ghee is likewise [presided over by] Kāśyapa, while cow’s curd is said to have Kauśika as its presiding deity.
Milk is from Bharadvāja, likewise cow dung is from Gautama;
cow urine is from Atri—thus it is proclaimed by the sages.
Milk is Sadyojāta, curd is likewise Vāmadeva,
cow-urine is Bahurūpa, and cow-dung is Puruṣa. (10)
One should perform the consecration with the great mantra Vyomavyāpin.
Clarified butter has Agni as its deity; a coconut [offering] is for the Gaṅgā;
O Goddess, rice-flour is for Uṣas, and turmeric is for * * * *.
Āmalaka, Lakṣmī, Kaśodaka, Manonmanī, and Pada—these indeed are the five sheaths; one should discipline them according to the four threads.
The wise one should install [the deities] starting from Īśāna and worship them within the very square;
with the Gāyatrī and other mantras, he should apply cow's urine, and with "Gandhadvārā," cow dung.
One should offer milk with the mantra "āpyāyasva," curd with "dadhikrāvṇo," clarified butter with "śukram asi jyotiḥ," and water with kuśa grass with "devasya tvā. (15)
The bath taken at dawn indeed destroys all sins;
however, the bath taken at midday is said to be exceedingly efficacious in every respect. (16)
Indeed, from the evening consecration, there is the destruction of all diseases;
having become gracious-faced, one should remain in the center of the pavilion. || 17 ||
One should prepare rice with śāli grains, likewise heating ghee in the center;
one should place cow dung in the east and cow urine in the south. (18)
Having placed curd in the west and milk in the north,
one should place honey in the southeast and a coconut in the southwest.

286) In the constellation Śūrpakṣa, under the lunar mansion Śroṇa, in the hand, and in the sky.
That was in the fourth part of that constellation, in the region of Kumudeśa.
Having observed the rising of Cancer, the knower of the Śiva-mantras should diligently collect earth from the temple of the sovereign of the desired kingdom.
In the center, in the middle of the village, in the stable for the chief horses,
and in the dwelling of the chief elephant, one should place [the image] together with a garment that touches the peak [of the linga].
At crossroads, near a treasury or a temple, in a village shrine, in a field, by a pond, or at the outlet of water; 23.
Having carefully collected earth from ten locations and having drawn it separately into individual vessels in one's own region or in a temple of the deity, (one should proceed).
Having covered it with a clean cloth, one should place it in the midst of śāli rice;
in that [vessel], during half a month or a month, as before, at the rising of Cancer.
Having made a firm resolve one day prior, or on the tenth or ninth day, having risen at the time of dawn and performed his bath according to the prescribed rules; || 26 ||
Having satiated [the deity] one thousand and eight times with the Śiva-mantra,
he then went to the temple of the god and prostrated before Mahādeva.
Having taken ten jars, one should wrap them with thread;
having rinsed them with the *praṇava* alone and fumigated them with the seed-syllable of Śiva.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred times for each portion, he should take up the earth;
having placed it in ten jars, he should cover the opening with a cloth.
(287) The wise man should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of the temple, or in the north, the northeast, or likewise the southeast, using two āḍhaka measures of rice.
Having sprinkled [the area] with the heart-mantra, one should place the jars upon it;
having covered them with a pure cloth, one should worship them with the flow-seed mantra (dhārābīja).
Having protected it with the mantra of the weapon (astra), one should display the cow-seal (dhenumudrā) [over the vessel] while seated comfortably on a pleasing seat, facing either east or north.

Having touched the water-pot with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass and having recited the five-syllabled mantra ten thousand times, one should perform the fire-oblation at the conclusion of the recitation.
The wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in a water-pot (kumbha) either in the east or in the north;
otherwise, he should conduct the entire preliminary ritual according to the previously stated procedure.
One should perform a thousand oblations consisting of coconut fruit, mung beans, sugar, and honey, combined with plantain and jackfruit.
One should feed nine, five, or even just one Brāhmaṇa there;
one should perform this practice specifically every day in this very manner. || 36 ||
Having determined the day prior [to the ceremony], at the conclusion of the recitation and fire-offerings,
one should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva, provided with sixteen pillars.
It was provided with four gates, adorned with four archways, furnished with garlands of *darbha* grass, and decorated with canopies and other ornaments. || 38 ||
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar occupying one part out of nine parts;
having covered the altar with a cloth, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with red rice.
One should strew rice, sesame seeds, parched grain, and *darbha* grass around the area;
having performed the ritual bath according to the rules, one should thereafter offer libations. (40)
At the conclusion of the recitation and the fire-oblation, the wise and discerning practitioner should enter the pavilion;
the learned one should then [worship] the Śivaliṅga with that which has been conquered through mental resolve (saṃkalpa).
Having bathed Mahādeva with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), having placed him upon a seat above the altar, one should worship him with *droṇa* flowers.
The wise one, having worshipped with a thousand [offerings] using the Śiva-mantra and the previous mantra, should present incense and a lamp along with *droṇa* flowers.
Having taken ten clay pots and purified them by means of inspection and other rites,
one should take up [the clay] with the Śiva-bīja mantra and smear the Lord with that clay.
Reciting the five-syllable mantra, he should worship with a thousand jasmine flowers by way of emanation, and offer boiled rice mixed with jaggery.
Having worshipped with all ritual offerings,
the supreme preceptor should then bring the arrow, having honored it with *droṇa* measures of jasmine flowers.
Having worshipped it himself with ten thousand, or half of that, or even half of that again, the practitioner should perform the "Hand of Śiva" (śivahasta).

The practitioner, knowing the mantra, should recite the kīla-mantra with devotion while placing his hand upon the head; having thus heated it, he should recite the great mantra beginning with "macakrānta."
By this method, one should first perform a vigil during the night;
when the day of the formal vow (saṃkalpa) arrives, one should remain with a mind fixed on its specific observances.
The wise man should cause food to be given to Brāhmaṇas and devotees of Śiva;
he should cause food and drink to be provided for the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others. (50)
When the previously mentioned time has arrived, the wise man should worship Gaṇeśa;
and at the appropriate time, the astrologer should inform the patron.
By the power of the *namaṅga* mantra, the presence of the Sacrificer is established;
one should surround [the area] nine times by way of the Guru’s *upasthāna*.
O Śāli, by this method, if a wise man sees the earth [marked with signs], he should consume that [earth] three times; by that means, he certainly obtains that kingdom. (53)
By the worship of a clay liṅga alone, a king obtains the earth situated amidst the four oceans; O Vāyu, this is not false. The worship of the clay liṅga has been declared;
now hear the procedure for the oral liṅga (mukhaliṅga).
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Worshipping the Clay Liṅga," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
I shall describe the propitiation of the sandals; listen to it, O Prabhajanas!
At the end of the worship during the half-yāma period, one should worship both sandals.
Having placed [the vessel] upon a stand, one should draw a bull in its center;
then, having invoked Śiva above it, one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, meat, and other offerings.
Having placed [the body] upon a palanquin, accompanied by the sounding of conchs, adorned with all ornaments, and attended by all musical instruments. || 3 ||
Accompanied by hymns and songs, one should enter the place of Śakti;
having performed the washing of the feet, one should offer water for the feet and water for sipping. (4)
Having taken water in his hand, he should sprinkle it over the bed;
then, having worshipped the goddesses according to the rule, the preceptor should invoke them with the Astra-mantra.
Having placed [the image] upon the bed, one should worship Śiva above it;
having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, one should present food and other offerings.
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should cause betel-leaf to be given with the Hṛdaya-mantra;
having worshipped the ten weapons all around, one should place the two sandals on the ground.
One should perform the rite of securing the door with a cloth alone;
having worshipped Śaṇḍeśvara, the Guru should enter his own home.
In this way, whatever a mortal performs, he shall attain a meritorious state.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Worship of the Sandals," in the Sūkṣma-śāstra.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for the protection of kings;
it is proclaimed to be of two kinds: the open and the concealed. || 1 ||
The "open" [rite] is performed with ashes, while the "closed" [rite] uses yellow pigment (rocanā) and so forth;
it should be done on the birth lunar day, under the birth asterism, or at the commencement of the sixty-year cycle.

During the solstices of the moon and sun, during eclipses, at the time of a family death-rite (kulakāla), in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth month, and also under an inauspicious asterism (śūlanakṣatra). || 3 ||
At the beginning and end of a battle, and when there is no occurrence of calamities such as spirits or diseases,
a wise man should worship for the protection of the king according to this rite.
On the ninth, seventh, or fifth day prior to the commencement of the ritual,
one should worship the image of Kṛṣṇa according to the prescribed rites for Śivarātri.
One should take cow dung that has fallen upon the ground with the *sadyojāta* mantra;
O Goddess, it should be accompanied by the *śikhā*, *bilva*, and the five limbs.
Having formed the *piṇḍa* with the *vāmadeva* mantra, the wise practitioner should perform its drying with the *bahurūpa* mantra and its ripening with the *puruṣa* mantra alone.
The wise one should cause the Lord to be grasped and consecrate him with the syllables of the Kalās;
then he should place him in an earthen vessel or a copper vessel with the Heart mantra.
Having wrapped the face with a cloth and adorned it with perfumes and flowers,
one should perform the circumambulation of the village while wearing all one's ornaments.
The wise and discerning practitioner should place [the object] at the tip of his crest-lock after first performing the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana);
he should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the root mantra alone.
Then, having reached the pavilion adorned with canopies and other ornaments,
and having broken through the center of the spread-out ground with joy, one should seize the station of space (vyomapada) in the middle.
In each of the four directions, it should be provided with auspicious Śiva-ornaments,
one cubit in height, and resembling the surface of a mirror.
The procedure for the elevation of the directions is that it should be made four parts less than that;
the pedestal (upavedi) should be constructed with a portion equal to one-fourth of that.
The wise man should cause nine fires, or five fires, or even a single fire to be prepared; he should arrange the sacrificial pits there according to the previously mentioned procedure. (14)

Having smeared the ground with cow dung, the wise man should decorate it with rice grains; he should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made, accompanied by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should sprinkle [the site] with the Puruṣa-sūkta and recite the Pāvamāna hymns;
then the wise man should have a sacrificial mound constructed using eight droṇas of śāli rice.
Having eaten half of that amount of rice and also half of that amount of sesame seeds,
one should scatter parched grain and flowers and fill [the vessel] with five-colored [powders].
Having covered that altar with cloths and adorned it with various ornaments,
one should fashion a lotus in its center, provided with eight petals.
Having taken nine jars, he should wash them with the Astra-mantra;
he should wrap them all around with thread, making them resemble a man from head to foot.

In the northeastern quarter of the pavilion, one should offer libations and place the *toraṇa*-vases with their openings facing downward, as well as the guardians of the directions in their proper order.
The preceptor should worship each [element] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using its respective mantra.
Then, having worshipped the seat of Śiva upon the altar with perfumes and other offerings, [he should proceed]. || 21 ||
Whether on the ground, in the intermediate space, or even at the site of a battle,
one should draw a mandala measuring twelve finger-breadths and adorned with svastikas.
Alternatively, one should fashion a svastika joined with two lingas, possessing white and red weapons, or else endowed with yellow and red. || 23 ||
Having recited the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should sprinkle [the area] with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra.
There, a sacrificial mound (*staṇḍila*) should be prepared with pure *śāli* rice grains. (24)
A wise person should place there, upon a small stand, an image made of gold, silver, copper, or even bell-metal, fashioned from rice-flour.
The best of those skilled in ritual procedure should fashion a bull, complete in all its limbs, measuring twelve finger-breadths in size and provided with a couch.
Having adorned it with five-colored ornaments and decorated it with all kinds of jewelry,
[he should place] the ears on the two horns of the donkey and the testicles on the two excesses.
The tips of the horns, the tail, and the ends of the feet are adorned with yellow color;
it is traditionally taught that the eyebrows and the lines of that same measurement are black in color. (28)

Having prepared a seat for Śiva with dark-colored materials, with the remaining limbs [of the deity] being white in color, and having adorned it with all kinds of flowers, provided with incense and lamps. || 29 ||
Having offered water for the feet and other items with their respective root mantras, the wise one should receive the bull from the preceptor accompanied by the sounding of a conch shell.
One should place [the vessel] facing either east or north in the center of the altar,
together with eight thousand white unbroken grains of rice and the tips of *dūrvā* grass.
Having worshipped the bull with the mantra for consuming sins,
he should then offer an oblation consisting of split mung beans.
Having offered water for drinking and water for rinsing the mouth, the wise man should offer incense and a lamp;
then, having offered a temple accompanied by song and instrumental music.
Having taken up a jar of ashes, one should place it in Pūrvabhadrā;
one should establish it in Navakadākṣiṇabhadra as before, with the mantra. (34)
The wise practitioner should place Daśapuṣpa in the west and Nirāñjana in the north, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having recited the demon-destroying mantra beginning with "kṛṇuṣva," perform the recitation;
having worshipped with incense and lamps, one should offer pure food.
Then, having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit, one should begin the consecration;
perform the rites from the arrival [of the bride] until the marriage according to the previously stated procedure. (37)
In the midst of that [lotus], one should meditate upon the Lord of the Gods of gods, endowed with five faces, resembling a pomegranate flower in color, and possessed of ten arms. || 38 ||
Clad in yellow garments and adorned with yellow garlands and unguents, he holds in his right hands a vajra, a trident, an axe, and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). || 39 ||
On the left side are the hooded serpent, the boon-granting gesture, the noose, and the goad;
he is joined with Manonmanī and endowed with the fivefold enclosure.
The preceptor should worship each [deity] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using their respective mantras;
[he should offer] fuel, clarified butter, sacrificial wood, broth, curd, barley, and honey.
Sesame, parched grain, jujube, mung bean, flour, cooked rice, fruit, white sugar, copper, and the tips of five types of dūrvā grass— these are the eighteen substances for the fire-oblation (homa).
One should consecrate all the ritual substances in sequence with the half-mantra of Mṛtyuñjaya;
for each, one should perform a hundred, or fifty, or even twenty-five oblations.
Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblation at the end of the substances, the Guru should likewise touch the jar of ashes;
having worshipped it with perfumes and flowers, he should offer incense and a lamp.
Thus, having remained awake during the night, one should perform the ritual bath at dawn;
having worshipped the canopy-like [image] with all the necessary materials, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti*.
Having worshipped with scents and flowers, one should dismiss the deity of the fire.
Taking up the jar of ashes, adorned with all ornaments, accompanied by the sound of the Vedas and endowed with the sound of hymns of praise. || 47 ||
Having performed a circumambulation of the temple accompanied by song and instrumental music,
one should prepare a mandala before Śiva, adorned with all ornaments.
Having placed everything on my left, one should arrange the ashes in front;
having placed the nine items on the right, the lustration (nīrājana) should then be performed on the north.
The best of instructors should place ten flowers in the west;
thereafter, he should worship Gaṇeśa and honor the deities of the doorway.
Then, having performed the purification of the *liṅga* with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the nectars (*amṛta*),
the wise practitioner should worship it with its own mantra until the offering of lamps.
One should bathe the deity while recollecting the root mantra;
then, having offered the mantra-flower, one should present the mantra-food.
One should worship the Supreme Lord with garments, ornaments, garlands, and other offerings;
then, taking the water and ashes from the jars, one should apply them to the top of the Liṅga.
Having smeared the liṅga on all sides with the mantra "bṛhat sāma," one should offer the five-colored oblation and then provide water for drinking and rinsing the mouth.
Then, having entered the pavilion, the preceptor should offer oblations to the bull,
having worshipped him with incense and lamps while reciting the Vṛṣa-mantra.
One should praise the Lord of Vṛṣabha with hymns, songs, dances, and so forth;
then, at the time of the evening meal, concluding with incense and lamps.
Taking the *nīrājana* lamp, the wise one should place it before Śiva;
he should then worship [the deity] with perfumes and flowers using the mantras of the *kalās*, beginning with Nivṛtti.
One should display the lotus and the trident mudrās in the presence of the lamp, accompanied by fragrant incense and combined with *gulma*, *lūghṛta*, and other offerings. (58)
The wise one should show the three worlds above the top of the *liṅga* at the tip of the *veda*;
having descended slowly with the root mantra, [he should do so] three times.
Having performed the circumambulation as before one, two, or three times, the wise one should dismiss [the deity] with the syllable *praṇava*. || 60 ||
Having had it carried by Brahmins or Vādhanāris, the wise man should then perform a circumambulation accompanied by the sound of musical instruments. || 61 ||
At the front of the pedestal, or at the front of the gateway, or at a triple-pathway, or at a crossroads,
having set aside the ritual waving of lights (nirājana), one should meditate upon the Lord of manifold forms.
The Guru should perform a sprinkling all around with the ordinary arghya water;
having washed his feet, he should enter the temple.
Having worshipped Śiva with ten flowers and the ten seed-syllables, the preceptor,
having offered three handfuls of flowers, should request the Guru for his desired boon. (64)
Having set aside the bull during the interval of the twilight rite, one should cast the ashes into the middle of the water and, while reciting the *tāra* mantra, place half of them into the vessel.
Having protected [the body] with armor, one should wrap the face with a cloth;
then, taking up the sacrificial vessel (sāḍhya), one should prepare a firm seat.
Having meditated upon Anugraha-Śiva, facing either east or north,
one should gaze with the root mantra from the crest down to the feet.
The wise practitioner should place a jar of ashes on the right side;
having taken a quantity equal to one niṣka, he should place it above the head of the person to be treated.
The supreme preceptor, having sprinkled [the disciple] three times with the *praṇava*, [should do so] from the crest to the feet and from the feet to the crest. (69)
One should perform the pervasive ritual three times with the mantra that consumes sin;
one should devoutly practice the six-limbed yoga and mutter the Amṛtyuñjaya mantra.
One should protect the measure by means of exactly three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas);
having accomplished this and touched the heart, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
The wise man should recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra with the Brahma-mantras of Śiva’s limbs;
that mortal who acts in this way shall attain a meritorious state.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Method for the Protection of Kings," in the *Sūkṣmaśāstra*.
(298) O Lord Prabhāñjana, listen to how the deity Rakṣādīpa is;
tell me all that you have asked, O Master. (1)
The protective lamp is especially distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior;
it is considered to be threefold: pacifying, nourishing, and the granting of desires. (2)
It may be made of gold, silver, iron, or even brass;
it should be fashioned in the form of a shallow bowl and measure twenty finger-breadths [in length].
One should arrange five jars from the center to the northern limit;
each should be ten finger-breadths in height and ten finger-breadths in width.
Above that, having placed a lamp, the best [practitioner] should fashion the pinnacle;
its base should be five finger-breadths in width, and its height should be equal to that.
One should prepare the lamp-vessel with such an extent and in this manner;
having placed it upon a tripod, one should then set up the protective lamp.
Thus has the rite for pacification (śāntika) been described; now hear the procedure for nourishment (pauṣṭika).
The measurement of the sacrificial mound (sthalikā) is said to be twenty finger-breadths in width.
This lamp-stand made of rice-flour is fivefold;
thus is the rite for nourishment (pauṣṭika) described. Now hear from me that which grants desired objects.
The width should be twenty-four units, and the vessel should be perfectly round and excellent;
one should diligently arrange five, seven, nine, or one lamp-stand.
One should arrange either cow-dung or flour in seven vessels;
specifically, there should be nine lamps upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one prastha and a quarter.
Having cooked it in due order, [he should place] the *kuḍupa* and the central lump; all the oblation prepared in every direction is [offered] successively in the eight directions. (11)
Having painted it with five colors, or else with red pigment,
and having applied a raised rim above that, one should sprinkle it with cow's ghee alone.
One should properly perform [the rite] at nightfall through the path of the eye-remnants;
especially every day, on the ground that brings victory for kings.
The rite for pacification (śāntika) should be performed daily, either in a consecrated sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or elsewhere;
at evening one should go to bed and worship Yakṣeśī properly.
To its west, there is a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should place a small vessel there, joined with the Netra-mantra;
one should then sprinkle it with either oil or cow’s ghee that has been consecrated.
Thereafter, one should kindle the fire in the sacrificial pit by means of the mantra, or else one should plant the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ) as the central lamp. || 17 ||

Having recited the "Pervading the Sky" mantra (*vyomavyāpin*) with the mantras for the directions starting from the east and ending with the north, one should worship the universal lamp (*sarvadīpa*).
Or one should propitiate a courtesan or a temple servant with an offering of a lamp-vessel;
accompanied by the threefold musical instruments, the courtesan should perform a dance.
Accompanied by the sound of the Vedas and joined with all kinds of musical instruments,
one should perform a circumambulation of that lord of the Vedas in his presence.
Having recited the *astramantra*, the Guru should worship the lamps;
at the conclusion of the incense and lamps, however, he should recite the protection mantra (*rakṣāmantra*). (21)
Having worshipped the linga and other icons with eight flowers, one should then perform the circumambulation;
one should move slowly around three or more times.
Furthermore, one should cast [the offerings] before the pedestal of the sacrificial oblation (balipīṭha) along with courtesans and others.
Thus, the rite for pacification (śāntika) has been described; now hear about that for nourishment (pauṣṭika). || 23 ||
In front of Śiva, specifically at the mandala, my wise [disciple] should,
by means of mantra, place the goddess Rakṣā upon a small pedestal.
Having recollected the Netra-mantra, one should sprinkle [the area] with the auspicious water (śivāmbhas);
then, having reached the inner sanctum (garbhageha), one should worship it with the Astra-mantra. || 25 ||

Having recollected the protective deity (rakṣādevī), one should then circumambulate the image (bera) and other objects, starting from the primary deity (ādi-devī), by moving in the sequence of one, two, or three circuits. Then follows the [general] circumambulation.
Then, at that time, one should cause the ashes to be distributed along with the ritual dismissal (visarjana),
having performed the protection of Śiva which brings benefit to all living beings.

Thus, having first described the rite for nourishment (pauṣṭika), listen now to that which is performed in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or again within the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha). || 28 ||
One should perform the rite in seven vessels and worship them with lamps;
according to the sequence for nourishing rites, one should worship the supreme deity. (29)
O Lord, listen as I relate to you how, by joining the lamp with Śiva during the rite of dismissal (visarjana), it becomes a granter of desires, as has been declared. 30.
The lamp is declared to be of three types: the best is said to be seven *aṅgulas* in height;
the middling should be five *aṅgulas*, and the smallest should be three *aṅgulas*. (31)
Cow's ghee is declared to be the best, while that from a goat is middling; oil is said to be the lowest, and one should perform the rite using only clarified [oil].
Having applied dūrvā grass and having joined a mirror with sacred ash,
one should then offer the water for the feet and other honors to Śivā in the proper sequence, following the act of visualization.
O Prabhajana, listen likewise to the true form of Yakṣeśvarī:
it is joined with the sound *ya* and endowed with the essential sound of *rakṣa*. (34)

Beginning with the syllable Oṃ and ending with "namas," with the seed-syllable of the Lord of Protection (Rakṣeśi) in the middle—this mantra, more supreme than the supreme, has been revealed to you in this hymn. (35)
He has two arms, one face, two feet, and two eyes;
he is adorned with a crown and a casket, possessing a gentle form and a smiling countenance. (36)
One should place the Goddess in the middle of the lamp with the añjali-mudrā;
having meditated thus, the knower of mantras should worship the Goddess and the Protectress Goddess. (37)
One should worship the eight powers, Vāmā and the others, in order starting from the east; having fully worshipped Soma, Aṅgāraka, and the rest, one should place them in the second enclosure.
Having fully worshipped the world-protectors and others, one should place them in the third enclosure;
in this very same sequence, the wise person should worship the Lord of the Guardians (Rakṣeśin).
Having thus resolved, the wise man should prepare his bed at nightfall, having first applied ashes to his body and offered this prayer for the sake of all people.
(302) It removes all sins, is meritorious, and serves to please all the gods.
Having thus joined [the elements] in this sequence, one should perform the protective lamp ritual. 41.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter in the Sūkṣmaśāstra, titled "The Ritual for the Protective Lamp."
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the instruments;
for it would be impossible for an agent to perform an action without all the necessary instruments.

Therefore, the sacrificial implements should be fashioned according to their defining characteristics; likewise, the characteristics of the fire-pits (kuṇḍas), as well as those of the large and small wooden ladles (sruk and sruva), must be established.
The characteristics of the sacrificial vessels and likewise of the enclosing sticks (paridhi), as well as the characteristics of the darbha grass for strewing and of the fuel-sticks (samidh). || 3 ||
Then [he should determine] the measure of the oblations and of the water for bathing,
as well as the water for washing the feet, the water for sipping, and especially the arghya offering.

One should offer perfume, flowers, incense, and lamps according to the prescribed rule; likewise, the characteristics of the canopy and the characteristics of the hanging cloth [should be observed]. || 5 ||
The characteristics of the incense burner with its great sounding bell are as follows:
the ritual procedure is of two kinds, namely external and internal. (6)
The measurement of the pedestals for all the jars and their characteristics,
as well as the measurement of the flagstaff and the characteristics of the ritual offering (bali), [are now described].
I shall describe these according to their characteristics as determined by the scriptures;
furthermore, one should draw three lines, one pointing eastward and one pointing northward.

On a field made square, one should construct the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) according to their defining characteristics; having divided the diagonal cord (karṇasūtra) into four parts, one should draw [the center] with one part.
One should also place a measurement exceeding half the field on both sides;
one should deposit a seventh part of the diagonal cord toward the eastern direction.
By laying two lines on the sides, the pit (kuṇḍa) takes the form of a womb (yoni).
Having divided the field into forty parts and having drawn a diagonal line from the center, [the construction proceeds].
Then, having set aside half of the field, one should divide the remainder into three parts;
joining it with one part, one should then unite it with the half of the field.
By means of that cord, one should draw a circle; it is called a *kuṇḍa*.
Having likewise [drawn] a square there as before by means of the diagonal (*karṇa*), [one proceeds]. 13.
The circular pit (kuṇḍa) that has been described there is said to be half a bow in measure;
it is one-eightieth part together with half of half the measurement of the field.
By this very [method], the thread for the triangle is one-third of the [original] thread;
having divided the field into seven parts, one should place one part outside.
Therefore, having taken the middle point and likewise rotated [the cord] around the circle,
that which becomes the half-ear here shall be joined with one-eighth of the half-ear.
In that case, there would be this [shape]: with five [sides], it should have five arms;
by means of five lines starting from the east, the wise one should fashion a pentagon. (17)
Likewise, having divided the field into ten parts, one should place one part on the outside; then, from that center, the wise man should draw a circle with a thread.
One should join one sixteenth part of the field with half of the field;
having thus drawn the thread, there shall be a side in a heptagon. (19)
By means of seven lines starting from the east, a clearly defined heptagon is formed;
this, within a circle, is equal to a lotus, complete with a pericarp and petals.
Thus has the supreme characteristic of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) been briefly described.
Furthermore, the large and small sacrificial ladles (sruk-sruva) should be made either of vaikaṅkata or khadira wood.
Alternatively, O wise one, the sacrificial ladle (sruk) and spoon (sruva) should be made by the ritualists from trees such as the Palāśa,
Khadira, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Udumbara, and Candana.
The vaikaṅkata, śamī, and bilva—these nine are the sacrificial trees.
Having then divided them into two parts, one should measure them well with a cord.
Then, having made it square, the wise one should fashion the characteristic marks; its length should be one cubit (aratni), and there should be an offering at each of its four corners.
A staff with a circumference of six aṅgulas is prescribed at its base;
its neck should have half that girth, and the flower-head should be like the base.
The supreme scent, resembling cow dung, is equalized by the nose; it is joined with the two nostrils and filled with a karṣa of incense.
The characteristic of the *sruva* has been declared; now the characteristic of the *sruka* is being stated:
it should be thirty-six finger-breadths in length and eight finger-breadths in width.
Its height should be half of that, measured accurately with a cord;
its mouth, according to my view as well, should be seven finger-breadths in width.
One-third [of the width] should be at the base, and one-third at the top; having made the front one-third, one should discard the remainder. (29)
The two ears (karṇas) should be two finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width;
the altar (vedikā) should be eight finger-breadths in length, with its width being of that same measure.
In its center, one should fashion a strength [or base] measuring four finger-breadths;
one should make a well-rounded cavity with eight petals and a pericarp.
On all sides, outside the *bali*, there should be a band half a finger-breadth wide;
outside that, there should be a lotus petal, one barley-corn deep and variegated.
Outside of that, there should be a band measuring two barley-corns;
in the middle, the pedestal (vedikā) should have an aperture of the measure of the little finger. || 33 ||

The width of the *yava* should be six *aṅgulas*, while the depression for the offering (*bali*) should be one *balimāna*. The staff (*daṇḍa*) should be six *aṅgulas* in circumference, and at the tip of the staff there should be three small rods (*daṇḍikā*).
Increasing by half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula), it should be made four fingers wide;
at the base of the staff, there should be a jar (ghaṭa) with a length of thirteen fingers.
The pitcher (kumbha) should be two finger-breadths [in height], and its circumference (nāha) should be known as ten finger-breadths;
by means of that [measurement] in the middle of the altar, the characteristics of the vessel for the pitcher are described.
O you who possess the power to shatter [obstacles], listen as I describe the ritual for the thousand-fold common [worship]:
after the bath, whether it be obligatory, occasional, or for the sake of a specific desire, one should worship Maheśvara.
Bathing with the thousandfold stream is certain to increase prosperity and good fortune;
this is the most excellent of streams, that supreme power beyond the supreme.

Having caused [the substance] to flow into the thousand-faced vessel and having collected it in the form of the deceased, one should then take up the vessel; its characteristics are now described here. (39)
Beginning from seven finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths at each step,
the width of the blade (pātra) is said to extend up to twenty-seven finger-breadths.
Alternatively, it may be three finger-breadths thick, or five finger-breadths thick with ghee;
the thickness of the base of the foot-moulds should be one finger-breadth all around its width. || 41 ||
It may be provided with four rings, or have two sides equipped with rings; it may be joined with iron chains or furnished with leather thongs. || 42 ||
Gold, silver, or copper—these three types of metal may be used;
O Wind, one should have them fashioned in the order of superior and so forth.
For Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, [the offering] of gold and other materials is prescribed;
for kings, however, gold or silver is specifically intended. (44)
If he is unable [to do so], the one most skilled in ritual procedures should fashion it out of copper;
he should prepare that vessel as either square or perfectly circular.
Alternatively, it should be made triangular, or else twenty-five squares;
if it is circular, especially, it is the means for accomplishing all desired aims. (46)
It bestows long life, nourishment, and prosperity, and is auspicious;
specifically, within the center of the vessel, there should be a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
Increasing by one finger-width at a time, the rule for the three-finger measurement is that one should fashion a gem encased in gold, joined with a surrounding lotus design.
Having placed a gem in the center, it is considered firmly set and completely released;
outside of that, one should fashion a hollow opening with the measurement of a mere needle. (49)
One should rotate the thread around the finger for the sake of the thirteen [deities], measuring either the size of a barley grain or even the size of a black mustard seed.
In the eastern part there should be a vajra, and in the southeast a firm pearl;
in the south a puṣyarāga, and in the southwest a blue sapphire.

In the western quarter (Vāruṇa) there is indeed a *spuṭi*, and in the north-western (Vāyava) a *vaiḍūrya*; in the northern (Saumya) there is the head (*mastaka*), and in the north-eastern (Aiśānya) there is indeed a *nīla*.
Then, having properly applied gold that is well-refined, firm, and of the highest quality, there are thirteen coverings; now hear from me the number of the apertures. || 53 ||

In the first [cakra], there are eight apertures (randhra), with the Vasus as their presiding deities (adhidevatā). In the second, there are sixteen apertures, with the Kalās as their presiding deities.
In the third [cakra], there are twenty-four [pores] with the King of Serpents as their presiding deity;
in the fourth, there are thirty-two pores with the Great Gaṅgā as their presiding deity.
In the fifth enclosure, there are fifty-one apertures;
one should worship Yamunā as the presiding deity of all the apertures.
In the sixth enclosure, there are fifty-four quarters;
Godāvarī is presided over by the deities, and there is fitness in all the apertures.
The junction is ordained as the presiding deity of the apertures;
and in the seventh enclosure, the sixtieth aperture occurs.
One should worship Sarasvatī, whose presiding deity she is, in the apertures in due order;
and in the eighth enclosure, there are eighty-two [deities], with an additional pair.
Surrounded by [his retinue], one should worship the hollow space as having Dadhīca as its presiding deity;
in the ninth enclosure, the cavity is traditionally said to consist of ninety-six [parts].
Success shall come through the presiding deity in all the apertures according to their fitness,
and likewise in the tenth enclosure, which is endowed with one hundred apertures.
One should sequentially join the *kāvera* [vessel] to the apertures according to the deities;
thereafter, if there is a covering, it shall consist of one hundred and four [parts].
One should join all the apertures with deities such as those of the holy fords (puṇyatīrtha);
the wise one should perform the placement by assigning [deities] to all the apertures.
At the twelfth enclosure, there should be one hundred and eight [deities];
they have Icchā-śakti as their presiding deity, especially at every aperture.
It is declared to have thirteen vowels, two hundred and sixty [consonants],
the presiding deity of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), and to be endowed with all the apertures.
In this manner, that which is called the "opening" (randhra) should be determined according to the measure of the mantra-fingers;
in the center of the square, there shall be seven steps on each side.
In the central square, there should be a lotus made of ruby, pearl, diamond,
sapphire, lapis lazuli, emerald, and topaz.

One should fashion a single square of twenty-five finger-breadths, with a hollow center, extending from the middle to the northeast (Īśāna) and ending at the southeast (Agni), using crystal and coral. || 68 ||
In this very way, the final syllables of each word correspond to each three-word phrase;
they are endowed with a thousand streams, having the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) as their presiding deity. (69)
One should construct a swinging apparatus (ḍolayantra) joined with four strong ropes;
or else, listen to another method, O Prabhajana. (70)
That vessel is said to be of three kinds, corresponding likewise to the triad beginning with the lowest;
thus, one measuring twelve finger-breadths is proclaimed as the best.
A width of seven finger-breadths is proclaimed as the middling [size],
while a width of three finger-breadths is proclaimed as the lowest.
Thus, the width of the bowl and the height of the wall are described;
a height of one *aṅgula* is proclaimed as the best. (73)
An elevation of half a finger-breadth is proclaimed as the medium [size];
however, an elevation of one-quarter of a finger-breadth is also known as medium. (74)
In this very same sequence,
the wise one should state that [the thickness] is equal to the height of a barleycorn, and likewise, by that same sequence, it is declared to be merely a barleycorn in density.
Taking a leaf with both hands, one should sprinkle it upon the top of the *liṅga*;
[the vessel] may be made of gold, silver, or copper, and may be either square or circular. (76)
One should carefully construct a square of nine compartments with a hollow space in the center,
surrounded by eight other hollow spaces, forming a single unit.
Outside the footprints and specifically within the middle of the lines,
one should fashion the ear-cavity with a measurement of only a needle's breadth.
p.
310) Make twelve other hollows within the middle sections;
one hundred and eight is prescribed, and one less than fifty [is another]. 79.
In that vessel there are nine compartments, with the middle compartment being the central one;
it is unenclosed and has eight openings, especially on its exterior.
Within each individual word, there are five arrows and nine apertures; thus, it is said that there are fifty arrows and twenty-five apertures.

That leaf [diagram] should have nine compartments, with a hollow space precisely in the center; in the other [compartments], however, make a slightly oblique hollow space within the middle of the square.
The square has been described; now the circle is being explained.
In this manner, the vessel is to be made as before, provided with six petals and a pericarp.
In this manner, place the eight [syllables] starting from the east within the pericarp;
then, outside of that, place them in the middle of the petals. || 84 ||
Outside of that, there is likewise a square; thus, in the great directions, there shall be four squares.
In this manner, the hollow space is said to consist of one hundred and eight [units] in sequence.
One should arrange fifty and twenty-five as before;
this is declared to be the minor [mandala], whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others. (86)
Thus, while for the sake of others it is indeed auspicious, one should not consider it so for one's own sake; whether out of joy or even through ignorance, one may consecrate an unworthy vessel.
One should cause longevity, prosperity, fame, and stability to melt away during the dark fortnight;
one should worship that vessel with water from a conch shell while reciting the root mantra. || 88 ||
In this very same manner, by means of this sequence alone, there is the consecration of five hundred [monks]. (88½)
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Thousandfold Stream," in the Sūkṣmaśāstra.
I shall describe the characteristics of the *nāga*; listen to that, O Prabhajana. [It may be made] of gold, silver, copper, stone, or brick. (1)
One should fashion a serpent out of ten types of wood,
beginning with a single cubit and increasing by eight finger-breadths [for each subsequent type].
One should fashion the length of the serpent for twenty-four cubits; one should adopt an auspicious measurement endowed with beauty in its proportions and so forth. || 3 ||

Dividing that measurement into one hundred parts, one part shall be two finger-breadths (dvaṅgula). From the measurement of the face, which consists of four parts, the width of the face shall be eleven parts (rudrāṃśa).
The height of the neck should be eight parts; the width of the hood should be fifty parts;
the distance between the nostrils should be one quarter (of the total); and the tip of the nose should be one-eleventh part.
Equal to that, it should be long and wide, with a circle for the eyes consisting of one-sixteenth of the sky-measure;
in its center, one should fashion a black circle measuring one barley-corn.
The *jyotirmalakā* should be half the measure of its width;
its length should be two parts, and its width one part of Śiva (eleven parts).

The height of the wing should be two and a half finger-breadths, while the distance from the ear to the edge of the wing should be one finger-breadth; the width of the lion's ear should be four parts, according to the skillful measurement of the ear.
(312) It should be joined with four tusks, and its length from tusk to tusk should be one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
The tip of each tusk should be half a finger-breadth; one should fashion it like the tusk of Airāvata.
Alternatively, it may have a basket-shaped crown or the form of variegated garments;
in the center, according to the measurement of half a hood, there should be a side-hood.
It is taught that one should perform either seven hoods or three hoods;
the circumference [of the base] should indeed not be sixteen finger-breadths, but rather the length of the tail should be two finger-breadths.
Above the lotus-seat, however, there is a triple fruit adorned with ornaments;
the central thread of the nose is like the tip of a hair, a straight line. (12)
Whether it be one part, two parts, or three parts, a slight deficiency or excess does not constitute a fault;
one should execute every limb with skill, endowed with beauty and strength. (13)
The characteristics of the serpent have thus been described; now hear the measurements for the pavilion.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Characteristics of Nāgas," in the *Sūkṣmaśāstra*.
I shall describe the procedure for the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha); listen to it, O Prabhajana!
It is said to be of two kinds, the auspicious (bhadra) and the minor (kṣudra); the minor one is indeed the small pedestal. || 1 ||
The great seat (mahāpīṭha) has been declared as Bhadra, and the liṅga as Traiyyekarūpaka;
now the characteristics of the minor seats (kṣudrapīṭha) between these two will be described.

Regarding the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) for a Śiva-liṅga, it is said that one-ninth of the liṅga's height is the standard; of this, seven parts are declared excellent, while five parts are remembered as middling.
One-third [of the total] is reckoned as the width of the small pedestal (kṣudrapīṭha);
each individual height of the pedestal is one-fourth of that width. (4)
According to the measure of the *mānāṅgula*, it consists of eight units of *rasa* (six) mantras;
when the height of the distressed [section] has been divided into five parts by the measure of its own portion... || 5 ||
One should fashion the pericarp with one [part], and the other according to another rule.
One skilled in measurement should fashion [the image] entirely with the luster of a full-blown lotus;
whether it be without a pedestal or provided with one, it should be appropriately joined.
The improper [arrangement] has been described as before; the proper lotus-seat is four or six finger-breadths wide, or it may be as broad as seven seats.
The characteristics such as being elevated and so forth have been proclaimed as before;
however, the measurement of the intervals between those [features] is traditionally held to be one *aṅgula*.
Having first completed all this— the procedure for the retinue as declared in the Bhadrapīṭha-vidhi— one should perform the rite of installation (pratiṣṭhā).
The installation of the pedestal at the door should be performed in the first and second [chapters],
and the installation of the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) should be carried out according to the Samatantra.
Or one may perform it according to the rules with four components using separate tantras;
however, it must be performed by a single preceptor at a single time in a single location.
One should perform the rites for the seed-syllable (aṅkura), the sacrifice to the site (vāstuyāga), and so forth, according to the general tantra;
one should construct the pavilion (maṇḍapa) according to the prescribed rule in the eastern direction of the temple.
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar (*vedikā*) measuring one cubit;
it is called the *rudravedī*, and its width and height should be equal. (14)
One should fashion a sacrificial altar according to the rules in the four directions starting from the east of that [site],
or one may construct it equal to this [altar] according to the method prescribed for it.
In this very manner, one should properly prepare the pavilion;
one should perform the rite of germinating seeds (aṅkura) on the ninth day, or the fifth, or the third.
Having abandoned a dilapidated pedestal, one should then install a new one;
that dilapidation is said to be of three kinds: cracked, chipped, and broken. (17)

The auspicious pedestal (bhadrapīṭha) is especially endowed with major and minor limbs; furthermore, there are the footstool (upānaha), the base (jagatī), the lotus (kumuda), and the neck-band (kaṇṭhapaṭṭikā).
The lotus and its pericarp are proclaimed as the *mahāṅga* (major limb);
the petals, sub-petals, faces, and so forth are proclaimed as the *upāṅga* (minor limbs). || 19 ||

One should avoid [defects] in the major limbs; however, O Wind, if they cannot be abandoned, one may accept small seats and the like, provided they are free from those [major defects]. One should avoid them when they are deficient.
I shall describe its extraction and the sequence [of worship] within the southern mandala of the seat;
having mentally prepared the throne and invoked [the deity], one should perform the mantra-worship. (21)
To the east of that, having prepared a sacrificial mound with auspicious circles made of rice,
one should draw a lotus in its center, complete with eight petals and a pericarp.
The wise one should place jars filled with water (droṇas) in their midst;
having invoked the deities from the pedestal, he should then install them within the jars.
p.

315) Having completed the offering of the *naivedya* and so forth, according to the procedure prescribed for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), and having performed the rites from the kindling of the fire (*ādhāna*) up to the marriage (*vivāha*), as well as the offerings of honey and clarified butter; 24.
Reciting the mantra of each respective deity, one should offer oblations separately with dūrvā grass and rice—
either one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five of each.
One should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the primary seed-syllable of the *kṣurikā*;
then, one should offer the *jayā* and other oblations, as well as the *āghāra*, and subsequently offer the *bhūta-homa* in due order.

One should conclude the rites by placing [the image] upon the fire, within a mandala, or in the center of a sacrificial pit; alternatively, one may bury them in the ground or cast them into the oceans.
One should perform that rite with the thought, "I am born from the ancient seat (pīṭha) and so forth.
Then, having performed the purification of the seat (pīṭha-śuddhi) with the five products of the cow, the five earths, and bilva fruits, [one should proceed].

The auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) is the special feature; standing before it with mirrors, one should perform the consecration by pouring streams [of water] while reciting the "śuddhair uddhṛtaiḥ" mantra.
First, one should perform the Vāstuhoma, the Bali offering, and the worship of the pavilion;
then, having performed the binding of the protective thread, [one should place the deity] upon the pericarp of the auspicious throne.
Or one may perform it on other seats, or even without them;
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) upon the altar using eight *droṇas* of rice.
It was joined with half that amount of rice and half of that with sesame seeds;
it was beautifully adorned, strewn with parched grain, flowers, sesame, and *darbha* grass.
To the east of that, one should worship Nandin, Mahākāla, and the Bull in sequence upon the pitchers on the altar, from south to north to the center.
Then, on the southern side, in all the sacrificial jars upon the altar,
one should worship Durgā, Astra, Vighneśa, Varada Skanda, and Vadhāva. (34)
One should worship Caṇḍeśa in the southeast, Śānta at the beginning [of the directions], Bhūteśa in the center,
Dharaṇīdhara in the intermediate directions, and Bhujageśvara upon the altar-pitchers.
In the four intermediate directions of the Dharmadeva enclosure, one should place Indra, Vaiśvānara, and Yama, respectively, in the pitchers upon the northern altar.
One should worship Maheśvara, known as Nirṛti, Pāśī, Padhvin, Indu, and Vaṭuka,
as well as Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha, beginning from the east.
In their midst, upon the altars and jars, [one should worship] Āmoda,
Pramodaka, Sumukha, Durmukha, Avighna, and Vighnanāyaka.
One should properly worship her, joined with the seats, the primary forms, and so forth, located at the northeast petal, the southwest petal, the Rudra direction, the pericarp, and above. || 39 ||
In a location to the north of that [main] altar, one should perform the preliminary consecration (vāsana) of the minor seats and so forth;
there is a special procedure for the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), and one should perform the consecration in its place.
One should perform the mastery of the Vedas preceded by the installation of the water-pot;
one should carry out everything beginning with the establishment of the sacred fire (agnyādhāna) as prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya). || 41 ||
One should offer sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), mustard seeds (sarṣapa), barley (yava), and sesame seeds (tila),
using the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅga) derived from their respective root-mantras, as well as the Pavamāna and Tryambaka mantras.
Having touched [the vessel], one should offer oblations there while recollecting the root mantra;
thus, one should keep vigil at night and perform the ritual bath at dawn.
One should worship all the vessels, such as the arches and so forth, with perfumes and flowers.
I shall now describe the procedure for the consecration of small pedestals; listen to that. (44)
Having taken his place in the middle of the palace, within the center of the inner mandala,
he should worship [the deities] beginning with Durgā and ending with Caṇḍapīṭha, from the southeast to the northeast.
O Agni, wherever there is Vṛṣasthala, one should perform that *pīṭha* rite;
the preceptor, having established the *pīṭha* of Bhūtanātha upon its back according to the prescribed measurement. (46)
Specifically at each door, one should worship the Lord of the Door (Dvāreśa) located in the region of the pedestal;
this constitutes the inner mandala alone for Dharmeśa, who is the nectar of the Bull (Vṛṣa).
The Indrapīṭha extends from the mouth [of the central deity] to the Bhadrapīṭha;
its connection to the boundary of that location is according to the measurement of the inner maṇḍala. || 48 ||

One should establish the deities beginning with Agni in the seven directions between Soma and Īśa; in the Nairṛta direction, one should install the Viṣṇupīṭha according to the measurement of the staff.
In the northeast, one should install the Brahma-pīṭha measuring one cubit;
in the second enclosure, one should arrange the pīṭhas in this very same manner.
The consecration of the auspicious throne has been declared, as well as the characteristics of the enclosure wall;
thereafter, one should worship the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
One should provide teachers and attendants according to one's means, honoring them with upper garments and the like, and adorned with turbans. (52)
Then, having carried on his head the jars previously established and accompanied by all [the musical instruments], he should circumambulate the temple.
Having recited each respective root mantra and consecrated [the disciple] at each respective seat,
one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), for there is a special procedure for the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha). || 54 ||
I shall describe the procedure for the gopura; listen, O Prabhañjana!
Starting from the inner maṇḍala, it extends up to the boundary line at the end of the salaka.

For the sake of beauty and for protection, one should construct the door-hall (dvāraśālā) and so forth. The door-hall, the door-decorations, and the pavilion-terrace (harmyakam) at the entrance [are to be made]. || 56 ||
These are proclaimed as the fivefold types of gate-towers (dvāragopura), beginning with the twelve-pillared and ending with the palace (harmya), for the sake of beauty and protection. || 57 ||
One should specifically design some variation for the great gatehouse (*mahāgopura*),
ranging from one to three stories in height, for the purpose of ritual bathing.
From eight up to seven, one should provide garments and ornaments;
from eight up to five, one should arrange them for the purpose of a bed.

One should arrange the thirteen [deities] beginning with Rudra, as well as the Gausabha and Arsha [measures], starting from three tālas up to the ground level; thus one should construct the gateway and the temple.
One should construct the gateway-tower (dvāraharmya) extending to a height of six tālas;
the great gatehouse (mahāgopura) is desired to terminate at the level of the kalā-stage.
Alternatively, for all the *sālā* [structures], the number of *muni* [verses] would be the measure of the *tala*;
